beginner.definition: In cloud platforms, identity and access management controls what each account or role may do. A principal is any identity, such as a user, a service, or a role. A policy is the written list of permissions. This detection flags permissions being attached to a principal that never held them before.
beginner.whyItMatters: Cloud permission changes last until somebody reverses them. A password reset does not remove a role that an intruder gave to a quiet account. Such a grant survives your clean-up and becomes a way back in later. These changes are often the moment stolen credentials turn into lasting control. Watching them gives you a signal that password rotation cannot erase.
howItWorks: Cloud platforms write an audit record for every identity change, naming who did it and what changed.
The detection reads those records for policy attachments, new roles and trust changes.
It extracts the acting identity and the identity that received the new permissions.
It compares that pair against the last few months of similar changes in the same account.
A brand-new pair raises an alert, with more weight when broad permissions were granted.
The tool then searches the following hours for actual use of the new permissions.
beginner.example: An office building issues badges that open specific doors. An administrator adds a new door to somebody's badge, and that change keeps working for months. If an intruder reaches the badge system, they quietly add their own account to the room holding the servers. Changing every employee password afterwards does not remove that door access. Somebody must review the permissions themselves.
takeaways: Permission grants outlive password resets, so they need their own alert.
A permission change made outside your normal automation is worth a look.
Check whether the new permission was actually used soon afterwards.

topics.title: DNS TXT Beaconing Periodicity
topics.summary: DNS TXT beaconing periodicity detection identifies recurring queries for TXT records that follow a regular timing pattern toward the same parent domain or a small set of parent domains, which is the characteristic signature of command and control or data transfer tunnelled through the Domain Name System. The behaviour matters because DNS is almost universally permitted outbound, is rarely inspected beyond basic reputation filtering, and is handled by infrastructure that neither authenticates the requester nor understands the payload carried in record data, so an operator can both task an implant and receive results without ever opening a conventional network connection to an unfamiliar address. The telemetry required is DNS query and response logging from recursive resolvers, the endpoint DNS client cache or sensor, or passive network capture of DNS traffic, retaining the queried name, record type, response size, response code and the requesting host, together with a source of timing aggregation so periodicity and jitter can be measured rather than inferred. The signal survives common evasion because tunnelling still requires a sustained exchange of queries and answers; even an implant that introduces jitter must remain within the beacon interval the operator needs for practical interactivity, and adding jitter reduces but does not eliminate measurable regularity in the same destination. Domain fronting, long label payloads and rapid parent-domain rotation do change the observable distribution, but rotation itself produces an anomalous pattern of newly registered parents on the resolver. The detection breaks down in practice because many benign applications resolve on fixed schedules: telemetry agents, update checkers, endpoint management clients and messaging clients all poll on intervals. Shared resolvers also mask which internal host issued a query when logging is aggregated, and encrypted DNS removes query visibility entirely at the network layer. Practical reliability comes from combining timing regularity with query characteristics such as TXT record focus, unusually long or high-entropy labels, high unique-subdomain counts per parent, and rare-parent-domain age, and from accepting that encrypted DNS requires endpoint-side logging to remain detectable.
objectives: Explain why DNS is a durable command and control channel and which record types are most abused for bidirectional exchange.
Measure beacon periodicity and jitter from resolver logs and choose statistics that tolerate normal scheduling drift.
Combine timing regularity with label entropy, unique subdomain count and parent domain age to reduce false positives.
Identify which hosts in the estate bypass local resolver logging through encrypted DNS and describe the compensating control.
Correlate DNS anomalies with endpoint process telemetry to attribute queries to a specific binary and parent.
Rank a suspected tunnelling channel against other active incidents using data volume, target asset criticality and confidence.
dataSources: Recursive DNS resolver query logs containing queried name, record type, response code and requesting client address
Endpoint DNS client telemetry associating each query with the process that issued it
Passive network capture of DNS requests and responses with response length and timing
Domain registration and reputation enrichment providing parent domain age, registrar and hosting classification
Proxy and firewall logs showing whether the same host used other egress channels in the same window
topics.logic: Group DNS queries by requesting host and parent domain, restrict attention to record types that carry data such as TXT, and compute whether successive queries to the same parent arrive at a stable interval with low variance relative to the host's normal traffic. Raise an alert when periodicity is combined with data-bearing record types, unusually long or random-looking labels, a high count of distinct subdomains under one parent, or a parent domain that is recently registered or heavily queried from a single host. Then attribute the queries to a process using endpoint telemetry so the responder knows whether the source is a known agent or an unexplained binary, and cross-check for other egress activity in the same window before deciding severity.
topics.pseudoQuery:
title: Periodic DNS TXT Queries To A Single Parent Domain
id: det-dns-txt-beaconing
status: training
logsource:
  category: dns_query
detection:
  txt_queries:
    RecordType: TXT
  label_characteristics:
    QueryName|re: '^[A-Za-z0-9+/=_-]{20,}\\.'
  periodicity:
    condition: stdev(query_interval) < 5s and count() by Hostname, ParentDomain > 30 within 1h
  high_diversity:
    condition: count(distinct QueryName) by Hostname, ParentDomain > 50 within 1h
  condition: txt_queries and periodicity and (label_characteristics or high_diversity)
fields:
  - Hostname
  - QueryName
  - RecordType
  - QueryLength
  - ResponseCode
level: high
falsePositives: Endpoint management, patching and telemetry agents that poll vendor services on a fixed schedule
Anti-abuse and reputation services that issue repeated lookups to the same provider as part of normal operation
Content filtering and secure web gateways that validate domains through their own resolver pipeline
Application health checks and service discovery that resolve infrastructure names at a constant interval
Email security platforms performing repeated sender domain and record validation
topics.tuningNotes: Build a per-host periodic-query baseline and allow-list the destination parents used by signed agents, but exclude only the specific host-and-parent pair rather than the host entirely, so a compromised workstation running legitimate agents can still generate an alert for a different parent. Relax the variance threshold in environments where schedulers drift, and compensate by tightening the label entropy and subdomain diversity conditions, which are harder for legitimate software to satisfy accidentally. Keep TXT as a strong weighting factor rather than a hard requirement, because tunnelling also occurs over other record types, and review the rule monthly against the current top parent domains so that newly adopted cloud services do not produce sustained noise. Where encrypted DNS is deployed, ensure the compensating endpoint logging source is onboarded before relying on this detection for compliance reporting.

beginner.definition: The domain name system is the internet service that turns a name such as example.com into an address. One of its record types, called TXT, can carry short pieces of free text. This detection looks for a computer asking for TXT records again and again. The requests go to the same domain on a regular rhythm, which suggests hidden messages.
beginner.whyItMatters: Almost every network allows name lookups out, and few inspect them closely. The service does not check who is asking. It also does not care what text comes back. An attacker can send instructions to a program inside your network. Stolen data comes back the same way, with no normal connection to a strange address. This channel is quiet and easy to overlook.
howItWorks: Your name servers and endpoint tools record each lookup, including the name asked for and the machine that asked.
Queries are grouped by machine and by the parent domain they belong to.
Timing between repeats is measured, because malicious tools often call home at a fixed interval.
The detection also looks for TXT questions carrying long, scrambled labels that resemble encoded data.
Regular TXT lookups to one domain, with many different subdomains, stand out.
Endpoint records are then used to name the exact program responsible for the queries.
beginner.example: A prisoner may send one letter home every Monday at noon, and the reply arrives every Thursday. The guards read the envelopes but never open them. The return address is one they recognise. So the prisoner keeps a regular conversation with the outside, hidden in plain sight. The rhythm itself is the giveaway, not the words on the page.
takeaways: Regular lookups to the same domain on a fixed rhythm deserve a check.
Text records can hide data in a channel most filters never read.
Make sure your logs can tie a lookup back to the program that asked.

topics.title: Impossible Travel Sign-In
topics.summary: Impossible travel sign-in detection identifies authentication events for the same account from two geographically distant locations within a time window that makes physical travel between them infeasible, which is a long standing indicator that credentials are being used by more than one party. The behaviour matters because it applies after the credential theft has already happened and does not depend on the attacker using tools on an endpoint: a valid account used from an unexpected place will authenticate successfully, satisfy most policy checks, and appear in logs as a normal user unless the spatial and temporal relationship between consecutive sign-ins is evaluated. The telemetry required is identity provider or directory sign-in logs containing the account, timestamp, source address, resolved location, client application, authentication method and outcome, plus an address geolocation source with accuracy metadata and a device or session identifier where the platform provides one so that concurrent sessions can be distinguished from sequential ones. The signal survives common evasion because credentialed access from a remote network must traverse the internet and will be geolocated to that network's registered location; virtual private network and proxy use changes the apparent origin but does not remove the discrepancy when the legitimate user is simultaneously active, and the discrepancy often becomes larger, not smaller, when commercial hosting ranges are used. The detection breaks down in practice for well documented reasons: mobile carrier routing, corporate virtual private network egress points that concentrate users in one datacentre, satellite links, and inaccurate geolocation databases all produce apparent travel that never happened. Authentication through a shared egress also means many accounts can appear to move simultaneously, which is a strong signal that the location source, not the user, moved. Ineffective handling of these cases causes rapid alert fatigue, so mature implementations combine distance and time thresholds with a check for whether the same address serves many accounts, treat virtual private network and known egress ranges as neutral rather than anomalous, and require a second signal such as an unfamiliar device, a failed multi-factor challenge, or a suspicious post-authentication action before escalating to an incident.
objectives: Compute travel velocity between consecutive sign-ins and choose thresholds that reflect realistic commercial travel.
Identify systemic geolocation artefacts such as corporate egress concentrators and carrier routing that cause mass false positives.
Interpret simultaneous or overlapping sessions for one account as stronger evidence than sequential location change.
Combine travel anomalies with device familiarity, authentication method and post-authentication activity to set severity.
Describe the containment and verification steps for a confirmed stolen credential, including session revocation and token invalidation.
Assess the effect of virtual private network, proxy and hosting network usage on the reliability of geolocation indicators.
dataSources: Identity provider sign-in logs containing account, timestamp, source address, application and outcome
Geolocation enrichment data providing country, region, city and accuracy radius for each source address
Device and session metadata including device identifier, join state, client application and token lifetime
Multi-factor authentication challenge logs recording method used and challenge result
Directory audit logs recording subsequent identity or mailbox configuration changes made by the account
topics.logic: For each account, order successful sign-ins chronologically and compute the distance between consecutive source locations and the time elapsed, alerting when the implied travel speed exceeds a realistic maximum such as commercial aviation. Neutralise known corporate egress ranges and hosting providers before comparison, and detect the systemic case where many accounts appear to move at once by grouping events per source address rather than per user. Escalate when the anomaly coincides with an unfamiliar device, a weaker authentication method than the user normally uses, or administrative action taken shortly after the second sign-in.
topics.pseudoQuery:
title: Impossible Travel Between Consecutive Successful Sign-Ins
id: det-impossible-travel
status: training
logsource:
  product: identity
  service: signin
detection:
  successful_signin:
    ResultType: Success
  geo_enriched:
    GeoLatitude|exists: true
    GeoLongitude|exists: true
  velocity_anomaly:
    condition: distance_between_consecutive_signins(AccountName) > 800km and elapsed_time < 60m
  neutral_sources:
    SourceNetworkCategory:
      - corporate_egress
      - known_vpn
  condition: successful_signin and velocity_anomaly and not neutral_sources
fields:
  - AccountName
  - SignInTime
  - SourceIpAddress
  - GeoCity
  - AppDisplayName
  - DeviceId
level: medium
falsePositives: Corporate virtual private network and secure web gateway egress that concentrates users at a small number of datacentre locations
Mobile carrier networks that route subscriber traffic through a distant regional gateway
Satellite and in-flight connectivity that reports registration points unrelated to the user's actual position
Inaccurate geolocation database entries for recently allocated or reassigned address ranges
Users operating concurrent sessions from a workstation and a remote desktop or virtual desktop environment
topics.tuningNotes: Start by identifying which addresses routinely serve large numbers of accounts and classify them as neutral egress rather than excluding the accounts that use them, since a user on corporate virtual private network may still generate a genuine anomaly from a different address. Avoid pure distance thresholds; require both a high implied velocity and one supporting signal such as an unknown device, a change in authentication method, a first-seen country for that user, or an administrative action immediately afterwards, which removes most of the noise while retaining the cases that warrant investigation. Suppress repeat alerts for the same account and location pair within a shift so that one travelling user does not consume the queue, and record known travel in the identity platform where the tooling supports it rather than maintaining exclusions in the query. Finally, confirm that geolocation accuracy radius is respected, because events resolved only to a country level should not be used to calculate distance.

beginner.definition: This detection watches sign-in records for one account and compares the places and times of those sign-ins. The same account may appear in two distant places within minutes. No real journey could cover that distance so quickly, so the pair is flagged. The name comes from that impossible speed.
beginner.whyItMatters: It catches the problem after credentials have already been stolen. The intruder signs in with a valid password, so nothing is broken and no malware needs to run. Even a correct multi-factor code will not help, because the attacker may have it too. Comparing consecutive sign-in locations is one of the few ways to notice that two different people are using one account.
howItWorks: Your identity system logs each successful sign-in with a timestamp and a source address.
An enrichment step turns each address into a rough location, such as a city.
Sign-ins for one account are sorted in time order to build a simple journey.
The distance between two consecutive sign-ins is divided by the time between them.
If the implied speed beats what a commercial flight could do, an alert is raised.
Known corporate network exit points and hosting providers are marked as neutral before the alert is scored.
beginner.example: Maya signs in from the London office at nine in the morning. Twelve minutes later the same account signs in from a city in another country. Nobody can cross that distance so quickly, yet both sign-ins used her correct password and her correct code. The sensible conclusion is not that Maya flew, but that somebody else now holds her credentials. Check for two sessions running at once.
takeaways: Two sign-ins that are far apart in place and close in time need a human check.
Many accounts moving at once usually means the location data is wrong.
Confirm stolen credentials by revoking sessions and resetting, not only by resetting.

topics.title: Kerberoasting SPN Request Spike
topics.summary: Kerberoasting SPN request spike detection identifies a single account requesting service tickets for an abnormal number and diversity of service principal names within a short window, which is the defining pattern of offline cracking of service account credentials in a Kerberos environment. The behaviour matters because the request path is entirely legitimate: any authenticated principal may ask the domain controller for a service ticket, and the returned ticket is encrypted with the service account's key, so an operator can take the encrypted material away and crack it at leisure without touching the target host at all. The telemetry required is domain controller Kerberos service ticket issuance events including the requesting account, the target service name, encryption type and source address, combined with account metadata that identifies which of the targeted principals are user accounts with registered service names rather than genuine computer accounts, and privilege data showing which of those accounts hold elevated rights. The signal survives common evasion because the volume and diversity of requests is what distinguishes the attack; an operator who requests a single ticket for a single service looks exactly like normal application behaviour, so the detection is strongest against the broad sweep and weaker against careful targeting. Requesting only weak encryption types, or filtering for targets whose keys are crackable, still produces a cluster of requests that differs from baseline in target diversity and encryption negotiation. The detection breaks down in practice because service ticket volume is enormous in some environments and legitimate application servers, monitoring platforms, backup software and vulnerability scanners request tickets across wide service populations every day. Ticketing patterns are also bursty and change with business cycles, so static thresholds age badly. Effective tuning requires per-requesting-account baselines, suppression of host and service accounts that behave like scanners, and a focus on requests originating from workstation subnets or interactive user sessions, where wide service ticket acquisition has no routine explanation.
objectives: Explain the Kerberos service ticket request flow and why the request itself is authorised and therefore invisible to access control.
Build a per-account baseline of service ticket request volume, target diversity and encryption type distribution.
Distinguish interactive user requests from machine and service account requests and prioritise the former.
Identify which targeted service accounts hold elevated privileges so that crackable findings can be risk ranked.
Describe the response options for a suspected roasting event, including service account credential rotation and detection of subsequent reuse.
Assess how encryption type negotiation and targeted requests change the detectability of the technique.
dataSources: Windows Security event 4769 Kerberos service ticket request including account name, service name and ticket encryption type
Windows Security event 4768 ticket granting ticket issuance for source address and account correlation
Directory service records identifying user accounts with registered service principal names and their group memberships
Domain controller network logon events linking the requesting account to a source host or workstation subnet
Identity governance data classifying service accounts, their owners and their review status
topics.logic: Track service ticket requests per requesting account over a rolling window and alert when one account obtains tickets for many distinct service names, or when the same account requests tickets for service names belonging to privileged user accounts rather than computer accounts. Weight the alert by whether the requesting account is an interactive user on a workstation subnet, whether requests used weak encryption types, and whether the targeted services belong to accounts with administrative rights or stale passwords. Suppress the machine accounts and application servers that legitimately enumerate large service populations, but keep their activity logged at a low severity so an outlier day is still reviewable.
topics.pseudoQuery:
title: Kerberos Service Ticket Request Spike Across Many Service Names
id: det-kerberoasting-spn-spike
status: training
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  service_ticket:
    EventID: 4769
  weak_encryption:
    TicketEncryptionType:
      - '0x17'
      - '0x18'
  target_is_user_service:
    # service name does not end with a machine account marker
    ServiceName|endswith: '$'
  spike:
    condition: count(distinct ServiceName) by TargetUserName > 15 within 10m
  condition: service_ticket and spike and not target_is_user_service
fields:
  - TargetUserName
  - ServiceName
  - IpAddress
  - TicketEncryptionType
level: high
falsePositives: Application servers and middleware platforms that authenticate to many downstream services in one session
Monitoring, vulnerability scanning and inventory platforms whose service accounts enumerate large service populations
Backup and replication agents that contact multiple file and database services during a schedule window
Administrative scripts run by a human operator during troubleshooting across several services
Single sign-on and federation gateways that broker tickets for many relying parties at logon time
topics.tuningNotes: Build the baseline per requesting account over at least thirty days and express the threshold as a multiple of that account's normal distinct-service count rather than as an absolute number, which keeps the rule useful in both small and large directories. Separate computer accounts and known application service accounts into a low severity lane with a much higher threshold, and keep interactive user accounts under an immediate page because wide service ticket acquisition by a human account is rare and highly indicative. Use encryption type as a ranking factor instead of a hard filter, since some legacy applications negotiate weak types routinely and excluding those events would also hide the attack. Pair this detection with monitoring for subsequent authentication as the targeted service accounts, and with a review of how many service accounts have passwords that are old, shared, or set to never expire, because that inventory determines the real risk behind any alert.

beginner.definition: Kerberos is the system Windows uses to prove who you are on a network. A service ticket is a small pass the domain controller issues so you can use a service. A service principal name is the label for that service. This detection flags one account asking for tickets to an unusual number of different services in a short time.
beginner.whyItMatters: Every service ticket is encrypted with the password key of the service account behind it. An attacker may request any ticket they are entitled to receive. They take those tickets away and crack the keys offline at their own pace. No server is touched, so nothing looks broken. Spotting the broad sweep of requests is often your only early warning.
howItWorks: Every service account in a directory has a name, and clients use that name to ask for access.
An attacker first lists the service names that exist, then requests a ticket for each one.
The domain controller issues the tickets, because any signed-in account may ask for them.
Each ticket is encrypted with the target service account's secret, so it can be cracked offline.
Your detection counts how many distinct services one account asked for inside a short window.
One account asking for many services is urgent, but spikes from machine accounts rank lower.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel reception desk that hands out spare keys. Any guest may ask for the key to the room they booked. Now imagine one guest asking for a copy of every room key in the building. They take the whole set away. Nothing was stolen on the spot, because the plan is to copy the keys elsewhere. That is why the number of requests matters.
takeaways: A request for many service tickets by one account is a strong warning sign.
Real users rarely sweep a whole directory, so weight human accounts as high risk.
Rotate the passwords of targeted service accounts once an alert is confirmed.

topics.title: LSASS Handle Access
topics.summary: LSASS handle access detection identifies non-standard processes opening a handle to the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service with access rights that permit reading its memory, which is the prerequisite step for extracting cached credential material on a Windows host. The behaviour is high value to an attacker because a successful read yields password hashes, Kerberos tickets or plaintext secrets that can be reused elsewhere in the estate, so it typically appears in the credential access phase shortly after a foothold and before lateral movement. The telemetry required is kernel-level process access auditing, delivered either through a native audit policy that emits object access events for the target process or through an endpoint detection sensor that records source process, target process, requested access mask and granted access, alongside process creation records so the requesting binary can be resolved to a file path, signer and parent. The signal survives common evasion because the access itself is the operation the attacker needs; even fully fileless tooling that never writes a payload to disk must still open the handle and request read permissions from the kernel. Tools that duplicate an existing handle from a privileged process or that inject into a trusted signed binary create a different anomaly in the same telemetry family, where the request originates from an unexpected source image. The detection breaks down in practice because legitimate security products, backup agents, monitoring tools and administrative utilities all read process memory, so the access mask alone is not sufficient and must be combined with source process reputation, signer validity, and whether the source executable lives in a user-writable directory. Sensor coverage is also uneven: without kernel driver telemetry or configured audit policy the event may simply not exist, and access mask values reported by third-party tools vary, so tuning must be done against the actual field semantics of the deployed pipeline rather than against a generic specification.
objectives: Explain which Windows access rights indicate an attempt to read process memory versus normal handle usage, and why the distinction drives severity.
Build a query that returns source process, requested access mask and signer status for handle opens against the credential process.
Establish a benign baseline of security products, backup agents and management tooling that legitimately read process memory in your estate.
Detect handle duplication and injection-into-trusted-process variants that do not originate from an obvious credential dumping binary.
Decide when to escalate to host isolation based on concurrent signals such as new service creation or outbound authentication from the same host.
Describe which audit policies and sensor capabilities must be deployed before this detection has any chance of firing.
dataSources: Kernel process access telemetry from an endpoint sensor recording source image, target image and granted access mask
Windows Security event 4656 and 4663 handle requests for the credential process object when object access auditing is enabled
Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing to resolve the requesting binary and its parent
Authenticode signature and file path metadata for the requesting executable
Windows Security event 4624 logon records on the same host used to correlate access with subsequent authentication activity
topics.logic: Alert when a process opens a handle to the credential subsystem image requesting memory-read or full-access rights, then immediately enrich the event with the requesting process path, its signature status and its parent. Exclude the signed security and management binaries that appear in the local baseline, and rank everything else by whether the source image sits in a user-writable directory, whether the signature is absent or invalid, and whether the account is an interactive user rather than a system service. Escalate the finding when the same host shows new service creation, scheduled task registration, or outbound authentication to other hosts within a short window, because those indicate the extracted material is being used rather than merely collected.
topics.pseudoQuery:
title: Suspicious Handle Access To Credential Process
id: det-lsass-handle-access
status: training
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_access
detection:
  target_process:
    TargetImage|endswith: '\\lsass.exe'
  memory_read_rights:
    GrantedAccess|contains:
      - '0x1010'
      - '0x1410'
      - '0x1438'
      - '0x143a'
      - '0x1fffff'
  known_good_source:
    SourceImage|endswith:
      - '\\MsMpEng.exe'
      - '\\csrss.exe'
      - '\\svchost.exe'
      - '\\wininit.exe'
  condition: target_process and memory_read_rights and not known_good_source
fields:
  - SourceImage
  - TargetImage
  - GrantedAccess
  - CallTrace
  - User
level: critical
falsePositives: Endpoint protection and antivirus engines that inspect process memory as part of their normal scanning loop
Backup, disaster recovery and virtualisation agents that snapshot process state including the credential subsystem
Enterprise monitoring and performance agents that enumerate process memory counters across all running processes
Administrative troubleshooting tools and debuggers legitimately attached to the process during support sessions
Remote management platforms that perform credential hygiene or local password rotation routines
topics.tuningNotes: Do not tune by removing the access mask condition; instead maintain an explicit allow-list keyed on the requesting binary path, its valid signature and, where the sensor supports it, the specific account and host role that performs the access. Suppress by repeated behaviour, for example treating a source image that requests the same access on hundreds of hosts per day as tooling while still alerting on its first appearance on a server class host. Add a complementary rule for unsigned or user-directory source images that does not depend on the allow-list at all, and keep it at critical severity because that combination has almost no benign explanation. Track call trace availability, since sensors that expose the module responsible for the access substantially reduce false positives from injected threads and should be preferred when choosing tooling.

beginner.definition: LSASS is a Windows process that holds login secrets in memory while people are signed in. A handle is a request for permission to work with another running program. This detection looks for unusual programs asking for a handle to LSASS. It focuses on requests that allow reading its memory, the step before stealing passwords.
beginner.whyItMatters: If an attacker reads the memory of that process, they can walk away with password hashes or login tickets. Those can be reused to sign in as other people. They also allow movement between machines, without touching the victim again. This happens early, right after an intruder gets a foothold. Catching it early breaks the chain.
howItWorks: When you sign in, Windows stores secret material inside the LSASS process so other programs can use it.
An attacker who already has a foothold asks the operating system for a handle to that process.
The request includes which rights are wanted, and reading memory is one of those rights.
With auditing or an endpoint sensor in place, that handle request is recorded with both programs named.
Your detection filters out the known security and backup products that legitimately read process memory.
What remains, especially an unsigned program started from a user folder, is treated as urgent.
beginner.example: A hospital keeps a locked office with the master keys to every ward. Staff walk past it all day without a thought. One afternoon a visitor in a borrowed uniform asks the desk for that key. They say they only want to look inside. The request itself is the warning. No thief needs to break the door down when the key can be handed over politely.
takeaways: The LSASS process is a prime target because login secrets live inside it.
An unsigned program in a user folder reading that process is a red flag.
You need a sensor or special auditing turned on, because ordinary logs miss it.

topics.title: Mass File Rename With High Entropy
topics.summary: Mass file rename with high entropy detection identifies a single process rapidly modifying, renaming or extending the names of many files across one or more directories where the resulting names exhibit high character entropy and consistent suffix patterns, which is the observable fingerprint of automated data encryption for impact. The behaviour matters because it is one of the last chances to interrupt an intrusion before recovery becomes expensive: once the rewrite completes across servers and backups the organisation is reduced to restoring from offline copies. The telemetry required is file system auditing or endpoint file-operation telemetry that captures the acting process, the parent process, the original and resulting file names, the operation type and the directory, together with process creation records for identity and a time-series aggregation capability so that rate per minute can be computed rather than evaluated file by file. The signal survives common evasion because the operation is inherently bulk and inherently fast; even a deliberately throttled encryptor must rename or rewrite thousands of files within a short window to be effective, and slowing down enough to avoid rate thresholds extends the attack to an impractical duration. Directories excluded from encryption to preserve a ransom note still produce a distinctive cluster of untouched paths. The detection breaks down in practice because legitimate software performs bulk rename operations routinely: archive extraction, media transcoding pipelines, document management migrations, development build systems, and backup rotation all write or rename many files quickly. Distinguishing them requires examining name entropy, suffix uniformity, the presence of an accompanying note file, whether the process deleted or created recovery artefacts, and whether shadow copies or backup services were affected in the same window. Coverage gaps also arise where telemetry is sampled, where network attached storage does not forward file auditing, and where the target is a database file rewritten in place rather than renamed, which produces far fewer file events.
objectives: Describe the file-system event patterns that distinguish automated encryption from ordinary bulk processing.
Compute a per-process rename and write rate from file telemetry and choose thresholds that balance delay against detection.
Measure name entropy and suffix uniformity and explain why they distinguish encrypted output from archive extraction.
Correlate mass file modification with recovery inhibition activity such as deletion of local backup state or shadow copies.
Plan containment decisions including process termination versus host isolation and the effect of each on evidence quality.
Produce a written incident timeline for a ransomware event using file, process and service telemetry.
dataSources: Endpoint file operation telemetry capturing process, target path, operation type and resulting file name
Windows Security file system auditing events for object creation, rename and write operations on monitored shares
Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing to identify the acting binary and its parent
Service control manager events recording unexpected stop of backup, database or volume shadow copy services
Storage and network share access logs showing distributed write bursts from a single host or account
topics.logic: Aggregate file create, rename and write events by acting process and host into short rolling windows, then alert when a single process exceeds a rate baseline that is implausible for interactive work. Score the alert higher when the resulting file names share a uniform suffix, when their characters are unusually random, when the same process touched multiple directories or mapped drives, and when recovery related services stopped or their state was cleared within the same window. Lower the score when the process is a known archiving or build tool operating inside its expected working directory chain, and require human confirmation before automatic containment on hosts where such tooling is normal.
topics.pseudoQuery:
title: Mass File Rename With High Entropy Names
id: det-mass-file-rename-entropy
status: training
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  bulk_rename:
    EventType:
      - rename
      - create
      - write
    # grouped by process and host
  rate_threshold:
    condition: count(distinct TargetFilename) by ProcessGuid > 300 within 10m
  high_entropy_names:
    TargetFilename|re: '\\[A-Za-z0-9]{8,}\\.(locked|enc|encrypted|crypt|[a-z0-9]{3,5})$'
  recovery_artefacts:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - 'RECOVER'
      - 'DECRYPT'
      - 'README'
  condition: bulk_rename and rate_threshold and (high_entropy_names or recovery_artefacts)
fields:
  - ProcessImage
  - ParentImage
  - User
  - TargetFilename
  - Computer
level: critical
falsePositives: Archive and compression tools expanding or creating large numbers of files inside an expected working directory
Media transcoding, rendering and image pipeline jobs that write thousands of uniformly named output files
Source control checkouts, build systems and package managers materialising dependency trees in bulk
Document management migrations, bulk renames by administrators and data classification tooling
Backup and synchronisation agents that stage, rename or rotate large file sets on a schedule
topics.tuningNotes: Baseline the rename, create and write rate for every process family that routinely touches more than a few hundred files per window, and apply those baselines per host role so build servers are not compared against workstations. Do not suppress the alert entirely for such processes; instead downgrade to a low severity event that still records the activity so that a ransomware binary masquerading as a signed tool produces a visible anomaly. Tier thresholds by criticality so a database server or domain controller crossing a modest threshold pages immediately while a developer workstation requires a higher count, and always keep the entropy and recovery-artefact conditions as separate boosts rather than as prerequisites. Finally, verify that file telemetry covers network shares and mounted volumes, because a detection limited to local drives will miss the fastest spreading events.

beginner.definition: Entropy is a measure of how random a piece of text looks. This detection watches for one program renaming or rewriting hundreds of files very quickly. The new names look like random strings and share the same ending. That pattern is the fingerprint of ransomware encrypting your files.
beginner.whyItMatters: Encryption runs fast because the attacker wants it finished before anyone notices. Catch the wave while it is still running, and you can stop the program. That saves the files it has not reached yet. Miss it, and recovery may mean restoring from offline copies or paying. This is one of the last chances to interrupt an attack.
howItWorks: Your endpoint tools or file auditing record who changed which file, and when each change happened.
Events are grouped by the program that made the change, over short windows such as ten minutes.
The detection counts how many files that one program touched inside the window.
It compares that number against what is normal for that program on that kind of machine.
It then checks whether the new names look random or share one odd file extension.
A high rate plus random names plus files touched across several folders is treated as critical.
beginner.example: Imagine a person walking along every library shelf and rewriting each book title as a random code. They work through the whole room in minutes, never pausing and never reading anything. A normal archivist may relabel many books too. But they work slowly, one section at a time, and keep names people can read. Speed, randomness and coverage are what give the intruder away.
takeaways: Watch the rate as well as the name, because encryption is bulk work done fast.
Random names plus one shared extension make a rename wave far more suspicious.
Names alone are not enough, since build and backup tools rename files in bulk too.

topics.title: New Service Installation
topics.summary: New service installation detection identifies the creation of a Windows service or the modification of an existing service's binary path where the referenced executable is not part of an approved software baseline, which is a common and durable route to both persistence and privileged code execution. The behaviour matters because a service installation requires administrative rights to complete, so it evidences either privileged access already obtained or an elevation technique that has just succeeded, and the resulting service starts automatically or at boot, granting the payload execution in a system context that survives logoff and often survives reboots. The telemetry required is service installation auditing events with the service name, image path, start type and account, process creation records for the binaries that install services including their full command line and parent, file creation or write telemetry for the referenced executable so its origin can be established, and signature and reputation enrichment for that file. The signal survives common evasion because the operating system must still record the service in its configuration store for the service to run; an operator may install it through a signed management binary, through a remote procedure call from another host, through a scripting interface, or by modifying an existing service's path rather than creating a new one, and all of these leave configuration and process evidence. The detection breaks down in practice because legitimate software installs and upgrades services constantly, and software deployment systems, monitoring agents, database engines and security products all create services as part of normal operation. Service names are attacker-chosen and often imitate vendor conventions, so name matching alone is weak, and remote installation through management interfaces can attribute the change to a system account rather than the initiating user, blurring accountability. Durable tuning therefore depends on matching the service image path to a signed binary in an approved directory, on noticing services that point into user-writable locations, temporary directories or script interpreters, and on treating modification of an existing service path as equivalent in severity to creating a new one.
objectives: Describe the event sources that record service creation and modification and the fields needed to assess risk.
Evaluate a new service by image path, signer, parent process and the account the service will run as.
Detect modification of an existing service binary path as a persistence technique distinct from creation.
Recognise service installations that reference scripting interpreters, temporary directories or remote paths.
Correlate service creation with the process that installed it and reconstruct the execution chain afterwards.
Recommend least privilege controls that constrain who may install services and from where.
dataSources: Windows Security event 4697 service installation with service name, image path and service account
Windows System log service control manager events recording service creation and configuration change
Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing to identify the installing process
File creation telemetry and Authenticode signature metadata for the executable referenced by the service
Software deployment and change management records used to distinguish approved installations from unapproved ones
topics.logic: Alert on any service installation or service configuration change and immediately resolve the referenced image path to a file, checking whether it is signed, whether it resides in a protected program directory, and whether the installing process is a known deployment agent. Raise severity when the image path points into a user profile, temporary directory or network share, when the binary is unsigned or newly created, when the service account is a privileged local or domain account, or when the installation happened on a host and at a time outside the change calendar. Lower severity to an informational record for installations that match an approved deployment signature and path pair, and always query the process tree around the installation time so that any subsequent execution of the service binary can be tied back to a specific origin.
topics.pseudoQuery:
title: Unapproved Service Installation With Untrusted Image Path
id: det-new-service-installation
status: training
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  service_installed:
    EventID: 4697
  untrusted_path:
    ServiceFileName|contains:
      - '\\Users\\'
      - '\\AppData\\'
      - '\\Temp\\'
      - '\\ProgramData\\'
      - '\\Windows\\Temp\\'
      - '\\\\'
  interpreter_path:
    ServiceFileName|contains:
      - 'cmd.exe'
      - 'powershell'
      - 'rundll32'
      - 'mshta'
  approved_installer:
    # installer binary corresponds to a signed deployment agent path
    condition: installer_is_known_deployment_agent
  condition: service_installed and (untrusted_path or interpreter_path) and not approved_installer
fields:
  - ServiceName
  - ServiceFileName
  - ServiceAccount
  - SubjectUserName
  - Computer
level: high
falsePositives: Software deployment and patch management agents installing or updating services across the estate
Endpoint protection, backup and monitoring products that register services during installation and upgrade
Database and application servers configured manually by administrators during approved builds
Driver and hardware support packages that add helper services from vendor installation directories
Development and test systems where engineers iterate on service-based components frequently
topics.tuningNotes: Key exclusions on the pair of installer binary and service image path, both resolved to signed files in approved directories, rather than on the service name, because names are easily imitated and change between product versions. Treat any service whose image path resolves to an unsigned file or a user-writable directory as a separate high severity rule that is not subject to the deployment agent allow-list, since signed deployment tooling should never produce that combination. Where remote installation is possible, ensure that the service events are collected with subject account information and that the originating host is correlated through logon events, otherwise the change will appear attributable only to a machine account. Finally, review the rule whenever the endpoint agent or management platform changes its own service configuration, because those upgrades generate predictable bursts of alerts that erode analyst trust if they are not handled.

beginner.definition: A Windows service is a background program that starts with the computer and runs without anyone signing in. Installing one normally needs administrative rights. This detection flags new services, or changes to an existing service. It looks at the program the service points at, checking whether that program is part of your approved software.
beginner.whyItMatters: A service gives an attacker code that runs as a powerful system account. It restarts after a reboot and keeps the installer hidden in the background. Installing one also proves that somebody held admin rights or just gained them. Adding a service is quieter than many other tricks. Without this alert, an intruder can stay for a long time.
howItWorks: Windows writes an audit record whenever a service is installed or its settings are changed.
The record includes the service name, the path of the program it runs, and the account it runs as.
The detection resolves that path to a real file and checks whether the file is digitally signed.
It also checks whether the file sits in a protected program folder or in a user folder.
The installing program is identified, so a known deployment agent can be recognised.
Services pointing at unsigned files in user folders are treated as high risk.
beginner.example: A company installed a new monitoring tool. During the setup it created a service that started automatically, which is completely normal for that type of software. The alert fired anyway, because the program sat in a temporary folder and carried no digital signature. Investigators then saw that the installer was the approved package. The folder also matched the vendor default, so they recorded an exception.
takeaways: A new service means background code that survives a reboot.
Judge the image path, the signature and the installing program, not the service name.
Trusted software creates services often, so build an allow-list instead of ignoring the event.

topics.title: Office Spawning Child Shell
topics.summary: Office spawning child shell detection identifies productivity suite processes creating a command interpreter, scripting host or living-off-the-land binary as a direct child, which is the classic post-exploitation pattern following malicious document execution, macro abuse or an exploited document renderer. The behaviour matters because document-borne intrusion remains one of the most common initial access routes, and the transition from a document handler to a system shell is the moment when a contained file becomes an interactive foothold with the user's rights and network position. The telemetry required is process creation with parent process identification and full command lines, including parent integrity level, the document or template path where available, the signed status of the child binary, and file and network telemetry to establish what the child then did. The signal survives common evasion because the operating system records the parent-child relationship at process creation regardless of how the shell was invoked; an operator may use a scripting host, a signed system binary that loads script content, a component object model invocation, or a template injection that reaches the same result, but the parent remains the document handling process. The detection breaks down in practice because legitimate documents and add-ins do spawn processes: template management, document comparison, mail merge, citation managers, digital signature workflows, and vendor add-ins for accounting, legal and engineering tools all create child processes from the office application. Environments with heavy add-in use therefore require an allow-list keyed on the specific child binary, its signer and the parent's loaded modules. Coverage also depends on whether process telemetry includes suppressed or short-lived processes, since many malicious children exit within seconds, and on whether the parent process identifier is preserved rather than reused, which some collection pipelines do not guarantee.
objectives: Explain why the parent-child process relationship is a durable signal even when the child is a signed system binary.
Query process telemetry for office parents creating shells, script hosts or signed system binaries and enrich with signer data.
Build an allow-list of legitimate document add-in child processes and describe the risks of over-excluding.
Correlate the child process command line with follow-on network, file or credential activity to establish intent.
Handle short-lived child processes and process identifier reuse in collection pipelines.
Describe immediate containment steps and the evidence to preserve when a document-driven shell is confirmed.
dataSources: Endpoint detection agent process creation telemetry with parent image, command line and integrity level
Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing enabled
Authenticode signature and file path metadata for both the document handler and the spawned child binary
Endpoint network telemetry recording outbound connections initiated by the child process
Mail gateway and file share metadata identifying the document source, sender and delivery time
topics.logic: Alert whenever a document handling process appears as the parent of a command interpreter, scripting host or signed system binary commonly abused to launch code, and attach the child's full command line, its signature status and its immediate network activity to the alert. Score higher when the child command line references temporary directories, encoded content, remote addresses, or archive and download utilities, and when the parent document originated from an external sender or an untrusted share. Score lower only for child binaries and signers that appear in the reviewed add-in allow-list, and keep those events at low severity for periodic review rather than discarding them outright.
topics.pseudoQuery:
title: Document Handler Spawning A Shell Or Script Host
id: det-office-child-shell
status: training
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_creation
detection:
  office_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\\winword.exe'
      - '\\excel.exe'
      - '\\powerpnt.exe'
      - '\\outlook.exe'
  suspicious_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\\cmd.exe'
      - '\\powershell.exe'
      - '\\wscript.exe'
      - '\\mshta.exe'
      - '\\rundll32.exe'
      - '\\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\\certutil.exe'
  suspicious_arguments:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'http'
      - '\\AppData\\'
      - '\\Temp\\'
      - 'frombase64string'
  known_addin:
    condition: child_matches_approved_addin_list
  condition: office_parent and suspicious_child and not known_addin
fields:
  - ParentImage
  - Image
  - CommandLine
  - User
level: high
falsePositives: Document management, citation and template add-ins that launch helper or updater processes
Mail merge, mailto and hyperlink handling that opens a command or protocol handler from a document
Enterprise add-ins for finance, legal and engineering tools that spawn signed companion binaries
Digital signature and document comparison workflows that invoke local utilities
User-initiated macros in internally authored spreadsheets that call out to approved internal tools
topics.tuningNotes: Allow-list on the exact combination of parent image, child image and child signer, and require that the approved entries be reviewed and owned by a named team, because a broad parent-only exclusion removes the detection entirely in add-in heavy environments. Keep the excluded events flowing at low severity so that a change in the allowed child's arguments or its network behaviour still generates a visible anomaly. Weight severities using the document origin, since alerts from documents delivered by external mail or downloaded from the web carry materially higher risk than those from internal shares, and block macros from internet-origin documents as a preventive control that reduces alert volume at the same time. Finally, verify that process telemetry captures short-lived children, and where process identifier reuse is possible in the pipeline, join on process start time in addition to identifier to avoid misattributing activity.

beginner.definition: Documents open in programs such as Word or Excel. A child process is a program started by another program. A shell is a command interpreter that can run further instructions. This detection flags a document program starting a command interpreter or scripting tool. That is often the sign of a harmful document running its payload.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attacks that arrive inside documents are still a common way intruders get in. The moment a document handler starts a shell, a harmless file becomes a live foothold. It gains that user's rights and that user's network position. Catching that single step stops the chain early. It stops before the attacker downloads tools, adds accounts, or reaches shared folders.
howItWorks: Endpoint sensors record each new process along with the program that started it.
The detection selects starts where the parent program is a well-known document handler.
It then checks the child, looking for command interpreters and scripting tools.
The child's full command line is reviewed, because web addresses and temporary folders are warning signs.
The digital signature of the child program is checked, since signed system tools are often borrowed.
Only child programs on a reviewed add-in list are treated as routine, and even they are logged.
beginner.example: You open a letter and it asks you to sign a form. You sign, and the letter phones a stranger to say the door is unlocked. A document is only paper until something else starts on its behalf. When a spreadsheet quietly launches a command interpreter, the file stops being a document and starts doing work. That jump is unusual, and it is exactly why this alert exists.
takeaways: A document program should not normally start a command interpreter.
The parent and child pair matters, even when the child is a signed system program.
Treat documents that arrived by email with more suspicion than files from internal shares.

topics.title: RDP Logon From New ASN
topics.summary: RDP logon from a new autonomous system number detection flags successful interactive remote desktop sessions where the source network has never previously appeared in the organisation's remote access history for that host, account or user population. The behaviour matters because stolen credentials are frequently valid, correctly typed and correctly MFA-challenged, so the only observable difference between a legitimate administrator and an intruder is often where the session originates and whether the ASN, country or hosting provider is consistent with that account's history. The telemetry required is authentication logging from the remote access path itself, including source address, account, session outcome and negotiated protocol, combined with an enrichment source that maps addresses to autonomous system numbers and network ownership, plus asset inventory so the target host's business function is known. The signal survives common evasion because residential proxy services and commercial hosting providers are themselves registries with stable ASN values, so an operator routing through a bulletproof host or a cloud virtual machine still produces a source that stands out against an enterprise user base; even a compromised home router in a previously unseen ASN deviates from the account baseline. The detection breaks down in practice for a well known set of reasons: travelling staff, remote work relocations, mobile carrier address pools that rotate ASN frequently, and legitimate use of VPN egress concentrators all generate genuine first-seen ASNs. It also fails when enrichment data is stale or when the source address seen by the collector is a load balancer or gateway rather than the true client, which is common where a reverse proxy terminates the session. Effective use therefore depends on scoring first-seen ASN alongside impossible travel, account privilege, MFA method used, and post-authentication behaviour rather than alerting on first-seen alone.
objectives: Explain why source network reputation and ASN history remain useful when credentials and MFA are both valid.
Build a query that joins successful remote desktop authentication to an ASN enrichment table and computes first-seen combinations.
Score alerts using account privilege, host business function, hosting-origin flag and MFA method rather than geography alone.
Identify telemetry blind spots created by reverse proxies, jump hosts and VPN concentrators that obscure the true client address.
Distinguish a compromised but valid session from credential misuse by examining post-authentication actions on the target host.
Document an investigation timeline for a suspected remote access intrusion suitable for a formal incident report.
dataSources: Windows Security event 4624 logon records with logon type 10 for remote interactive sessions, including source address
Remote desktop gateway or jump host operational logs recording client address, account and session duration
Identity provider sign-in logs containing source address, applied conditional access policy and authentication method
Address-to-ASN and network ownership enrichment table refreshed from a commercial or public routing registry
Asset inventory mapping host names to business function, environment and data classification
topics.logic: Take every successful remote interactive authentication, resolve the source address to an autonomous system and country, and compare the combination against the historical set of ASNs seen for that account, that host and the tenant as a whole. Raise an alert when the source ASN is new for the account or host, and add weight when the origin belongs to a hosting or proxy provider, when the account holds administrative rights, when the target is a server rather than a workstation, or when the sign-in used a weaker authentication method than the account normally uses. Correlate the session with actions taken on the target host afterwards so that a genuinely suspicious remote session can be distinguished from a travelling employee connecting from a hotel network.
topics.pseudoQuery:
title: Remote Desktop Logon From Previously Unseen ASN
id: det-rdp-new-asn
status: training
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  successful_rdp:
    EventID: 4624
    LogonType: 10
    # status field indicates success
  source_enriched:
    SourceAsn|exists: true
  first_seen_asn:
    condition: source_enriched and asn_not_in_historical_baseline(AccountName, SourceAsn, 90d)
  risky_origin:
    AsnCategory:
      - hosting
      - proxy
      - anonymiser
  privileged_account:
    AccountName|endswith:
      - '-adm'
      - '-da'
  condition: successful_rdp and first_seen_asn and (risky_origin or privileged_account)
fields:
  - AccountName
  - SourceIpAddress
  - SourceAsn
  - TargetHostName
  - AuthenticationMethod
level: high
falsePositives: Employees travelling or relocating who connect from a genuinely new network provider
Mobile broadband and carrier grade NAT pools that present different ASNs across sessions
Vendors and contractors connecting from their own corporate ranges for the first time
Cloud hosted jump hosts or administrative workstations provisioned in a new region
Users on dynamic residential connections whose ISP reassigns address blocks between providers
topics.tuningNotes: Set the historical baseline window long enough to cover seasonal working patterns, commonly ninety days or more, and compute it per account and per host rather than only per tenant so a new workstation does not immediately generate alerts for every user. Treat hosting and anonymising ASN categories as a separate higher severity rule rather than folding them into the base rule, which keeps the general detection useful without paging on every business trip. Feed known corporate egress ranges, VPN concentrators and vendor ranges into an explicit allow-list and revisit it monthly, and normalise the source address at the collector so that reverse proxies and gateways do not mask the true client. Finally, cap the number of alerts per account per day so that a single user on a rotating mobile connection cannot flood the queue.

beginner.definition: Remote Desktop lets you control another computer over the network, and each connection comes from an internet address. An autonomous system number is a label for the network that owns that address. This detection flags a successful remote desktop login from a network that is new for that account or that computer.
beginner.whyItMatters: Stolen passwords are often typed correctly, so a login can look perfectly normal. Multi-factor authentication may even pass if the attacker holds the code. The strongest remaining clue is where the session comes from. An account may always connect from one city, then suddenly arrive from an unknown provider abroad. That change deserves a look before the intruder moves deeper.
howItWorks: Your systems log every successful remote desktop login, including the source address and the account used.
An enrichment step turns each address into the network provider that owns it and the country it sits in.
You store the usual networks for each account and each computer over the past weeks or months.
A comparison step checks whether the network behind a new login has ever appeared before.
The alert ranks higher when the network is a hosting or proxy provider, not a home internet line.
Analysts then confirm whether the account holder was travelling or whether the session came from a stranger.
beginner.example: Think of an office where everyone badges in at the front door. Security knows which door each person normally uses. One morning a badge appears at a service entrance on the far side of the building. That person has never touched that door before. The badge is real and the door is real, yet the guard should still walk over and look. A first-time network is a reason to check, not proof of guilt.
takeaways: When passwords and codes can be stolen, where a session starts is a useful clue.
A new source network is a signal to investigate, not a verdict.
Many new networks at once usually means your records moved, not your users.

topics.title: Scheduled Task Created by Non-Admin
topics.summary: Scheduled task created by a non-administrative account detection identifies task registration activity where the creating account is an ordinary user or a service identity that has no legitimate business reason to establish persistence, autostart or system level execution on the host. The behaviour matters because scheduled tasks are one of the most reliable and least disruptive persistence mechanisms on Windows: they survive reboot, they can run under a privileged context through stored credentials, and they are frequently used for recurring beaconing, dropper staging and privilege escalation through writable task definitions. The telemetry required is process creation for the task scheduling utility along with its command line, scheduled task operational events recording task name, creating account, action to execute and the principal the task runs as, and process creation correlated to the task engine so that the executed child process can be attributed back to the task definition. The signal survives common evasion because registration is an unavoidable step: an operator may use the command line tool, a scripting interface, a management API or a signed binary proxy, but all of these result in a task definition written to the task store, and the resulting execution appears as a child of the task scheduling service. Attackers who avoid the task store by using alternative autostart locations still remove themselves from this detection's scope, which is why it belongs in a family of autostart detections rather than standing alone. The detection breaks down in practice because non-administrative users in many organisations legitimately create their own logon tasks, software installers register per-user update tasks constantly, and cloud connected productivity and collaboration clients rebuild their scheduled entries after every upgrade. Task names are also attacker-controlled, so name-based matching produces both false positives and false negatives. The workable approach is to score on the creating account's privilege relative to the task principal, the writability of the executable path referenced, and the relationship between task creation and surrounding process activity, rather than on the existence of the task alone.
objectives: Explain why the relationship between the creating account and the task principal matters more than the task name.
Query task registration telemetry to extract the executing path, the run-as principal and the trigger configuration.
Identify task definitions that reference user-writable directories, script interpreters or remote content.
Baseline legitimate per-user updater tasks from productivity and collaboration software in your environment.
Correlate task execution with the originating process tree to attribute running payloads back to the schedule.
Recommend hardening measures that restrict non-administrative task creation without breaking vendor updaters.
dataSources: Windows Security event 4698 scheduled task creation including task name, content and creating subject
Process creation telemetry for the task registration utility with full command line
Task Scheduler operational log entries recording task registration and execution start
Windows Security event 4688 process creation capturing the task engine spawning the configured action
Account group membership data identifying whether the creating account holds administrative rights
topics.logic: Alert when a task registration event is attributed to an account that does not hold administrative rights, or when the task principal is more privileged than the creating account, and enrich the alert with the executable or script path the task will run. Add severity when the referenced path is inside a user profile, temporary directory, or other location writable by non-administrators, when the action invokes a scripting interpreter or downloads remote content, and when the task is configured to run at logon or on a short repeating interval. Reduce severity for tasks created by known software updaters with signed binaries in program directories and a stable name pattern, and correlate the alert with the process that the task engine actually launched so that running payloads can be attributed and collected.
topics.pseudoQuery:
title: Scheduled Task Registered By Non-Administrative Account
id: det-scheduled-task-non-admin
status: training
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  task_registered:
    EventID: 4698
  non_admin_creator:
    SubjectUserName|endswith:
      - '$'
    # creator is not a member of the local administrators group
  suspicious_action:
    TaskContent|contains:
      - 'powershell'
      - 'cmd.exe /c'
      - 'wscript'
      - 'mshta'
      - 'rundll32'
      - '\\AppData\\'
      - '\\Temp\\'
      - '\\Users\\Public\\'
  condition: task_registered and (non_admin_creator or suspicious_action)
fields:
  - TaskName
  - SubjectUserName
  - TaskContent
  - Computer
level: high
falsePositives: Cloud synchronisation and collaboration clients that register per-user update or maintenance tasks
Software installers and updaters running in user context that recreate their scheduled entries after upgrade
Administrative scripts running under a delegated service account that is not in the local administrators group
Endpoint management agents that register inventory or compliance tasks on behalf of a system service
Developer tooling that schedules builds, test runs or cleanup jobs under the interactive user account
topics.tuningNotes: Build the exclusion set from the pair of task name pattern and executable path rather than from the task name alone, because attacker chosen names frequently imitate vendor naming conventions. Where the deployment supports it, resolve the creator's effective group membership at alert time instead of relying on the account name suffix, since delegated and just-in-time administrative accounts do not follow naming rules. Keep severity low, but do not discard, tasks whose action references a signed binary in a protected program directory; instead route them to a weekly review so that a compromised updater change is still visible. Supplement the rule with detection of task modification and deletion events, since operators increasingly modify an existing benign task instead of creating a new one, and that behaviour is invisible to a creation-only rule.
