beginner.definition: A scheduled task is an instruction Windows runs later, either once or on a repeating timetable. An administrative account is one with broad control over a computer. This detection flags tasks created by ordinary accounts. It also flags tasks set to run as a more powerful account than their creator.
beginner.whyItMatters: Tasks are a favourite way to stay on a machine, because they survive a restart. They also look like ordinary system behaviour. An attacker can register one quietly, then let Windows relaunch their program every hour or at each sign-in. Many organisations let normal users create tasks. This activity therefore sits inside allowed behaviour, so it needs its own alert.
howItWorks: Windows writes an audit record whenever a new scheduled task is registered.
That record names the task, the account that created it and the command the task will run.
It also shows which account the task runs as, which may be more powerful than the creator.
The detection compares the two accounts and checks whether the creator normally holds admin rights.
It also looks at the target path, because files in user folders and temporary areas are common hiding places.
High-risk tasks are correlated with what the task actually launched later, so running code can be traced.
beginner.example: Think of an apartment building where any tenant may leave a written instruction at the front desk. One tenant leaves a note for the maintenance crew. It asks them to unlock the manager's office at two in the morning. The crew is allowed to do it and the tenant is allowed to leave notes. Nothing about either action looks broken. Yet the combination is wrong, and the manager should ask why.
takeaways: Scheduled tasks are a durable way to stay on a machine across restarts.
Compare who created the task with the account it will run as.
Judge a task by its target path and command, not by its name.

topics.title: Shadow Copy Deletion
topics.summary: Shadow copy deletion detection identifies execution of commands or interfaces that remove volume shadow copies, resize the shadow storage allocation, or disable the recovery services that maintain them, which is a preparatory step that removes the fastest local recovery path before data is encrypted or destroyed. The behaviour matters because it converts a recoverable incident into an unrecoverable one: with local snapshots intact an organisation can often restore without paying, and attackers know this, so recovery inhibition reliably precedes impact activity by minutes to hours and provides a rare opportunity to interrupt the campaign. The telemetry required is process creation with full command line for the binaries and script hosts that expose shadow management functionality, including their parent process and user context; service control manager events recording stop, disable or deletion of recovery related services; scheduled task and service creation records that show the deletion being wrapped into a recurring job; and storage management interface activity where it can be collected. The signal survives common evasion because the operation must reach the volume snapshot provider through a documented interface; an operator may script it, invoke a management tool, call a backup product's own utility with destructive arguments, or load the interface through a signed binary, but the recovery service state or the storage configuration still changes and the initiating process still appears in process telemetry. The detection breaks down in practice because legitimate administration does delete snapshots: storage reclamation, imaging workflows, backup software that prunes old snapshots, and troubleshooting scripts all produce similar commands. Distinguishing malicious from routine use requires context such as the parent process, the account, the timing relative to other suspicious events, and whether the deletion was paired with disablement of recovery services or deletion of backup catalogues. Environments where the command line is not captured, or where the destructive action is taken through a remote management interface that logs nothing locally, will not be covered by process telemetry alone.
objectives: Explain why recovery inhibition is a high confidence precursor to destructive attacks and how to prioritise it accordingly.
Identify the process, service and storage telemetry that reveals shadow copy deletion and service disablement.
Distinguish administrative snapshot pruning from malicious deletion using parent process, account and timing context.
Correlate deletion activity with simultaneous service configuration changes and backup catalogue tampering.
Describe containment actions appropriate at the first confirmed deletion event and the sequencing of evidence collection.
Assess detection coverage gaps where deletion is performed through remote management or backup product interfaces.
dataSources: Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing enabled
Endpoint detection agent process telemetry including parent process, integrity level and loaded modules
Service control manager events recording service stop, configuration change and removal
Windows Security event 4697 service installation and related service configuration auditing events
Storage and volume management telemetry showing shadow storage configuration change or snapshot removal
topics.logic: Alert when a process invokes a shadow copy management interface with arguments that remove snapshots or alter storage allocation, or when the recovery related services are stopped, reconfigured or deleted outside an approved maintenance window. Enrich the alert with the parent process chain and account, and escalate immediately when the same host or account also shows mass file modification, service disablement, or deletion of backup catalogues within the surrounding hour. Downgrade known backup and imaging products operating from their signed installation paths under their service accounts, but log them so that a change in their invocation pattern remains visible.
topics.pseudoQuery:
title: Volume Shadow Copy Deletion Or Recovery Service Disablement
id: det-shadow-copy-deletion
status: training
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_creation
detection:
  shadow_tool:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\\vssadmin.exe'
      - '\\wmic.exe'
      - '\\wbadmin.exe'
      - '\\diskshadow.exe'
      - '\\bcdedit.exe'
  destructive_arguments:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'delete shadows'
      - 'shadowcopy delete'
      - 'delete catalog'
      - 'resize shadowstorage'
      - 'recoveryenabled no'
      - 'ignoreallfailures'
  service_disablement:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'config'
      - 'start= disabled'
  condition: shadow_tool and (destructive_arguments or service_disablement)
fields:
  - Image
  - ParentImage
  - User
  - CommandLine
  - Computer
level: critical
falsePositives: Backup and disaster recovery products that prune expired snapshots as part of their normal schedule
Storage reclamation and capacity management scripts run by infrastructure teams during maintenance windows
Imaging and migration workflows that delete snapshots before converting or cloning a volume
Troubleshooting and remediation scripts that reset shadow storage after corruption or capacity exhaustion
Sandbox, test and laboratory systems where snapshot cleanup is performed routinely by automation
topics.tuningNotes: Allow-list by the combination of signed binary path, service account and host role, and require that the exclusion also match an approved maintenance window, so the same command outside the window still alerts. Never exclude the destructive argument set alone, because that is precisely the behaviour a masquerading binary would exhibit. Where backup products perform deletion through their own executables rather than system tools, extend the detection to those binaries with their delete and prune arguments and validate with the backup team which invocation patterns are expected. Because this behaviour is often the last warning before impact, keep it at critical severity, route it to an out-of-hours queue with an automatic page, and verify that endpoint telemetry captures command lines for script host processes where the deletion is commonly wrapped.

beginner.definition: A shadow copy is a saved snapshot of your files that Windows keeps so you can restore an earlier version. This detection watches for commands that delete those snapshots or switch off the recovery service that manages them. Removing snapshots is a common step attackers take just before they encrypt or destroy data.
beginner.whyItMatters: Snapshots are usually the fastest way to recover without paying anyone. When they are gone, a bad day turns into a disaster. This activity often happens minutes before files are locked. That makes it one of the last clear warnings you will get. Treating it as urgent gives you a real chance to cut off the attack.
howItWorks: Windows keeps a record of the commands it runs, including the exact options typed after each command.
A short list of built-in tools can remove snapshots or change how much space they are allowed.
The detection looks for those tools being used with options that delete snapshots or free their storage.
It also watches for the recovery service being stopped, disabled, or set to never start again.
Each alert carries the account, the parent program and the machine so you can judge whether it was planned work.
A suspected deletion should be paired with a check for sudden mass file changes on the same machine.
beginner.example: A cleaner comes into your house and quietly removes the fire extinguishers. They also unscrew the batteries from every smoke alarm. Nothing has burned yet and the building looks untouched. But the moment a fire starts, you have no way to fight it and no warning. Anyone who removes your recovery options first is telling you what they plan next.
takeaways: Deleting snapshots is a late warning sign, so it should wake someone up immediately.
Legitimate tools can do this work, so judge by account, timing and parent program.
Keep backup copies that an attacker cannot reach from inside the network.

topics.title: Suspicious PowerShell EncodedCommand
topics.summary: Suspicious PowerShell EncodedCommand detection identifies execution of PowerShell where the command payload is supplied as a Base64-encoded string rather than readable script text, typically through the -EncodedCommand parameter, its documented short forms, or by piping decoded content into Invoke-Expression. The behaviour matters because encoding is one of the cheapest and most common ways an operator hides intent from casual console review, from simple string-based content filters, and from responders reading a process list under time pressure. The telemetry required is process creation with full command line captured, ideally from endpoint detection agents or Windows Security event 4688 with command line auditing enabled, plus PowerShell script block logging and module logging where available so the decoded body can be reconstructed after the fact. The signal survives common evasion because the encoding step happens before the shell ever evaluates the script, so the obfuscated string is what appears in the process command line; variants that read an encoded blob from a file, an environment variable, or a remote download still produce a distinctive parent-child pattern and an unusually high proportion of non-alphanumeric characters. It also survives because legitimate administrative tooling rarely needs encoding at all. The detection breaks down in practice on three fronts: automation platforms and configuration management agents use encoded commands perfectly legitimately and at high volume, so baseline allow-listing by parent process and signing certificate becomes mandatory; short payloads produce short command lines where entropy and length thresholds are unreliable; and adversaries who switch to script block logging evasion, downgrade attacks against logging policy, or in-memory assembly loading can leave a decoded payload that never appears in the command line at all, which is why this rule should be paired with script block content analysis and AMSI-related telemetry rather than used alone.
objectives: Explain what PowerShell command encoding does at the shell level and why the encoded form, not the decoded script, is what appears in process-creation telemetry.
Write a query that correlates encoded-command execution against parent process, user context and host role to separate automation from interactive abuse.
Identify which command-line tokens indicate encoding and describe how each family of tokens behaves across PowerShell editions.
Assess when command-line length and character-distribution heuristics add value and when they produce unacceptable noise.
Describe how script block logging and module logging recover intent that the encoded command line conceals.
Recognise logging-policy tampering and language downgrade behaviour as an escalation signal alongside the initial encoded execution.
Prioritise encoded-command alerts using follow-on activity such as network egress, credential access attempts or scheduled task creation.
dataSources: Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing enabled
Endpoint detection agent process telemetry including parent process, integrity level and signing certificate
PowerShell script block logging events capturing reconstructed script text
PowerShell module logging and transcription output where administrative policy enables them
Windows Security event 4104 correlated with the originating process identifier on the same host
topics.logic: Look for any process whose image name is a PowerShell host and whose command line contains an encoding parameter, then enrich the alert with the parent process, the user context and whether the host is a build agent or management server. Strip the ordinary automation parents that appear in the environment baseline, and score what remains higher when the command line is unusually long, when it is dominated by non-alphanumeric characters, or when the same host shows download or credential-access activity within the surrounding window. If script block logging is available, join the decoded content to the process and surface keywords that indicate reconnaissance, remote download or defence evasion rather than attempting to match on the encoded text.
topics.pseudoQuery:
title: Suspicious PowerShell EncodedCommand
id: det-powershell-encodedcommand
status: training
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_creation
detection:
  encoded_param:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\\powershell.exe'
      - '\\pwsh.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'encodedcommand'
      - ' -enc '
      - ' -e '
      - ' -ec '
  pipe_decode:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'frombase64string'
      - 'invoke-expression'
  automation_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\\sccmexec.exe'
      - '\\wsexec.exe'
      - '\\msiexec.exe'
  condition: encoded_param and not automation_parent
fields:
  - Image
  - ParentImage
  - User
  - CommandLine
level: high
falsePositives: Configuration management and software deployment agents that pass installation logic to PowerShell as encoded commands
Monitoring and inventory agents that poll local system state through encoded one-liners on a schedule
Backup, patching and virtualisation management consoles that wrap vendor scripts in encoded commands
Administrator-written scheduled jobs that encode a script to survive quoting problems with spaces and special characters
Managed endpoint tooling and remote support sessions that issue encoded commands from a signed binary
topics.tuningNotes: Build the benign baseline from parent image path, file signature and the account that executes the command, then exclude those combinations rather than excluding the encoding parameter itself, because excluding the parameter removes the entire detection surface. Threshold on repetition per host per hour so a legitimate agent that runs every minute is suppressed while a single unusual encoded invocation on a workstation is still surfaced. Keep short command lines in scope but lower their severity and require a second signal such as network egress, a new scheduled task or a service installation before paging anyone. Re-review the allow-list quarterly against signed binaries only, and raise an independent alert when PowerShell logging policy or transcription settings change on a host that previously had them enabled.

beginner.definition: PowerShell is a built-in tool on Windows that runs commands and small scripts. An encoded command has been translated into a long block of letters, numbers and symbols before the computer runs it. This detection looks for PowerShell being started with its instructions in that scrambled form instead of plain, readable text.
beginner.whyItMatters: When the instructions are scrambled, nobody watching can see what the command really does. Attackers use this trick because it hides intent from a quick glance at a screen. It also slips past simple filters that search for known bad words. If you ignore it, a machine can run harmful code while the console shows a meaningless block of characters.
howItWorks: Windows records each program it starts, together with the full command line that started it.
Some of those command lines begin with PowerShell followed by a parameter that means the command is encoded.
The recorded line then contains a long block of characters that looks nothing like normal English.
Your monitoring tool raises a flag whenever that parameter appears on a machine with no reason to use it.
For a clearer picture, turn on PowerShell script logging so the decoded text of the command is saved too.
Check which program started it and who was signed in, because software deployment tools often encode commands for honest reasons.
beginner.example: Picture a postcard that anyone in the post office can read, and picture the same message written entirely in shorthand. The postman still delivers it, but nobody along the way can tell what it says. An encoded command works like that shorthand. The computer understands it perfectly, while a person reading the screen sees only gibberish. That is why you should decode it before deciding whether it is harmless, and why you check who sent it.
takeaways: An encoded command is not proof of an attack, but it does hide what the command will do.
Turn on PowerShell script logging so you can read the decoded command later.
Allow trusted deployment tools by parent program rather than ignoring encoding altogether.

topics.title: APT1
topics.summary: APT1 is the designator given in a widely cited 2013 private-sector report to a long-running intrusion set that the report attributed with high confidence to a specific unit of the Chinese People's Liberation Army, an attribution that has since been debated by other analysts and should be treated as a third-party assessment rather than an established fact. The same activity cluster has been published under names including Comment Crew, Comment Panda, Byzantine Candor, and the Shanghai Group, and later research has questioned whether all of it represents one organisational entity or several overlapping clusters sharing tooling and infrastructure. Open reporting describes a breadth-first targeting model rather than narrow sector focus: hundreds of victim organisations across government, defence, aerospace, energy, technology, media, legal, and consulting sectors, concentrated in the United States and other English-speaking countries, with additional victims reported across Asia and Europe. The tradecraft described is comparatively straightforward and repetitive, which is itself the analytic point. Reporting characterises heavy reliance on spearphishing email with malicious attachments or links as the dominant initial access method, followed by remote access through established footholds, use of publicly available and custom remote administration tooling, credential theft from the local host, and long-dwell collection of email and documents. Persistence has been described through service creation and scheduled execution, and exfiltration largely over the same channels used for command and control. Because tooling overlapped with commodity malware and reused infrastructure, defenders face an attribution problem: overlap does not by itself prove a shared operator. For detection planning, the enduring value of studying APT1 is that it illustrates a high-volume, low-sophistication campaign where classic controls such as email attachment filtering, egress restriction, and rapid detection of remote access tooling still carry most of the defensive weight. Many of the specific indicators published in the original report are long obsolete, so the durable lessons are behavioural, not indicator-based.
objectives: Explain why breadth-first targeting changes how defenders prioritise detection engineering compared with a narrowly sector-focused threat.
Analyse spearphishing attachment and link delivery chains and identify the log sources that reveal each stage of the chain.
Detect unauthorised remote administration tooling installed by a user or malware and distinguish it from sanctioned administrative software.
Explain how long-dwell collection of email and documents is detected through volume and access-pattern anomalies rather than signature matching.
Describe how reused infrastructure and commodity tooling create attribution ambiguity and how to state that ambiguity in a threat assessment.
Evaluate why published indicators decay and design a detection portfolio that survives indicator rotation.
Explain the role of egress filtering and protocol restriction in limiting damage from an established foothold.

beginner.definition: APT1 is a tracking name for a very active spying group described in a widely read 2013 report from a security company. That report linked the group to a unit of China's military. Other analysts have debated this claim since then. Treat the link as a third-party opinion, not a proven fact.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group attacked hundreds of organisations instead of a few chosen ones. It used simple, repeated methods that still worked. The letters A P T stand for advanced persistent threat, a funded attacker that does not give up. Blocking harmful email attachments and limiting what can leave your network stops a lot of damage.
howItWorks: Attackers send email with a harmful attachment or a link to many employees.
One person opens it, and a hidden program starts running on the computer.
That program lets the intruder control the machine and add more tools.
Stolen usernames and passwords help them reach other computers in the network.
They read email and copy documents for months, or sometimes for years.
Data leaves the network over the same channels used for control, so it looks normal.
beginner.example: Picture a thief who does not study one house. He walks down a long street and tries every door handle. Most doors are locked, but he only needs one that is not. Because he targets so many places, the police cannot warn everyone in time. Good locks on every door matter more than knowing his face.
takeaways: Simple attacks repeated at scale can be more dangerous than clever ones.
Filter harmful email attachments and control what data can leave.
Do not treat a published group name as proof of who did the attack.

topics.title: APT12
topics.summary: APT12 is a designator applied to an intrusion set that public reporting, largely from vendor research and catalogued in the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base, associates with activity assessed by third parties as Chinese state-interest espionage. The cluster is also tracked as IXESHE, DynCalc, Numbered Panda, and Calc Team, and the historical reporting base is comparatively thin relative to better-documented groups, so the boundaries of the label and the strength of the sponsorship assessment should be treated as moderate rather than settled. A distinctive feature of the public record is that several tracking names derive directly from tooling and naming conventions observed in the campaigns rather than from victimology, which is a reminder that naming often reflects an analyst's first observable rather than an organisational truth. Reporting describes targeting concentrated in East and Southeast Asia, with victims in government, defence, electronics and technology manufacturing, media, and, in earlier waves, organisations associated with political and policy issues, alongside a smaller number of victims reported in North America and Europe. The tradecraft described is classic document-borne espionage: spearphishing with malicious documents that exploit application vulnerabilities or abuse embedded scripting to trigger a downloader, followed by command and control over common web protocols, use of multiple redundant backdoors on a single victim host, and collection of documents from local and network file stores. Reporting has described the deployment of more than one implant family concurrently as a resilience measure, so the discovery of a single implant should not be taken as evidence that the host is clean. For defenders, the practical lessons are to treat email attachment chains as a primary detection surface, to hunt for multiple concurrent implants after any confirmed compromise, and to avoid over-relying on campaign-level indicators that have long since decayed. Analysts should also be careful not to attribute new activity to this label purely on the basis of a shared tooling name.
objectives: Explain how malicious document delivery chains are reconstructed from mail gateway, endpoint, and network telemetry.
Detect concurrent deployment of multiple implant families on a single host and explain why single-implant removal is insufficient.
Analyse command and control over common web protocols and describe the network behaviours that still provide detection value under encryption.
Evaluate the evidentiary strength of a vendor tracking label when the naming derives from tooling rather than victimology.
Build a hunting hypothesis for document and file share collection using access and staging anomalies.
Explain how application vulnerability exploitation in document readers is mitigated and where those mitigations fail.
Draft a threat assessment that separates observed behaviour from sponsorship inference and states confidence explicitly.

beginner.definition: This group, tracked as APT12, is a label used by security companies for a spying group. The short form A P T means advanced persistent threat, which is a patient attacker with money and time. Several companies link the group to state interests in China. The public evidence is thin, so treat that claim as an opinion.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group shows how one simple method can still work: a harmful document sent by email. The attackers also place more than one backdoor on the same computer. If you remove only one, the others stay and the intruder returns. That single lesson is worth more than any list of file names.
howItWorks: A person in a target office receives an email that looks normal and useful.
The attached document asks to run a script, or a link opens a fake login page.
A small downloader fetches a backdoor, a hidden program that gives remote control.
The attackers install a second backdoor, so removing one still leaves access.
The backdoors talk to the internet using normal web traffic, so they blend in.
Files and email are copied out slowly, and the long-term spying continues for months.
beginner.example: Imagine a visitor who wants to keep entering a building. The front desk takes away the key they find in his pocket. He smiles and leaves. The next night he walks in through a side door, because he hid a second key under a flowerpot weeks earlier. That is why a team must search the whole building before saying it is clean.
takeaways: After one hidden program is found, keep looking, because others may remain.
Email attachments are a main way intruders get their first foothold.
Names for attacker groups come from analysts and can change over time.

topics.title: APT28
topics.summary: APT28 is a long-running suspected Russian state-sponsored intrusion set that multiple government and vendor reporting tracks attribute with moderate to high confidence to a unit of Russia's military intelligence service, commonly identified in public reporting as Unit 26165 of the GRU. Vendors have published under many overlapping names, including Fancy Bear, Sofacy, STRONTIUM, Sednit, Pawn Storm, and Forest Blizzard, and the boundaries between those labels are not perfectly consistent across publishers, so defenders should treat alias convergence as approximate rather than exact set equality. Reporting has repeatedly described the group targeting government ministries, military and defence contractors, diplomatic missions, political organisations, election-related bodies, media outlets, think tanks, and, in some campaigns, hospitality, logistics, and aviation-sector supply chains. Observed regional focus clusters around Europe, North America, the Middle East, and Central Asia, with activity also reported against organisations in the Caucasus and Eastern Europe. The tradecraft described in open reporting is broad rather than narrowly specialised: spearphishing with malicious attachments and links, credential harvesting through lookalike authentication pages, password spraying against exposed services including webmail and VPN portals, exploitation of public-facing applications, and abuse of legitimate remote services and valid accounts for access. Post-compromise behaviour attributed to the group includes extensive use of command and scripting interpreters, living-off-the-land binaries to blend into administrative activity, credential theft from browsers and mail clients, deployment of custom implant families with modular downloaders, and interest in network infrastructure such as routers and mail servers as both access vectors and collection points. Several reporting streams also describe operational security mistakes, including reused infrastructure and registration artifacts, which have supported attribution. For defenders, the practical consequence is that detection investment should concentrate on identity and authentication telemetry, public-facing service exploitation, email-borne initial access, and outbound command-and-control patterns rather than on any single malware signature. Attribution is contested in some cases and assessed with only moderate confidence in others, and some activity bundled under the label may reflect distinct sub-units or copycat operations.
objectives: Compare the tradecraft attributed to APT28 in vendor and government reporting and explain which intrusion phases carry the strongest analytic confidence.
Explain how password spraying against webmail, VPN, and other exposed authentication services is detected using identity telemetry rather than endpoint signatures.
Build a detection hypothesis for credential phishing delivered through lookalike authentication pages and evaluate where such detections produce false positives.
Identify the living-off-the-land binaries and scripting interpreters most often associated with this group and explain how to baseline their legitimate administrative use.
Assess the risk that network edge devices and mail infrastructure become both initial access vectors and long-term collection points, and prioritise hardening accordingly.
Construct SIEM queries that surface anomalous authentication patterns consistent with state-sponsored credential access in a hybrid identity environment.
Explain the supply-chain and third-party access risk described in reporting on this group and how to scope vendor trust accordingly.
Evaluate the limits of attribution in public reporting and describe how to write a threat assessment that states confidence levels honestly.

beginner.definition: APT28 is a tracking name for a long-running spying group. Many governments and security companies link it to Russia's military intelligence service. The same activity appears under names such as Fancy Bear, Sofacy and Forest Blizzard. Those names overlap, so treat the link as an assessment, not a proven fact.
beginner.whyItMatters: The letters A P T stand for advanced persistent threat, meaning a patient attacker with money and time. This group guesses passwords on login pages that face the internet, such as webmail and remote access portals. Weak passwords and missing multi-factor authentication (a second proof, such as a code on your phone) are what let it in. Fix those two things and you remove its easiest path.
howItWorks: The group sends email with a harmful file or a link to a copy of a login page.
People type their password into the fake page, and the attacker now has it.
The group also tries one common password on many accounts, hoping one works.
With a real account, the intruder looks like a normal worker on the network.
They use tools already built into the system, so no strange program appears.
Mail and documents are collected slowly, often over a very long period.
beginner.example: Think of a large office with a staff entrance. A stranger stands outside and politely asks people for their door code. He also tries the same simple code on fifty different doors, because someone always picks an easy one. Once inside, he wears the same uniform as everyone else, so nobody stops him. That is why a second proof of identity matters.
takeaways: Turn on a second proof of identity for every account that faces the internet.
Teach staff that a login page can be a careful copy of the real one.
Watch for tools already on the system used at unusual times or by odd accounts.

topics.title: APT29
topics.summary: APT29 is a long-running intrusion set that multiple government and vendor reporting streams attribute with moderate to high confidence to a Russian foreign intelligence service, commonly identified in public reporting as the SVR. Published under names including Cozy Bear, The Dukes, NOBELIUM, Midnight Blizzard, YTTRIUM, and Iron Hemlock, the aliases reflect overlapping but not identical scopes as different publishers refined their tracking. Reporting describes sustained targeting of government agencies, diplomatic and foreign-policy institutions, think tanks, healthcare and research organisations, technology and managed service providers, and, in several documented waves, supply chains where a trusted software vendor or cloud service provider becomes the means of reaching downstream victims. The geographic emphasis in reporting is North America, Europe, and multilateral diplomatic organisations, with activity also observed against organisations in Asia and the Middle East. The tradecraft emphasised in public reporting is patient and identity-centric: password spraying and credential stuffing against exposed authentication endpoints, abuse of valid accounts including service and application identities, heavy use of cloud and identity provider APIs for discovery and persistence, token and certificate theft in some described cases, and custom implant families known for long dwell and low-noise lateral movement. Reporting has repeatedly highlighted novel persistence paths added to cloud identity platforms and the use of trusted service providers for command and control, which means endpoint-centric detection alone is insufficient. Analysts have also documented the group's preference for operating within existing administrative tooling and protocols rather than deploying conspicuous malware, complicating triage for teams whose detection strategy is signature-driven. Attribution of any given intrusion is often assessed at moderate confidence, and some activity published under these aliases may involve different operators or be contested, so defenders should distinguish between the confidence in an attribution and the confidence in the observed behaviour when writing assessments and setting detection priorities.
objectives: Explain how supply-chain and managed-service-provider access changes the victim's detection perimeter and what telemetry must be collected to compensate.
Detect password spraying and credential stuffing against cloud identity providers using sign-in risk, failure distribution, and user-agent telemetry.
Analyse cloud and identity provider audit logs to identify persistence mechanisms created through APIs rather than endpoint malware.
Explain how token, certificate, and application credential theft is detected and what revocation steps limit blast radius.
Evaluate detection coverage for adversary activity that relies on legitimate administrative tooling and explain where gaps remain.
Compare public reporting on this group's cloud tradecraft and identify which observables are durable versus environment-specific.
Build a threat hunting hypothesis for trusted service provider command and control and describe the network evidence that would confirm or refute it.
Draft a confidence-qualified attribution statement that separates observed behaviour from assessed sponsorship.

beginner.definition: APT29 is a tracking name for a patient spying group. Many governments and security companies link it to Russia's foreign intelligence service. The same activity appears as Cozy Bear, The Dukes and Midnight Blizzard. The group is known for signing in with stolen accounts instead of dropping obvious malware on computers.
beginner.whyItMatters: The letters A P T mean advanced persistent threat, a well-funded attacker that waits. This group often uses real accounts and cloud services, so nothing looks broken. Endpoint tools that only look for bad files may see nothing at all. You must watch sign-in records, permission changes and application keys, because that is where the group works.
howItWorks: The group guesses common passwords across many accounts on services open to the internet.
One sign-in works, and the attacker now has a valid account and an active session.
They add their own way back in, such as a new application key or a changed setting.
They read mail and files through normal cloud interfaces, so the traffic looks routine.
Sometimes they enter through a trusted software supplier, reaching many customers at once.
They move slowly between systems, keeping noise low and staying for many months.
beginner.example: Think of a large office tower where everyone uses a badge. A stranger watches people type their codes at the door and learns one that is simple. Now he walks in with a valid badge. He does not break windows or force doors. He sits in meeting rooms, reads files and quietly makes himself a spare badge for later.
takeaways: Watch sign-in records for many failed attempts followed by one success.
Treat cloud settings, application keys and permissions as places intruders hide.
A valid account can be more dangerous than any piece of malware.

topics.title: APT32
topics.summary: APT32 is an espionage intrusion set that commercial vendors and independent researchers have attributed with high but not absolute confidence to Vietnam-based activity, generally assessed as operating in support of state strategic interests rather than for financial gain. Reporting places the group's activity from roughly the middle of the last decade onward, with targeting concentrated on private-sector corporations, foreign governments and diplomatic missions, media organisations, and domestic dissident and civil-society groups, with a geographic emphasis on Southeast Asia and a secondary footprint in Europe and North America. The group is notable in public reporting for its investment in bespoke tooling and delivery infrastructure: researchers have described custom downloaders and backdoors, abuse of legitimate cloud and content-delivery services for command and control, malformed or weaponised documents delivered by spearphishing, and watering-hole activity against websites likely to be visited by intended targets. Reporting also describes the use of compromised websites and fake domains to build credible lures, and the targeting of macOS as well as Windows, which is unusual for a regional espionage actor and relevant to defenders who treat Apple endpoints as out of scope. The practical defensive message is that cloud service abuse makes network-perimeter blocking insufficient: command and control may arrive from reputable hosting and SaaS address space. Detection should focus on process behaviour, execution of files from uncommon document-adjacent directories, anomalous use of legitimately signed binaries, and outbound sessions to cloud endpoints that are inconsistent with the organisation's normal usage. Attribution statements about APT32 should be read as third-party assessments, and the group's tooling overlaps with other regional clusters in ways that make single-indicator attribution unreliable.
objectives: Explain how abuse of legitimate cloud and content-delivery services undermines domain and IP block-list defences.
Build detections for malicious documents spawning interpreters and for execution from document-adjacent directories.
Describe watering-hole methodology from the defender's perspective and the controls that reduce exposure.
Extend macOS and cross-platform endpoint monitoring to cover tradecraft that is not Windows-specific.
Correlate phishing infrastructure indicators with endpoint telemetry to distinguish targeted from commodity activity.
Assess the confidence language used in regional attribution claims and how to represent it in internal reporting.
Prioritise detection coverage for an organisation in media, civil society, or diplomatic sectors facing targeted espionage.

beginner.definition: APT32 is a tracking name for a spying group that several security companies link to Vietnam. Researchers describe purpose-built tools, fake websites and harmful documents sent by email. The group also targets Apple computers, which many teams forget to protect. The country link is an assessment from companies, not a proven fact.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group hides its control messages inside popular cloud services and content networks. Blocking a list of bad web addresses will not help, because the traffic goes to well-known companies. It also compromises websites that its targets often visit. That means your browser, your documents and your cloud sessions are all in scope, not only your network edge.
howItWorks: The attackers build fake websites and send emails that look like real news or files.
A person opens the document, and a program runs behind the scenes.
That program downloads a hidden backdoor from an ordinary cloud storage service.
The backdoor sends and receives instructions through cloud services that most networks allow.
They may also add harmful code to a website their targets visit often.
They copy documents and messages, including from Apple computers, for many months.
beginner.example: Think of a courier who never uses a hidden alley. He walks into a busy post office with a normal parcel and a normal receipt. Nobody stops him, because the post office handles millions of parcels every day. His secret is not the hiding place, but the crowd. To spot him, you must notice what is unusual for your own office.
takeaways: Blocking known bad web addresses fails when traffic goes to popular services.
Protect Apple devices with the same care as Windows computers.
Watch for documents that start other programs when they are opened.

topics.title: APT39
topics.summary: APT39 is a long-running espionage intrusion set that multiple commercial threat intelligence vendors have assessed as linked to the Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security, an assessment that rests on infrastructure overlap, targeting patterns, and shared tooling rather than on any public technical proof, so it should be treated as a vendor judgement of moderate to high confidence rather than an established fact. Reporting describes sustained targeting of telecommunications providers and travel-related industries, with secondary interest in aviation, hospitality, and IT service providers, and victim organisations identified across the Middle East, Europe, Asia, and North America. The operational logic attributed to the group is intelligence collection rather than disruption: telecommunications metadata and subscriber information, and travel itineraries and booking systems, have both been described as collection priorities in vendor reporting. Tradecraft commonly described includes spearphishing for initial access, use of custom backdoors alongside commercially available or commodity remote access tools, credential theft from browsers and mail clients, and persistence via scheduled tasks and autostart mechanisms. The group is also reported to reuse infrastructure and tooling associated with other Iran-nexus clusters, which complicates attribution and means indicators frequently overlap across multiple tracked actors. For defenders, the reliable signal is behavioural rather than infrastructural: unexpected outbound beaconing from endpoints in telecom or travel environments, mail client credential store access, and the presence of remote administration tooling that the organisation has no legitimate reason to deploy. Detection programmes should also account for the group's history of long dwell times and low-volume collection, which makes volume-based alerting weak.
objectives: Describe the collection priorities attributed to Iran-nexus espionage activity against telecommunications and travel sectors.
Recognise why attribution based on infrastructure overlap carries lower confidence than attribution based on unique tooling.
Build detections for credential theft from browser and mail client stores on managed endpoints.
Hunt for low-volume, long-dwell command and control beaconing in environments where volume thresholds are ineffective.
Explain how commodity remote access tools are abused for persistence and why allow-listing is fragile.
Assess detection coverage gaps that arise when an actor reuses infrastructure shared with other tracked clusters.
Prioritise logging sources for a telecommunications or travel-sector environment facing state-sponsored espionage.

beginner.definition: APT39 is a tracking name for a spying group that security companies link to Iran's intelligence ministry. It is also called Chafer and Remexi. The group targets phone companies and travel businesses, because those hold call records and travel plans. The country link is a company assessment, not a proven fact.
beginner.whyItMatters: Telephone records and travel bookings reveal who talks to whom and who goes where. That is valuable intelligence. This group collects slowly and quietly, so alarms based on large data volumes often stay silent. It also reuses tools and servers shared with other groups. That makes simple blame unreliable, so focus on behaviour inside your own network.
howItWorks: An email with a harmful attachment or a link starts the intrusion.
A backdoor is installed and contacts its server a few times each day.
The group then steals passwords kept by web browsers and mail programs.
They add a scheduled task so their access returns after a restart.
They read mail and copy records in small amounts, avoiding large transfers.
Collection can continue for many months before anyone notices that anything is odd.
beginner.example: Imagine a librarian who wants the information in a private archive. He never carries out a big box of files. Each night he photocopies two or three pages and puts everything back exactly as it was. The shelves look untouched, and the daily totals look normal. Only a pattern over many months gives him away.
takeaways: Look for small, regular outbound connections rather than huge transfers.
Protect saved browser and mail passwords on every managed device.
Shared tools and servers make blame hard, so trust your own evidence.

topics.title: APT41
topics.summary: APT41 is a prolific intrusion set that the United States Department of Justice and multiple commercial vendors have publicly linked to China-based activity, with reporting describing a dual mission of state-directed espionage alongside financially motivated intrusions carried out by the same or overlapping personnel. That combination is unusual and is the reason the group appears in both espionage and cybercrime reporting; analysts should treat the dual-mission characterisation as a widely reported assessment rather than something directly observable in telemetry. Reported targeting spans healthcare and pharmaceutical research, telecommunications, technology and software providers, gaming, media, and logistics, with victims identified across North America, Europe, and Asia. Tradecraft described in public reporting includes exploitation of internet-facing applications and web-facing servers for initial access, abuse of valid accounts and credentials obtained from prior compromises, custom malware and loaders that are frequently updated, digital code-signing certificates abused or stolen to sign malicious binaries, and supply-chain compromise of software build and update processes. The group has also been reported to deploy ransomware for impact, which blurs the line between espionage and extortion and makes the affiliate-versus-state distinction operationally less useful for defenders. Practical defensive implications are that certificate trust is not a security control in itself, that software supply chains must be treated as an attack surface with provenance and build integrity controls, and that detection should emphasise anomalous code-signing behaviour, unusual child processes from web server software, and credentials used from unexpected locations. Attribution statements about APT41 are third-party assessments, and overlap between this cluster and other China-nexus tracking names is acknowledged in public reporting.
objectives: Explain why the espionage-and-financial dual-mission model changes how an intrusion is scoped and escalated.
Build detections for web server processes spawning command interpreters and administrative utilities.
Assess code-signing abuse and describe the provenance and build-integrity controls that reduce supply-chain exposure.
Identify anomalous certificate use, including unexpected signers and signing events outside the release pipeline.
Map supply-chain compromise scenarios onto ATT&CK techniques and identify which are detectable at the enterprise layer.
Rank containment options when an intrusion has both intelligence-collection and destructive objectives.
Explain how credential reuse from unrelated prior compromises shortens attacker time to lateral movement.
Write an attribution paragraph that separates observed behaviour from third-party assessment of sponsorship.

beginner.definition: APT41 is a tracking name for a very active group that security companies and the United States government link to China. It is unusual because it does both spying and money-making crime. It also abuses code-signing certificates, the digital stamps that prove software came from a trusted maker. That dual purpose is a widely reported assessment.
beginner.whyItMatters: Because this group both spies and commits crime, an intrusion can turn destructive without warning. It has signed harmful programs with stolen certificates, so a trusted signature is not proof of safety. It has also tampered with software build systems, meaning your own product could carry the intruder to your customers. Protect your build process like a vault.
howItWorks: The group finds and exploits a weakness in a server that faces the internet.
They install tools that let them run commands and move inside the network.
They steal usernames, passwords and digital signing keys wherever they find them.
With those signing keys they stamp harmful programs so the files look trusted.
They may also add code to a software update that customers download and install.
Sometimes they lock files and demand money, mixing spying with plain extortion.
beginner.example: Imagine a border guard who trusts one thing: an official stamp on a passport. A forger copies the stamp perfectly and puts it on any document he likes. The guard waves each one through, because the mark looks right. That is what a stolen code-signing certificate does for harmful software. The stamp is only as good as the key behind it.
takeaways: A valid digital signature means the file was signed, not that it is safe.
Guard build systems and signing keys like the keys to your company.
Plan for both spying and destructive goals in the same incident.

topics.title: FIN7
topics.summary: FIN7 is a financially motivated intrusion set tracked by multiple vendors under names including Carbon Spider, Sangria Tempest, ELBRUS, and Navigator Group. Unlike state-sponsored groups, attribution here is largely a criminal-tracking exercise rather than a question of state sponsorship, and several individuals associated with the activity have been publicly charged in the United States, which gives the group an unusually concrete legal dimension compared with most clusters. Reporting describes a long-running campaign against the retail, hospitality, restaurant, and gaming sectors, with additional targeting of banking, insurance, and healthcare organisations, concentrated heavily in the United States with victims also reported in Europe and Australia. The group's best-documented tradecraft is social engineering at scale: telephone calls and email approaches impersonating legitimate service providers, catering suppliers, or IT support, used to persuade employees to open documents or install remote management software. Reporting has described both malicious document delivery exploiting application features and, in later waves, the use of legitimate remote monitoring and management tooling as an initial access vector, which is significant because it makes the intrusion look like normal administrative activity. Post-compromise behaviour in public reporting includes the deployment of custom point-of-sale malware in earlier campaigns, a shift toward ransomware and extortion activity including through affiliates, credential theft, reconnaissance of payment and email systems, and lateral movement using standard administrative protocols. The group has been described as operating with a structured organisational model including separate teams for intrusion and monetisation, and has been reported selling or granting access to other criminal operators. For defenders in retail and hospitality, the practical priority is detecting abuse of remote management software, unusual outbound payment-related traffic, and social engineering that arrives through voice channels that email-focused controls do not cover.
objectives: Explain how abuse of legitimate remote monitoring and management tooling differs from malware-based initial access and how to detect it.
Analyse telephone-oriented social engineering against help desk and finance functions and design verification controls that resist it.
Detect point-of-sale and payment environment reconnaissance using network segmentation and process telemetry.
Explain how criminal access brokers change the threat model for an organisation that may be a secondary rather than primary target.
Build detection coverage for credential theft and lateral movement in a flat retail network and prioritise segmentation work.
Compare the group's documented shift from payment card theft to ransomware and extortion and explain the defensive implications.
Explain how legal and law enforcement reporting can inform but not replace technical threat intelligence.

beginner.definition: FIN7 is a tracking name for a criminal group that targets money, not state secrets. Security companies also call it Carbon Spider and Sangria Tempest. Several people linked to the activity have been charged in the United States. The group is known for phone calls and emails that pretend to come from suppliers or technical support.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group often asks staff to install remote support software, which is a legitimate tool. Nothing is broken into, and no malware signature appears. A worker simply follows a friendly request. It also targets restaurant, hotel and retail chains, where payment systems hold valuable data. Teach staff to verify before they install anything.
howItWorks: Someone calls a help desk and pretends to be a trusted supplier or a manager.
They ask for a small favour, such as installing a support tool to fix a problem.
That tool gives the caller remote control of the computer with the user's permission.
From there they search for payment systems, mail accounts and saved passwords.
They move quietly between computers using ordinary administrator tools and shared accounts.
Later they steal card data, or they lock files and demand a payment.
beginner.example: Imagine a busy restaurant kitchen during the dinner rush. A man in a delivery uniform walks in with a clipboard and says the new card machine needs a quick update. The manager is too busy to check, so she lets him plug in a laptop. He is polite, confident and helpful. Being busy is exactly what he was counting on.
takeaways: Verify callers through a number you look up yourself, never one they give.
Remote support tools are useful, so control who may install them.
Keep payment systems on their own network, away from everyday computers.

topics.title: HAFNIUM
topics.summary: HAFNIUM is an intrusion set that Microsoft and other vendors have attributed to a China-based nexus, and the cluster became widely known in early 2021 after reporting described mass exploitation of vulnerabilities in on-premises internet-facing Microsoft Exchange Server deployments. The group is best understood by its initial access method rather than by a distinctive malware family: public reporting describes opportunistic scanning for vulnerable Exchange servers followed by server-side exploitation that allowed attackers to run commands, drop web shells, and reach credentials and mailbox data without needing to phish a user. Victims reported at the time spanned infectious disease researchers, law firms, defence contractors, policy think tanks, and non-governmental organisations, with a concentration in the United States; subsequent reporting described follow-on activity against additional Exchange flaws and against other internet-facing products. Tradecraft attributed to the group includes web shell persistence on compromised servers, credential theft from the host including from memory, lateral movement using remote administration tooling, and the use of compromised infrastructure for further operations. Because the initial access vector is an unpatched or unreachable-to-patch perimeter service, the defender's central problem is inventory and patch velocity for systems that are exposed to the internet but are often not covered by standard endpoint agents and may lack adequate logging. Detection effort should target web server process trees, file-write events in application directories, authentication from unusual sources, and mailbox access patterns inconsistent with user behaviour. Attribution is a third-party assessment and the group's publicly known tooling is not unique to the cluster.
objectives: Explain why on-premises, internet-facing and agentless servers are a persistent blind spot in detection coverage.
Build detections for web server processes spawning command interpreters and for web shell file-write behaviour.
Describe what Exchange server compromise exposes beyond the host itself, including mailbox and credential material.
Design logging and inventory requirements for perimeter services that fall outside standard endpoint tooling.
Prioritise patch and mitigation work using exposure data rather than severity scores alone.
Sequence containment for a compromised perimeter server while preserving volatile evidence for investigation.
Explain how credential theft from an exploited server enables follow-on access to other enterprise systems.

beginner.definition: HAFNIUM is a tracking name for a group that security companies link to China. It became well known in early 2021 for attacking mail servers that organisations ran themselves and exposed to the internet. The group did not need to trick any user with an email. It reached the server directly and took mail and passwords.
beginner.whyItMatters: Servers that face the internet are often missed by endpoint tools, because no standard agent runs on them. They may also be hard to patch quickly. If such a server falls, the intruder gains mail, passwords and a path deeper into the network. So keep a list of exposed servers, and patch them fast.
howItWorks: The group scans the internet for mail servers that have a known weakness.
They send a specially crafted request that runs commands on the server.
They drop a web shell, a small file that accepts commands through the website.
Using it, they read mail and steal passwords and access keys from the machine.
They move to other systems with stolen credentials and remote administration tools.
They keep access by adding hidden accounts or startup entries on the server.
beginner.example: Imagine a warehouse with a main gate that guards watch carefully. At the back there is a small service window that nobody monitors. A visitor reaches through the window, unlocks the door and walks in. The front gate was never the problem. You must know about every opening in the building.
takeaways: Keep a current list of every server that the internet can reach.
Patch exposed servers quickly, because attackers scan for them automatically.
Put logging on those servers, since they are often a blind spot.

topics.title: Ke3chang
topics.summary: Ke3chang is a long-running espionage intrusion set that multiple commercial vendors assess as China-based and state-aligned, with public reporting tracing activity back more than a decade and describing sustained targeting of government ministries, diplomatic organisations, military-adjacent entities, and, more recently, non-governmental organisations and media outlets. Victim concentrations reported by vendors include the Middle East, Europe, and North America, with a stable interest in diplomatic and governmental communications. The group is most often described in reporting for its malware families rather than for a distinctive initial access trick: researchers have documented layered backdoors and downloaders that have been rewritten and recompiled repeatedly over the years, with components reported under names such as TidePool and RoyalCli, alongside credential theft from browsers and mail clients. Initial access is commonly described as spearphishing with malicious documents or links, sometimes combined with credential phishing pages that mimic legitimate webmail or file-sharing services, and persistence is reported through registry-based autostart mechanisms and scheduled tasks. The defender-relevant characteristic is longevity and iteration: the same intrusion set recurs against similar targets with refreshed tooling, so detections tied to specific file names or hashes decay quickly while behavioural detections remain useful. Detection effort is best spent on document-to-interpreter process chains, unusual autostart registry modification, anomalous outbound sessions from office and mail applications, and credential access patterns on endpoints belonging to diplomatic or executive staff. Attribution statements are third-party assessments and should be presented with their confidence level rather than as established fact.
objectives: Describe how iterative malware rewriting defeats indicator-based detection and what detection strategy survives it.
Build detections for registry autostart persistence and scheduled task creation on managed endpoints.
Recognise credential phishing pages that impersonate legitimate webmail and file-sharing services.
Hunt for office and mail applications initiating network connections inconsistent with baseline behaviour.
Prioritise monitoring for high-value diplomatic and executive accounts given the group's targeting pattern.
Assess the value of long-horizon retro-hunting when a recurring actor refreshes tooling with shared code.
Explain why vendor naming conventions for this cluster vary and how to reconcile them in reporting.

beginner.definition: Ke3chang is the name researchers use for a long-running spying group. Several security companies believe it works for a state, and they link it to China. The group is known less for clever tricks and more for patience. It keeps attacking similar targets for many years.
beginner.whyItMatters: Spying groups like this one do not disappear. They wait, learn and return with new tools. If your team only blocks known file names, the next version slips past you. Understanding this group teaches you to watch behaviour, not just names. It also reminds you that reports from security companies are opinions, not proven facts.
howItWorks: The group sends emails with a harmful document or a link to a fake login page.
A person opens the file or types a password, and the attacker gets a way in.
Small helper programs, called backdoors, are placed on the computer to keep access.
The backdoor starts again after a reboot by hiding in a startup setting or a scheduled task.
The attackers copy passwords saved in browsers and mail programs so they can reuse them.
They quietly collect email and documents for a long time before anyone notices.
beginner.example: Think of a person who wants to read the post in a large office. The guards once learned his face, so he grew a beard and changed his coat. The guards had memorised the old coat. The visitor still walks the same corridor, at the same quiet hour, and still asks for the same room. Watch the behaviour, because the coat will change again.
takeaways: Watch how intruders behave, because file names and hashes change quickly.
Treat company reports about who is behind an attack as opinions, not proof.
Protect saved browser and mail passwords, since they let attackers log in as staff.

topics.title: Lazarus Group
topics.summary: Lazarus Group is an umbrella designator applied by vendors and governments to a broad collection of intrusion activity that public reporting attributes, with varying confidence, to North Korean state-sponsored operators. The United States government has formally attributed specific activity and campaigns to North Korean state actors under the HIDDEN COBRA label, while the vendor ecosystem splits the wider cluster into sub-clusters such as Diamond Sleet, Zinc, Labyrinth Chollima, and Guardian of Peace, each with distinct tooling and mission focus. The scope of this grouping is therefore genuinely contested: analysts disagree about which campaigns share operators, infrastructure, and funding lines, and some activity labelled Lazarus in early reporting has since been reassigned. Reporting describes a uniquely wide target set driven by revenue generation as well as espionage, including financial institutions, cryptocurrency exchanges and payment platforms, defence contractors, aerospace and engineering firms, media and entertainment companies, healthcare and pharmaceutical organisations, and government agencies. Geographic reporting concentrates on South Korea, the United States, Japan, India, and Southeast Asia, with cryptocurrency-focused activity reported globally. Described tradecraft spans spearphishing of individuals with credible lures including job offers and social media contact, exploitation of public-facing applications and widely deployed software, supply-chain compromise of trusted update mechanisms, abuse of valid credentials, custom backdoors and loader families, destructive and disruptive operations including ransomware deployment and wiper activity, and monetisation through cryptocurrency theft and the use of front companies. The group's operational diversity means defenders cannot rely on a small set of behavioural rules; the defensible common threads are supply-chain trust, third-party developer tooling, and identity-based access to financial and administrative systems.
objectives: Distinguish the government-attributed HIDDEN COBRA activity from the wider vendor-tracked sub-clusters and explain why the umbrella label is contested.
Analyse supply-chain compromise of software update and build mechanisms and identify the controls that would detect or prevent it.
Explain how social-engineering lures such as fraudulent job offers are recognised and countered in a recruitment-heavy organisation.
Detect destructive or disruptive activity patterns early by identifying the precursors that precede them in the intrusion lifecycle.
Assess the risk of third-party developer tooling and dependency compromise when defining build pipeline trust boundaries.
Explain how cryptocurrency and payment fraud objectives change the assets a defender must protect and monitor.
Prioritise detection coverage for an organisation that holds both intellectual property and financial transaction capability.
Evaluate the reliability of public reporting when a tracking label spans multiple distinct operational clusters.

beginner.definition: Lazarus Group is an umbrella name for a wide mix of activity that governments and security companies link to North Korean state operators. The United States has publicly blamed North Korean actors for some campaigns. Vendors split the same activity into smaller clusters with their own names. Because the label covers so much, treat any single claim with care.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group steals money as well as information, so banks, payment platforms and cryptocurrency services are targets. It has also attacked software update systems, which means a trusted download can carry an intruder. It has used destructive tools that wipe data. That combination means you must protect your data, your money paths and your suppliers all at once.
howItWorks: The attackers study a target and send a message that fits, such as a job offer.
The person opens a file or follows a link, and hidden code starts running.
The code contacts a server and waits for instructions from the operator.
The group steals passwords, then moves to other systems with normal administration tools.
Sometimes they hide harmful code inside a software update that people already trust.
Finally they steal money, lock files for ransom, or wipe data completely.
beginner.example: Imagine an office that orders printer paper every month from the same supplier. One month the box contains a hidden device that copies every document. Nobody questions the delivery, because the van looks right and the paperwork is correct. Trust in a familiar supplier is exactly what makes this approach so effective.
takeaways: Trusted software updates are an attack path, so check what you install.
Be careful with unexpected job offers and social messages at work.
Keep backups that attackers cannot reach, and test that they restore.

topics.title: menuPass
topics.summary: menuPass is a long-running intrusion set that vendors and, in at least one notable case, a national government have linked to Chinese state-sponsored activity, with the United States Department of Justice announcing charges against individuals described as associated with the group. The cluster is tracked under names including APT10, Stone Panda, Red Apollo, Potassium, and Cicada, and the boundaries of those labels vary between publishers, particularly where the group is described as supporting other operators by granting or reselling access. Public reporting describes targeting of managed service providers and information technology outsourcing firms, defence and aerospace contractors, telecommunications operators, healthcare and pharmaceutical organisations, and government agencies, with victims reported across North America, Europe, Japan, and Southeast Asia. The most consequential tradecraft described in reporting is abuse of trusted third-party relationships: managed service providers with legitimate remote administrative access to multiple downstream customers became the entry path to those customers, and in some described waves the group is assessed to have obtained and used service provider credentials and tooling for that purpose. Other reported behaviour includes spearphishing with malicious documents, exploitation of public-facing applications, use of custom backdoors and loaders with modular, extensible designs, abuse of legitimate remote administration software, credential harvesting and use of valid accounts, and long-dwell collection of documents and email before exfiltration to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Reporting has also described the group selling or providing network access to other state-interest operators, which complicates attribution because the actor that gains entry is not always the actor that exploits it. For defenders, the central lesson is that outsourced administration is a trust boundary: provider credentials, jump hosts, and remote management tooling deserve the same monitoring rigour as internal privileged access.
objectives: Explain how managed service provider trust is abused and what monitoring must exist on provider-connected administration paths.
Design detection for legitimate remote administration tooling used with stolen provider credentials and separate it from routine support activity.
Analyse the risk that network access is sold or handed to another operator and how that affects incident scoping and attribution.
Detect modular backdoor and loader behaviour through host telemetry when static signatures do not apply.
Explain how credential harvesting from administrator workstations enables downstream victim compromise across an outsourcing relationship.
Evaluate contractual and technical controls for third-party access, including just-in-time provisioning and session recording.
Build a threat hunting plan for long-dwell document and email collection using access-pattern anomalies.

beginner.definition: menuPass is a tracking name for a long-running spying group that security companies and at least one government have linked to China. It also appears as APT10, Stone Panda and Red Apollo. The group is best known for entering through outside companies that manage other companies' computers. Reports say it also sold access to other operators.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many organisations let an outside company run their computers and networks. That provider holds powerful keys. If the provider is breached, every customer can be reached through a door that already exists. This makes the supplier a trust boundary, not just a helper. You must log and limit what provider staff can do inside your systems.
howItWorks: The group first breaks into a company that provides technical services to others.
From there they steal the provider's passwords, keys and everyday support tools.
Those details let them log in to customer systems without breaking a single lock.
Once inside, they read mail and documents and copy what interests them.
They use built-in administration tools, so their activity looks like routine support work.
They stay for a long time, and sometimes they hand access to another group.
beginner.example: Think of an office block where one cleaning company has master keys for every floor. The cleaners are trusted, so their van passes the gate without a check. If someone copies those master keys, they can walk into every office in the building. The weakest point is not any single door, but the master key ring.
takeaways: Treat outside support staff as a high-value path into your systems.
Log and limit provider access, and remove it when the work is finished.
Long, quiet collection of mail and documents is the usual goal.

topics.title: Storm-0501
topics.summary: Storm-0501 is a financially motivated intrusion set tracked by Microsoft under its weather-themed naming convention for unattributed or partially attributed clusters, and also reported by other vendors under the Vanilla Tempest and DEV-0501 designations. Public reporting describes the group as a ransomware affiliate and operator that has moved across multiple ransomware ecosystems over time, which is characteristic of the affiliate model where the same intrusion crew rents or switches payloads depending on access to builders and negotiation infrastructure. Reported targeting concentrates on United States organisations across healthcare, education, manufacturing, government, and retail, with a documented emphasis on hybrid cloud environments where an on-premises identity tier is synchronised to a cloud tenant. The tradecraft described in vendor reporting includes exploitation of internet-facing applications and remote access services for initial access, abuse of valid accounts, credential theft and dumping, and lateral movement using native remote administration tooling before impact. A recurring theme in reporting is the abuse of the identity control plane: compromising privileged on-premises accounts, manipulating or creating accounts to establish persistence, and using the hybrid trust relationship to reach cloud subscriptions and storage. For a defender, that pattern argues for treating identity as the primary detection surface, specifically anomalous privileged role assignments, unexpected directory synchronisation changes, and mailbox or storage access from unfamiliar hosts. Attribution of this cluster is less settled than for state-sponsored groups and the naming itself signals that vendor confidence in a durable identity is limited, so behavioural detections transfer better than actor-specific indicators.
objectives: Describe the ransomware affiliate operating model and why the same crew appears under multiple ecosystem names.
Trace how compromise of an on-premises identity tier leads to control of a synchronised cloud tenant.
Construct detections for suspicious privileged role assignment, account creation, and directory synchronisation changes.
Prioritise triage of alerts in hybrid identity environments where on-premises and cloud telemetry must be correlated.
Explain how credential dumping and valid-account abuse shorten the time from initial access to impact.
Draft a containment sequence for a hybrid identity compromise that preserves evidence and limits ransomware staging.
Evaluate why vendor cluster names such as Storm-xxxx carry limited attribution meaning and how to write actor-agnostic detections.
