beginner.definition: Storm-0501 is a tracking name from a security company for a criminal group that uses ransomware (software that locks files until you pay). The same activity also appears as Vanilla Tempest and DEV-0501. The generic name shows that the company is not fully sure who the group is. It targets hybrid setups where local accounts also control cloud services.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many organisations run a local identity system that is copied into a cloud service. Attackers who take over a powerful local account can often reach the cloud side too. From there they create accounts, grant themselves roles and lock data for ransom. Watching only computers is not enough, because the damage is done in the identity system.
howItWorks: The group gets in through an exposed service or a stolen set of credentials.
They steal more passwords from the machines they reach, including administrator ones.
With a powerful local account, they change settings in the identity system.
Because local and cloud identities are linked, those changes affect cloud access.
They create new accounts or add roles, so they can return later.
Then they lock files and demand payment, often after copying the data first.
beginner.example: Imagine a company where one badge opens the office and also the company bank account. A thief copies that badge from a desk drawer. He does not need to break any window. He lets himself in, adds his own name to the account, and only then asks for money. The badge was the real target all along.
takeaways: Protect the accounts that link your local systems to cloud services.
Alert on new privileged roles and new accounts, then check them.
Keep offline backups, because ransomware can reach anything that stays online.

topics.title: Threat Group-3390
topics.summary: Threat Group-3390 is a long-running intrusion set that public reporting, including work published by several vendors and by MITRE ATT&CK, associates with activity widely assessed by third parties as linked to a Chinese state-interest nexus, though no government has formally indicted or sanctioned the activity under this name, so the sponsorship claim rests on vendor analysis rather than official attribution. The cluster is tracked under many overlapping names, including Emissary Panda, Lucky Mouse, Bronze Union, Earth Smilodon, and APT27, and different publishers have drawn the boundaries of those labels differently over time, with some activity reassigned between clusters as new evidence emerged. Reporting describes targeting of government ministries and agencies, defence and aerospace organisations, energy and critical infrastructure operators, gaming and technology companies, and organisations in the Middle East, Central Asia, Southeast Asia, and Europe, with additional victims reported in North America. The group is notable in open reporting for combining web-facing exploitation with heavy use of publicly available remote access tooling, which lowers the cost of operations and blurs the line between targeted intrusion and commodity compromise. Described tradecraft includes exploitation of public-facing applications for initial access, abuse of external remote services including web shells and remote management interfaces, credential dumping and reuse of valid administrator accounts, lateral movement over standard administrative protocols, scheduled task and service-based persistence, and exfiltration staged to attacker-controlled or legitimate third-party web services. Several reporting streams describe usage of custom downloaders alongside commodity tooling and an interest in harvesting intellectual property and email. Defenders should note that the group's reliance on administration-facing protocols means detection strategies centred on endpoint malware alone will miss significant portions of the intrusion lifecycle, and that the use of legitimate remote services makes allow-listing decisions consequential.
objectives: Explain how web shell persistence on an internet-facing server is detected and how to prioritise containment once found.
Detect abuse of external remote services and administrative protocols that blend with legitimate management traffic.
Analyse the risk of credential dumping and administrative account reuse when designing tiered administration controls.
Build detection logic for scheduled task and service creation used for persistence and evaluate its false positive profile.
Explain how staged exfiltration to legitimate third-party web services evades protocol-based egress controls and what replaces those controls.
Describe how cluster boundaries shift as vendors reassign activity and why that matters for indicator sharing.
Prioritise detection effort across web-facing exploitation, identity abuse, and lateral movement for an organisation in a targeted sector.

beginner.definition: Threat Group-3390 is a tracking name for a long-running spying group that security companies link to state interests in China. It is also called Emissary Panda, Lucky Mouse and APT27. No government has formally named it, so the country link rests on company analysis. Different companies draw its edges differently.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group breaks into servers that face the internet, then leaves a small web page that works like a remote control. It also uses free, widely available administration tools. That mix makes its activity look like normal technical support work. If you only look for known malware, you will miss it. Watch your servers and your administrator accounts.
howItWorks: The group finds a weakness in a public website or server and exploits it.
They upload a web shell, a small script that runs commands through the website.
With that access they steal administrator passwords that are stored on the machine.
Those passwords let them log in to other computers using normal administrator tools.
They add scheduled tasks or services so their access survives a restart.
Stolen files are uploaded to ordinary web services, which rarely look suspicious.
beginner.example: Picture a shop with a public front door and a small back room. Someone slips a note under the door that says, trade this note for any item you like. Staff read the note and hand goods through the wall, because it looks like a normal order. Nobody broke a lock. The shop was simply never designed to notice a strange instruction.
takeaways: Keep internet-facing servers patched, and watch for files added to web folders.
Treat administrator tools used at odd hours as a possible intrusion.
Stolen data often leaves through ordinary websites, so watch uploads as well.

topics.title: Turla
topics.summary: Turla is one of the longest-documented espionage intrusion sets, assessed by multiple governments and vendors as associated with Russian state security services, most commonly linked in public reporting to the Federal Security Service. That association rests on third-party analysis of infrastructure, tooling, and targeting, and although several national authorities have stated it with high confidence, it remains an attribution judgement rather than an observable technical fact. Reporting describes targeting of government and diplomatic entities, military organisations, research and defence-industrial bodies, and, in later campaigns, entities in Europe, the Middle East, Asia, and North America. The group is known in public reporting for technically distinctive tradecraft: satellite-based and hijacked-network command and control paths, including abuse of other actors' infrastructure; the Snake framework, a long-lived modular implant documented extensively in national advisories; DNS-based covert channels; custom rootkit components; and the use of compromised legitimate websites and cloud services to blend with normal traffic. It has also been reported to co-opt and operate implants on networks already compromised by other intrusion sets, which means victim telemetry may show two distinct actors and incident scope must be established carefully. For defenders, the group's emphasis on low-and-slow collection and network-layer concealment makes host-only monitoring insufficient. Detection effort should include DNS anomaly analysis, hunting for long-lived encrypted sessions to unexpected destinations, review of egress paths for unauthorised tunnels, and integrity monitoring of core system components. Attribution of this cluster should be presented with explicit confidence language, and the overlapping vendor naming schemes should be reconciled before comparing campaigns.
objectives: Describe how hijacked network infrastructure and DNS covert channels complicate network-layer attribution.
Build detections for DNS tunnelling indicators and long-lived anomalous encrypted egress sessions.
Explain the operational risk of acting on a network that a second, unrelated intrusion set has also compromised.
Assess endpoint integrity monitoring options for detecting kernel-level or boot-level persistence.
Evaluate egress filtering and outbound allow-listing as controls against covert channel abuse.
Interpret national advisory attribution language and translate confidence levels accurately into internal reporting.
Prioritise log sources for a low-and-slow espionage threat with multi-year dwell time.
Explain why decommissioning a legacy implant requires both host remediation and infrastructure-side action.

beginner.definition: Turla is a tracking name for one of the oldest known spying groups. Several governments and security companies link it to Russian state security services. It is famous for hiding its secret communications inside normal network traffic. The same reporting describes very long, quiet stays inside victim networks. The link is an assessment, not a proven fact.
beginner.whyItMatters: Turla hides its control messages inside ordinary internet lookups and other normal traffic. A firewall (a guard that checks network traffic) may wave this through, because it looks harmless. The group also stays for years and collects slowly, so alarms based on large volumes stay silent. You need to understand normal traffic before you can spot the strange parts.
howItWorks: The intruders get a first foothold, often through email or a stolen password.
They install a hidden program that hides deep in the operating system.
That program wraps its secret messages inside requests that look completely normal.
Because the traffic looks ordinary, simple filters and block lists miss it.
The attackers may also take over servers owned by other people to hide their origin.
They quietly collect documents for years, and they almost never rush their work.
beginner.example: Imagine a delivery van that arrives at a warehouse every day. On the outside it looks like every other van, with normal boxes and normal paperwork. Inside one box, hidden between layers of cardboard, is a small message. Guards who check only the outside of the van never see it. To catch this, you must open a few boxes.
takeaways: Learn what normal network traffic looks like, so quiet oddities stand out.
Watch for connections that last a very long time to unexpected places.
Spying campaigns can last years, so keep your logs for a long time.

topics.title: Volt Typhoon
topics.summary: Volt Typhoon is a state-sponsored intrusion set that multiple Western government agencies have publicly attributed to a People's Republic of China nexus, described in joint advisories as a prepositioning threat aimed at critical infrastructure rather than at espionage for immediate intelligence gain. Reporting consistently characterises the targeting as spanning communications, energy, transportation, water and wastewater, and maritime sectors, with victims identified across the continental United States as well as in Guam and other Indo-Pacific locations. The group's defining tradecraft is living-off-the-land: it relies heavily on native command interpreters, built-in administrative utilities, and legitimate remote access mechanisms rather than deploying bespoke malware, which means much of its activity can look superficially like routine administration. Reporting describes long dwell time, use of compromised small-office and home-office network devices such as routers and edge appliances as operational relay infrastructure, and attempts to obtain credentials and map the target environment. The practical consequence for defenders is that signature-based detection has limited value here. Detection effort is better spent on baselining normal administrative behaviour, alerting on unusual combinations of native tooling invoked from unexpected parent processes, monitoring for authentication from residential or hosting-provider address space, and treating edge-device integrity as a first-class control. Attribution of Volt Typhoon is stated by those governments with high confidence, but it remains a political and analytical judgement rather than a technical fact observable in telemetry, and the group shares tooling overlap with other China-nexus activity, so analysts should separate behaviour from attribution when writing detections.
objectives: Explain why living-off-the-land tradecraft defeats signature-centric detection and what compensating controls remain effective.
Identify behavioural indicators in process ancestry and command-line telemetry that distinguish native-tool abuse from legitimate administration.
Describe how compromised edge and small-office network devices are used as operational relay infrastructure and how to hunt for the resulting traffic.
Build a baselining approach for administrative accounts and service accounts so deviations become visible.
Assess the residual risk to operational technology and critical infrastructure environments when credential access succeeds without malware.
Explain the difference between behavioural evidence in telemetry and government attribution statements, and how to represent confidence honestly in reporting.
Prioritise detection engineering effort across identity, endpoint, and network telemetry for a low-signature, long-dwell threat.

beginner.definition: Volt Typhoon is a tracking name for a state-linked group that several Western governments link to China. Joint advisories describe it as preparing for possible future disruption of critical services, not just stealing information. It uses tools already built into the operating system, so it brings very little of its own. That link is a government assessment.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group avoids custom malware almost entirely. It uses built-in commands that administrators use every day. Signature checks therefore find nothing, and its activity can look like normal maintenance. The only way to catch it is to know what normal looks like in your environment, then notice small differences in who runs what, and from where.
howItWorks: The group gains access through weak credentials or an unpatched network device.
It then uses commands that are already part of the operating system.
Those built-in commands list users, map the network and collect stored passwords.
Small home and office routers may be taken over and used as quiet relays.
The group logs in from ordinary internet addresses, so location rules fail.
It stays quiet for a long time, waiting for orders rather than stealing data.
beginner.example: Think of a workshop where every worker uses the same set of tools from a shared rack. A stranger walks in, picks up a normal hammer and does normal-looking work in the corner. Nothing he carries is unusual. The only oddity is that he is not on the staff list, and nobody has seen him before.
takeaways: Learn how your administrators normally work, so odd sessions stand out.
Patch and replace small routers and edge devices, then watch them.
Alert on logins from unexpected addresses, even when the password is valid.

topics.title: AES GCM
topics.summary: AES-GCM is an authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) mode that combines the AES block cipher in counter mode with a GHASH-based universal hash to produce ciphertext plus a 128-bit authentication tag, so confidentiality and integrity are delivered by a single key. The construction takes a 128-bit block cipher key (AES-128, AES-192 or AES-256), a unique nonce of typically 96 bits, the plaintext, and optional associated data that is authenticated but not encrypted. Decryption fails closed: if the tag does not verify, no plaintext is released, which is why GCM is preferred over unauthenticated modes such as CBC in modern protocols like TLS 1.3, IPsec ESP, and 802.11 WPA3. The security proof of GCM depends absolutely on nonce uniqueness per key; reusing a nonce with the same key leaks the XOR of plaintexts and, worse, exposes the GHASH authentication subkey, letting an attacker forge arbitrary messages. Other practical failure modes are truncating the tag too aggressively, ignoring tag verification in application code, reusing keys across contexts, and exhausting the 96-bit counter space on long-lived high-volume keys. Implementations also vary in constant-time behaviour, so side channels during GHASH multiplication matter on embedded and shared hardware. For defenders this means key and nonce lifecycle management, per-message key derivation, envelope encryption patterns, and reliable detection of downgrade or fallback to legacy cipher suites are all first-class operational concerns rather than implementation details.
objectives: Explain how AES-GCM composes counter-mode encryption with GHASH authentication and what the authentication tag guarantees.
Describe exactly what breaks when a nonce is reused with the same key, and how that failure surfaces in captured traffic.
Choose appropriate tag lengths and associated data for a protocol, and justify why tag truncation is a risk decision.
Recognise downgrade and fallback behaviour in TLS or IPsec logs that indicates traffic is no longer protected by an AEAD mode.
Design envelope encryption and per-message key derivation so that high-volume services never exhaust nonce space.
Evaluate a code review finding where a GCM tag is computed but not actually verified before use.
Map cryptographic weakening of transport encryption to adversary techniques for collection and command and control.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-38D: Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation - GCM and GMAC
NIST Cryptographic Standards and Guidelines landing page

beginner.definition: AES GCM is a way to lock data so nobody can read it and nobody can change it. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) scrambles the data. GCM, short for Galois Counter Mode, adds a tamper seal as well. If anyone edits even one bit, the seal breaks and the data is refused.
beginner.whyItMatters: Encryption alone is not enough. If an attacker can flip bits in your scrambled data, they may change a payment amount or a message without reading it. AES GCM solves both problems at once: it hides the data and proves nobody touched it. That is why modern secure connections prefer it over older modes that only hide data.
howItWorks: The sender and receiver share one secret key, which both sides must keep private.
For each message, a unique number called a nonce is chosen. A nonce must never repeat with the same key.
AES scrambles the message using the key and the nonce, turning readable text into unreadable output.
A second calculation builds a short seal, called a tag, over the scrambled message and the key.
The receiver checks the tag first. If it does not match, the message is thrown away without being read.
beginner.example: Think of a sealed courier box. The contents are hidden inside, and the lid carries a wax seal with a unique pattern. The courier writes a fresh code on the seal for every delivery, because reusing the same code would let someone copy it. When the box arrives, you check the wax seal before opening it. If the seal is cracked or the pattern is wrong, you do not trust the contents at all.
takeaways: AES GCM both hides data and detects tampering, so use it instead of plain encryption.
Never reuse a nonce with the same key. Reuse breaks both secrecy and the seal.
Always check the seal before trusting data, and reject the message if the check fails.

topics.title: Alert Fatigue
topics.summary: Alert fatigue is the degradation of analyst attention and judgement caused by a detection pipeline that raises more alerts than a team can meaningfully examine. It is not simply a volume problem. Fatigue sets in when alerts are numerous and individually low-yield, so that the rational response becomes pattern matching on the alert title, batch-closing whole categories, and treating the queue as work to be cleared rather than as evidence to be assessed. The operational consequences are measurable: rising time to acknowledge the alerts that matter, missed true positives hidden inside noisy detections, analyst burnout and turnover, and a dangerous normalisation of anomalous activity. The root causes are structural. Rules built on a single event with no threshold, no entity context and no business weighting will fire on legitimate administrative behaviour. Log sources with poor parsing produce malformed fields that make every alert look identical. Duplicate detections from overlapping content raise the same activity several times. Suppressions are applied permanently instead of with an expiry, so detections quietly die and nobody notices the resulting blind spot. Because fatigue is a measurement and content-quality problem, the treatment is engineering rather than exhortation. Teams track per-rule alert volume against per-rule confirmed-true rate, retire or rewrite rules below a usefulness threshold, add allow-listing with mandatory expiry, enrich alerts with asset and identity context before an analyst ever sees them, and consolidate overlapping detections. Detection content then becomes a maintained product with owners, review dates and a documented reason to exist.
objectives: You will be able to explain how alert volume, low yield and duplicate content interact to produce analyst over-trust in titles and batch closures.
You will be able to measure per-rule alert volume against confirmed-true rate and use it to identify content that should be rewritten or retired.
You will be able to add entity context and thresholds to a noisy rule without destroying its ability to catch the behaviour it targets.
You will be able to design suppressions with mandatory expiry, ownership and a review condition rather than permanent exclusions.
You will be able to evaluate the operational cost of a detection before deploying it, including expected daily volume at current estate scale.
You will be able to argue a defensible case for retiring a detection while documenting the compensating control for the coverage it removes.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-61, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

beginner.definition: Alert fatigue is what happens when a security team gets far more alerts than it can properly check. People start skimming titles instead of reading the evidence. They close whole groups of alerts at once. Over time, real attacks hide inside the noise, and nobody notices them.
beginner.whyItMatters: An alert is only useful if someone actually looks at it. When the queue is too long, your team learns to ignore it. Bad alerts also cost money and time, and they burn people out. Attackers know this, so some of them deliberately create noise. Tuning your alerts is not optional.
howItWorks: Every day, your detection tools send alerts into one shared queue for analysts to review.
If the queue grows faster than people can read it, they start judging alerts by title only.
Rules that fire on normal admin work add many useless alerts and push real ones down.
Duplicate alerts about the same event make the pile look bigger than it really is.
Teams fix this by measuring which rules produce useful alerts and which only create noise.
They rewrite weak rules, add short-lived exceptions, and add context so analysts decide faster.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital reception desk with one nurse and five hundred patients arriving every hour. Most of them are fine. The nurse quickly learns to wave people through without asking questions. Then one person with a serious injury walks in, and they get waved through too. A security queue works the same way. Too many alerts do not make you safer. They teach your team to stop looking.
takeaways: A long alert queue trains people to stop reading carefully.
Measure each rule by how many useful alerts it really produces.
Add exceptions with a short expiry date instead of blocking an alert forever.

topics.title: Alert Triage
topics.summary: Triage is the first analytical pass over an alert or a queue of alerts, in which an analyst decides what the signal means, how urgent it is, and what happens next. It is a bounded activity with a defined output, not open-ended investigation: for each alert the analyst produces a disposition, a confidence statement, the evidence that supports it, and an escalation decision. Good triage follows a fixed sequence. Validate that the alert is real and not a duplicate, a scheduled job or a known test; establish the entities involved, meaning accounts, hosts, source addresses and business context; reconstruct the timeline from raw logs rather than trusting the alert's own summary; look for corroborating or contradicting telemetry from independent sources such as identity, endpoint and network records; and only then decide whether the activity is benign, suspicious or confirmed malicious. The consistent failure modes are well understood. Analysts anchor on the alert title and never open the underlying events. They accept an enrichment field as fact when it is stale or unverified. They close an alert because a similar one was benign last month. They escalate too early and burn responder capacity, or too late and let a foothold mature. Effective SOCs reduce these errors structurally: clear severity and escalation criteria, checklists for the highest-volume alert types, suppression with an expiry date rather than permanent closure, and requirement that the disposition evidence be written down so a reviewer can reproduce the judgement. Triage quality is best measured not by alerts closed but by escalation precision and by whether real incidents were initially triaged as benign.
objectives: You will be able to apply a repeatable triage sequence that validates, contextualises, reconstructs and corroborates an alert before disposition.
You will be able to reconstruct an event timeline from raw telemetry instead of relying on an alert's generated summary.
You will be able to write a disposition that records evidence, confidence and escalation rationale in a form another analyst can reproduce.
You will be able to prioritise a mixed queue using asset criticality, identity privilege and observed adversary behaviour rather than raw severity labels.
You will be able to recognise and correct common triage biases such as title anchoring, stale enrichment trust and precedent-based closure.
You will be able to decide when to suppress rather than close an alert, and specify an expiry and review condition for the suppression.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-61, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

beginner.definition: Triage is the first careful look at an alert. The analyst decides what the alert really means, how urgent it is, and what should happen next. Each alert ends with a written decision, the evidence behind it, and a note on whether to escalate. It is a bounded task, not an open-ended investigation.
beginner.whyItMatters: Triage is where a real attack is either caught or missed. A rushed decision sends a serious incident home as harmless, and the attacker gets days of quiet time. A careless escalation floods the response team with nothing. Doing triage the same careful way each time is what makes a security team reliable.
howItWorks: Check that the alert is real and not a duplicate or a known scheduled job.
Identify the entities involved: which accounts, machines and network addresses are named.
Open the raw logs and rebuild the timeline yourself instead of trusting the summary.
Look for evidence from other sources that confirms or contradicts the alert.
Now decide whether the activity is harmless, merely suspicious, or confirmed malicious.
Write down your decision, your confidence and the evidence, then escalate if needed.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital emergency department. A nurse sees every patient first and sorts them fast: the chest pain goes straight in, the sprained ankle waits. The nurse does not treat anyone, but that quick sorting decides everything that follows. Alert triage is that first assessment. Get the sorting wrong, and the wrong patient waits while the serious one sits in the chairs.
takeaways: Read the raw logs; never decide based only on the alert title.
Write your reasoning down so another analyst can check it.
Sort the queue by asset importance and account privilege, not just severity.

topics.title: Anti Forensics
topics.summary: Anti-forensics is the set of techniques an adversary uses to frustrate, mislead or delay forensic analysis, either by destroying evidence, by making analysis uneconomic, or by planting artefacts that send investigators down the wrong path. The category spans data destruction such as secure wiping, free-space overwriting and the deletion of logs; artefact manipulation including timestamp alteration, log tampering and the removal of entries from event or audit trails; concealment through encryption, steganography, alternate data streams, hidden partitions and packed or obfuscated binaries; tool subversion, where malicious code interferes with the very utilities a responder would run, including kernel-mode rootkits and the disabling of security logging; and attribution attacks such as the deliberate use of another organisation's naming conventions or living-off-the-land binaries to blend into normal activity. For defenders, anti-forensics matters less as a list of tools than as an interpretive warning: the absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, and the failure of a standard tool to find something may itself be a finding worth pursuing. Investigations respond by collecting volatile data before artefacts can be altered, corroborating every conclusion across independent sources, validating acquisition and analysis tools against known-good behaviour, and treating inconsistencies in timestamps or log continuity as investigative leads. Reporting anti-forensic indicators, including gaps, tampering and tool anomalies, alongside substantive findings protects the credibility of the case and informs detection engineering, because these techniques often require behaviour that can be detected even when the artefacts themselves cannot be recovered.
objectives: Categorise anti-forensic techniques by whether they destroy, manipulate, conceal or misattribute evidence.
Interpret missing, discontinuous or inconsistent artefacts as investigative findings rather than as proof of innocence.
Adapt collection order and tooling when an environment may contain kernel-level or tool-subverting implants.
Corroborate conclusions across independent evidence sources so they withstand deliberate artefact manipulation.
Map observed anti-forensic behaviour to adversary tactics and identify the detection opportunities it creates.
Document and communicate confidence limits when evidence integrity or completeness is in question.
Brief stakeholders on how anti-forensics affects scope estimates, investigation timelines and legal defensibility.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK - adversary tactics and techniques knowledge base
SANS Institute - digital forensics and incident response resources
NIST Computer Security Resource Center - forensic examination guidance

beginner.definition: Anti-forensics is the set of tricks an attacker uses to confuse, delay, or mislead an investigation. Some tricks destroy evidence, such as wiping files or clearing logs. Others hide evidence using encryption or hidden storage. Others plant false clues. If you investigate incidents, anti-forensics tells you when to trust your tools.
beginner.whyItMatters: When evidence is missing, it is easy to assume nothing happened. That is a dangerous mistake. Anti-forensics means the absence of evidence is not proof of innocence. An attacker who deletes logs, changes file times, or hides code can make a clean-looking machine hide a real break-in. If you ignore this, you may close an incident that is still active.
howItWorks: The attacker gains access and then works to slow down anyone who investigates later.
They destroy evidence, for example by wiping free disk space or deleting security logs.
They hide evidence by encrypting files, using hidden storage areas, or packing programs so tools cannot read them.
They change file times and log entries so your timeline no longer matches what really happened.
They may also break the tools you rely on, so your own software reports nothing suspicious.
You respond by collecting fragile evidence first and checking every finding against a second source.
beginner.example: Think of a burglar who breaks into a house, then tidies up before leaving. The chairs sit straight, the dishes are washed, and the door is locked again. Nothing looks wrong, so you assume nobody came in. Then you notice the clock on the wall shows the wrong time and the garden gate is open. Anti-forensics works the same way. The missing signs and the strange details are your real clues.
takeaways: Missing evidence is itself a clue, never proof that nothing happened.
Collect fragile data early, before an attacker or a reboot removes it.
Always confirm important findings with a second and independent evidence source.

topics.title: Antimalware Scan Interface
topics.summary: The Antimalware Scan Interface is a Windows interface that lets applications and scripting runtimes hand content to the installed antimalware provider for inspection before that content is executed, interpreted or loaded. Its importance comes from the gap it fills: script engines and dynamic runtimes do not necessarily write a file to disk before running code, so a traditional file scanner sees nothing to inspect. By calling into AMSI, a participating host such as a scripting engine, an office macro runtime, or a dynamic scripting component can submit the script text, the decoded buffer or the module being loaded, and the antimalware provider can return a verdict that causes the host to abort. AMSI is not itself a detection engine; it is a broker, and its effectiveness depends entirely on the provider behind it and on the host actually calling it with useful content. That dependency is the source of its well-known weaknesses. Bypass research concentrates on preventing the scan rather than defeating the signatures: corrupting the in-memory state of the interface so that calls fail open, patching the provider's scanning function inside a process, or structuring code so that the meaningful payload never appears in a single buffer that gets submitted. Because several of these approaches leave distinctive artefacts, AMSI remains valuable to defenders: failures of the interface, unexpected patching of its components, and mismatches between what a script claims to do and what the provider observed are all high-signal events when the relevant logging is enabled, and AMSI output frequently feeds straight into endpoint detection platforms.
objectives: Explain what AMSI is, how a participating host submits content, and why the design closes a scripting visibility gap.
Identify which runtimes and applications call AMSI and what each contributes to endpoint detection.
Describe the classes of AMSI bypass at a conceptual level and the artefacts each tends to leave behind.
Detect tampering with AMSI components by monitoring module integrity and provider load failures.
Assess the limitations of AMSI against encoded, segmented or encrypted content that never reaches it intact.
Integrate AMSI verdicts and errors into endpoint alert triage alongside script block and process telemetry.

beginner.definition: AMSI stands for Antimalware Scan Interface. It is a Windows feature that lets programs hand over the content they are about to run to your antivirus tool for a quick check. If the check fails, the program stops instead of running the code.
beginner.whyItMatters: Scripts and macros often run without ever being saved as a normal file. A classic file scanner has nothing to look at, so the bad code slips past. AMSI closes that gap by asking the antivirus to inspect text and memory just before it runs. It is not a scanner itself. It is a messenger, so it only works when the app calls it and the antivirus answers.
howItWorks: A program that runs scripts, such as a command shell, prepares some code to run.
Before running it, the program sends the text or memory content to AMSI.
AMSI passes that content to the antivirus product installed on the machine.
The antivirus checks the content and sends back a verdict of clean or harmful.
If the verdict says harmful, the program cancels the action instead of running it.
Because the scan happens in memory, no file needs to exist on the disk.
beginner.example: Picture an airport security queue. Before you reach the gate, an officer looks inside your bag. The gate itself does not check anything. It only opens for people who passed the earlier check. The scanning interface plays that officer for scripts. When a script is about to run, the program asks the security software to look at it first. If the officer says stop, the script never reaches the gate. If the app never asks, nothing gets checked at all.
takeaways: AMSI is a messenger, not a scanner; the antivirus behind it does the real work.
It exists because scripts can run in memory without leaving a file behind.
Watch for apps that fail to call AMSI, because that gap can hide harmful code.

topics.title: Attribute-Based Access Control
topics.summary: Attribute-based access control (ABAC) is an access control model that evaluates a policy against attributes of the subject, the resource, the action and the environment at the moment of the request, rather than relying solely on a pre-assigned role. Typical subject attributes include department, clearance, employment status, device compliance state and manager, while resource attributes include classification, owner, tenant and data residency, and environment attributes include time, network origin, authentication strength and risk score. Because the decision is computed rather than looked up, ABAC can express rules such as permitting access only when the requesting device is managed, the user is a current employee in the owning department, and the request arrives from a trusted network during business hours. That expressiveness is also the model's principal operational hazard: policies interact, and a rule written to satisfy one business case can silently widen access when combined with another. Policy authoring therefore needs the same rigour as code, including version control, review, automated testing against representative request scenarios, and documentation of the attribute sources that feed each decision. Attribute quality becomes a security dependency, because a stale human resources feed or a device compliance signal that fails open can convert a correct policy into an incorrect decision. Implementing ABAC usually starts alongside existing RBAC, using roles as coarse-grained building blocks and attributes as fine-grained conditions, and this is the pattern most cloud identity platforms and policy engines such as Open Policy Agent and Cedar-family languages support.
objectives: You will be able to define subject, resource, action and environment attributes and map them to real access requirements.
You will be able to write and test an attribute-based policy and reason about how it composes with existing role grants.
You will be able to identify attribute sources whose staleness or failure mode could cause a policy to fail open.
You will be able to explain how policy-as-code review, version control and automated tests reduce misconfiguration risk.
You will be able to compare ABAC with RBAC for a given decision and justify a hybrid design.
You will be able to troubleshoot an access denial by tracing which attribute evaluation caused the decision.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-162: Guide to Attribute Based Access Control Definition and Considerations
AWS documentation: IAM policy evaluation logic

beginner.definition: Attribute-based access control is a way to decide who may use a system. Instead of only checking a person's job title, it checks many details about the person, the data, and the moment. Each request is judged on its own.
beginner.whyItMatters: Job titles change and people move between teams. A fixed title can leave someone with too much access for years. Attribute-based control closes that gap, because the decision uses live details. It also lets you say yes more often, in safer ways. If you ignore it, old permissions quietly pile up.
howItWorks: A person asks to open a file, a report, an application, or a cloud service.
The system collects attributes, which are facts such as department, device health, time of day, and location.
A written rule checks those facts together and then returns either allow or deny.
The rule can also ask for extra proof, such as a stronger sign-in, before it allows the request.
Every decision is logged, so you can see later which facts caused it.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital ward. A nurse may open the medicine cabinet, but only during a shift, only on the ward where they work, and only after scanning their badge. A cleaner with the same badge cannot open it at all. The rule is not based on the job title alone. It also looks at the place, the time, and the task. That is attribute-based control in daily life.
takeaways: Attributes are just facts about the user, the data, and the moment of the request.
Write policies like code: review them, version them, and test them before they go live.
A stale fact can grant wrong access, so keep your data sources fresh.

topics.title: Attribution
topics.summary: Attribution is the analytic judgement that links a set of observed activity to a responsible actor, and it is one of the most overclaimed products in cyber threat intelligence. Analysts distinguish at least three questions that are routinely conflated: technical attribution of tooling and infrastructure to a cluster of activity, operational attribution of that cluster to a consistent set of people and their tradecraft, and strategic or political attribution of those people to a state, sponsor or criminal organisation. Each step is weaker than the last and requires evidence of a different kind, so confidence should fall as the claim becomes more consequential. The core technical difficulty is that tooling, malware families, infrastructure and even credentials are shared, resold, stolen or deliberately planted. False flags are cheap: strings, language artefacts, time zone artefacts and reused code can all be inserted to mislead. Mature practice therefore relies on corroboration across independent sources, on clustering by infrastructure and capability rather than by a single indicator, and on structured analytic techniques that force the analyst to argue the alternative hypothesis. Naming conventions matter as well. Tracking a cluster with a neutral designator keeps the technical analysis separable from the attribution claim, whereas reusing a named actor label imports assumptions about intent and sponsorship that the evidence may not support. Public attribution also carries legal, diplomatic and operational consequences, so it is normally a leadership decision informed by intelligence rather than a side effect of a technical report. Defensively, attribution rarely changes the immediate response, because containment, eradication and recovery depend on what the adversary can do, not on who they are, though it does shape long-term risk, control investment and intelligence sharing.
objectives: You will be able to separate technical, operational and strategic attribution and state the evidence each requires.
You will be able to argue an alternative hypothesis and identify the false flag opportunities in a given evidence set.
You will be able to cluster activity by infrastructure and capability instead of relying on a single indicator.
You will be able to write an attribution judgement with explicit confidence and a clear statement of assumptions.
You will be able to explain why neutral cluster designators reduce analytic bias compared with named actor labels.
You will be able to describe how attribution affects long-term risk decisions while leaving incident response largely unchanged.

beginner.definition: Attribution is the work of deciding who is behind a cyber attack. You study the clues and try to name the person, group or country responsible. It is a judgement, not a fact, so you should always say how sure you are.
beginner.whyItMatters: Knowing who attacked you rarely changes how you clean up. You still remove the malware and reset the passwords. Attribution matters for the long game. It shapes which risks you track, where you spend money and who you warn. Bad attribution is dangerous. If you blame the wrong group, you may miss the real threat and make a serious political mistake.
howItWorks: Collect the evidence. Gather file names, network addresses, timestamps and the tools the attacker used.
Group the activity into a cluster. Give it a neutral name like Cluster A, so you do not bias yourself.
Separate three questions. Which tools, which people, and which sponsor or state? Each answer needs stronger proof.
Look for false flags. Attackers plant other languages and time zones to make you blame someone else.
Check independent sources. One report is weak, but several sources that agree raise your confidence.
State your judgement with a confidence level, and list the evidence that would prove you wrong.
beginner.example: Imagine a threatening note is pushed under your door. The handwriting looks foreign, but anyone can copy a style. It might be a neighbour, or someone far away trying to frame that neighbour. You would not accuse anyone based on one clue. You would look for fingerprints, camera footage and a motive. Cyber attribution works the same way. One clue is never enough, and clever attackers leave misleading clues on purpose.
takeaways: Attribution is a careful judgement with a confidence level, never a certain fact.
Attackers plant false clues, so cross-check several independent sources before you blame anyone.
Who attacked you rarely changes your cleanup, but it shapes long-term risk decisions.

topics.title: BGP Hijacking
topics.summary: The Border Gateway Protocol is the routing protocol that exchanges reachability information between autonomous systems on the internet, and it operates on trust: a network announces the address prefixes it can reach, and its neighbours generally believe the announcement. BGP hijacking exploits that trust by announcing a prefix the attacker does not legitimately control, or by announcing a more specific prefix that wins longest-prefix matching, so traffic destined for the real owner is delivered elsewhere. The consequences range from denial of service, because traffic is blackholed or dropped, to interception, because the attacker forwards traffic onward while observing or modifying it. A route leak, where a network accidentally re-announces routes learned from one provider to another, produces similar effects without malicious intent and is a frequent cause of large-scale incidents. Because the protocol has no built-in origin authentication, a bad announcement can propagate globally within minutes and is corrected only after the legitimate operator and its providers respond, which means detection speed matters as much as prevention. Prevention uses cryptographic or registry-based attestation of route origin: a resource public key infrastructure with route origin authorisations lets a network publish which autonomous system may originate which prefix, and BGPsec aims to protect the path itself, although adoption remains uneven. Filtering at the edge, rejecting announcements for prefixes a peer is not authorised to originate and applying maximum prefix limits, prevents a large share of accidental leaks. Detection complements prevention through public route monitoring services, looking-glass queries, and comparison of observed paths against expected paths. For defenders outside routing teams, hijacking matters because it can redirect traffic to an attacker-controlled network, support impersonation of a domain or service, and enable interception of sessions whose protection depends on the endpoints involved.
objectives: You will be able to explain how prefix announcements and longest-prefix matching make hijacking possible.
You will be able to distinguish a malicious hijack from an accidental route leak by evidence.
You will be able to assess whether an anomaly should be described as denial of service or interception.
You will be able to describe how route origin authorisation and BGPsec constrain unauthorised announcements.
You will be able to design edge filtering and maximum prefix limits for peers and customers.
You will be able to use route monitoring and looking-glass data to detect and report an anomalous announcement.

sources.label: RFC 6480: An Infrastructure to Support Secure Internet Routing

beginner.definition: BGP hijacking is when someone tells the internet's routing system that they own a block of internet addresses they do not really own. Routers believe the claim and send traffic to the wrong place. Border Gateway Protocol, or BGP, is the set of rules networks use to swap these route claims.
beginner.whyItMatters: The internet has no central referee for routes. A wrong claim can spread worldwide in minutes. Traffic meant for a bank or a government site may quietly flow through a stranger's network. That can take a service offline, or let someone read and change data in transit. You cannot fix this alone, but you can watch for it and report it fast.
howItWorks: Every network on the internet owns blocks of addresses, called prefixes, and announces them to its neighbours.
Neighbours pass those announcements along, so a route claim spreads across the world within minutes.
Routers always prefer the most specific route, so a smaller fake prefix beats the real, larger one.
In a hijack someone announces a prefix they do not own, and traffic is delivered to them instead.
Sometimes a network does this by accident; we call that a route leak, and the effect looks similar.
Defenders compare watched routes with expected ones and publish signed proof of who may announce what.
beginner.example: Imagine you move house and file a change of address form with the post office. A stranger files the same form for your street, and the post office believes whoever filed last. Now all your letters go to the stranger's door. They can throw your post away, which is like an outage, or open it, copy it and send it on, which is like interception. Routing works the same way, because networks trust announcements unless someone checks them.
takeaways: Internet routing runs on trust, so a false claim can redirect real traffic.
Hijacks cause outages or interception, and both are serious.
Watch your routes, and report strange changes to your provider quickly.

topics.title: Business Impact Analysis
topics.summary: A business impact analysis is the structured study that determines how the loss or degradation of each business process, and the resources that process depends on, would affect the organisation over time. It is the analytical foundation of business continuity and disaster recovery planning because it produces the numbers that drive every later decision: the maximum tolerable period of disruption, the recovery time objective, the recovery point objective, the minimum acceptable service level and the priority order for restoration when resources are scarce. A competent analysis works process-first rather than asset-first. It starts from the organisation's products and services, breaks them into business processes, identifies the people, applications, data, facilities, suppliers and infrastructure each process needs, and then models impact across several dimensions: financial, regulatory and legal, operational, customer and reputational, and safety where relevant. Impact is assessed over a time axis because most disruption is tolerable for minutes and intolerable after days, and that curve is what makes a recovery objective defensible rather than arbitrary. Practitioners should insist on named process owners providing input, because a BIA produced solely by the security team will encode technical assumptions that no part of the business has agreed to. The output feeds continuity strategies, dependency mapping, third-party risk assessment, recovery testing scenarios and the risk register, and it should be refreshed when the business changes rather than on a fixed multi-year cycle alone.
objectives: You will be able to derive business processes and their dependencies from products and services rather than from an asset list.
You will be able to model impact across financial, regulatory, operational, customer and safety dimensions.
You will be able to build an impact-over-time curve that justifies a maximum tolerable period of disruption.
You will be able to run structured interviews with process owners that produce evidence rather than reassurance.
You will be able to derive recovery priorities and dependencies that shape continuity and recovery strategies.
You will be able to spot where an untested dependency or single supplier invalidates a stated recovery objective.

beginner.definition: A business impact analysis is a study of how much harm your company would suffer if a business process stopped working. It asks what each process needs, such as people, data and systems, and how the damage grows over time. The result guides recovery priorities.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most teams guess which system to fix first after an outage. Guessing puts effort in the wrong place and keeps the important work offline longer. A business impact analysis replaces opinion with evidence from the people who run each process. It also gives you numbers, so leaders can decide what recovery speed is worth paying for.
howItWorks: Start with the products and services your company sells, not with a list of servers.
Break each product into the business processes that deliver it to customers.
Ask the owner of each process what people, data, systems and suppliers it depends on.
Estimate the harm caused by an outage of one hour, one day and one week.
Compare those costs to find how long each process may safely stay offline.
Use the answers to set recovery orders and to check them with the business.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital. If the pharmacy system goes down, nurses can write paper orders for a short time. After a few hours, mistakes become dangerous and patients wait longer. So the pharmacy system is ranked as urgent, while the staff canteen till can wait until tomorrow. A business impact analysis is the conversation that produces those rankings before anything breaks, using patient safety and delay as the measure.
takeaways: Start from business processes, not from a list of technical assets.
Impact grows with time, so measure harm at several points during an outage.
Process owners must give the input, or the numbers will be guesses.

topics.title: C2 Beacon
topics.summary: A command-and-control beacon is the component of an intrusion that maintains a channel between implanted code on a victim host and infrastructure the operator controls, periodically checking in for instructions or waiting to be activated. The beacon's design goal is reliability under adverse conditions: it must survive intermittent connectivity, survive the loss of individual servers, and remain inconspicuous in network and host telemetry. That produces a recognisable set of behaviours worth studying. Beacons poll on a schedule, frequently with a randomised jitter component so that intervals do not look machine-generated. They blend into permitted traffic by using common application protocols over ports that are rarely blocked, or by tunnelling through domain name resolution, and they frequently use legitimate third-party services as relay points rather than bespoke infrastructure. They also tend to fail in characteristic ways: repeated connections to a hostname that resolves to a documentation-range address or a domain registered very recently, a steady byte-size profile in both directions, TLS sessions with unusual parameters, or a process that talks to the internet at regular intervals with no user interaction. Defenders have two complementary angles. Network analytics and flow metadata can surface beaconing periodicity and long-lived low-volume channels without any payload inspection, which is valuable when traffic is encrypted end to end. Host and identity telemetry can surface which process is making the connection, under which account, and what it did immediately before and after. Because the channel is what makes dwell time possible, disrupting or detecting it early is often the single most consequential intervention available to a defender, and it is also the point at which an adversary's operational security is most exposed.
objectives: Explain what a C2 beacon does on a victim host and why periodic check-in shapes its observable behaviour.
Identify beaconing characteristics in flow data, including interval regularity, jitter and consistent payload sizes.
Recognise abuse of legitimate services and protocol tunnelling as a means of blending into permitted traffic.
Build detections that combine network periodicity with host process and account attribution.
Assess domain-age, destination reputation and TLS metadata signals while accounting for false positives from legitimate software.
Decide when to disrupt a channel versus continue monitoring, and justify the tradeoff in a written recommendation.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (T1041)

beginner.definition: A command-and-control beacon is a small piece of code on an infected machine that quietly contacts a server the attacker controls. It checks in on a regular schedule to ask for new orders or to wait until it is needed. The word beacon comes from the idea of a signal that keeps repeating.
beginner.whyItMatters: That channel is the attacker's lifeline. It lets them send new commands, move to other machines, and steal data over days or weeks. If you cut the channel, the intrusion goes blind. Because beacons repeat on a timer, they leave a pattern in network records. Learning that pattern helps you find intruders even when all traffic is encrypted.
howItWorks: Harmful code gets a foothold on a machine, often through a document or a weak password.
It reaches out to a server the attacker controls, using a common protocol like web traffic.
The server replies with instructions, or simply says wait for now.
The code waits a fixed time, plus a small random delay, then checks in again.
Small amounts of stolen data may ride out along the same channel.
That regular timing creates a pattern that network records can slowly reveal.
beginner.example: Think of a spy in a hotel who must report in every night at a slightly different time. Too regular, and the front desk notices. So the spy varies the minute a little. The spy never gets a long message, just a short call, a code word, and a hang-up. If the calls stop, the handler knows something is wrong. A command-and-control beacon behaves the same way. It is quiet and repeating, easy to miss one at a time, but obvious once you plot the timings on a chart.
takeaways: A beacon is the attacker's ongoing connection, not the first break-in.
Regular check-in timing, with small random delays, is its clearest signature.
Look for a process talking to the internet at a steady rhythm with no user activity.

topics.title: Certificate Pinning
topics.summary: Certificate pinning is the practice of restricting which certificates or public keys a client will accept for a given service, instead of trusting every certificate authority in the platform trust store. The client embeds or is configured with an expected leaf certificate, a public key, a hash of either, or the identity of a specific issuing authority, and it rejects any chain that does not match. This closes the gap left by the CA model, where any trusted authority, or anyone who can convince one to issue, can produce a certificate that validates for a hostname the attacker does not control. Pinning is common in mobile applications, thick clients, embedded device firmware, service meshes and internal API calls. It is also one of the more brittle controls in wide deployment, because pins must be updated in lockstep with certificate rotation and clients that cannot be updated will fail closed at renewal time. Common failures are pinning only the leaf certificate with no backup pin, storing pins in a configuration file that is itself updated over the network, pinning by common name rather than key material, implementing pin checks in a layer that can be bypassed by hooking or proxying, and failing to test pin mismatch handling. Defenders care about pinning from both directions, since a sudden wave of pin validation failures across clients may indicate an interception attempt, a misissued certificate, or a botched deployment.
objectives: Distinguish leaf certificate pinning, public key pinning and issuing-authority pinning, and state the tradeoffs of each.
Explain how pinning mitigates CA compromise and misissuance without replacing the rest of chain validation.
Design a pin set with backup pins and an update strategy that survives certificate rotation without client lockout.
Diagnose why a pinning implementation can be bypassed through dynamic instrumentation or a user-installed root.
Interpret a spike in client pin validation failures and separate attack indicators from deployment errors.
Balance pinning against operational risk in mobile, embedded and service mesh environments.

sources.label: OWASP Mobile Application Security - Network Communication
NIST SP 800-52 Rev 2: Guidelines for TLS Configurations

beginner.definition: Certificate pinning means a client accepts only one specific certificate, or one specific public key, for a service. It ignores every other certificate, even ones signed by a trusted authority. The client remembers exactly what it expects and refuses anything else.
beginner.whyItMatters: Normally your device trusts hundreds of certificate authorities. Any one of them can issue a certificate for any website. If one is tricked or hacked, an attacker can pretend to be your bank and your device will believe it. Pinning removes that wide trust and checks for one exact identity instead. The trade-off is that pins must be updated carefully.
howItWorks: The service owner decides which certificate or key the app should always expect.
That expected value is built into the app, or stored in a place the app reads at startup.
When the app connects, it receives the server certificate as usual and checks the signature chain.
Then it compares the certificate, or its public key, against the stored expected value.
If they do not match exactly, the app stops the connection and shows an error.
You should also store a backup pin so renewal does not lock every user out.
beginner.example: Picture a nightclub with a guest list. The bouncer does not accept any official identity card from any country. He accepts only the exact person on his list, checked by name and photo. That is very strong, but it has a cost. If the club changes its list and forgets to tell the bouncer, loyal regulars are turned away at the door. Backup pins are the second name on the list.
takeaways: Pinning trusts one exact certificate or key instead of every authority on the device.
Always keep a backup pin, or a routine renewal will lock out every user.
A sudden wave of pin failures can mean interception or a broken rollout, so check both.

topics.title: Chain OF Custody
topics.summary: Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken record of who collected a piece of evidence, when and where it was collected, how it was handled and stored, who accessed it afterwards, and how it was transferred between custodians. In digital forensics the evidence is usually a disk image, a memory capture, a mobile extraction, a log export or a set of network captures, and the record takes the form of a custody form supported by artefacts such as write blockers, hash values, sealed storage, signed transfer receipts and case management timestamps. The purpose is to make the evidence defensible: in a disciplinary hearing, a civil dispute, a regulatory investigation or a criminal prosecution, opposing counsel will challenge whether the artefact presented is the same artefact that existed at the scene, and an unbroken chain with matching cryptographic hashes is the standard answer. Chain of custody begins before acquisition with authorisation and scope, continues through the use of validated tools and write blockers, and extends into analysis, where working copies are made and originals remain sealed. Breakpoints - an unexplained gap, a missing signature, an analyst who examined the original without documenting it, storage in an uncontrolled location - do not automatically make evidence inadmissible, but they weaken its weight and can be fatal in the strictest proceedings. Good practice treats custody as a habit rather than as paperwork: hash on acquisition and again on every transfer, log every access, store in access-controlled locations, and never let convenience override the record.
objectives: Explain what chain of custody must record and why each element affects admissibility and evidential weight.
Document the acquisition, transfer, storage and analysis of digital evidence using a defensible custody record.
Apply cryptographic hashing at acquisition and at each transfer to demonstrate that evidence is unaltered.
Use write blockers and validated tooling so that original media is never modified during examination.
Identify common custody breakpoints and assess how each one weakens the evidence in a hearing or investigation.
Coordinate custody handling with legal counsel, HR and law enforcement expectations before collection begins.
Design storage and access controls that keep sealed originals separate from analyst working copies.

sources.label: NIST Computer Security Resource Center - forensic evidence handling guidance
SANS Institute - digital forensics and incident response resources

beginner.definition: Chain of custody is the written record of who handled a piece of evidence, when, where, and why. For digital evidence, that could be a disk copy, a memory capture, a log export, or a disk image. The record shows every transfer and every person who accessed it. It proves the evidence you present is the same evidence you collected.
beginner.whyItMatters: Evidence only helps if people trust it. In a disciplinary meeting, a lawsuit, or a police case, the other side will ask how you know the files were not changed. A tidy record, with matching fingerprint values called hashes, answers that question. A gap in the record, even an honest one, weakens your case and may make the evidence useless.
howItWorks: Before you touch anything, confirm you have written permission to collect the evidence.
Write down what you took, the exact time, the place, and the device it came from.
Make a copy and never work on the original, so the original stays untouched.
Create a hash, a digital fingerprint, and record it so any later change becomes obvious.
Log every handover with a signature, a date, and the reason for the transfer.
Store the evidence in a locked, access-controlled place and review who opened it.
beginner.example: Imagine handing a sealed hospital sample to a lab. The nurse signs a form, the courier signs it, and the lab signs again on arrival. Every step has a name and a time. If the seal is broken or a signature is missing, the result cannot be trusted. Digital evidence works the same way. The form and the seal are your record.
takeaways: Write down every handover, with a name, a time, and a reason.
Always work on a copy and keep the original sealed and untouched.
Record a hash so any later change to the evidence is easy to spot.

topics.title: Cloud Security Posture Management
topics.summary: Cloud security posture management is the continuous discovery, assessment and remediation of configuration risk across cloud accounts, covering identity grants, network exposure, storage permissions, encryption settings, logging coverage and compliance against a chosen baseline. A CSPM capability connects to provider APIs with read-only credentials, enumerates every resource in scope, evaluates each against policy rules, and reports the drift between intended and actual state with enough context to prioritise. Its output is deliberately different from a vulnerability scanner: rather than finding flaws in code, it finds misconfiguration in deployed infrastructure, which is the dominant cause of cloud incidents. Effective implementations depend on several disciplines. Rules must be mapped to recognised benchmarks so that findings carry external meaning, and they must be tuned so that each alert corresponds to a real risk, because unmanaged volume produces alert fatigue and silent suppression. Ownership has to route to the team able to fix the resource, and the tool must distinguish misconfiguration that is exploitable now from latent risk. Coverage itself is a risk area, since accounts and regions excluded from scanning are invisible, and a new account created outside the pipeline arrives unmonitored. Mature programmes treat posture findings as code defects, feeding them back into templates and guardrails so the same mistake cannot be redeployed.
objectives: You will be able to explain what CSPM evaluates and how it differs from vulnerability scanning, CSPP and cloud infrastructure entitlement work.
You will be able to map posture findings to a recognised benchmark and justify the priority assigned to each.
You will be able to tune noisy rules without suppressing genuine exposure, and identify the tradeoff each suppression introduces.
You will be able to detect coverage gaps such as unscanned accounts, regions and newly created subscriptions.
You will be able to write a posture finding report that a platform team can act on without further triage.

beginner.definition: Cloud security posture management is the practice of continuously checking your cloud accounts for risky settings. It looks at who has access, what is exposed to the internet, how storage is shared, and whether logging and encryption are on. It compares what you have with what you intended.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most cloud incidents start with a simple setting mistake, not clever malware. Someone leaves a storage bucket open, or grants far more access than needed. These gaps are invisible in code review because they live in the live account. Posture management finds them early, before an attacker does, and shows your team what to fix first.
howItWorks: You connect the tool to your cloud account with read-only access, so it can look but not change.
It lists every resource, such as storage buckets, virtual machines, accounts and network rules.
Each resource is compared against written rules that describe a safe setting.
Anything that breaks a rule becomes a finding, with a severity and the reason it matters.
The finding is sent to the team that owns that resource so they can correct it.
The best teams then fix the template that created it, so the same mistake cannot return.
beginner.example: Imagine a large block of flats. The landlord checks the building once a month: are any doors unlocked, are windows open, are fire exits blocked? Nobody broke in, but the survey still finds real risk. Cloud posture management is that monthly walk-through, except it runs continuously and checks every flat at once.
takeaways: Posture management finds configuration mistakes in your live cloud accounts, not in code.
Connect it with read-only access and fix noisy rules so alerts stay useful.
Feed findings back into templates so the same mistake is never deployed again.

topics.title: Cloud Workload Protection Platform
topics.summary: A cloud workload protection platform protects the running compute layer of a cloud estate, covering virtual machines, containers, serverless functions, and increasingly the orchestration control plane that schedules them. Where posture management examines configuration, workload protection examines behaviour at runtime: process execution, file integrity, network connections, privilege changes, memory anomalies, image contents and package vulnerabilities across the whole lifecycle from build to retirement. Typical capability clusters include agent or agentless vulnerability assessment of images and hosts, file and process integrity monitoring, runtime threat detection with behavioural rules, network microsegmentation and flow visibility, container image scanning with admission control, serverless function analysis, and integration of findings into the same incident pipeline as endpoint detection. The operational challenge is that cloud workloads are ephemeral and horizontally scaled, so host-centric assumptions break: a compromised container may live for minutes, identifiers change on every deploy, and an analyst cannot rely on a single stable hostname. Effective programmes therefore anchor detection on immutable artefacts such as image digests, workload identity, service accounts and deployment metadata, and they connect runtime signal to the pipeline that produced the workload. Without that linkage, teams see unusual activity but cannot attribute it to a build, a team or an image, and remediation becomes guesswork.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish what a workload protection platform covers from what posture management and entitlement analysis cover.
You will be able to explain why ephemeral workloads break host-centric detection and what identifiers to anchor on instead.
You will be able to design runtime detection for containers, virtual machines and serverless functions.
You will be able to evaluate agentless and agent-based approaches and state the coverage each misses.
You will be able to triage a runtime workload alert and link it back to the image, pipeline and owning team.
You will be able to feed workload findings into admission control and build gates rather than only into tickets.

beginner.definition: A cloud workload protection platform is a tool that watches the programs actually running in your cloud. It looks at virtual machines, containers and serverless functions while they work, not just how they are set up. It spots strange behaviour, such as unexpected processes or new network connections, and raises an alert.
beginner.whyItMatters: Cloud workloads are short-lived and always changing, so you cannot treat them like fixed servers. A container might live only minutes, then disappear. If nothing watches what runs inside it, an attacker can work quietly and you will never see it. Workload protection gives you that missing view.
howItWorks: You install a small agent, or connect a read-only feed, so the tool can see activity on your workloads.
The tool records what each workload does, such as which programs start and which addresses they connect to.
It compares that behaviour with a baseline of normal activity for that kind of workload.
When something clearly unusual happens, it raises an alert and links it to the image and team that built it.
It also scans the images before they run, so known vulnerable packages are found early.
Your team then investigates, and can feed the result back into the build pipeline as a block.
beginner.example: Think of a busy food court. The health inspector who only checks the plans and licences is doing posture work. The inspector who walks past the counters during service, watching how food is handled right now, is doing workload protection. Both are useful, but only the second one catches a cook leaving food uncovered today.
takeaways: Workload protection watches behaviour while things run, not just their settings.
Cloud workloads are short-lived, so tie alerts to images and owning teams.
Route workload findings into your build pipeline, not only into tickets.
