topics.title: Code Signing
topics.summary: Code signing is the use of a digital signature over a software artifact so that a consumer can verify who produced it and whether it has changed since it was signed. The signer hashes the artifact with a cryptographic digest and signs that digest with a private key; the verifier checks the signature with the corresponding public key, validates the certificate chain to a trusted root, and confirms the artifact digest matches. Signing is the mechanism behind operating system and package manager trust decisions, driver and installer approval, browser extension and mobile application distribution, container image trust policies and artifact repository promotion rules. For a practising engineer the interesting part is everything around the cryptography. Which identity signs, how that identity is proven to the certificate authority, where the private key lives, how the signing operation is authorised and logged, and how the trust decision is enforced at the point of installation or deployment all determine whether signing provides real assurance or merely ceremony. Weaknesses that keep recurring are long-lived unprotected private keys, signing services reachable from a compromised build job, verification that checks a signature exists but not whose it is, timestamping omitted so signatures expire with the certificate, and revocation infrastructure that is never consulted. Modern practice moves towards short-lived keys held in hardware or a managed signing service, keyless signing bound to a workload identity, transparency logs that record every signing event, and build provenance that binds an artifact to the exact source revision and build definition that produced it.
objectives: You will be able to explain the signing and verification flow, including certificate chain validation, digest comparison and the role of timestamping.
You will be able to describe how signing trust is consumed by operating systems, package managers, container runtimes and browsers.
You will be able to design a signing key custody model using hardware modules or managed signing services with authorised, logged use.
You will be able to identify common verification failures, such as accepting any valid signature regardless of signer identity or skipping revocation checks.
You will be able to explain build provenance and how it binds an artifact to its source revision and build definition.
You will be able to assess what a signing programme would and would not prevent if a build system were compromised.

sources.label: RFC 5280: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile
RFC 3161: Internet X.509 PKI Time-Stamp Protocol

beginner.definition: Code signing is the practice of adding a digital signature to a software file so people can check who made it and whether anyone changed it. Think of it as a tamper-evident seal on a package. Your device checks that seal before it trusts the file.
beginner.whyItMatters: Without signing, you cannot tell a real update from a fake one. An attacker could swap a download for malicious software that looks identical. Signing gives your operating system, browser, or package manager a way to say yes or no before running code. It protects millions of users from silent tampering, and it makes attackers work much harder.
howItWorks: The software maker creates a unique private key (a secret code only they hold).
They run a hash, a math function that turns the file into a short fingerprint.
The private key signs that fingerprint, and the signature is published with the file.
Your device rebuilds the fingerprint and checks it against the signed one.
It also checks the certificate chain, the linked proof that the signer is who they claim.
If all checks pass, the file is trusted and the software is allowed to run.
beginner.example: Imagine you order a medicine online. The bottle arrives with a sealed cap and a printed batch number. If the seal is broken, you do not take the medicine. Code signing works the same way. The seal is the signature, and the batch number is the fingerprint of the file. A pharmacy that checks the seal before selling protects you. Software that checks a signature before installing protects your computer the same way.
takeaways: A signature proves who built a file and that nobody changed it.
Always verify the signer identity, not just that a signature exists.
Keep signing keys in hardware or a managed service, never on a laptop.

topics.title: Conditional Access
topics.summary: Conditional access is a policy engine that evaluates signals about a sign-in attempt and then decides whether to allow it, block it, or allow it only after additional requirements are satisfied such as multi-factor authentication, a compliant device or a trusted network location. The signals typically include user or group membership, application being accessed, device platform, device compliance or join state, client application type, source IP address and named location, and sign-in risk or user risk computed by the identity provider. This is the mechanism that turns identity from a binary decision into a graded one, and it is the practical enforcement point for zero trust principles in most enterprise estates today because it can require stronger evidence for sensitive applications while keeping low-risk access frictionless. The security outcome depends entirely on policy coverage and on how exceptions are managed: a policy that excludes a service account, a legacy protocol client or a break-glass identity creates a path that does not require the control, and adversaries deliberately hunt for those paths by attempting authentication through older client stacks that cannot satisfy modern requirements. Policy design therefore needs both a default posture that blocks what is not explicitly permitted and a deliberate, documented set of exclusions with compensating monitoring. Orchestration between policies matters too, since many platforms combine all applicable policies and require satisfaction of every grant control they contain, so an apparently narrow policy can change behaviour for a large population. Defenders rely on the resulting telemetry, because sign-in logs annotated with policy outcomes allow alerting on repeated policy failures from one identity, on successful sign-ins that bypassed an expected control, and on new or modified policy definitions that quietly weaken posture.
objectives: You will be able to enumerate the signals available to a conditional access policy and select the ones relevant to a stated requirement.
You will be able to distinguish grant controls from session controls and explain how multiple applicable policies combine.
You will be able to design a policy set with a blocking default and documented, monitored exclusions.
You will be able to identify bypass paths created by legacy authentication clients, service accounts and break-glass identities.
You will be able to detect policy weakening by monitoring changes to policy definitions alongside sign-in outcomes.
You will be able to troubleshoot a user access failure by reading policy evaluation results in the sign-in log.

beginner.definition: Conditional access is a gate that checks each sign-in attempt before it lets someone in. It looks at signals, which are clues about the request. Then it allows access, blocks access, or asks for extra proof before continuing.
beginner.whyItMatters: A password alone cannot tell you if the person signing in is the real owner. Conditional access adds context, so a stolen password is often not enough. It keeps normal work smooth while guarding sensitive systems. Without it, every account becomes an all-or-nothing door that anyone can open with one secret.
howItWorks: Someone tries to sign in to an application, usually with a username and password.
The system gathers signals, such as the device, the location, and the risk of the sign-in.
Rules written by your team are checked against those signals one by one.
The result is allow, block, or allow only after the user passes another check.
Sensitive applications can demand stronger proof, while routine work stays quick and simple.
beginner.example: Picture an airport security queue. Everyone shows a passport, which is like a password. But some travellers are pulled aside for a bag search, a fingerprint check, or extra questions. The decision depends on the destination, the ticket, and the risk on the day. Nothing is banned outright. Instead, the same door opens with different levels of proof.
takeaways: Conditional access decides each sign-in using clues, not just a password.
Exclusions in a rule become open doors, so review and monitor every exception.
Start from a blocking default and allow only what you have clearly agreed.

topics.title: Confidence Level
topics.summary: Confidence is the explicit, calibrated expression of how much weight an analytic judgement should carry, and it is distinct from the likelihood that an event will occur. A useful threat intelligence product states both: how reliable the sourcing is, and how strongly the analysis supports the conclusion. It then uses consistent estimative wording so consumers can rank competing claims against each other. Source reliability and information credibility are frequently assessed with a two-axis scheme that rates the source from completely reliable to unreliable and the information from confirmed to improbable, which produces a compact code an analyst can attach to each statement. Analytic confidence is a different judgement. It reflects the quality and quantity of evidence, the coherence of the argument, the soundness of the methods used, and the extent to which alternatives were considered. Established intelligence community standards for analytic writing require that judgements be sourced, that uncertainty be expressed in words with defined meanings, and that probability be distinguished from confidence. In practice, teams define a small vocabulary and keep to it, for example low, moderate and high confidence paired with stated reasons, and they avoid vague hedges such as possibly or could be, which carry no ranking information. Common failure modes include overconfidence driven by a single vivid source, anchoring on an initial vendor attribution, and treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence when collection was never attempted. Calibration improves by recording judgements and later scoring them against outcomes, by peer review that challenges the reasoning rather than the conclusion, and by writing estimative statements a reader can falsify. For defenders, confidence determines action: high-confidence judgements may justify immediate blocking or escalation, while low-confidence reporting should generate hunting, monitoring or collection requirements rather than disruptive change.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish source reliability, information credibility, analytic confidence and likelihood within one product.
You will be able to apply a defined confidence vocabulary consistently and state the reasoning behind each rating.
You will be able to replace vague hedging with ranked estimative wording that a reader can falsify.
You will be able to identify overconfidence, anchoring and absence-of-evidence fallacies in a draft assessment.
You will be able to map confidence levels to proportionate defensive action, from monitoring through to blocking.
You will be able to design a simple calibration record that scores past judgements against observed outcomes.

sources.label: NIST Computer Security Resource Center publications

beginner.definition: A confidence level is a label on a piece of threat intelligence. It says how much weight that claim should carry. It describes how strong the evidence is, not how likely an attack is. Teams often use words like low, moderate and high, and they explain their reasons.
beginner.whyItMatters: Threat reports arrive from many places, and they often disagree with each other. Without a confidence level, you cannot rank them. You might block a harmless address because of one weak rumour. Or you might ignore a serious warning that came from a strong source. A shared confidence vocabulary lets a whole team act in proportion. High confidence can justify immediate blocking, while low confidence should start a hunt instead.
howItWorks: Ask two separate questions. How trustworthy is the source, and how credible is this specific piece of information?
Rate the source. A well-known research team is stronger than an anonymous forum post.
Rate the evidence itself. Was it seen directly, or is it only a rumour passed along?
Choose a confidence word from a small fixed list, such as low, moderate or high.
Write down your reason, and name the evidence that would change your mind.
Match the action to the level. Block on high confidence, and hunt quietly on low confidence.
beginner.example: Think about a weather forecast. A presenter might say there is a high chance of rain tomorrow. That is a probability. Separately, you trust the forecast more when several models agree and the sky already looks grey. That is confidence. The two ideas are different. A forecast can be very likely and still be low confidence if the data is thin. Threat intelligence works exactly the same way, so you should report both.
takeaways: Confidence describes the strength of your evidence, not the chance an attack will happen.
Use a small fixed set of confidence words, and always write down your reason.
Let the confidence level decide the response, from quiet hunting up to immediate blocking.

topics.title: Container Escape
topics.summary: Container escape is the class of techniques by which a process confined to a container reaches the underlying host, another tenant's container, or the cluster control plane, converting a workload compromise into infrastructure compromise. Containers share the host kernel, so the boundary is enforced by kernel features such as namespaces, control groups, capabilities, mandatory access control profiles and seccomp filters rather than by a hypervisor, and escape generally follows from a configuration or kernel flaw that weakens those controls. Recurring categories include privileged containers that hold effectively all capabilities and device access, containers mounting the host filesystem or the container runtime socket, excessive Linux capabilities combined with writable host paths, host namespace sharing for networking or process identifiers, kernel vulnerabilities reachable from within a container, and misconfigured runtime or orchestration components that trust client input excessively. The consequences of a successful escape are severe because the host usually holds credentials: node identity, cluster service account tokens, cloud instance role credentials reachable through the metadata endpoint, and secrets mounted for other workloads. Defensive practice therefore concentrates on preventing the conditions rather than only detecting the technique: forbid privileged mode and host path mounts, drop capabilities, run read-only root filesystems, apply seccomp and mandatory access control, isolate with user namespaces or sandboxed runtimes, restrict access to the runtime socket, and assume that any workload with host access has already compromised the node.
objectives: You will be able to explain why containers share the host kernel and how namespaces, capabilities and mandatory access control form the boundary.
You will be able to identify workload configurations that make escape trivial, including privileged mode, host paths and runtime socket mounts.
You will be able to design admission policy that blocks the preconditions for escape before deployment.
You will be able to describe what credentials and mounted secrets become reachable after a node is compromised.
You will be able to triage container escape indicators such as host namespace access and unexpected device usage.
You will be able to rank escape paths by realistic exploitability and business impact for a report.

beginner.definition: A container escape happens when a program trapped inside a container breaks out and reaches the machine underneath it. Containers share the same operating system kernel (the core of the system), so the wall between them is thinner than a full virtual machine. A mistake in settings or in the kernel can let someone step outside.
beginner.whyItMatters: If a container escape succeeds, the attacker is no longer stuck in one small app. They can reach the host machine, other customers' containers, or the cluster control plane. The host often holds valuable keys, such as cloud credentials and tokens for other services. One escape can turn a small problem into a whole-platform problem.
howItWorks: An attacker first gets code running inside a container, often through a bug in the app.
They look for weak settings, such as running in privileged mode, which grants almost full control.
They also check for the host disk or the runtime socket being mounted inside the container.
Using that access, they try to read host files, kernel features, or the cloud metadata endpoint.
If it works, they can steal node credentials and move to other workloads in the cluster.
Defenders prevent this by blocking privileged containers and host mounts before deployment.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel. Each guest room is a container, and the corridor and master keys belong to the host. Normally a guest stays in their room. But if the room door was fitted badly, the guest can step into the corridor, try other doors, and perhaps reach the staff office with the master key cabinet. That is a container escape.
takeaways: Containers share the host kernel, so the boundary depends on correct settings.
Privileged mode and host mounts are the most common escape preconditions.
Block risky settings at deployment time, not only after an alert.

topics.title: Containment
topics.summary: Containment is the incident response phase in which a team deliberately limits the spread, impact and persistence of an active intrusion while preserving both the evidence and the business functions needed to recover. It is a risk decision made with incomplete information: the analyst usually knows that at least one host or identity is compromised and does not yet know the full scope, so containment trades some operational disruption for a reduced chance that the adversary moves laterally, exfiltrates data or re-establishes access from a foothold nobody has found. Short-term containment is applied within minutes to hours and is usually blunt - network isolation of an endpoint, disabling an account, blocking a command-and-control destination at the egress proxy or DNS resolver, revoking active sessions and tokens, or rotating exposed credentials. Long-term containment keeps the environment stable while eradication and recovery are planned, often by segmenting affected subnets, applying temporary compensating controls, or standing up clean rebuild infrastructure. Effective containment depends on decisions made long before the incident: who has authority to take production systems offline, how isolation is technically performed without tipping off the adversary, and how forensic images and volatile data are captured before a rebuild destroys them. Containment carries risk of its own, because an attacker who detects isolation may accelerate destructive action, so timing and sequencing matter. Teams document every containment action with a timestamp, an owner and a rationale, because those records support later scoping, legal hold and regulatory reporting.
objectives: Define containment in terms of the spread, impact and evidence tradeoffs it is intended to manage.
Differentiate short-term and long-term containment and select the appropriate approach for a given intrusion stage.
Identify the pre-approved authority, contacts and tooling required to isolate a production system without delay.
Sequence containment actions so that volatile evidence is captured before rebuilds, reboots or log rotation destroy it.
Recognise the operational and adversary-detection risks created by isolation, account revocation and traffic blocking.
Document containment decisions so they support later scoping, legal hold and regulatory notification.
Evaluate whether a proposed containment action is proportionate to the scope of compromise that has actually been confirmed.

sources.label: CISA - Incident response and cyber defense resources
NIST Computer Security Resource Center - incident handling and contingency guidance
Microsoft Learn - security operations and endpoint isolation documentation

beginner.definition: Containment is the incident response step where you deliberately limit an active attack. You try to stop the attacker from spreading, causing more damage, or keeping a way back in. At the same time you protect evidence and keep the business running. It is a fast risk decision made with incomplete information.
beginner.whyItMatters: Every minute an intruder stays connected, they can steal more data or move to another system. Containment buys you time and limits the damage. But you rarely know the full scope, so you must act while some facts are unknown. Without a plan, nobody knows who may switch off a production server.
howItWorks: Confirm at least one compromised host or account, then decide how urgent the situation is.
Choose short-term actions that stop the spread, such as isolating a machine from the network.
Disable or reset the affected accounts and end their active login sessions.
Block the network destinations the attacker used, so their remote control channel stops working.
Capture memory and logs before you rebuild, because cleanup destroys evidence.
Move to longer-term containment, such as splitting networks, while you plan full removal.
beginner.example: Picture water pouring from a burst pipe in your kitchen. You do not stop to find the exact crack first. You shut the main valve, which stops the flood but also cuts water to the whole house. Later a plumber fixes the pipe and you turn the water back on. Containment is that valve. You accept some disruption now to prevent a much bigger loss.
takeaways: Containment limits spread and damage while you still lack full facts.
Decide in advance who can isolate a system, so nobody wastes time.
Save evidence before cleanup, because rebuilding a machine erases memory.

topics.title: Control Gap
topics.summary: A control gap is the measurable difference between the protection an organisation believes it has and the protection that is actually implemented, operating and effective. Three distinct failure modes hide inside that single phrase, and separating them is the core skill. A design gap exists when no control addresses the risk at all, for example no privileged access review for a tier-zero identity store. An implementation gap exists when a control is defined but not deployed everywhere it is needed, such as endpoint detection present on workstations but absent on the servers that hold the crown jewels. An operating effectiveness gap exists when the control is deployed but does not function as intended, which covers disabled logging, alert rules that never fire, exceptions that quietly became permanent, and configuration drift after a change. Practitioners find gaps through several converging sources: control testing and walkthroughs, framework crosswalks against a target baseline, attack-path or red-team findings, audit and assessment reports, incident and near-miss analysis, and telemetry coverage checks that compare an asset inventory against the systems actually reporting logs. Ranking gaps requires more than counting, because a missing detection on an identity provider that can reach everything matters more than a missing hardening baseline on an isolated lab. Good gap registers record the evidence, the affected scope, the residual risk, the remediation owner, the acceptance criteria and the verification method that will prove closure, and they distinguish genuine remediation from documentation that merely restates the intent.
objectives: You will be able to separate design, implementation and operating effectiveness gaps when reviewing a control failure.
You will be able to build a telemetry coverage comparison between asset inventory and systems actually reporting logs.
You will be able to derive gaps from framework crosswalks, control testing and red-team findings rather than opinion.
You will be able to rank gaps by reachability and business impact instead of by raw count.
You will be able to write remediation entries with owners, acceptance criteria and a defined verification method.
You will be able to detect where a compensating control or accepted exception has become a permanent silent gap.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-53 security and privacy controls

beginner.definition: A control gap is the difference between the protection you think you have and the protection that truly works. The safeguard may be missing by design, deployed in only some places, or present but broken. Finding the real difference is what keeps a security plan honest.
beginner.whyItMatters: You can pass a checklist review while still being exposed. A gap hides in the space between the written policy and what runs on the machines. If nobody measures that space, you spend money on paper and get no real protection. Finding gaps early lets you fix the important ones before an attacker finds them for you.
howItWorks: List the risks you care about and the safeguards meant to reduce each one.
Check whether a safeguard exists at all, which is a design gap.
Check whether it runs everywhere it is needed, which is a coverage gap.
Test whether it truly works today, because that is an effectiveness gap.
Gather proof from control tests, audits, incidents and log coverage reports.
Rank the gaps by reach and business harm, then give each one an owner.
beginner.example: Imagine a building with a fire alarm policy on the wall. The policy says every floor has a smoke detector. On inspection, one floor has none, which is a design gap. Another floor has detectors that were never wired to the alarm panel, which is a coverage gap. A third floor has detectors with dead batteries, which is an effectiveness gap. Reading the policy alone told you nothing true.
takeaways: A written policy is not proof that a safeguard is installed or working.
Separate missing, partial and broken controls, because each needs a different fix.
Rank gaps by what an attacker could reach, not by how many you found.

topics.title: Cyber Kill Chain
topics.summary: The Cyber Kill Chain is a seven-stage model of an intrusion that describes how an adversary progresses from reconnaissance to mission impact. The stages are reconnaissance, weaponisation, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives. Its purpose is not to describe every intrusion precisely but to give defenders a shared vocabulary and a set of choke points where activity can be detected or disrupted before the adversary reaches the final stage. The model rests on an asymmetry: the adversary must succeed at every stage, while defenders need to break only one link, which reframes defence as cost imposition rather than perfect prevention. In practice the chain is most useful for structuring detection coverage reviews, sequencing incident narratives and choosing controls. Hardening the external attack surface targets reconnaissance. Mail and web filtering target delivery. Patch management and exploit mitigations target exploitation. Application control and endpoint hardening target installation. Network monitoring and egress control target command and control. Data loss prevention, backup integrity and segmentation limit actions on objectives. The model has well-known limitations. It was written with perimeter intrusion in mind, so it maps awkwardly to cloud identity attacks, supply-chain compromises, insider activity and hands-on-keyboard operations that skip or reorder stages. It is also linear, while real intrusions loop, repeat and run stages concurrently. Analysts therefore commonly pair it with ATT&CK for technique-level detail and with the Diamond Model for actor and infrastructure context. Used with those caveats, the kill chain remains a durable briefing tool because non-specialist stakeholders can follow it, and it exposes where an organisation has no detection at all rather than merely where its tools are noisy.
objectives: You will be able to name the seven Cyber Kill Chain stages and place observed activity into the correct stage.
You will be able to identify the choke points where a control or detection can break the chain before impact.
You will be able to explain why the model fits perimeter intrusions better than cloud identity or supply-chain attacks.
You will be able to translate a kill-chain coverage review into a prioritised list of missing controls.
You will be able to combine kill-chain narrative structure with technique mapping in a single incident write-up.
You will be able to brief non-specialist stakeholders using chain stages without overstating the model's precision.

sources.label: NIST Computer Security Resource Center publications

beginner.definition: The Cyber Kill Chain is a seven step model of how an intrusion unfolds. It starts with planning and ends with the attacker reaching their goal. Each step is a chance for defenders to break the attack. The steps are reconnaissance, weaponisation, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives.
beginner.whyItMatters: The attacker must succeed at every step, but you only need to stop one. That is a huge advantage. The model helps you see where your defences have holes. Maybe you detect delivery well but never notice an attacker quietly controlling a machine. Naming the stages also gives your team and your managers a shared language. You can then fix the weakest link instead of buying more tools.
howItWorks: Reconnaissance. The attacker studies your company, your staff and your public systems before doing anything.
Weaponisation and delivery. They build a harmful file or link and send it by email or a fake website.
Exploitation. A bug in your software lets the attacker run their code on one of your machines.
Installation. The attacker plants something on the machine so they can return after a restart.
Command and control. The infected machine quietly calls home to receive its orders.
Actions on objectives. The attacker steals data, encrypts files or damages your systems.
beginner.example: Think of a burglar trying to enter your home. First they watch the house and note when you leave. Then they pick a lock or copy a key. Then they slip inside. Once in, they prop open a back door so they can return easily. Finally they carry out your television. You could stop this at any point. A light on a timer spoils the watching, a strong lock spoils the entry, and a loud alarm spoils the escape.
takeaways: The attacker must win at every stage, while you only need to break one link.
Use the seven stages to find where your detection coverage is missing.
The model fits older network attacks better than cloud, supply chain or insider threats.

topics.title: Dark Web Monitoring
topics.summary: Dark web monitoring is the systematic collection and analysis of content from sources that mainstream search engines do not index, including criminal forums, illicit marketplaces, paste sites, private messaging channels, ransomware leak sites and credential dumps, in order to detect exposure, fraud enablers and threats to an organisation. For defenders it supports four main use cases: discovering leaked or stolen credentials and session material before it is used, identifying brand impersonation and phishing infrastructure, learning about planned or ongoing campaigns that name the organisation or its suppliers, and gathering adversary tradecraft that can be turned into detection. Collection is harder than it first appears. Sources are ephemeral and hostile, registration often requires vouching or payment, access carries legal, contractual and personal safety risk, and much of the content is recycled, fabricated or seeded by criminals and by researchers themselves. Verification is therefore the core analyst skill: a credential listing proves nothing until a controlled check confirms it is current, and a forum post claiming an intrusion may simply be a sales pitch. Sound programmes use dedicated isolated collection environments, maintain strict separation between collection identities and corporate infrastructure, operate under rules of engagement approved by legal and leadership, and handle material that may contain personal data in line with privacy regulation. Output is only valuable when it reaches a workflow, so mature teams route validated findings into identity remediation, takedown requests, fraud monitoring and intelligence reporting, and they record which sources produced results and which produced noise.
objectives: You will be able to define collection requirements that connect dark web monitoring to specific defensive decisions.
You will be able to explain the legal, privacy and personal safety constraints that govern covert collection and reporting.
You will be able to validate leaked credential and access listings before triggering remediation or escalation.
You will be able to distinguish genuine exposure from recycled, fabricated or researcher-seeded content.
You will be able to route validated findings into identity, fraud, takedown and intelligence workflows.
You will be able to measure source productivity and retire collection that generates noise without decisions.

sources.label: NIST Computer Security Resource Center publications

beginner.definition: Dark web monitoring means watching hidden online places for signs that your organisation has been exposed. These places include criminal forums, marketplaces and leak sites that normal search engines do not list. The goal is to find stolen passwords or plans against you early. Then you can act before the attacker does.
beginner.whyItMatters: Stolen passwords are often sold long before anyone uses them. If you find them first, you can reset them and lock the account. That removes an easy way in. Monitoring also reveals fake websites that copy your brand to trick customers. Ignoring all this leaves you blind. You may learn about a leak only when a criminal logs in, which is far too late.
howItWorks: Set a clear question first. Decide what you want to learn, such as leaked staff logins.
Collect carefully, using isolated machines and research identities that stay away from work accounts.
Treat everything as untrusted. Much of this content is old, copied, fake or planted by other researchers.
Verify before you act. Check whether a leaked password still works, using an approved and safe process.
Route real findings to the right team, such as identity, fraud or legal, with a deadline.
Record which sources gave useful results, and stop paying for the ones that only make noise.
beginner.example: Imagine you lose your wallet. Someone finds it and sells your bank card details to a stranger online. You do not know yet, and nothing bad has happened. A monitoring service is like a friend who watches those market stalls. They see your card listed and tell you at once. You call the bank and cancel the card before anyone spends your money. That early warning is the whole value.
takeaways: Find stolen credentials early so you can reset them before an attacker logs in.
Treat dark web content as unverified, because much of it is old or fake.
Only collect within agreed rules, and keep your research identity away from work systems.

topics.title: Detection as Code
topics.summary: Detection as code is the practice of managing detection content, meaning rules, correlation logic, enrichment mappings and the tests that validate them, with the same engineering discipline applied to application source code. Detection logic lives in a version control repository rather than being clicked into a console. Changes arrive as reviewed pull requests with an author, a reviewer and a written rationale. Every rule carries structured metadata: an identifier, a description, the ATT&CK techniques it addresses, the required log sources, a severity and a documented owner. A continuous integration pipeline validates syntax against the target platform's schema, lints for required fields, checks that referenced log sources exist, executes unit tests against sample events that should and should not fire the rule, and then deploys through environments in a controlled fashion. The benefits are concrete rather than aesthetic. History answers when a detection changed, who changed it and why, which is exactly what an incident review needs. Tests catch the regression where a well-meaning edit to shared logic silently breaks unrelated rules. Portability improves because content expressed in a vendor-neutral format can be translated to several query languages instead of being rewritten by hand. The genuine difficulties are also concrete: keeping the tests' sample telemetry representative of production, handling secrets and environment-specific values without committing them, preventing repository drift from what is actually deployed in the console, and staffing the review process so that it does not simply become an approval rubber stamp. Detection as code therefore succeeds only when the pipeline and the review culture are real, not when a repository is created and left to diverge.
objectives: You will be able to explain how version control, peer review and automated validation change the lifecycle of a detection rule.
You will be able to author a rule with structured metadata that identifies its owner, required log sources, severity and ATT&CK coverage.
You will be able to write positive and negative test cases for a rule and explain why both are required to catch regressions.
You will be able to build a continuous integration check that validates rule syntax and schema before deployment.
You will be able to detect and remediate drift between the content repository and the rules actually deployed in production.
You will be able to design a review process that produces substantive feedback rather than routine approval.

sources.label: Sigma: generic signature format for SIEM systems

beginner.definition: Detection as code means treating your security detection rules like software source code. Rules live in a shared code repository instead of being clicked into a console. Every change is reviewed by another person and tested automatically. This gives you a clear history of what changed, who changed it, and why.
beginner.whyItMatters: Detection rules are small programs, and small programs break. Someone edits a shared part, and ten unrelated rules quietly stop working. Without a written history, nobody can tell when a rule changed or who approved it. Version control and automated tests catch these mistakes before an attacker benefits from them.
howItWorks: You write each detection rule as a text file and store it in a code repository.
The file includes metadata: what the rule finds, which logs it needs, and who owns it.
When you want to change a rule, you open a pull request that a colleague reviews.
An automated pipeline checks the rule's syntax and runs test data through it.
The test data includes events that should match and events that should never match.
Only after the checks pass does the pipeline deploy the rule to the live platform.
beginner.example: Think of a restaurant kitchen with a shared recipe book. Any chef who wants to change the soup recipe writes the change on paper, and the head chef reads it first. If the new recipe is bad, the old page is still there. Nobody scribbles over the book in secret. Detection as code is that recipe book for security rules. You can always see what the soup used to be.
takeaways: Store detection rules in a repository, not only inside a tool console.
Every rule needs an owner, a purpose and a review date.
Test rules with good and bad sample events before you trust them.

topics.title: Diamond Model
topics.summary: The Diamond Model is an intrusion analysis framework that describes every malicious event as the interaction of four core features: an adversary, a capability, an infrastructure and a victim. The adversary is the actor or group directing activity. The capability is the tool, malware, exploit or credential the actor wields. The infrastructure is the physical or logical channel used to deliver the capability and control it, such as a domain, mail service, virtual private server or compromised host. The victim is the target, whether a person, organisation, account, asset or data set. Each event is drawn as a diamond with those four vertices. The value of the model lies in its edges and the pivots they permit: given any single known vertex, an analyst can reason about the others, and a confirmed link on one edge strengthens hypotheses along the rest. If two events share infrastructure and a capability but differ in victim, that suggests a broader campaign. If two share a victim and a capability but use different infrastructure, that suggests the actor is rotating channels defensively. The model also carries a socio-political meta-feature layer and, in the extended form, a technology meta-feature, acknowledging that adversary motivation and victim characteristics shape activity as much as tools do. Because the Diamond Model is event-centric, it complements rather than replaces kill-chain and ATT&CK views: it answers who did what to whom using what, while ATT&CK answers how. In practice, analysts use it to cluster events, generate collection requirements, prioritise intelligence gaps and document confidence. Its limits are equally important. The model is descriptive, so it imposes no analytic rigour by itself, and pivoting from infrastructure alone is prone to the same false attribution traps as any single-source inference.
objectives: You will be able to label the four Diamond Model vertices and the edges between them for a given intrusion report.
You will be able to pivot from a known infrastructure vertex to defensible hypotheses about capability and adversary.
You will be able to cluster multiple events into a campaign by comparing shared and divergent vertices.
You will be able to explain how the Diamond Model complements ATT&CK and kill-chain analysis instead of replacing them.
You will be able to identify intelligence gaps as missing vertices or unsupported edges and turn them into collection requirements.
You will be able to document an intrusion narrative that keeps observed events separate from inferential claims.

sources.label: NIST Computer Security Resource Center publications

beginner.definition: The Diamond Model is a way to describe a single attack using four parts. They are the adversary (the attacker), the capability (the tool), the infrastructure (the channel) and the victim (the target). Every event has all four, and drawing them as a diamond shows the links between them.
beginner.whyItMatters: One alert on its own tells you very little. The Diamond Model pushes you to ask the missing questions. Who did this? With what tool? Through which channel? Against whom? When you can fill all four corners, you understand the event much better. It also helps you connect separate alerts into one campaign. That turns scattered noise into a story you can act on.
howItWorks: Write the four corners for the event you are studying: adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim.
Mark what you actually observed, and leave the corners you are only guessing clearly empty.
Pivot from a known corner. If you know the domain, ask which tool and which victim connect to it.
Compare events. Two events that share infrastructure and tool may belong to one campaign.
Note the gaps. Missing corners become questions for your next round of collection.
Keep facts apart from guesses, and record how confident each link between corners is.
beginner.example: A hospital analogy. A patient arrives with a fever. The nurse records four things: who the patient is, what the symptoms are, how the illness arrived and what the likely cause is. Any single detail alone is weak. Together they point to a diagnosis. If three more patients arrive with the same symptoms from the same street, the nurse spots an outbreak. The Diamond Model links single events into patterns in the same way.
takeaways: Every attack event has four corners: adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim.
Known corners let you make careful, testable guesses about the unknown ones.
Shared corners across events suggest one campaign rather than many separate incidents.

topics.title: Disk Imaging
topics.summary: Disk imaging is the process of creating a bit-for-bit copy of a storage device, or of a defined set of allocated and unallocated regions, so that examination happens on a working copy while the original remains sealed and unmodified. The image captures everything the file system exposes plus what it does not: deleted file remnants, slack space, partition and boot sectors, volume snapshots, swap and hibernation files, and file system metadata such as timestamps and journal records. Because a single capture preserves all of that in one verifiable artefact, imaging is preferable to live file copying whenever the media can be removed or safely quiesced, and it is frequently the only way to recover deleted or partially overwritten material. Acquisition runs through a write blocker, either hardware or a validated software equivalent, and the resulting image is verified with a cryptographic hash computed at acquisition and again after transfer, since a mismatch invalidates the copy. Formats matter for practicality: raw images are simple and widely supported but large, while compressed or segmented formats with embedded metadata suit evidence transport and long-term retention. Logistics are as important as tooling, including capacity estimation, planning downtime for servers that cannot simply be taken offline, documenting the exact device and range captured, labelling media, and storing images in access-controlled locations. Analysis then covers file system parsing, deleted file recovery, artifact extraction and correlation with memory, log and network evidence.
objectives: Explain what a bit-for-bit image captures that a live file copy does not, including unallocated and slack space.
Select an acquisition approach, image format and tool for a given device, downtime window and evidence volume.
Perform a write-blocked acquisition and verify it with cryptographic hashes at acquisition and after transfer.
Document device identity, captured range, tooling, operator and hash values in a defensible acquisition record.
Plan storage, labelling and retention for large images with sensitivity and legal-hold requirements in mind.
Recover deleted and partially overwritten artefacts from an image and explain their evidential limits.
Correlate disk artefacts with memory, identity and network evidence to support a scoped incident narrative.

sources.label: SANS Institute - digital forensics and incident response resources
NIST Computer Security Resource Center - forensic media acquisition guidance

beginner.definition: Disk imaging means making an exact, bit-for-bit copy of a storage device. Every part is copied, including deleted files, empty space, and hidden system areas. You then examine the copy and leave the original safe. The copy is called an image, and it acts as your evidence.
beginner.whyItMatters: Deleted files often still sit on the disk, and a normal file copy misses them. An image keeps that hidden material in one verifiable package. It also protects the original device from accidental changes. Without imaging, your analysis may destroy the very clues you need, and nobody can check your work later.
howItWorks: Decide what to copy and whether the machine can be safely taken offline first.
Connect the drive through a write blocker, a device that allows reading but blocks writing.
Copy every sector of the drive into one image file, including unused space.
Calculate a hash, a fingerprint of the image, right after the copy finishes.
Calculate the hash again before analysis, and check that both values match.
Examine only the copy, and store the original drive sealed and labelled.
beginner.example: Think of photographing a messy room before anyone cleans it. One wide photo of everything is better than a few close-ups. If you tidy first, small details are gone forever. A disk image is that wide photo. It captures the whole scene, including the corners you did not know mattered. Later you can zoom in as often as you like.
takeaways: An image copies everything, including deleted files and unused space.
A write blocker stops you from accidentally changing the original drive.
Matching hashes before and after copying show the image is unchanged.

topics.title: Distributed Denial of Service
topics.summary: A distributed denial of service attack attempts to make a service unavailable by exhausting a resource, using many sources so that no single host can simply be blocked. Volume-based attacks saturate network links with floods of packets or bytes. Protocol attacks consume state on network devices or servers, for example by exhausting connection tables or abusing a handshake so that half-open sessions accumulate. Application-layer attacks send requests that look individually legitimate but are expensive to serve, such as repeated searches, login attempts or interface calls that trigger heavy database work, so modest traffic volumes can still cause outages. Modern campaigns are frequently multi-vector and short, blending floods with application requests to defeat single-layer defences, and they are sometimes paired with extortion, used as distraction from another intrusion, or used as cover for data theft. Mitigation is layered and depends on where capacity actually exists. Upstream scrubbing services and content delivery networks absorb volumetric traffic and filter close to the source, which is essential because local links are usually far smaller than the attack. On-premises appliances handle smaller floods and can act quickly, but they cannot exceed the size of the circuits they protect. Application defences include caching, rate limiting per identity rather than per address, restricting expensive endpoints, and requiring a challenge for suspicious clients. Preparation matters more than any single tool: a written runbook that names who can enable scrubbing, how traffic is rerouted and how providers are contacted turns a panic into a procedure. Monitoring should include baseline traffic profiles, alerts on abnormal connection counts and response latency, and periodic testing of failover and mitigation paths, while post-incident review should separate genuine capacity failures from outages caused by a mitigation that blocked legitimate users.
objectives: You will be able to classify volumetric, protocol and application-layer attacks and the resource each exhausts.
You will be able to baseline normal traffic and recognise the onset of an attack from monitoring data.
You will be able to design layered mitigation across upstream scrubbing, local appliances and application controls.
You will be able to write and rehearse a mitigation runbook with clear decision rights and provider contacts.
You will be able to distinguish a real capacity failure from an outage caused by over-blocking.
You will be able to rank multi-vector attack scenarios by business impact for a given service.

sources.label: SANS Institute Research and White Papers

beginner.definition: A distributed denial of service attack, or DDoS, is an attempt to knock a service offline by flooding it with traffic from many machines at once. The word distributed matters, because the requests come from thousands of places. You cannot simply block one address and make it stop.
beginner.whyItMatters: Any service that people depend on can be pushed offline, from a shop to a hospital booking system. Attackers may also use a flood as a distraction while they steal data somewhere else. Without preparation, your team will panic and guess. With a written plan and upstream help, the same attack becomes a routine event you can absorb.
howItWorks: Attackers build a botnet, which is a large group of infected computers they can command remotely.
They point all those machines at one target and send far more traffic than it can handle.
Some floods fill the network link; others exhaust connection tables or slow application logic.
Real users then cannot connect, so the service looks broken even though nothing was hacked.
Your provider diverts traffic through a scrubbing centre, which filters the flood and passes good traffic.
You also rate-limit and cache at the application, then review what happened afterwards.
beginner.example: Picture a small shop with one door. Ten customers can come and go comfortably. Now imagine a thousand people crowded into the doorway, not buying anything, just standing there. Real customers cannot get in, and the shop loses money without anything being stolen. That is a flood attack. If you hired a bigger doorway and a doorman who only lets genuine shoppers through, you would be doing what a scrubbing service does.
takeaways: DDoS means many machines flooding one service until real users cannot get in.
You cannot absorb a large flood locally; upstream filtering does the heavy lifting.
Write and rehearse the plan before the attack, not during it.

topics.title: DNS Tunnelling
topics.summary: DNS tunnelling is a technique for carrying arbitrary data inside DNS queries and responses, exploiting the fact that name resolution is permitted almost everywhere, including networks where most other outbound traffic is blocked. An adversary who controls an authoritative name server can encode payload in the leftmost labels of a query, for example a long high-entropy subdomain, and receive data back through the response, producing a bidirectional covert channel without ever opening a direct connection to an external host. The same mechanism supports exfiltration, with stolen data chunked across successive queries, and it can carry a command channel, which is why defenders usually treat it as DNS-based command and control or exfiltration over DNS rather than as a standalone intrusion technique. Detection rests on behaviour rather than payload, because the queries themselves are well formed. Useful signals include sustained query volume to a single domain, unusually long or random-looking labels, high randomness in subdomain strings, unusual record types, elevated rates of non-existent domain responses, and low-and-slow patterns designed to stay under rate thresholds. Tuning is difficult because legitimate services share some of those characteristics: content delivery networks, endpoint telemetry agents and software update mechanisms all generate high query volume to a small set of names, and security products themselves use DNS for reputation lookups. Effective detection therefore combines several weak signals, baselines per host and per domain, and enrichment with reputation, registration age and resolution history rather than relying on any single rule. Mitigation is layered: restrict recursive resolvers to internal clients, block direct outbound DNS from endpoints, log and retain query data centrally, monitor authoritative servers for the organisation's own domains, and use response policy zones to block known malicious names.
objectives: You will be able to explain how data is encoded into DNS queries and responses and why the channel bypasses egress filtering.
You will be able to build detection queries using label length, entropy, volume and response-code patterns.
You will be able to baseline legitimate high-volume DNS consumers and reduce false positives.
You will be able to distinguish exfiltration over DNS from beaconing and from ordinary resolution failures.
You will be able to design resolver, egress and response policy controls that constrain tunnelling without breaking resolution.
You will be able to assess why a hard block of DNS is rarely acceptable and what compensating controls apply.

sources.label: RFC 1035: Domain Names, Implementation and Specification

beginner.definition: DNS, the Domain Name System, is the internet's address book. It turns a name like example[.]com into an address. DNS tunnelling hides other data inside those name lookups. Because almost every network allows DNS out, an attacker can slip stolen files or secret commands through a channel that looks like ordinary browsing.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most networks block unusual outbound traffic but must allow DNS, or nothing works. That makes DNS a quiet exit route for stolen data and hidden control messages. It is hard to spot because the lookups are valid. You need to watch the shape of DNS traffic, not just its content, and keep good records so you can look back later.
howItWorks: A program on an infected machine builds a strange name, such as a long random string, and asks for it.
That name reaches a name server the attacker controls, which reads the hidden data inside it.
The server replies with another crafted name, so information travels back the same way.
Many small lookups follow, so no single one looks large or suspicious on its own.
Defenders spot the pattern instead: long labels, odd characters and heavy traffic to one domain.
They then restrict which servers can answer and block the domain at the resolver.
beginner.example: Think of a school where notes are banned, but students may ask the office for a lost item's name. A clever pair sends messages by asking about made-up names, one letter at a time. Each question sounds innocent, yet the answers spell out whole sentences. That is DNS tunnelling: ordinary-looking questions carrying a secret conversation past a rule that only checks the envelope.
takeaways: DNS is allowed almost everywhere, which makes it useful for hiding data.
Look for long random names and heavy traffic to one domain.
Log DNS queries and restrict which resolvers clients may use.

topics.title: Dynamic Application Security Testing
topics.summary: Dynamic application security testing is the automated assessment of a running application, sending crafted requests or driving a browser and analysing the responses for security weaknesses such as injection, broken authentication, insecure session handling, misconfigured headers, exposed administrative interfaces and unsafe redirects. Because it exercises the deployed artifact, DAST observes the same surfaces an attacker would, which makes it strong at finding configuration, authentication and session problems that static analysis cannot see. The trade-off is coverage and certainty in the other direction: black-box scanning only reaches what it can discover, it cannot reason about code it cannot see, and destructive or stateful techniques risk corrupting test data, so scans are usually run against a dedicated environment seeded with representative content and credentials. Authenticated scanning is the single biggest determinant of value; an unauthenticated scan of a modern single-page application typically crawls a login page and little else. For a practising engineer the operational questions are environment fidelity, credential handling, scan scope, rate limiting, and how findings are de-duplicated across runs so a repeated issue is not rediscovered as new. Pairing DAST with an API specification gives far better coverage than crawl-only scanning, and pairing it with static analysis closes the loop between code-level and runtime evidence. Common failure modes include scanning production during peak hours, scanning an environment with debug features enabled so results do not reflect production, and reporting every informational header finding as if it carried the same weight as a confirmed injection.
objectives: You will be able to explain what running the application adds over static analysis and which defect classes it uniquely exposes.
You will be able to configure an authenticated DAST scan with a safe test account, a scoped target and rate limits that protect the environment.
You will be able to evaluate environment fidelity and state why scanning a debug-enabled staging copy can produce misleading results.
You will be able to interpret a DAST report, separating confirmed findings from informational observations and scanner heuristics.
You will be able to define a de-duplication and retest process so recurring findings are tracked rather than rediscovered.
You will be able to combine API-specification-driven scanning with crawl-based scanning to improve endpoint coverage.

beginner.definition: Dynamic application security testing checks a running application for security weaknesses. A tool sends test requests to the live program and studies the replies. It looks for problems like broken login, weak sessions, and injection flaws, where user input changes a command. Because it tests the real thing, it sees what an attacker would see.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many security bugs only appear when the software is running and connected to real data. Static tools read code and often miss them. Dynamic testing finds configuration and login mistakes that code review cannot see. It also shows how your system behaves under real requests. Skipping it leaves a blind spot attackers happily use.
howItWorks: You point the scanner at a test copy of your running application.
The scanner crawls the site, following links and mapping every page it finds.
It sends unusual requests, such as odd characters or missing login details.
It studies each reply for signs of a flaw, such as error messages or leaked data.
A report lists findings by severity so you can fix the worst problems first.
You can also give the scanner a login so it can test pages behind the sign-in.
beginner.example: Think of a building inspector who does not read the blueprints. Instead, she walks through the finished house. She opens every door, turns on every tap, and checks the locks herself. She finds the window that will not close and the back door left unlocked. A dynamic scanner does the same for your website. It visits the live site like a curious guest and reports the doors that are not locked.
takeaways: Dynamic testing checks the running app, not just the source code.
Always scan with a login, or you will only test the login page.
Test a copy that matches production, never live traffic during peak hours.

topics.title: ECDSA
topics.summary: ECDSA is the elliptic curve analogue of the Digital Signature Algorithm, producing signatures whose security depends on the hardness of the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem rather than integer factorisation. A signature is generated from a private scalar, a per-signature secret nonce, and the message hash; verification uses the public point and the curve parameters. Because the security per bit is higher than RSA, ECDSA keys are far smaller for equivalent strength, which is why it dominates TLS certificates, code signing, SSH keys and hardware-backed authentication on mobile devices. The critical operational property is that the nonce must be unique and unpredictable for every signature made with a given private key. Reusing a nonce across two signatures over different messages allows the private key to be recovered algebraically from the two signatures alone, and this is not a theoretical concern: it has happened repeatedly through flawed random number generation and through code paths that derive the nonce deterministically but incorrectly. Other practical hazards include weak or duplicated entropy on embedded devices, curve parameters that are not the standardised NIST or Curve25519 family, malleable signature encodings that break naive transaction or protocol logic, and libraries that accept a public key without validating that it lies on the curve. Defensive practice therefore centres on vetted libraries, deterministic nonce generation, hardware key storage, and inventorying where signatures are produced.
objectives: Explain how ECDSA signing and verification use the curve, the private scalar and the per-signature nonce.
Describe how nonce reuse across two signatures reveals a private key and what evidence of that failure looks like.
Compare ECDSA key sizes and performance with RSA and state where each is still the better operational choice.
Validate curve parameters and public key encoding during a review of a signature verification implementation.
Recognise malleable signature encodings and explain why canonicalisation matters to protocol logic.
Plan a migration from classic curves to modern alternatives while preserving certificate and key continuity.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1: Recommendation for Key Management

beginner.definition: ECDSA stands for Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm. It is a way to prove that a message really came from you and was not changed on the way. You keep a private key secret and share a public key. The maths works with points on a curve.
beginner.whyItMatters: Digital signatures are how software, websites and messages prove their origin. ECDSA gives you the same trust as older methods but with much smaller keys. Smaller keys mean faster connections and less storage, which matters on phones and small devices. It also has one strict rule: the secret value used for each signature must never repeat.
howItWorks: You create a key pair. The private key stays with you and the public key is shared openly.
To sign a message, you first hash it, which turns it into a short fixed value.
You combine that hash with your private key and a fresh random number for this signature.
The result is a signature that only your private key could have produced.
Anyone with your public key can check the signature against the same message hash.
If the random number is ever reused, an attacker can work out your private key.
beginner.example: Think of a special pen that only you own. When you sign a document, the ink changes shape depending on the exact paper and the exact time. Anyone can look at the signature and the document and confirm it is genuine. But if you ever sign two documents at the same recorded moment, anyone can copy your pen. That moment is the random number, and it must always be different.
takeaways: ECDSA proves who sent a message using a small, efficient key pair.
Each signature needs a fresh random value. Reusing it exposes your private key.
Use a well-tested library, because this maths is very easy to get wrong by hand.

topics.title: EDR
topics.summary: Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) is a class of endpoint agent that continuously records process, file, registry, network and identity telemetry from a host, applies behavioural analytics and signature logic to that stream, and gives responders the ability to query, isolate and remediate the endpoint remotely. Unlike legacy antivirus, which largely evaluated files at rest or on execution, EDR treats sequence and context as the primary signal: a signed administrative utility writing to a run key, a shell spawning from an office productivity process, or a credential store being read by an unexpected parent are all interesting regardless of whether any single artefact matches a known bad hash. Modern deployments typically combine a lightweight kernel or platform-level sensor, a local detection engine for offline resilience, and a cloud backend that correlates across the estate, performs retroactive hunting over retained telemetry, and drives automated response actions. Practitioners care about EDR because it is the main source of truth for host-level investigation: it answers who ran what, as whom, from where, and what happened next. Its weaknesses are equally important to understand. Coverage varies by operating system and kernel version, sensor tampering and driver-level evasion can blind the agent, high-volume environments generate alert fatigue that buries real intrusions, and telemetry retention windows constrain how far back an analyst can hunt after a slow-burn compromise is discovered. EDR also raises its own governance questions around data residency, privacy, and the handling of employee endpoint data, and its value collapses if the deployment is partial, the exclusions list is unmanaged, or nobody owns tuning. Effective programmes pair EDR with strong identity telemetry, network metadata and a documented triage workflow rather than treating the console as a self-contained security solution.
objectives: Explain what an EDR sensor collects at kernel and user level, and how that differs from classic antivirus file scanning.
Describe the detection pipeline from raw telemetry through behavioural analytics to an alert a tier-one analyst can action.
Design a triage workflow that uses process lineage, parent-child relationships and user context to separate true positives from benign administrative activity.
Identify the practical blind spots of EDR coverage, including unsupported platforms, kernel-level evasion and stale or over-broad exclusions.
Evaluate retention, data residency and privacy constraints when planning retroactive threat hunting on endpoint telemetry.
Write a containment procedure that uses EDR isolation and remote remediation without destroying volatile evidence needed for investigation.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-61: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations

beginner.definition: EDR stands for Endpoint Detection and Response. An endpoint is any device a person uses, such as a laptop or a server. EDR is a software agent on that device that records what happens there, spots suspicious behavior, and gives your team tools to investigate or isolate the machine remotely.
beginner.whyItMatters: Older antivirus mainly compared files against a list of known bad ones. That fails when an attacker uses a trusted tool in a strange way. EDR watches the story instead: which program started which other program, under which account, and what happened next. It is usually the main source of truth when you investigate an incident on a device.
howItWorks: A small agent is installed on the device and starts collecting activity in the background.
It records process starts, file changes, network connections, and the account involved.
Rules and behavior models compare that stream against what normal activity looks like.
When something looks wrong, the agent raises an alert with the surrounding context.
An analyst reviews the alert and decides whether it is a real threat.
The analyst can then isolate the device or clean it up, all from the console.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital with a wristband system. The band does not just say who you are. It records every test, every dose, and every ward you visit. When something odd happens, staff can replay the whole story instead of guessing. EDR is that record for a computer. Antivirus might only check whether the doctor's badge is genuine. EDR notices that the same badge opened the pharmacy at three in the morning, which is the part that matters.
takeaways: EDR watches behavior over time, not just whether a file is known to be bad.
It gives your team remote tools to isolate and clean an infected device.
Its blind spots are real, so pairing it with identity and network logs helps.

topics.title: Eradication
topics.summary: Eradication is the incident response phase in which the team removes the adversary's ability to continue operating in the environment: malware, tooling, persistence mechanisms, created or compromised accounts, malicious configuration, and the initial access vector that let them in. It is the phase most often declared too early. Deleting a dropped binary or rebuilding a single workstation addresses a symptom rather than the foothold; if the adversary planted a scheduled task, a rogue service, a federated identity token, a malicious OAuth application, an additional SSH key or a shadow administrator account, that access survives the cleanup and the incident simply restarts. Sound eradication begins with scoping evidence: which accounts authenticated where, which persistence locations exist across the estate, which systems share the compromised credential or the vulnerable component. Root cause then has to be closed rather than merely observed - patching the exploited service, rotating every credential the adversary could have touched, removing malicious identity objects, and confirming that the initial access path no longer works. Eradication actions are destructive to evidence by nature, so forensic collection precedes them, and each action is recorded with a timestamp, an operator and a verification result. Verification is the crux: after cleanup the team must re-hunt using the adversary's known tactics, techniques and procedures to demonstrate absence rather than assume it. Only when eradication is verified does recovery begin, and even then detection coverage and monitoring are raised rather than relaxed.
objectives: Describe what eradication must remove beyond malware, including persistence, identity objects and the initial access vector.
Scope persistence across endpoints, identity providers, cloud control planes and network infrastructure before cleanup begins.
Determine which credentials, tokens and secrets require rotation after a confirmed compromise and justify the scope.
Sequence forensic collection and eradication so that destructive cleanup does not destroy evidence.
Verify eradication with threat hunting driven by the adversary's observed tactics, techniques and procedures.
Explain why restoring a rebuilt host without closing the root cause usually produces a repeat incident.
Record eradication actions with timestamps, operators and verification results suitable for audit and legal review.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK - adversary tactics and techniques knowledge base

beginner.definition: Eradication is the incident response step where you remove the attacker from your systems completely. That means the malicious software, the ways they stayed hidden, the accounts they created, and the weakness they used to get in. You also fix the original problem. Only then can the environment be trusted again.
beginner.whyItMatters: Teams often clean up too early and declare victory. Deleting one bad file or rebuilding one laptop does not remove a hidden task, a rogue service, or a spare login the attacker left behind. Access survives, and the incident simply starts again a week later. Proper eradication closes every door, not just the obvious one.
howItWorks: Collect and save the evidence you need, because cleanup destroys it.
Search widely for hidden access, such as startup tasks, new services, and extra accounts.
Change every password and key the attacker might have seen, not only the obvious ones.
Remove the malicious files, the hidden access, and any accounts they created.
Fix the original weakness, for example by patching the software they abused.
Hunt again using what you learned, to prove nothing is left rather than assume it.
beginner.example: Imagine weeds in a garden. Pulling the leaves off leaves the roots in the soil, and the weeds return in days. To solve the problem you dig out the roots and check the whole bed, not just the spot where you first noticed green. Eradication is that careful digging. It is slower, but the weeds do not come back.
takeaways: Malware is only one piece; hidden access and created accounts must go too.
Rotate every credential the attacker could have touched during the intrusion.
Hunt again after cleanup to prove the attacker is really gone.

topics.title: Evasion
topics.summary: Evasion is the set of techniques used to avoid, delay or defeat detection and analysis rather than to achieve an objective directly, and it is best understood as a tax on defenders' visibility rather than a single action. Practitioners group it by what is being evaded: signature matching, behavioural analytics, logging, and human investigation. Common patterns include altering the on-disk representation of code so known signatures no longer match, obfuscating scripts and command lines, abusing signed system utilities so actions appear under a trusted name, masquerading files and services as legitimate software, tampering with or blinding telemetry so evidence never reaches a central store, and encrypting or tunnelling command-and-control traffic so content inspection becomes useless. Because evasion targets the collection layer, the most effective counters are architectural. Centralised, append-only logging with strict access control removes the advantage of tampering on a single host. Tamper protection and health monitoring on endpoint agents expose attempts to disable them. Application control and script block logging shrink the space in which obfuscated code can run at all. Behavioural detections that correlate across hosts and identities survive cosmetic changes better than any signature. Finally, analysts should treat absence of evidence as a signal in itself: a host that stops reporting, a log source that goes quiet, or a gap in a timeline is a detection opportunity, and treating those gaps as alerts is one of the highest-value habits a security operations team can build.
objectives: You will be able to classify evasion techniques by whether they target signatures, behaviour, logging or investigation.
You will be able to identify signs that telemetry has been disabled, blinded or tampered with.
You will be able to explain why centralised, append-only logging defeats many host-level evasion tactics.
You will be able to design behavioural detections that survive cosmetic changes to tooling.
You will be able to treat monitoring gaps and silent hosts as actionable detection signals.

beginner.definition: Evasion means changing how an attack looks so that security tools do not notice it. It does not achieve the goal by itself. Instead it delays or prevents detection, giving the intruder more time. Evasion targets many things: file signatures, behaviour patterns, logging, and the humans who investigate alerts.
beginner.whyItMatters: Security tools are only useful if they can see what is happening. Evasion attacks that visibility directly. An intruder may rename tools, hide inside trusted programs, or switch off logging on one machine. If your logs live only on that machine, the evidence disappears with them. Central logging and tamper protection keep the record safe. Treat a silent host as a warning sign, not as peace and quiet.
howItWorks: The intruder studies which security tools watch the machines they want to use.
They change their tools so that known detection patterns no longer match.
They hide their actions inside trusted programs that already run on the system.
They try to turn off, blind or delete the logging on the affected machine.
If detection is delayed, they gain quiet time to reach their real goal.
beginner.example: Think of a burglar who puts on a delivery driver's uniform. The neighbours see a familiar van and a friendly wave. Nothing about the scene feels wrong, so nobody calls the police. The uniform did not open the door by itself. It simply stopped people from looking too closely. Malicious activity that hides behind trusted system tools works the same way. The lesson for defenders is to watch behaviour, not just names and appearances.
takeaways: Evasion does not attack your data, it attacks your ability to see.
Send logs to a central place that intruders cannot edit.
A host that stops reporting is a signal worth chasing.
