topics.title: Exfiltration
topics.summary: Exfiltration is the unauthorised transfer of data from an environment the organisation controls to a destination it does not, and it is usually the point at which an intrusion becomes a reportable breach. The activity normally follows a recognisable sequence: locating and collecting data of value, staging it on an intermediate system, reducing its size or obscuring its content through compression and encryption, splitting it into transferable chunks, and moving it over a channel that is likely to be permitted. Channel choice is a trade-off between volume and stealth. Large transfers over ordinary web or file-sharing protocols are fast but visible; low-and-slow transfers over DNS, commodity cloud storage or a long-lived command-and-control channel are quieter but take longer and depend on the destination remaining available. Defences fail most often at the egress boundary, where broad allow-lists for web traffic, personal cloud storage and remote access tools make almost any destination reachable. Detection combines data-side and network-side evidence: unusually large or oddly timed transfers, access to repositories the account does not normally touch, new external destinations, protocol use that does not match the port, and anomalous DNS query volumes or label lengths. Mitigations that work are egress filtering with explicit allow-lists, data classification with controls that follow the data, scoped credentials that limit what a single identity can read, and monitoring of cloud storage and collaboration platforms rather than only the corporate perimeter.
objectives: You will be able to describe the collect, stage, compress and transfer sequence and the evidence each step creates.
You will be able to compare common exfiltration channels by volume, stealth and detectability.
You will be able to evaluate egress controls and explain why permissive allow-lists undermine them.
You will be able to use flow, DNS and cloud audit telemetry to build exfiltration detections.
You will be able to prioritise data classification and credential scoping as exfiltration mitigations.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (T1041)

beginner.definition: Exfiltration is the act of copying data out of a network without permission. The data leaves a place the organisation controls and arrives somewhere it does not. When this happens, a security incident usually becomes a reportable data breach. It is often the final and most damaging step of an attack.
beginner.whyItMatters: Your data is the reason attackers break in. If they can copy it out, the harm continues even after you remove them. Permissive outbound rules make this easy, because almost any website is reachable. If you allow all web traffic, an intruder can hide a data theft inside normal browsing. Watching what leaves your network matters as much as watching what enters it.
howItWorks: The intruder first finds and collects the files that look valuable to them.
They copy that collection onto one middle system they already control.
They shrink the files, often by compressing or encrypting them into one package.
They split the package into smaller pieces to avoid sudden large transfers.
They send the pieces out over a channel that is likely to be allowed.
beginner.example: Picture someone moving furniture out of an office at night. They cannot carry a sofa through the front door without being noticed. So they take it apart, wrap the pieces in ordinary boxes, and carry one box out with the normal rubbish each evening. Nothing looks strange on any single day. Weeks later, the office is empty. Data theft often works the same way: small, regular, boring transfers that no one questions.
takeaways: Watch outbound traffic as carefully as you watch inbound traffic.
Large or oddly timed uploads from your network deserve a closer look.
Limit what each account can read, and limit where data can go.

topics.title: Fileless Malware
topics.summary: Fileless malware is malicious logic that executes without a conventional malicious file ever being written to disk in a form that a scanner can inspect, instead living in memory, in registry values, in system configuration stores, or in the command lines and scripts passed to legitimate interpreters already present on the host. The category is best understood as a spectrum rather than a binary property. A purely memory-resident payload injected into another process leaves no artefact for a file-based scan, while a script launched from a registry key or a scheduled task leaves configuration artefacts that are fileless only in the narrow sense that no executable was dropped. The common thread is abuse of trusted, signed, ubiquitous components: the operating system shell, PowerShell or another scripting interpreter, Windows Management Instrumentation, the .NET runtime, and increasingly cloud-hosted script sources fetched at run time. Detection therefore shifts from content matching to behaviour and lineage. Analysts look at which parent process spawned which interpreter, whether the command line contains encoded or obfuscated content, whether a process downloaded and immediately invoked remote content, whether script block logging or module logging is even enabled, and whether memory contains executable regions that are not backed by a file on disk. Prevention leans on application control, constrained language modes, signed script enforcement and the removal of unnecessary interpreters from servers and user workstations. Memory acquisition capability and a solid understanding of logging gaps matter, because once the process exits the evidence often exits with it.
objectives: Explain the fileless spectrum from purely memory-resident payloads to registry- and task-based script execution.
Identify the trusted interpreters and system components most commonly abused for diskless execution.
Build detections from process lineage, command-line entropy and script block or module logging telemetry.
Recognise the specific logging gaps that make fileless activity invisible on an unconfigured estate.
Describe how application control and interpreter hardening reduce the attack surface available to fileless techniques.
Plan volatile evidence capture so memory-resident artefacts are preserved before a host is rebooted.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

beginner.definition: Fileless malware is harmful code that runs without ever being saved as a normal file on the disk. Instead it lives in memory, in registry settings (the Windows configuration store), or in commands sent to tools already built into the system. Because no suspicious file appears, a traditional file scanner has nothing to examine.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most older protection works by scanning files. When the harmful logic never lands on disk, that protection sees nothing. The attacker also borrows trusted programs that are already installed and signed, so nothing looks out of place. You need to watch behavior and origin instead of file contents, and you need logging switched on before the event, because once the process ends the evidence often ends with it.
howItWorks: The attacker gets a command to run on the machine, often through a document or a script.
That command uses a trusted tool already installed, such as a Windows scripting engine.
The tool loads the harmful logic straight into memory rather than saving it.
Because nothing is written to disk, a file scan finds no trace to flag.
The code may store a small piece of itself in a registry key to return later.
Defenders look instead at which program started which, and what arguments were used.
beginner.example: Think of a burglar who never breaks a window. Instead, they learn the code to the front door and walk in wearing the building manager's uniform. Nothing is damaged, no alarm trips, and the security guard nods them through. Fileless malware works the same way. It uses programs your computer already trusts, like a scripting engine, and gives them unusual orders. The room looks untouched. You only notice later by reviewing who entered, and at what time.
takeaways: No file on disk does not mean no infection; memory and settings can hide code.
Watch which trusted program started which, and check command arguments closely.
Turn on script logging before an incident, because memory evidence disappears on reboot.

topics.title: Firewall
topics.summary: A firewall is a network security control that enforces an explicit policy over which traffic may pass between two zones by inspecting packet headers and, in modern products, application-layer content. Classic packet filters evaluated a five-tuple of source address, destination address, source port, destination port and protocol against an ordered rule list, stopping at the first match and falling through to an implicit deny. Stateful inspection added a connection table so that return traffic belonging to an established session is permitted without a matching inbound rule, which removed many of the permissive workarounds that plagued early deployments. Next-generation firewalls identify applications rather than ports alone, attach user and group identity to flows, decrypt selected TLS sessions, and integrate intrusion prevention and threat intelligence, so the operational boundary between firewall, proxy and IPS has largely dissolved. Defensive value depends almost entirely on policy quality. A rule base that ends in any-any, that carries shadowed rules which can never match, or that accumulates temporary exceptions long after a project closes provides little assurance regardless of the hardware. Effective programmes enforce default deny between zones, document the business owner and expiry of every permit, review the rule base on a schedule, and forward accept and deny logs to a central platform where volume and destination changes are correlated. Firewalls remain necessary but are not sufficient: they cannot see inside encrypted traffic they do not decrypt, they cannot reliably distinguish a trusted internal host that has been compromised, and they are bypassed entirely when users and workloads leave the perimeter.
objectives: You will be able to explain how stateful inspection differs from stateless packet filtering and why rule order determines the effective policy.
You will be able to read a firewall rule base and identify shadowed, redundant and overly permissive rules.
You will be able to design a zone-based policy that defaults to deny and permits only documented business flows.
You will be able to interpret accept and deny logs when triaging an alert or scoping an incident.
You will be able to describe where application identification succeeds and where it fails for tunnelled or encrypted traffic.
You will be able to explain the operational risks created by policy drift, temporary any-any rules and weak change control.

beginner.definition: A firewall is a security control that sits between two networks and decides which traffic may pass. It checks each connection against a list of rules you write. Anything not clearly allowed is blocked by default. Modern firewalls also look at the application behind the traffic, not just the address and port.
beginner.whyItMatters: Without a firewall, every machine on your network is open to every other machine and to the internet. One infected laptop could then reach your file servers, backups and management consoles. A firewall limits that reach and gives you logs of what was blocked. But a rule list full of wide allowances is almost as bad as no firewall at all, so review your rules often.
howItWorks: You split your network into zones, such as users, servers and guests.
For each zone pair you write rules that describe allowed traffic and its purpose.
The firewall reads each packet header and finds the first rule that matches.
If no rule matches, the final rule denies the traffic, which is the default deny idea.
Stateful firewalls remember active connections, so replies come back without a new rule.
You send the accept and deny logs to a central place for review and alerts.
beginner.example: Think of a firewall as the doorman at a private club. The doorman holds a guest list that says who may enter, through which door and at what time. Someone not on the list is turned away, even if they look friendly. Once a guest is inside, the doorman remembers them and lets them leave and return without rechecking everything. If the guest list says everyone may enter, the doorman adds nothing.
takeaways: A firewall allows only the traffic your rules describe and blocks the rest.
Rule order decides the result, because the first match wins.
Wide rules and old exceptions quietly remove most of the protection.

topics.title: Flash Report
topics.summary: A flash report is a short, time-sensitive threat intelligence product published quickly to warn recipients about an urgent development and prompt a defensive decision. It is deliberately narrow: one topic, minimal background, and heavy emphasis on what changed, why it matters now, what recipients should do, and when the next update is expected. Flash traffic typically covers newly exploited vulnerabilities, active campaigns against a sector, credible reports of imminent activity, or a significant change in an adversary's tooling. Because speed is the point, a flash report is usually built from incomplete information, so it must state its confidence and its sourcing plainly, and it must be updated or formally superseded rather than silently edited after release. A workable structure includes a headline that states the change, a one-paragraph bottom line up front, key judgements with confidence, the technical detail analysts need in order to hunt, recommended actions ranked by effort and impact, indicators with a clear validity window, handling and distribution markings, and points of contact. Distribution is governed by handling caveats so recipients know whether they may forward the material, and by a defined list of who must be reachable outside business hours. The most common failure is noise: publishing everything urgently destroys the value of urgency, so teams set explicit triggers for what qualifies as flash and keep routine developments in a daily summary. The second failure is actionability, where a flash tells recipients that an actor exists without giving them a detection, a mitigation or a question to answer. Well-run teams keep a standing template, pre-agree who may approve release, and rehearse the workflow so a flash can be written, reviewed and distributed within an hour during an incident.
objectives: You will be able to identify the situations that genuinely meet a flash reporting trigger and those that belong in routine reporting.
You will be able to draft a flash report with a bottom line up front, stated confidence and ranked recommended actions.
You will be able to apply handling and distribution markings and explain what recipients may do with the product.
You will be able to convert technical findings into detection and hunting guidance a recipient can act on immediately.
You will be able to manage a flash lifecycle of publication, update, supersede and post-incident review.
You will be able to define release authority and out-of-hours routing so urgent warning is not delayed.

sources.label: NIST Computer Security Resource Center publications

beginner.definition: A flash report is a short warning sent quickly about an urgent threat. It arrives before the full picture is known. It focuses on what changed, why it matters now and what you should do today. Speed matters more than completeness. Teams keep a ready template so they can publish within an hour.
beginner.whyItMatters: Some threats cannot wait for a neat weekly summary. A new bug is being exploited right now, and your systems may be at risk. A fast warning gives people time to patch or to watch for the signs. If you warn about everything, nobody reads any of it. So you need strict rules for what counts as urgent. A flash report is that urgent channel, kept rare and sharp.
howItWorks: Check the trigger. Only publish a flash for a genuinely urgent, active and relevant threat.
Write the headline first, stating in plain words what has changed.
Add a short bottom line. Say what it means for your readers right now.
List the actions in order of effort, starting with the cheapest useful step.
State your confidence and your sources, because the information is still incomplete.
Send it to a defined list, then update or replace it later instead of editing it quietly.
beginner.example: Think of a fire alarm in an office. It is loud, short and impossible to ignore. It does not explain the chemistry of the fire. It tells you to leave now. Later, a full report explains what happened and how to prevent it. A flash report is the alarm, and a weekly intelligence summary is the report. If the alarm rang every day for small things, everyone would stop reacting.
takeaways: Publish a flash only when the threat is active, urgent and relevant to your readers.
Lead with what changed and what to do, not with background reading.
State your confidence clearly, and update or replace the report later.

topics.title: Foothold
topics.summary: A foothold is the first durable, repeatable point of access an intruder establishes inside a target environment, giving command execution and a base from which further objectives are pursued. It is deliberately distinguished from full compromise: a foothold may be a single low-privileged shell on an internet-facing host, a valid credential pair, a session on a remote access appliance, or code running inside a user's active browser session, and its value lies in reliability rather than breadth. The paths that produce footholds are well documented and defensive teams should treat them as a checklist for exposure: phishing with an attachment or link, exploitation of public-facing services, abuse of stolen or guessed credentials against remote access services, trusted relationships with suppliers, and misconfigured cloud or container endpoints. Immediately after access is obtained, the intruder's priorities usually shift to understanding the local context, confirming that the access survives normal session end, and hiding the channel that will carry later stages. Detection therefore rarely depends on a single alert. It comes from correlating identity telemetry with endpoint and network evidence: authentications from unexpected geographies or protocols, new remote access sessions on appliances that normally see none, unusual parent and child process relationships, and outbound connections to infrastructure the organisation has never used before. Because a foothold is small by design, containment decisions hinge on whether the access is a one-off session or something that will re-establish itself, which is why rapid scoping and credential rotation accompany every confirmed incident.
objectives: You will be able to define a foothold and distinguish it from persistence, privilege escalation and full compromise.
You will be able to map common foothold vectors to the telemetry that each one generates.
You will be able to correlate identity, endpoint and network evidence to confirm whether an intrusion has established stable access.
You will be able to choose proportionate containment actions for a suspected foothold without destroying evidence.
You will be able to explain why remote access appliances and valid accounts dominate real-world initial access.

beginner.definition: A foothold is the first stable way an intruder gets into a system. It is a small opening, not a full takeover. It might be one low-level session on a public server, a stolen username and password, or code running inside a browser. Its value is that it works again and again.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most big breaches start with one small opening. If you cannot spot that first access, you will not know an intruder is inside. A foothold often looks like normal activity, so it is easy to miss. Defenders should treat common entry paths as a checklist: phishing emails, exposed services, stolen passwords and weak cloud settings.
howItWorks: An intruder picks a way in, such as a phishing email or an exposed login page.
They send the first request and watch how the target answers it.
When it works, they get a small amount of control, like a user session.
They check what they can see and do from that one position.
They test whether the access survives a reboot, a logout or a password change.
beginner.example: Imagine you own a shop. A thief finds a small side window that does not lock. They climb in, but they do not empty the till yet. Instead they hide a key under a mat outside and learn the shop layout. That side window is the foothold. The shop is not robbed, but someone now has a way in whenever they want. This is why a small, quiet opening deserves a serious response.
takeaways: A foothold is stable access, not a full takeover of the network.
Watch your remote access tools and login pages closely.
Small and quiet access can grow into a very serious breach.

topics.title: GDPR
topics.summary: The General Data Protection Regulation is the European Union legal framework governing the processing of personal data, and it applies to organisations established in the EU as well as organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to, or monitor the behaviour of, people in the EU. Its obligations are built on principles rather than prescriptive controls: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; and accountability, where the organisation must be able to demonstrate compliance rather than merely assert it. For security practitioners the regulation matters in four operational areas. Article 32 requires appropriate technical and organisational measures proportionate to risk, which is where encryption, pseudonymisation, access control, resilience and testing of those measures land. Articles 33 and 34 set breach notification duties, with a seventy-two hour window to the supervisory authority once the controller becomes aware, so incident response runbooks must be able to answer what data, how many people, what categories and what residual risk within hours. Chapter IV introduces the data protection impact assessment for high-risk processing and the records of processing activities that underpin it. Chapter V governs transfers outside the EU and drives data residency, standard contractual clauses and transfer impact assessments. The security team's artefact trail, including detection records, containment timelines and post-incident reviews, is frequently the evidence that a supervisory authority examines.
objectives: You will be able to map the data protection principles onto concrete engineering and operational controls.
You will be able to determine what Article 32 appropriate measures mean for a given processing activity and risk level.
You will be able to run a breach assessment that produces the information a seventy-two hour notification requires.
You will be able to support a data protection impact assessment with accurate data flow and risk evidence.
You will be able to explain how international transfer restrictions change architecture and vendor selection.
You will be able to identify where a controller and a processor hold different obligations in an incident.

sources.label: OWASP Top 10 Web Application Security Risks

beginner.definition: The General Data Protection Regulation is a European Union law about personal data. Personal data means any information that can identify a living person. The law says how organisations may collect, use, store and share that information. It also gives people rights over their own data.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you handle data about people in Europe, this law applies even when your company sits elsewhere. A serious breach can lead to large fines and to lost trust. The law also sets a deadline, because you may need to tell a regulator within seventy-two hours of learning about a breach. That means your incident notes must be clear and fast to produce.
howItWorks: Decide why you need each piece of personal data and write that reason down.
Collect only what the reason requires, and delete it when the reason ends.
Protect the data with strong encryption, limited access and tested recovery plans.
Keep clear records showing what personal data you hold and where it flows.
If a breach happens, assess the risk to people and notify within the deadline.
Give people a way to see, correct and delete their own information.
beginner.example: Think of a gym that keeps member details. The gym needs your name and payment to bill you, but it does not need your medical history to sell a membership. If someone steals the membership list, the gym must work out how many people are affected and how serious the harm is. Then it may have to inform the privacy regulator quickly. Keeping less data made that job smaller.
takeaways: Collect the smallest amount of personal data that your purpose needs.
Know your breach deadline and keep evidence ready before you need it.
People have rights over their data, so build ways to answer them.

topics.title: Hardware Security Module
topics.summary: A hardware security module is a tamper-resistant device that generates, stores and uses cryptographic keys inside a boundary the host operating system cannot read across. Keys are created on the module, never leave it in plaintext, and are used through a constrained API that performs signing, decryption, key wrapping or random generation on behalf of an authorised caller. Because the key material exists only inside protected hardware, stealing the key requires physical or logical access to the module rather than a copy of a configuration file, and many modules zeroise their key store in response to detected tampering. HSMs underpin certificate authority private keys, payment key management, code signing, database transparent encryption, disk encryption key hierarchies and cloud KMS backends that offer dedicated or single-tenant hardware. The operational model introduces its own failure modes: poorly controlled administrator roles and quorum settings, weak or shared operator credentials that permit key export, misconfigured network exposure of the module's management interface, backup and restore procedures that either lose the key forever or replicate it into weaker storage, weak entropy on the first initialisation, and audit logging that is disabled or never reviewed. Availability also matters, since an HSM cluster that cannot fail over can take critical signing or payment flows offline, so redundancy and documented recovery are part of the security design rather than an afterthought.
objectives: Describe how an HSM protects key material through tamper resistance, restricted APIs and controlled key export.
Separate operator, administrator and auditor roles and explain why split knowledge and quorum controls matter.
Evaluate an HSM deployment for network exposure, entropy source, backup strategy and firmware currency.
Design high-availability key services so that hardware failure or cluster loss does not break signing or payment flows.
Review HSM audit logs to confirm key usage matches the applications and cryptoperiods that are expected.
Compare dedicated hardware modules, cloud KMS backends and software key stores for a specific key's risk profile.

sources.label: NIST FIPS 140-3: Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1: Recommendation for Key Management

beginner.definition: A Hardware Security Module (HSM) is a physical device that creates and stores cryptographic keys inside a sealed box. The keys never leave that box in readable form. Software asks the device to sign or decrypt something, and the device does the work internally. Many models erase their keys if someone opens the case.
beginner.whyItMatters: If a key is just a file on a server, anyone who copies the file owns the key. There is no way to tell the copy from the original. An HSM removes that risk, because the key cannot be copied out. This matters most for keys that sign certificates, approve payments or unlock whole databases. Losing or breaking the device can also stop your business.
howItWorks: The device is set up in a controlled way, often with several administrators acting together.
New keys are generated inside the device by its own random number source.
Software sends a request to sign, decrypt or wrap a key, using a limited interface.
The device checks whether the caller is allowed to use that specific key.
The operation happens inside the protected hardware and the result is returned.
Every action is written to an audit log that someone should review regularly.
beginner.example: Think of a bank vault with a strict clerk. You cannot take the gold home. You can ask the clerk to weigh a coin, stamp a document or move a bar to another shelf. The clerk records every request in a ledger. Several managers must agree before anything unusual happens. Breaking into the vault destroys the contents, so a thief gains nothing.
takeaways: An HSM keeps keys inside hardware so they cannot be copied out.
Split administrator duties and review the audit log, or the device is only a speed bump.
Plan for hardware failure and backups, because a dead module can halt signing.

topics.title: HIPAA
topics.summary: HIPAA is the United States federal law that governs the privacy and security of protected health information, and its security obligations are expressed through the Security Rule together with the Privacy Rule, the Breach Notification Rule and the Transactions and Code Sets Rule. The Security Rule is deliberately flexible and technology-neutral: it requires covered entities and their business associates to implement administrative, physical and technical safeguards that are reasonable and appropriate for their size, complexity and risk, and it sorts implementation specifications into required and addressable categories, where addressable means the organisation must either implement the specification or document why an equivalent alternative is reasonable and appropriate. The technical safeguards include access control, audit controls, integrity controls, person or entity authentication and transmission security, which in practice means unique user identification, role-based authorisation, emergency access procedures, automatic logoff, encryption in transit and at rest, and immutable audit logging of systems that touch electronic protected health information. Risk analysis is not optional and is the foundation of every other decision; a documented, current risk analysis tied to a remediation plan is the single artefact most often probed in an investigation. Business associate agreements extend obligations down the supply chain, and breach notification has a four-part risk assessment with defined timelines. Practitioners should treat ePHI data flow mapping as the prerequisite for meaningful segmentation and monitoring.
objectives: You will be able to separate the Privacy Rule, Security Rule, Breach Notification Rule and Transactions Rule obligations.
You will be able to classify an implementation specification as required or addressable and document the decision either way.
You will be able to perform and record a risk analysis that links threats, vulnerabilities and ePHI systems to remediation.
You will be able to implement technical safeguards including unique identification, emergency access and audit controls.
You will be able to run the four-factor breach risk assessment and determine notification obligations.
You will be able to manage business associate agreements and inherited responsibilities across a supply chain.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-66 HIPAA security rule resources

beginner.definition: HIPAA, short for the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, is a United States law that protects health information. That information covers records about treatment, diagnoses and payment for care. The law sets privacy and security rules for it. Clinics, hospitals, insurers and the companies serving them must follow those rules.
beginner.whyItMatters: Health records are valuable to criminals because they rarely change. A stolen name can be replaced, but a diagnosis cannot. The law expects you to study the risks to health data and to write down what you will fix. It also expects safeguards such as unique logins, audit logs and encryption. Missing those can bring heavy penalties.
howItWorks: Find every system that stores or moves health information about patients.
Study the risks to that information and write down what you find.
Apply safeguards such as unique logins, limited access and encryption in every place.
Keep audit records that show who opened which patient record and when.
Sign written agreements with any supplier that handles health data for you.
If data is exposed, assess the risk and notify people within the set time.
beginner.example: Picture a small clinic where every doctor uses the same shared login. It is convenient, but the audit trail cannot show who opened a patient file. If a celebrity's record leaks, the clinic cannot clear its staff or explain what happened. HIPAA expects each person to have their own account, so actions can be traced honestly.
takeaways: Know where health information lives, including inside your suppliers' systems.
Give every user a unique login so audit logs stay meaningful.
A written risk analysis is the foundation for every safeguard decision.

topics.title: HMAC
topics.summary: HMAC is a keyed message authentication construction defined in FIPS 198-1 and RFC 2104 that wraps an unkeyed hash function in a specific two-pass structure using inner and outer padding constants. It produces a message authentication code that proves both integrity and authenticity when the verifier holds the same secret key, and its security proof holds under weaker assumptions about the underlying hash than a naive secret-prefix construction, which is why it resists length extension attacks. HMAC-SHA-256 is the workhorse for API request signing, webhook verification, session token integrity, network protocol message authentication and key derivation through HKDF. Correct use depends on details that are easy to get wrong. The key must be generated randomly at an adequate length and stored as securely as any other credential, because possession of the key is possession of the ability to forge. Verification must be constant-time, since an early-exit byte comparison leaks how many leading bytes matched and enables forgery byte by byte. Truncated MACs reduce work for the attacker, and comparing a MAC that arrives in a client-controlled field without binding it to the request body, timestamp or nonce invites replay. Key rotation for HMAC secrets is operationally awkward when both sides must change simultaneously, so overlap windows and dual-key acceptance are standard practice, and log pipelines should alert on signature verification failures as a signal of tampering or credential misuse.
objectives: Explain the HMAC inner and outer padding structure and why it resists length extension attacks.
Implement secure MAC verification using constant-time comparison and explain the consequence of early-exit equality checks.
Design request signing for an API including key scope, timestamp binding, nonce handling and replay protection.
Choose appropriate MAC lengths and justify truncation only against a documented risk decision.
Plan an HMAC key rotation with overlapping key validity and no downtime for dependent services.
Analyse authentication failure telemetry to distinguish misconfiguration from active forgery attempts.

sources.label: NIST FIPS 198-1: The Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code (HMAC)
RFC 2104: HMAC - Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication

beginner.definition: HMAC stands for Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code. It is a way to prove that a message is genuine and unchanged. Both sides share one secret key. The sender mixes the message with the key and produces a short code. Anyone with the same key can check that code.
beginner.whyItMatters: A plain hash proves only that data did not change by accident. It cannot prove who sent it, because anyone can compute the same hash. HMAC adds a shared secret, so only someone holding the key can create a valid code. This protects requests between systems, webhook deliveries and session tokens. If the key leaks, an attacker can forge anything.
howItWorks: Both sides agree on one secret key and keep it safe, like any password.
The sender pads the key and mixes it with the message, then hashes the result.
Then it mixes the key again in a different way and hashes a second time.
The final short value is sent along with the message as the code.
The receiver repeats the same steps and compares the two codes carefully.
The comparison must take the same time for every attempt, so nobody can guess byte by byte.
beginner.example: Imagine a club where members share a secret stamp design. To send a note, you write it and stamp it with the shared design. The doorman compares the stamp with his own. A stranger can write a convincing note, but he cannot copy the stamp. If the stamp design leaks, everyone can forge notes, so you change the design regularly.
takeaways: HMAC proves both who sent a message and that it was not changed.
Treat the shared key like a password. Anyone who has it can forge messages.
Compare codes in constant time, or an attacker can guess them one byte at a time.

topics.title: IAM Policy
topics.summary: An IAM policy is a structured document that grants or denies permissions to a principal in a cloud platform, evaluated by the provider's authorisation engine on every API call. Policies typically bind a principal, an action or set of actions on a resource, and optional conditions such as source address, time, tags or whether multi-factor authentication was used, with an explicit effect of allow or deny. Cloud authorisation is generally default-deny, so access exists only where a policy grants it, and an explicit deny usually overrides any allow. Policies attach at several levels, including identity-based policies on users, groups and roles, resource-based policies on the target itself such as a bucket or key, permission boundaries, session policies and service control policies in an organisation hierarchy, which means the effective permission set is the intersection and union of several documents rather than any single one. Security professionals care because over-permissive policies are a leading cause of cloud compromise and because policy errors are invisible until an attacker or an auditor exercises them. Practical work includes least-privilege scoping, wildcard elimination, analysing cross-account trust relationships, reviewing role assumption chains, and detecting privilege escalation paths where one grant lets a principal modify a policy that grants more. Reviewing the effective permission of a principal, not the intent of a single document, is the discipline the topic teaches.
objectives: You will be able to read a JSON IAM policy and state precisely which principals, actions and resources it authorises.
You will be able to compute the effective permissions of a principal across identity, resource, boundary and organisation policies.
You will be able to identify privilege escalation paths created by policy modification rights.
You will be able to rewrite an over-permissive policy into a least-privilege form and justify each retained grant.
You will be able to explain how condition keys and explicit deny change authorisation outcomes.
You will be able to triage IAM-related alerts such as role assumption anomalies and policy change events.

sources.label: Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC

beginner.definition: An identity and access management policy, usually called an IAM policy, is a written rule that says who may do what in a cloud platform. It names a person or service, the actions allowed, and the resources those actions apply to. The cloud provider checks these rules on every request.
beginner.whyItMatters: Cloud accounts say no by default, so access exists only where a policy allows it. That is good, but a single careless rule can undo it. A policy that allows every action on every resource gives an attacker the whole account if they steal one key. Careful policy writing keeps each person and service to the smallest useful set of permissions.
howItWorks: A request arrives at the cloud provider, such as a service asking to read a file.
The provider works out who is asking, using a user, a role or a service identity.
It collects every policy that applies, from the identity, the resource and the organisation.
If any rule says deny, the request is refused, because deny beats allow.
If a rule allows the action on that resource, the request succeeds and is logged.
If nothing allows it, the request fails, since the default answer is no.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel key card. Your card opens your room, the gym and the front door during your stay. It does not open other guests' rooms or the manager's office. The front desk decides this when they program the card. An IAM policy is that programming, and a wildcard policy is like handing every guest a master key.
takeaways: Every cloud request is checked against policies, and the default answer is no.
An explicit deny always wins, so use denies for hard limits.
Give each person and service the smallest set of permissions that works.

topics.title: IDS and IPS
topics.summary: An intrusion detection system monitors network or host activity and raises alerts on behaviour that matches known attack signatures, deviates from a statistical baseline, or violates an explicit policy, while an intrusion prevention system sits inline and can drop the offending traffic in real time. Network sensors are usually deployed at chokepoints such as the internet edge, the data-centre core and the links between trust zones, fed by spans, taps or packet brokers, while host agents inspect system calls, file writes and process lineage that never appears on the wire. Detection logic spans signature matching, protocol anomaly checks, reputation feeds and behavioural models, and each family carries distinct failure modes: signatures miss novel variants and encoded payloads, while anomaly engines generate volume that overwhelms analysts. The dominant operational problem is rarely sensor coverage but triage capacity. A poorly tuned signature set produces thousands of low-value alerts every day, so genuine events are buried and mean time to detect degrades rather than improves. Mature teams suppress noisy signatures, tune thresholds against real baselines, enrich alerts with asset criticality and identity, and validate detection content with controlled tests before enabling prevention. Prevention deserves particular caution, because an inline device with a false positive becomes an availability incident, and an inline device with a decryption or evasion blind spot provides false assurance. Fragmentation, TCP evasion, protocol tunnelling, encrypted channels and high-throughput asymmetric paths all degrade inspection quality, so effective programmes treat detection and prevention as one detection-engineering discipline, keep content updates under change control, measure precision as well as coverage, and document the blind spots that remain.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish signature, anomaly and reputation-based detection and describe the failure modes of each.
You will be able to triage a sensor alert set by asset criticality, direction and expected business traffic.
You will be able to tune or suppress noisy signatures without creating an evasion gap.
You will be able to explain the operational risk of inline prevention and the conditions under which fail-open is acceptable.
You will be able to describe how fragmentation, encoding and encryption reduce inspection fidelity.
You will be able to evaluate detection coverage against a technique matrix and document the remaining blind spots.

sources.label: SANS Institute Research and White Papers

beginner.definition: An intrusion detection system, or IDS, watches network or host activity and raises an alert when something looks like an attack. An intrusion prevention system, or IPS, does the same but sits in the path of the traffic, so it can block the connection straight away. Detection means someone is told; prevention means the traffic never arrives.
beginner.whyItMatters: Your firewall allows traffic that matches your rules, but an attacker can hide inside allowed traffic, such as a web request that carries an attack. An IDS or IPS looks inside that traffic for known bad patterns and strange behaviour. The hard part is noise: a poorly tuned sensor produces thousands of useless alerts, and real events get buried. Tuning and measuring accuracy matter more than buying more sensors.
howItWorks: Sensors are placed at the points where traffic must pass, such as the internet edge.
Each sensor compares traffic with known attack patterns, called signatures, and with a normal baseline.
When something matches or stands out, the sensor writes an alert with the details.
An IDS only reports, so a human or another tool must decide what to do next.
An IPS blocks the traffic itself, which is faster but risky if the alert is wrong.
Teams then tune noisy rules, enrich alerts with asset value and test changes before enabling blocking.
beginner.example: Think of a night guard in an office building. A guard who only watches cameras and phones the manager is like an IDS. A guard who stands at the door and refuses entry is like an IPS. Cameras catch more without disturbing anyone, but the door guard stops trouble sooner. If the door guard mistakes ordinary staff for intruders and locks them out, you have created a new problem of your own.
takeaways: An IDS alerts you about suspect traffic; an IPS blocks that traffic in real time.
An IPS with a wrong rule becomes an outage, so test before you block.
Tuning beats volume: too many alerts hide the real attack.

topics.title: Incident Response Playbook
topics.summary: A playbook in security operations is a documented, versioned procedure that specifies how a defined class of alert or incident is handled, from the first acknowledgement through to closure and follow-up. It exists so that response quality does not depend on which analyst is on shift. A usable playbook is more specific than a policy and more procedural than a runbook index. It states the trigger conditions that invoke it, the roles and who has authority to act, the required inputs such as the alert payload and enrichment sources, the ordered steps with the exact queries and commands to run, the decision points with explicit criteria for each branch, the containment options available and their blast radius, the evidence to preserve and where, the escalation path with contact conditions and timeframes, and the closure criteria including what must be recorded. Two design principles separate playbooks that survive contact with reality from those that do not. First, enrichment precedes action: gather asset ownership, identity privilege, business function and recent related activity before disabling an account or isolating a host, because the outage can be worse than the incident. Second, every irreversible step has a named approver and a documented reversal path. Playbooks also decay. Infrastructure changes, log sources move, contact lists age and query syntax drifts, so each playbook needs an owner, a review date, and validation through tabletop exercise or live-fire test. Response metrics such as time to detect and time to contain are only meaningful when the underlying procedure is consistent and actually followed, which is the operational argument for maintaining them.
objectives: You will be able to define the required sections of an incident response playbook, from trigger conditions through closure criteria.
You will be able to write ordered response steps with explicit decision points and branch criteria instead of vague instructions.
You will be able to place enrichment before containment and justify the ordering in terms of outage risk.
You will be able to identify every irreversible action in a procedure and assign an approver and a reversal path to each.
You will be able to specify the evidence to preserve at each stage and the handling requirements that keep it usable.
You will be able to validate a playbook through tabletop exercise and record the gaps the exercise exposes.
You will be able to maintain playbooks against infrastructure drift with owners, review dates and change triggers.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-61, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
CISA Cyber Security Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks

beginner.definition: An incident response playbook is a written, step-by-step plan for handling one type of security incident. It starts at the first alert and ends when the case is closed. It lists who does what, in which order. The goal is that any analyst on shift handles the incident the same good way.
beginner.whyItMatters: During a real incident, people are stressed and the clock is running. Without a written plan, they guess, and they forget steps. A good playbook also slows you down in the right place. It reminds you to gather information before you take a big action that could knock a system offline.
howItWorks: The playbook opens with a trigger: the exact alert or situation that starts this procedure.
It names the roles involved and who has authority to approve risky actions.
It lists the information to collect first, such as who owns the machine and how critical it is.
Then it gives ordered steps with the exact commands or queries to run.
At each decision point it states the criteria for each branch, so choices are not guesswork.
It ends with closure rules: what evidence to save and what must be recorded.
beginner.example: Think of the safety card in an aeroplane seat pocket. It does not explain how planes fly. It shows you, in order, what to do if the cabin loses pressure. You read it once when calm, and then you follow it when you are not calm. An incident playbook is that card for a security team. It turns panic into a sequence of small, clear steps.
takeaways: Write a playbook for each alert type that happens often.
Always gather information before you disable an account or isolate a machine.
Give every playbook an owner and a review date, because systems change.

topics.title: Infostealer
topics.summary: An infostealer is malware whose primary purpose is to harvest and exfiltrate credentials and other valuable data from an endpoint quickly and with minimal footprint. Unlike ransomware, which seeks to disrupt, an infostealer is designed to be quiet: it typically runs for seconds or minutes, collects what it can, sends it out, and often removes itself. The target set is broad and highly specific at the same time. Browser stores are the richest source, including saved passwords, session cookies and authentication tokens, and the theft of live session cookies is particularly damaging because it lets an intruder reuse an already authenticated session and sidestep multi-factor authentication entirely. Beyond browsers, stealers target cryptocurrency wallet files, messaging and file-transfer application sessions, saved credentials in mail and remote-access clients, keylogging of anything typed, and bulk collection of documents and configuration files from user profiles. Distribution is usually opportunistic and consumer-oriented: cracked software, fake installers, malicious advertising, game cheat utilities and community-shared files, which is why an infostealer detections often first appear on a personal or unmanaged device before the stolen credentials are used against a corporate service. For defenders the implications are architectural rather than purely endpoint-focused. Stolen session cookies and tokens invalidate the comfortable assumption that multi-factor authentication makes credential theft survivable, so detection must include impossible-travel style session anomalies, first-time device and user-agent combinations, and token reuse from unexpected network locations. Response to a confirmed infostealer infection requires mass credential rotation, revocation of active sessions and refresh tokens, not just removal of the file.
objectives: Explain why infostealers prioritise browser credential and session-cookie theft over persistence or disruption.
Describe how stolen cookies and tokens let an attacker bypass multi-factor authentication at the session layer.
Identify high-value local data stores beyond browsers, including wallets, messaging clients and saved remote-access profiles.
Recognise the common distribution channels that place stealers on unmanaged or lightly managed endpoints.
Build detections for stolen-session reuse, including device, user-agent and network-location anomalies.
Run a post-infection response that revokes sessions and rotates credentials rather than only removing malware.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK: Credentials from Password Stores (T1555)
MITRE ATT&CK: Steal Web Session Cookie (T1539)

beginner.definition: An infostealer is malware built to steal valuable information from a device quickly and then disappear. It usually targets saved passwords, browser cookies (small files that keep you signed in), and session tokens. It does not lock your files or ask for money. It just takes the keys and leaves.
beginner.whyItMatters: Stolen cookies let an attacker reuse a session that is already signed in, so multi-factor authentication can be bypassed without breaking it. The theft often takes seconds, so there may be no obvious damage on the device. Later, someone logs into your company systems from far away using a real, valid session. If you only remove the malware, the attacker still holds working credentials and can return.
howItWorks: The stealer arrives, often hidden inside cracked software, a fake installer, or an online advert.
It runs quietly and copies saved passwords from browsers and other applications.
It also takes session cookies and tokens, which prove you already signed in.
Everything is packaged and sent to the attacker's server in a few seconds.
The program often deletes itself afterward, so the user notices nothing unusual.
Later, the attacker uses the stolen session or password to sign in as the victim.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel where the front desk gives you a wristband instead of a key card. The band opens your room and the pool for the whole week. Now imagine someone copies that band while you sleep. They never need your signature or your name. They just walk in and use your room as if it were theirs. Stolen session cookies work that way. The attacker skips the login and the second check, because the band already proves everything.
takeaways: An infostealer aims to be quick and quiet, not to damage your device.
Stolen session cookies can bypass multi-factor authentication without breaking it.
After an infection, reset passwords and cancel active sessions, not just the file.

topics.title: Infrastructure as Code Scanning
topics.summary: Infrastructure as code scanning is the automated static analysis of declarative infrastructure and configuration definitions, such as cloud resource templates, Kubernetes manifests, container build files, serverless definitions and policy bundles, looking for misconfigurations that would create security exposure when the code is applied. Because infrastructure definitions are machine-readable and describe the intended end state, scanners can reason about them far more reliably than they can reason about application logic, checking properties such as publicly reachable storage, permissive identity policies, unencrypted data stores, containers running as privileged or as root, absent network policies, disabled audit logging and hard-coded registry credentials. The category is closely related to cloud security posture management, with the key distinction that posture management assesses what is deployed while IaC scanning assesses what is about to be deployed, which is why it belongs in the pull request and in the pipeline before apply or sync. For a practising engineer the practical difficulty is drift and context. A scanner cannot see values injected at deploy time from a variable file, cannot know that a resource is internet-facing by design in a specific environment, and cannot tell whether an exception was granted deliberately. Effective programmes express policy as code with the same review process as application code, use environment-aware rule sets, classify findings by whether they affect a trust boundary, and detect drift between the repository and what the provider actually reports. Common failure modes are scanning only a subset of repositories, ignoring modules and nested templates, allowing unbounded inline suppressions, and treating a clean scan as evidence that the deployed environment is compliant.
objectives: You will be able to explain how static analysis of infrastructure definitions differs from cloud posture assessment of deployed resources.
You will be able to identify high-impact misconfiguration classes in cloud templates, Kubernetes manifests and container builds.
You will be able to integrate IaC scanning into a pull request and pipeline gate before apply or sync operations run.
You will be able to write policy as code with severity, environment scope and an exception process that expires.
You will be able to explain why variable interpolation, modules and cross-stack references produce scanner blind spots.
You will be able to describe how to detect drift between committed infrastructure code and the resources actually deployed.

beginner.definition: Infrastructure as code scanning reads your cloud and server setup files before they are used. These files describe servers, storage, and networks in plain text. The scanner looks for unsafe settings, such as open storage or containers running as root, the top administrator account. It catches mistakes at the pull request, long before anything is deployed.
beginner.whyItMatters: One wrong line in a setup file can expose all your data to the internet. A single public storage bucket has leaked millions of records in real incidents. Scanning before deployment costs seconds and stops the mistake reaching production. Without it, you rely on someone noticing by chance. That is not a plan, it is luck.
howItWorks: You write your servers and networks as text files in a repository.
Before the change is applied, a scanner reads those files line by line.
It compares each setting against a list of safe rules you chose.
It flags anything risky, such as open storage or a missing encryption setting.
You fix the file or record a written exception that expires later.
Only after the checks pass does the change get applied to your cloud.
beginner.example: Think of a building plan you submit before construction. An inspector reads the plan and spots a fire exit blocked by a wall. Nothing is built yet, so fixing the drawing costs almost nothing. If you had waited until the building opened, the same fix would mean knocking down walls. Infrastructure scanning is that plan review. It catches the blocked fire exit while it is still only a line on paper.
takeaways: Check setup files before deployment, not after the damage is done.
Write your safety rules as code so everyone reviews them.
A clean scan does not prove the live cloud is safe; check both.

topics.title: Instance Metadata Service Version 2
topics.summary: Instance metadata service version 2 is the session-oriented revision of the link-local endpoint that cloud instances query to obtain information about themselves, most importantly the temporary credentials associated with their attached role. The original interface answered any request arriving from the instance, which meant that a server-side request forgery flaw in an application running on that instance was sufficient to read the instance role credentials and use them from anywhere on the internet. Version two changes the exchange in two ways: the client must first issue a PUT request to obtain a limited-lifetime token that is unique to that session, and every subsequent metadata request must present that token in a header, with a configurable hop limit that additionally restricts whether requests can traverse a proxy or container network layer. Because a naive request-forgery payload cannot set custom headers or perform the required PUT, the token requirement breaks the common exploit chain, while the hop limit constrains forwarding through intermediate proxies and container namespaces. Security teams track adoption by measuring how many instances still permit the older interface, since the setting is enforced per instance and inherited at launch, and they apply it to container platforms through the node launch configuration. The topic also covers the practical migration problems: software that read metadata directly, custom agents that proxy metadata to pods, and the need to monitor metadata requests as a detection signal.
objectives: You will be able to explain how the token and hop limit requirements break credential theft through a server-side request forgery flaw.
You will be able to determine whether an instance or node pool still permits the legacy unauthenticated metadata interface.
You will be able to migrate applications and agents that read metadata directly without breaking startup.
You will be able to configure hop limits appropriately for proxies, containers and load balancers.
You will be able to use metadata access patterns as a detection signal for in-instance compromise.

beginner.definition: Instance metadata service version 2 is a safer way for a cloud server to ask about itself. The server calls a private address to learn its own name, network details, and short-lived login keys for its assigned role. Version 2 requires the server to prove it is a real session by fetching a token first.
beginner.whyItMatters: The old version answered any request that came from the server. That meant a web form bug could trick the server into fetching its own login keys and handing them out. Those keys often open other cloud services. Version 2 blocks that trick, because a simple forged request cannot get the token first.
howItWorks: A program on the server asks the metadata address, a link-local address, for a token.
The service replies with a token that expires after a short time.
The program then sends its real request and includes that token in a header.
A request without a valid token is refused, even if it comes from the server itself.
A hop limit setting controls how far requests can travel through proxies and containers.
Security teams count servers still allowing the old version and upgrade them.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel reception that hands out room keys. In the old system, anyone who phoned from inside the building and sounded like a guest got a key. In the new system, you must first collect a short-lived claim ticket in person, then show it at the desk. A prank caller cannot collect the ticket, so no key is handed over.
takeaways: Metadata holds temporary cloud credentials, so treat it as sensitive.
Turn on version 2 on every server and node pool you run.
Watch metadata requests, because unusual ones can signal a compromise.

topics.title: IOC
topics.summary: An Indicator of Compromise (IOC) is a forensic or telemetry artefact that provides evidence a system, account or network has been compromised, ranging from a file hash or hostile domain name to an anomalous authentication pattern or a registry key created by a loader. IOCs are the most shareable and the most perishable product of threat intelligence. They are trivially expressible in structured patterning, easy to push into a SIEM or EDR, and quick to automate, which is why they dominate machine-to-machine sharing; they are also the easiest thing for an adversary to change. A domain can be rotated in minutes, a payload recompiled to a new hash in seconds, and infrastructure can be rented and discarded. Treating an indicator list as a permanent blocklist therefore produces both alert fatigue and a false sense of coverage. Mature programmes classify indicators as atomic, computed or behavioural. Atomic values such as an IP address, domain name or file hash are volatile and should carry a short validity window and a confidence rating. Computed indicators, such as a hash of a decoded malware configuration or a distinctive transport fingerprint derived from a family, survive longer and support hunting. Behavioural indicators describe sequences of action and overlap heavily with adversary techniques. Operationally, an indicator is only useful when it is enriched with context: which actor family used it, which campaign, when it was first and last observed, and whether it is a genuinely exclusive artefact or a shared hosting address. Low-specificity indicators, especially IP addresses from commercial hosting or content delivery ranges, should drive hunts and correlation rather than blocklists, because blocking them breaks legitimate traffic. Indicators also age, so a feed that has not been reviewed recently should be filtered by first-seen date before it is trusted. Finally, defenders should be able to state which detection each indicator feeds and how it will be retired, because an indicator whose only consumer is a dashboard produces no security value.
objectives: You will be able to classify indicators as atomic, computed or behavioural and explain the operational lifetime and confidence each class deserves.
You will be able to build an indicator lifecycle covering enrichment, validation, deployment, review and retirement instead of permanent blocking.
You will be able to write detection and hunting logic that consumes indicators with context rather than matching bare IP addresses.
You will be able to explain why low-specificity indicators from hosting and content delivery ranges cause false positives when blocked.
You will be able to describe how indicators are expressed in structured patterning and shared through collections and feeds.
You will be able to assess a threat feed for freshness, specificity and overlap with existing coverage before onboarding it.

sources.label: NIST Computer Security Resource Center publications

beginner.definition: An indicator of compromise, or IOC, is a clue that a system may already be hacked. Examples include a strange file, a harmful web address or an unusual login time. It is technical evidence, not proof on its own. You should treat each clue as short lived, because attackers change them often.
beginner.whyItMatters: Indicators are easy to share and easy to load into your tools. That makes them popular. They also go stale very fast. An attacker can move to a new web address in minutes. If you treat a list of clues as a permanent blocklist, two bad things happen. You get flooded with false alarms, and you believe you are protected when you are not.
howItWorks: Collect the clue from a report, a log entry or an alert that your tools produced.
Add context. Note which attacker, which campaign and when it was first seen.
Decide the type. Some clues are single values, some are derived, and some describe behaviour.
Give it a validity window, because a single value may stop being useful in hours.
Push it to the right place. Strong clues can be blocked, while weak ones are only hunted.
Review and retire old indicators so your lists stay small and trustworthy.
beginner.example: Imagine a police appeal showing a suspect's car number plate. The plate is useful today. The suspect can swap plates tonight, so that appeal ages fast. A witness description is stronger. It says the suspect always limps and always wears a red cap. That behaviour may last for months. An IP address is the number plate, and a behaviour pattern is the description. Both help, but they age very differently.
takeaways: An indicator is a clue that something may be compromised, not proof that it is.
Indicators expire quickly, so give each one a validity window and review it.
Avoid blocking broad shared hosting addresses, because that breaks normal traffic.

topics.title: ISO 27001
topics.summary: ISO/IEC 27001 is the international standard that specifies requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an information security management system. It is a management-system standard rather than a control catalogue: it tells an organisation how to govern security through leadership commitment, documented scope, risk assessment, risk treatment, internal audit, management review and corrective action, while the accompanying guidance in ISO/IEC 27002 describes control objectives an organisation may select from. Certification is granted to the management system by an accredited certification body, not to a product, a data centre or a specific application, and it is issued against a declared scope and Statement of Applicability. For the security practitioner the practical consequences are concrete. Risk assessment must be repeatable and produce traceable treatment decisions; controls must be documented with owners, evidence and review cycles; Annex A control themes now cover organisational, people, physical and technological domains, and each selected or excluded control needs a justification. Auditors sample evidence rather than trust assertions, so operational artefacts such as access reviews, change tickets, incident records and supplier assessments become the real currency of the audit. Surveillance audits occur at least annually and a recertification audit happens on a three-year cycle, which means compliance is a continuous programme rather than a project with an end date. The standard pairs well with ISO/IEC 27017 and 27018 for cloud services and with ISO 27005 for risk methodology.
objectives: You will be able to explain how a risk assessment and risk treatment plan feed the Statement of Applicability and the audit programme.
You will be able to define an ISMS scope that matches the organisation's real legal, contractual and technical boundaries.
You will be able to map Annex A control themes onto existing operational controls and produce clause-level evidence.
You will be able to prepare for a stage 1 documentation review and a stage 2 evidence-based certification audit.
You will be able to run an internal audit and management review cycle that generates genuine corrective actions.
You will be able to identify the common failure modes where certification is achieved but security practice does not improve.

beginner.definition: ISO 27001 is an international standard for managing information security. ISO stands for the International Organization for Standardization, which publishes it. The standard does not list products to buy. Instead it describes how to build a management system: set the scope, assess risk, choose controls and keep improving. Certification covers that system.
beginner.whyItMatters: Customers and regulators often ask for proof that you manage security properly. Without a shared standard, every answer becomes a new questionnaire and a new argument. ISO 27001 gives you one agreed way to show how you decide what matters and how you check it works. It also creates steady habits instead of a yearly panic before an audit.
howItWorks: Define the scope: which teams, systems and locations the management system covers.
Assess the risks to information inside that scope and rank them clearly.
Choose controls that treat each risk, and write down why you chose them.
Record your decisions in policies, owners and evidence that auditors can check.
Run your own internal audits and management reviews on a regular schedule.
Fix what the reviews find, then repeat the cycle so the system improves.
beginner.example: Think of a restaurant kitchen with a food safety system. The kitchen does not just buy one good fridge. It sets rules, trains staff, records fridge temperatures, checks them and fixes problems. A health inspector then samples those records. ISO 27001 works the same way for information, and an auditor looks at your daily records rather than your promises.
takeaways: ISO 27001 certifies a management system, not a product or a building.
Risk assessment and written decisions are the core of the standard.
Auditors sample real records, so good daily habits matter more than documents.

topics.title: Just-in-Time Access
topics.summary: Just-in-time (JIT) access is an access management pattern in which elevation to a privileged role or entitlement is granted only for a bounded period, on request, and only after the requester has satisfied whatever approval, justification and authentication conditions the organisation defines. It replaces standing privilege, where an administrator holds powerful entitlements permanently and therefore holds them equally at three in the morning during a phishing campaign and during a planned maintenance window. A JIT workflow typically has four phases: request, where the user states the scope and reason and often a ticket reference; approval, which may be automatic when the request matches a pre-approved template or manual when it does not; activation, where the entitlement is attached for a fixed duration and is frequently accompanied by step-up authentication and a session recording; and expiry, where the grant is removed automatically by the platform rather than by human discipline. The security gain is measurable, because the window during which a stolen credential is useful narrows from indefinite to hours, and the population of accounts holding privileged rights at any instant becomes small enough to enumerate and monitor. The pattern also produces high-quality telemetry that rarely exists elsewhere: every request, justification, approval decision, activation and expiry is logged, so defenders can alert on activations outside change windows, on self-approvals where separation of duties is required, on repeated activations that suggest a workflow is being used as permanent access, and on direct use of the underlying privileged account that bypasses the broker entirely.
objectives: You will be able to describe the request, approval, activation and expiry phases of a just-in-time access workflow.
You will be able to design approval policies that keep routine work fast while reserving manual review for high-risk elevation.
You will be able to enforce maximum activation duration, step-up authentication and scope limits for each privileged role.
You will be able to detect activation anomalies such as out-of-window elevation, self-approval and repeated renewal.
You will be able to identify bypass paths where a privileged credential is used directly instead of through the broker.
You will be able to measure the reduction in standing privilege achieved after a JIT rollout.

sources.label: Microsoft Learn: Activate Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management roles
NIST SP 800-53: Access Control and least privilege controls

beginner.definition: Just-in-time access means you get powerful rights only when you need them. You ask for the right, explain why, and someone or something approves it. The right is removed automatically after a set time, so it never stays with you.
beginner.whyItMatters: Administrators often keep powerful rights all day, every day. If someone steals that account, the thief gets those rights too. Just-in-time access shrinks that window to a few hours. It also creates a clear record of who asked for what and why. That record is gold during an investigation.
howItWorks: You request a powerful role and write a short reason for needing it.
The system checks your request against the rules and your ticket reference.
An approver agrees, or the system approves automatically for routine work.
The role is switched on for a fixed time, often with a stronger sign-in.
When the time ends, the system takes the role away without human effort.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel master key. The manager does not carry it all day long. When a guest is locked out, the manager signs the key out at the front desk and returns it after the job. The log shows the time, the reason, and the room. If the key ever goes missing, staff know exactly who had it and when.
takeaways: Standing privilege is the problem; time-limited elevation is the fix.
Every request should carry a reason, an approver, and a short expiry time.
Watch for activations outside working hours or repeated renewals.
