topics.title: Kerberos
topics.summary: Kerberos is a network authentication protocol built on symmetric cryptography and a trusted third party, in which a client proves its identity to a service without sending a password across the network. The key distribution centre, composed of the authentication service and the ticket granting service, issues a ticket granting ticket after the client authenticates, and the client then presents that ticket to obtain service tickets for individual resources. Tickets carry a validity window and are encrypted with keys derived from account passwords or machine secrets, which is why Kerberos security is inseparable from the hygiene of those secrets. In Active Directory the protocol underpins almost all domain authentication, and its abuse paths dominate enterprise intrusions: requesting service tickets and cracking them offline because a service account password is weak, forging tickets when a service account key is stolen, relaying authentication to a service that does not enforce mutual verification, and taking advantage of delegation configured too broadly. Defensive practice centres on detecting anomalous ticket requests, especially bursts of service ticket requests with unusual encryption types or for services that a principal never normally contacts, and on eliminating the conditions that make those requests valuable. That means long random passwords for service accounts managed automatically where possible, removal of unnecessary privileged service principals, restriction of delegation, and monitoring of the domain controller security log for the ticket and credential events that indicate a principal is attempting to obtain material it should not need.
objectives: You will be able to describe the role of the authentication service, ticket granting service and service tickets in a Kerberos exchange.
You will be able to explain how ticket lifetime, renewable tickets and encryption type downgrades affect exposure.
You will be able to identify risky service principal configurations, including weak service account secrets and unnecessary delegation.
You will be able to build detection logic for anomalous service ticket requests and unusual encryption type selection.
You will be able to explain relay and coercion risks against services that do not verify authentication properly.
You will be able to prioritise remediation for Kerberos-related findings by blast radius rather than by count.

sources.label: RFC 4120: The Kerberos Network Authentication Service (V5)
Microsoft Learn: Windows security auditing and Kerberos authentication

beginner.definition: Kerberos is a way for computers to prove who they are without sending passwords across the network. A trusted service hands out tickets, which are short-lived passes. A computer shows a ticket to reach another computer safely.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many workplace networks rely on Kerberos, so its weaknesses affect almost everything. Weak service passwords let an attacker copy a ticket and guess the secret offline. Stolen keys let an attacker forge tickets that look real. If you ignore ticket hygiene, one weak service account can quietly open the whole network.
howItWorks: You sign in once, and a central service checks your password for you.
That service gives you a special ticket, called a ticket granting ticket.
When you need a file server, you show that ticket and ask for a service ticket.
You present the service ticket to the server, which checks it and lets you in.
Tickets expire after a short time, so a stolen ticket stops working soon.
beginner.example: Think of a members-only club. At the front desk you show your identity card once. The desk gives you a wristband for the evening. With that wristband you can enter the bar, the pool, and the dance floor without showing your card again. The doormen trust the wristband because the front desk issued it. Stolen wristbands only work until the club closes.
takeaways: Kerberos proves identity with short-lived tickets instead of sending passwords.
Service account passwords should be long, random, and rotated automatically.
Watch for sudden bursts of unusual ticket requests in your logs.

topics.title: Key Management Service
topics.summary: A cloud key management service is a managed, hardware-backed system for creating, storing, rotating and auditing cryptographic keys, and for performing encryption and decryption without ever exposing the key material to the caller. Applications and services call an API to encrypt or decrypt, and the service enforces authorisation through the same identity and policy machinery as the rest of the platform, so control of a key is a control of the data it protects. Two design patterns dominate practice. Envelope encryption wraps data with a data key, then wraps that data key with a long-lived key that never leaves the service, which allows large objects to be encrypted efficiently while keeping the root secret in hardware. Customer-managed keys add an explicit policy and lifecycle that the customer controls, enabling rotation schedules, automatic rotation, grants, cross-account access and the ability to disable a key and render data unreadable. Security professionals focus on several recurring problems: keys with policies that allow broad principal access, keys shared across environments, disabled or scheduled-for-deletion keys that break services, missing audit trails on decrypt operations, and key material that is replicated into a region an organisation did not intend to use. Because destruction is irreversible, key lifecycle decisions are treated as high-risk change, and separation of duties between those who can use a key and those who can delete it is a standard control.
objectives: You will be able to explain envelope encryption and why data keys are wrapped rather than used directly on large objects.
You will be able to read a key policy and determine which principals can encrypt, decrypt, manage or delete a key.
You will be able to design rotation, cross-account access and separation of duties for customer-managed keys.
You will be able to triage alerts on key policy changes, disabling and scheduled deletion.
You will be able to describe the blast radius when a key is destroyed and how to plan for recovery.
You will be able to verify that audit logging captures key usage and that encrypt and decrypt events are retained.

sources.label: AWS Key Management Service Developer Guide

beginner.definition: A key management service is a cloud service that creates, stores and uses encryption keys for you. Encryption keys are the secret values that lock and unlock protected data. The keys never leave the service, so your programs ask it to encrypt or decrypt instead of handling the key themselves.
beginner.whyItMatters: Encryption is only as strong as the protection of its key. If the key sits in a config file or a code repository, anyone who finds it can read everything. A key management service keeps keys in hardened hardware and records every use. It also lets you disable or delete a key, which instantly makes the data it protects unreadable.
howItWorks: You create a key in the service and write a policy saying who may use it.
Your program sends data to the service and asks it to encrypt that data.
The service returns scrambled data, called ciphertext, and never shows you the key.
For large files, the service first makes a data key, encrypts the file with it, then protects that data key with the main key.
When someone needs the data back, the service checks permission and returns the readable form.
Every use is written to an audit log, and rotation replaces keys on a schedule.
beginner.example: Think of a bank vault. You never carry the vault key around. Instead you ask a clerk to lock or unlock your box, and the clerk checks your identity first. The vault also keeps a written record of every visit. If you ever close your box permanently, nobody can open it again, not even you.
takeaways: Keep encryption keys in a managed service, never in code or config files.
Control who may use a key, because that controls the data itself.
Deleting a key is permanent, so protect that action with extra approval.

topics.title: Key Rotation
topics.summary: Key rotation is the scheduled or event-driven replacement of cryptographic keys, secrets and certificates so that the exposure window of any single key is bounded. Rotation limits the blast radius of an undetected compromise, satisfies compliance requirements that demand defined cryptoperiods, and reduces the value of a stolen key to an attacker who may already have exfiltrated it. A workable rotation process has four parts: generating new key material in an approved location, distributing it to every consumer without downtime, accepting both old and new material during an overlap window, and retiring the old material with proof that nothing still depends on it. The hard part is almost never the cryptography; it is discovery of every place a key is used, including configuration files, environment variables, CI pipeline secrets, cached tokens, backups, third-party integrations and human-held copies. Rotation that breaks production is the reason teams avoid it, so mature organisations automate issuance, treat keys as short-lived credentials, prefer key derivation per message or per tenant over one long-lived shared key, and monitor decryption or authentication failures that would reveal a consumer missed a rotation. Emergency rotation after a suspected compromise is a different exercise from scheduled rotation, since it must assume the attacker holds the old material and can observe the overlap window.
objectives: Design a key rotation policy covering generation, distribution, overlap acceptance and retirement with evidence.
Enumerate every consumer of a key across services, pipelines, devices, backups and third parties before rotating.
Automate rotation using a secrets manager or KMS while preserving availability for dependent systems.
Distinguish scheduled rotation from emergency rotation after suspected compromise and adjust the process accordingly.
Detect incomplete rotation through authentication, decryption and signature verification failures in telemetry.
Define cryptoperiods for different key types and defend those choices in an audit or control review.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1: Recommendation for Key Management
NIST SP 800-57 Part 2: Best Practices for Key Management Organizations
AWS Key Management Service documentation - Rotating keys

beginner.definition: Key rotation means replacing a cryptographic key with a new one on a schedule or after an incident. The old key is retired once nothing uses it. Rotation limits how much damage a stolen key can do. Even if an attacker copied the key, it stops working after the change.
beginner.whyItMatters: Keys do not last forever. People leave, laptops are lost, and logs sometimes leak a secret. A key used for years is a long opportunity for an attacker. Rotation shortens that window and is also required by many security standards. The hard part is not making the new key. It is finding every system, script and device that still uses the old one.
howItWorks: List every place the key is used, including apps, build pipelines, backups and partner systems.
Create the new key in an approved place, such as a key manager or hardware device.
Give the new key to every consumer while the old key still works.
Wait through a short overlap period so nothing breaks during the change.
Confirm from logs that every consumer has switched to the new key.
Disable and delete the old key only after you are sure nothing needs it.
beginner.example: Think of changing the locks on an office door. You tell every employee and cleaner about the new key before the old one stops working. You keep both keys valid for a week, so nobody is locked out. Then you check the door logs to confirm everyone used the new key. Only then do you throw the old key away. If you skip a step, people stand outside.
takeaways: Rotate keys on a schedule and immediately after any suspected leak.
Find every consumer first. Most rotation outages come from a forgotten script.
Accept both keys during a short overlap, then retire the old one with evidence.

topics.title: KQL and SPL
topics.summary: KQL, the Kusto Query Language, and SPL, the Splunk Search Processing Language, are the two query languages most commonly used by detection engineers and SOC analysts to interrogate security telemetry. Both are pipeline languages: a search begins with a source of events and a filter, then passes a tabular result through a chain of operators that project, extend, summarise, join, order and visualise. Their shared idioms matter more than their syntax. Progressive filtering keeps queries fast because the earliest stage should eliminate the most data. Time bounding is mandatory rather than optional, both for performance and because an unbounded query over a long retention window will time out or return misleading aggregates. Summarisation collapses many raw events into per-entity counts, which is how thresholds, rarity analysis and first-seen or last-seen logic are expressed. Joins between datasets such as endpoint process events and identity sign-in logs are what turn a weak single-source signal into a defensible detection. The differences are practical. KQL uses a pipe-forward style with tabular operators, has strong support for dynamic and JSON-typed columns, and is used across Microsoft security products and Azure services. SPL uses a search-command model with a large command library, is central to Splunk, and offers macros and lookups that many teams use to build reusable detection content. Fluency in either language is really fluency in a set of habits: knowing which fields carry trustworthy values, understanding how each platform handles timestamps and nulls, and testing query logic against deliberately constructed sample data before trusting it to raise alerts.
objectives: You will be able to read and construct pipeline-style queries that filter, project, extend, summarise and join security telemetry.
You will be able to translate a detection intent between KQL and SPL, accounting for differences in operator names and null handling.
You will be able to write threshold and rarity logic that uses summarisation rather than single-event triggers.
You will be able to join endpoint, identity and network datasets to corroborate a weak single-source signal.
You will be able to diagnose why a slow query is slow and restructure it for the platform's execution model.
You will be able to validate query logic against hand-built sample data before promoting it to a production detection.

sources.label: Microsoft Learn: Kusto Query Language overview

beginner.definition: KQL and SPL are two query languages used to search security logs. KQL stands for Kusto Query Language. SPL stands for Splunk Search Processing Language. Both let you ask questions of huge amounts of log data and get a table of answers back.
beginner.whyItMatters: A security team collects millions of log lines every day. Reading them by hand is impossible. Query languages let you filter that flood down to the few events that matter. They are also how detection rules are written. If you cannot write a query, you cannot check whether a rule is correct.
howItWorks: You start with a data source, such as sign-in logs or process events from laptops.
You add a filter to keep only the rows you care about, such as one user.
You add another stage that counts events, groups them, or adds a new column.
Each stage passes its table result to the next stage, like water through pipes.
You finish with a sort and a limit so you see the most important rows first.
Before using a query as a detection, you run it against sample data you built yourself.
beginner.example: Picture a library with a million returned books piled in the hallway. You do not read every book. You ask a helper for books returned last week by one person, then sort them by title, then show only the first ten. Each request narrows the pile a little more. KQL and SPL queries work in that same step-by-step way. Each stage makes the pile smaller and more useful.
takeaways: Always limit your query to a time range before you run it.
Filter as early as possible so the search stays fast.
Test a query on sample data before turning it into a detection.

topics.title: Kubernetes RBAC
topics.summary: Kubernetes role-based access control is the authorisation system that decides whether an authenticated request against the API server is permitted, by matching the requester's identity and group memberships against rules that name API groups, resources and verbs. Permissions are granted through Role objects scoped to a namespace or ClusterRole objects that apply cluster-wide, and they take effect only when bound to a subject by a RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding. Because the API server is the control plane's single entry point, RBAC governs far more than reading object lists: a subject that can create pods can often arrange for a pod that mounts a service account token or a host path, a subject that can read secrets can obtain credentials for other workloads, a subject that can create role bindings can grant itself anything, and permission to exec into pods or read pod logs provides a direct path to application secrets and internal services. These compound paths mean that reviewing individual rules in isolation is misleading and effective privilege must be computed across the graph of bindings, service accounts and default roles. Security teams inventory cluster-admin bindings and wildcard rules, examine default service account usage, restrict who may create workloads and bindings, and monitor the audit log for privilege-sensitive verbs. Good practice pairs authorisation tightening with authentication controls, since RBAC decisions are only as trustworthy as the identity source feeding them.
objectives: You will be able to explain how roles, cluster roles and bindings combine to authorise an API request.
You will be able to compute the practical privilege of a subject, including indirect paths through pod creation and secret reads.
You will be able to identify wildcard rules, cluster-admin bindings and default service account exposure in a cluster.
You will be able to rewrite over-broad bindings into namespace-scoped least privilege.
You will be able to use audit log evidence to triage privilege-sensitive API activity.
You will be able to explain why RBAC tightening depends on trustworthy authentication and workload identity.

beginner.definition: Kubernetes role-based access control, often shortened to RBAC, is the rule system that decides who may do what in a Kubernetes cluster. Kubernetes is a platform that runs containers across many machines. The rules name a person or service, the actions allowed, and the scope, such as one namespace or the whole cluster.
beginner.whyItMatters: Every request to a cluster goes through one entry point, the API server. If permissions are too wide, a small compromise grows fast. Someone who can create a container can often mount a login token or a host folder. Someone who can read secrets can take credentials for other services. Tight rules limit how far one stolen identity can reach.
howItWorks: A user or a service account sends a request to the cluster API server.
The server checks who the caller is, including the groups they belong to.
It gathers the roles bound to that identity, in the namespace or across the cluster.
A role lists resources, such as pods or secrets, and verbs, such as get or create.
If a bound role covers the request, it is allowed, and the action is written to the audit log.
If no role covers it, the request is refused and nothing happens.
beginner.example: Picture an office with one reception desk that approves every request. A junior staff member's badge opens their own floor and the shared kitchen. A manager's badge opens more doors. Nobody's badge opens everything. If a badge is lost, the damage depends on which doors it could open, so you keep each badge as small as the job needs.
takeaways: Roles describe permissions; bindings attach those roles to people or services.
Creating containers or reading secrets can be a path to more access.
Review admin bindings regularly and remove the ones nobody needs.

topics.title: Lateral Movement
topics.summary: Lateral movement is the progression from one compromised system or identity to others inside the same environment, performed to reach valuable data, higher authority, or a position from which the final objective can be achieved without returning to the internet. It rarely relies on a novel exploit; most real intrusions reuse credentials, sessions and administrative tooling that already exist. Typical mechanisms include interactive remote access over desktop, terminal or remote management protocols, authenticated file sharing and remote service creation, execution frameworks that push jobs to many machines at once, and control-plane operations in cloud or virtualisation platforms that reach many workloads through a single API. Credential reuse drives much of it, whether the material is a plaintext password, a password hash, a cached ticket or a long-lived API key, and it is frequently shared service accounts and duplicated local administrator passwords that make the movement cheap. Detection depends on joining authentication events to host and network context: a workstation authenticating to another workstation, an account logging in from a system it never normally touches, remote service or scheduled task creation, and east-west traffic that crosses a segmentation boundary. Mitigations reduce the number of usable hops rather than the number of alerts: segmented networks with default-deny rules between tiers, unique local administrator credentials, dedicated privileged access workstations, just-in-time administration, and removal of legacy authentication protocols. In cloud estates the same logic applies to role assumption paths and to network reachability between workloads.
objectives: You will be able to explain why lateral movement is dominated by credential reuse rather than exploitation.
You will be able to identify the authentication and host telemetry that reveals movement between systems.
You will be able to describe how segmentation, administrative tiering and unique local credentials reduce reachable paths.
You will be able to interpret east-west network flow data to spot traversal across trust boundaries.
You will be able to trace a role-assumption chain in a cloud tenant as a form of lateral movement.

beginner.definition: Lateral movement is the step where an intruder moves from one compromised machine or account to another inside the same network. They do this to reach valuable data, gain higher authority, or find a better position. It rarely needs a brand new software flaw. Most of the time it reuses existing passwords, sessions and admin tools.
beginner.whyItMatters: One stolen laptop should not unlock the whole company. But in many networks, one password works on many machines. Shared admin accounts and repeated local passwords make movement cheap for an intruder. If you cannot see logins between your own systems, you cannot follow the path they take. Network segmentation, which splits a network into smaller parts, limits how far a single password reaches.
howItWorks: The intruder starts on one machine they already control with a low-level account.
They search the machine for stored passwords, saved sessions and admin tools.
They try those credentials on other systems, often using normal remote access features.
When one works, they repeat the process from the newly reached machine.
Step by step, they approach systems that hold the data or rights they want.
beginner.example: Imagine an office building where every door uses the same key. A cleaner loses their key ring at the bus stop. The person who finds it can open the reception, then the finance office, then the server room. Each door feels safe on its own, but the shared key joins them all together. In networks, reused passwords and shared admin accounts are that same key ring. One small loss becomes a path through the building.
takeaways: Attackers usually move sideways with stolen credentials, not new exploits.
Give every machine its own unique local administrator password, not one shared one.
Log and review the logins that happen between your own internal systems.

topics.title: LDAP
topics.summary: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is an application protocol for accessing and maintaining distributed directory information services, and it remains the directory backbone behind Active Directory, OpenLDAP and most enterprise identity stores. Data is organised as a hierarchical tree of entries, each identified by a distinguished name and described by attributes constrained by a schema, with object classes determining which attributes are permitted. Clients bind to the directory to establish an identity and a level of access, then search with a base, a scope and a filter to retrieve or modify entries. Authentication outcomes depend on the bind and on transport: simple binds send credentials that are only protected by the transport, so LDAP over TLS or a SASL mechanism such as GSSAPI is required for any operation crossing an untrusted segment, and referrals and anonymous binds must be deliberately disabled unless a specific integration demands them. The dominant application-layer weakness in directory-connected software is filter injection, where unescaped user input is concatenated into a search filter so that an attacker can alter the logic of the query and, in badly written authentication code, bind as another user or enumerate the directory. Directory design carries its own risk: overly broad read permissions on the user object class enable reconnaissance of accounts, groups, service principals and delegation settings, and stale accounts or nested groups accumulate effective privilege that nobody intended to grant. Defenders monitor for anomalous bind failures, unusual search filters, high-volume enumeration and changes to privileged groups or directory-integrated objects.
objectives: You will be able to describe the directory information tree, distinguished names, schema and object classes well enough to read an LDIF entry.
You will be able to choose an appropriate bind mechanism and explain why simple binds require transport encryption.
You will be able to identify LDAP filter injection in application code and describe how input escaping prevents it.
You will be able to reduce directory exposure by restricting anonymous binds, referrals and overly broad read permissions.
You will be able to detect directory enumeration and privileged group modification from directory server logs.
You will be able to trace effective group membership for an account and explain why nested groups complicate least privilege.

sources.label: RFC 4511: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) - Protocol

beginner.definition: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, or LDAP, is a way to read and change information in a directory. A directory is a shared address book for computers. It stores users, groups, and devices in a tree of entries. Many sign-in systems use it behind the scenes.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most companies keep one central directory for accounts. If that directory is too open, an attacker can list every user and group in minutes. Bad code that mixes user input into a search can also let someone impersonate another account. Protecting the directory protects every system that trusts it.
howItWorks: A client connects to the directory server and asks to bind, which means to sign in.
The server checks the credentials and gives the client a level of access.
The client sends a search with a starting point, a depth, and a filter.
The server returns the matching entries and the attributes you are allowed to see.
If the connection crosses an untrusted network, it should be wrapped in encryption.
beginner.example: Think of a large public library. The catalogue lists every book, who borrowed it, and where it sits. Anyone may read the catalogue, but only staff may change the records. A careless clerk who reads a request too literally might hand over a private member file. Good rules about who may read and who may edit keep the library trustworthy.
takeaways: A directory is a shared address book, so treat its read permissions as important.
You should never send directory credentials over a connection without encryption.
Always escape user input before it reaches a directory search filter.

topics.title: Living Off the Land Binary
topics.summary: A living-off-the-land binary, commonly shortened to lolbin, is a legitimate, usually signed and pre-installed executable that an intruder abuses to perform an action such as downloading content, executing a payload, compressing data, or establishing persistence, without introducing a file that a signature-based control would flag. The same idea applies to scripts and libraries, which is why the broader terms living-off-the-land techniques and abuse of built-in tooling are often preferred. The defensive problem is structural: an allow-list that permits the operating system's own utilities implicitly permits every capability those utilities possess, and many of them are considerably more capable than administrators expect. Common abuse patterns include signed binaries that fetch remote content, utilities that proxy execution of another program, management and scripting interfaces that run arbitrary code, archiving tools used to stage collected data, and troubleshooting or installer executables that were designed to raise their own privilege. Detection cannot rely on the tool being present or on its signature. It relies on context: the parent process, the user account, the working directory, the full command line, the network destination contacted, and whether the invocation matches the organisation's baseline of how that tool is normally used. Practical controls include application control policies scoped to specific binaries and argument patterns, blocking specific utilities on server roles that never need them, script block logging, and prompt patching to remove known privilege-escalation paths in installer and troubleshooting components. Analysts should also expect deliberate argument obfuscation and path trickery, since adversaries know these names are watched.
objectives: Define living-off-the-land techniques and explain why signed, pre-installed binaries defeat content-based detection.
Recognise the capability categories adversaries seek in built-in tooling: download, execute, archive, persist and elevate.
Write detections keyed on process lineage, command-line arguments and network destinations rather than file reputation.
Build a baseline of legitimate administrative use so that deviations can be prioritised confidently.
Apply application control and role-based binary restrictions to reduce the abusable tool surface on servers.
Explain how argument obfuscation, path manipulation and renamed copies change the detection approach required.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

beginner.definition: A lolbin, short for living-off-the-land binary, is a normal, trusted program that is already installed on your system. Attackers use these programs to do their work instead of bringing their own harmful tool. Because the program is genuine and digitally signed, it does not look suspicious on its own.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you allow the operating system's own tools to run, you also allow every ability those tools have. Many of them can download files, run other programs, or compress data. An attacker who uses them never needs to drop a strange file that a scanner would catch. So you cannot judge safety by the tool alone. You must judge the situation it is used in.
howItWorks: The attacker first gains some way to run commands on the machine.
Instead of installing their own tool, they call a program Windows already provides.
That trusted program performs the action, such as fetching a file from the internet.
Any file-based check sees a legitimate, properly signed program at work.
Defenders must instead read the command line, the parent program, and the account used.
Unusual wording or timing for a normal tool is the real warning sign.
beginner.example: Imagine a building where staff may use the communal toolbox freely. A thief never brings a crowbar. They simply take the building's own screwdriver, use it, and put it back on the shelf. The toolbox list looks perfect and nothing is missing. The only clue is that the screwdriver was used at midnight, by someone who should not have been there, on a door it is never used on. Lolbins are that screwdriver, and context is the only clue you get.
takeaways: A signed system tool can still be used for harm; judge the context, not the file.
Build a baseline of how each built-in tool is normally used in your workplace.
Restrict tools on servers that never need them, and log full command lines.

topics.title: Macro Malware
topics.summary: Macro malware is malicious logic delivered inside a document or spreadsheet that uses the host application's built-in scripting facility to execute when the file is opened or when the user enables content. The classic form targets office productivity suites, where a document containing an embedded macro reaches a user as an email attachment, a link to a shared file, or a file hosted on a legitimate service, and relies on social engineering to persuade the recipient to click through the security warning. The technique persists because it sits inside a trusted, signed, universally deployed application and because a document is a natural thing for a user to open. Modern variants have widened well beyond the original form: some rely on external content relationships that pull a remote template or resource on open without any macro at all, some abuse document features to launch a companion file, and some target spreadsheet or presentation formats that fewer organisations remember to restrict. Defensive control has three layers. First, reduce the capability itself by disabling macros in documents originating from the internet, using mark-of-the-web and policy-based blocking rather than relying on user judgement. Second, restrict what the host process may do through attack surface reduction rules, application control, and blocking of child process creation from productivity applications. Third, detect the residue: document processes spawning shells or scripting engines, unusual outbound connections from a workstation's office application, external template retrieval, and files written to startup or temporary locations immediately after a document is opened. Email and web filtering help, but user reporting and rapid containment matter because macro campaigns are frequently the initial access step of something larger.
objectives: Explain how a document-hosted script gains execution and why the host application's trust makes it effective.
Compare macro-based delivery with template-injection and companion-file techniques that need no macro at all.
Configure mark-of-the-web and policy controls that block internet-origin macros without user discretion.
Write detections for productivity applications spawning interpreters, shells or unexpected network connections.
Investigate a suspected document incident from delivery through initial execution and follow-on activity.
Design user reporting and containment steps that shorten the window between opening a document and response.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK: User Execution: Malicious File (T1204.002)

beginner.definition: Macro malware is harmful code hidden inside a document or spreadsheet. A macro is a small script that the application can run for you, for example to format a table. Attackers abuse this feature, so that opening the file and allowing content starts their code. Delivery is often by email or a shared link.
beginner.whyItMatters: Documents are opened by everyone, and the application that opens them is trusted and installed everywhere. That makes a document a natural disguise. One click on an Allow button is enough to start an intrusion. Because the same feature is used for legitimate automation, you cannot simply ban all documents. You have to control which files may run macros, and watch what the application does afterward.
howItWorks: The victim receives a document by email, chat, or a link to a shared folder.
The file includes a message that encourages the reader to enable content.
When content is enabled, the built-in macro language runs the hidden script.
The script often downloads or starts another program in the background.
The document's application may also fetch a remote template without any macro at all.
Defenders watch for document programs starting shells or making network connections.
beginner.example: Think of a plain envelope that looks like a utility bill. Inside is not a bill but a set of instructions that only work if you read them aloud. The instruction sheet is harmless while sealed. The moment you speak it, you have given an order on someone else's behalf. A macro document is like that. It sits quietly until you click Allow, and that single permission turns a harmless-looking file into a starting point.
takeaways: A document can carry a script that runs when you enable content.
Block macros in files that came from the internet instead of trusting the user.
Watch closely for document programs that start shells or open network connections.

topics.title: Memory Dump
topics.summary: A memory dump is a capture of the contents of a system's physical or virtual memory, preserved as an image file for later analysis. It is the primary source for evidence that never touches disk: running and recently terminated processes, injected code regions, loaded drivers, kernel structures, network connections, command histories, encryption keys and, in many intrusions, the only surviving copy of fileless malware and its configuration. Dumps are taken either from a live host with a trusted acquisition tool, from a virtual machine through the hypervisor, from a cloud instance through provider snapshot or capture mechanisms, or from a crashed system via a configured crash dump or hibernation file. Fidelity depends on the method: hardware-assisted or hypervisor-level capture generally produces the most complete image, while software tools running inside a potentially compromised operating system may themselves be tampered with by a kernel-mode rootkit, so the trustworthiness of the tool and the order of acquisition both matter enormously. A defensible acquisition records the tool and version, the exact command, the memory range captured, a cryptographic hash of the image, the time of capture and the identity of the collector, because the image becomes evidence the moment it is written. Analysis then reconstructs process trees, extracts strings and configuration, looks for injected or unbacked executable regions, recovers credential material, and correlates findings with disk, identity and network evidence. Memory images are large and sensitive, so handling, retention and access controls are part of the process rather than an afterthought.
objectives: Explain what evidence a memory dump can recover that disk and log sources cannot.
Compare live, hypervisor, cloud-provider and crash-dump acquisition methods and their fidelity tradeoffs.
Perform a documented memory acquisition that records tooling, scope, capture time and cryptographic hash.
Assess whether a dump taken through a possibly compromised operating system can be trusted.
Analyse a memory image to reconstruct processes, network connections and injected code regions.
Correlate memory findings with disk, identity and network telemetry to build a defensible narrative.
Handle, store and retain memory images under access controls appropriate to their sensitivity and legal status.

sources.label: Microsoft Learn - Windows memory dump, crash dump and troubleshooting documentation
SANS Institute - digital forensics and incident response resources

beginner.definition: A memory dump is a saved copy of everything inside a computer's working memory, called RAM (random access memory). It is written to a file so you can study it later. It holds running programs, open network connections, and recent commands. Some evidence, including fileless attacks, exists only there.
beginner.whyItMatters: When you switch a computer off, memory is wiped in seconds. Anything that lived only in memory disappears with it. Attackers know this and use tools that never write a file to disk. If you reboot first, you may destroy the best evidence you had. A memory dump captures it before that happens.
howItWorks: Keep the machine running, because switching it off erases the evidence you want.
Run a trusted capture tool on the live system and write the image to external storage.
Record the tool name, its version, the exact command, and the time of capture.
Calculate a hash of the image, a fingerprint that shows it has not changed.
Analyze the image to list processes, network connections, and hidden code.
Store the large, sensitive image under strict access control with the case file.
beginner.example: Think about the steam rising from a hot cup of coffee. Once it cools, the steam is gone and you cannot get it back. Memory evidence behaves the same way. A reboot or a shutdown is like waiting for the cup to cool. A memory dump is you sealing the steam in a jar while it is still there.
takeaways: Memory holds evidence that never touches the disk at all.
Do not reboot a suspect machine before you capture its memory.
Record the tool, the command, the time, and a hash for every capture.

topics.title: MFA
topics.summary: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is an authentication control that requires a principal to present evidence from two or more distinct factor categories before a session is granted. The categories are knowledge (something you know, such as a password or PIN), possession (something you have, such as a hardware token, smart card or registered phone), and inherence (something you are, such as a fingerprint or face geometry), with location and behavioural signals sometimes treated as additional context rather than true factors. Because a stolen password alone satisfies only one category, MFA directly disrupts credential replay, password spraying and credential stuffing against externally exposed services, and it is one of the few controls that measurably changes the economics of initial access for ransomware operators. The strength of an implementation depends far less on the label than on the binding between factors: push notification approval, SMS one-time codes and email codes are all phishable or relayable, and adversary-in-the-middle toolkits that proxy the legitimate login page can capture a session token after the user completes a genuine prompt. Practitioners therefore evaluate MFA by the assurance properties it actually delivers: phishing resistance, number matching, origin binding, device-bound keys, and the telemetry the identity provider emits so that anomalous enrolment, factor reset and impossible-travel events can be alerted on. Deployment also has to survive operational reality, including service accounts, legacy protocols that cannot present a second factor, break-glass accounts, and help-desk enrolment fraud, which is why conditional access policy, number matching and FIDO2 security keys are typically combined rather than deployed in isolation.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish authentication factor categories and explain why two prompts of the same category do not constitute MFA.
You will be able to evaluate push, SMS, TOTP and FIDO2 authenticators by their resistance to phishing and adversary-in-the-middle relay.
You will be able to design an MFA rollout that covers privileged accounts, legacy protocols and break-glass access without creating lockout risk.
You will be able to build detection logic for MFA fatigue, factor enrolment changes, and successful sign-ins from new devices or geographies.
You will be able to explain how session token theft defeats MFA and what conditional access or token protection settings reduce that exposure.
You will be able to assess help-desk and self-service reset workflows for enrolment fraud and describe compensating verification steps.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-63B: Digital Identity Guidelines, Authentication and Lifecycle Management
Microsoft Learn: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication

beginner.definition: Multi-factor authentication, usually shortened to MFA, asks for two or more different kinds of proof before it lets you in. The kinds are something you know, something you have, and something you are. A password alone is only one kind.
beginner.whyItMatters: Passwords leak in large numbers, and attackers reuse them everywhere. A second kind of proof breaks that attack, because a stolen password is no longer enough. Most simple attacks stop at this step. Without it, one reused password can open your email, your files, and your work accounts.
howItWorks: You type your password first, which proves the thing you know.
The system then asks for a second kind of proof, such as a code or a key.
You approve the request on your phone or tap a small hardware key.
The system checks that both proofs belong to the same person.
Only then does it create your session and let you continue working.
beginner.example: Think of a bank safe deposit box. You need your own key and the bank's key to open it. One key alone does nothing. The bank clerk also checks your signature and your identification. Two separate things must be true at the same time. That is why a stolen key is not enough for a thief.
takeaways: Two prompts of the same kind are not multi-factor authentication.
Only approve a sign-in request when you started that sign-in yourself.
Security keys resist phishing far better than codes sent by text message.

topics.title: MISP
topics.summary: MISP is an open-source threat intelligence platform designed for storing, correlating, sharing and consuming structured indicators together with the context that makes them usable. Its central data structure is the event, a container that groups attributes describing an incident, campaign or sighting. Attributes are typed key-value pairs covering network indicators, file hashes and names, email artefacts, registry keys, financial data and free text, and they carry a category, a distribution setting and optional identifiers used for correlation. Objects extend attributes into structured bundles, so a file object can carry hashes, size and filename together instead of as loose rows. Taxonomies provide controlled vocabularies for classifying events, while galaxies attach knowledge such as ATT&CK techniques and threat actor clusters, which is what lets an organisation pivot from raw indicators to behavioural intelligence. Correlation is a core feature: when a newly ingested attribute matches an existing one, MISP links the events, surfacing relationships that a flat feed would hide. Sharing is governed by distribution levels, sharing groups and synchronisation with partner servers, and feeds can be pulled from external sources at configurable intervals. Warning lists are the practical counterweight to that automation, flagging values such as common public resolvers, popular domains and shared hosting ranges that are almost always benign. Effective MISP use depends on hygiene rather than features: consistent tagging, honest confidence and distribution choices, curated feeds, and periodic review of stale events. Because instances frequently exchange data with partners and public feeds, every ingested attribute should be treated as untrusted input, and correlation output should never drive automatic blocking without a validation step.
objectives: You will be able to model an incident as a MISP event with typed attributes and objects rather than loose indicators.
You will be able to apply taxonomies and galaxies so an event carries classification and technique context.
You will be able to configure distribution levels and sharing groups so intelligence reaches only intended partners.
You will be able to explain how correlation and warning lists change what an analyst sees and what gets blocked.
You will be able to evaluate and curate external feeds and retire stale events from an instance.
You will be able to assess the exposure created by publishing an event and choose the correct sharing setting.

beginner.definition: MISP is a free, open source platform for storing and sharing threat information. You keep each incident in a container called an event. Inside it you store typed clues, such as addresses, file names and email details. The platform links related events and controls who may see each one.
beginner.whyItMatters: Threat information is far more useful when it is shared. One team may spot a harmful address that another team has already met. A shared platform saves everyone from starting over. Context matters too. A bare address tells you very little, but the same address with an attacker name and a date becomes actionable. MISP keeps that context attached, so partners can trust and reuse your findings.
howItWorks: Create an event for the incident, and give it a clear title and date.
Add attributes, which are typed clues such as a network address or a file hash.
Attach labels from shared vocabularies so other teams can search and filter reliably.
Set the distribution. Choose whether the event stays private, goes to a group or is public.
Let the platform correlate. A new clue that matches an old one links the two events together.
Use warning lists to mute common values, such as popular public web services.
beginner.example: Think of a neighbourhood watch group with a shared notebook. Each neighbour writes down what they saw, when and where, instead of shouting a rumour. Because the entries are dated and labelled, patterns appear. Three streets report the same van on the same evening. The notebook also has privacy rules, so some pages are for the whole street and some are only for the committee. MISP is that notebook for security teams.
takeaways: MISP stores clues together with their context, not as a bare list of addresses.
Set the sharing level on every event, so information reaches only the right people.
Treat everything you receive from partners as untrusted until you check it.

topics.title: MTTD and MTTR
topics.summary: Mean Time to Detect and Mean Time to Respond are the two headline measures of security operations performance. Mean Time to Detect measures the elapsed interval between when malicious activity actually began and when it was first identified, while Mean Time to Respond measures the interval from identification to containment or resolution, depending on how the organisation defines the endpoint. Both are averages and both are therefore easily misread. A mean computed over a handful of incidents is dominated by outliers, so distributions, medians and percentiles communicate far more than a single number. The definitions themselves are the hardest part. Detection time cannot be measured from the alert timestamp unless you also determine when the activity started, which usually requires retrospective log analysis and often moves the start earlier once the incident is understood. Response end is equally ambiguous: is it containment of the immediate threat, eradication, restoration of service, or case closure. Without a written definition agreed with the business, teams optimise a metric they cannot compare over time. The measures are also gameable. Suppressing noisy detections lowers alert volume and can appear to improve response time while degrading detection. Closing cases quickly without corroboration improves the average and hides unresolved risk. The genuinely useful approach is to pair times with quality measures: the proportion of incidents found by internal detection rather than external notification, the fraction detected at each ATT&CK stage, dwell time distributions, and containment precision. Tracking MTTD and MTTR by incident class and detection source, and reviewing the specific incidents that set the extremes, converts an executive number into an engineering feedback loop.
objectives: You will be able to define detection start, detection point, containment and closure precisely enough that the metric is comparable over time.
You will be able to explain why means alone mislead and use medians, percentiles and distributions when reporting response performance.
You will be able to compute dwell time for an incident by reconstructing the true start of activity from retrospective log evidence.
You will be able to identify how suppressing alerts or closing cases prematurely can artificially improve these metrics.
You will be able to complement timing metrics with detection-source and coverage-quality measures such as internal versus external discovery.
You will be able to segment MTTD and MTTR by incident class and use the worst cases to drive specific detection or playbook improvements.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-61, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

beginner.definition: Mean Time to Detect is the average time between an attack starting and your team noticing it. Mean Time to Respond is the average time from noticing it to containing it. Together they are the two headline numbers for how well a security team performs. Mean simply means average.
beginner.whyItMatters: These numbers tell leadership whether the security team is getting faster or slower. They also show where the weak points are. A slow detection time means your sensors or rules are missing things. A slow response time usually means your procedures are unclear. Without measuring, you are guessing about your own readiness.
howItWorks: First, agree on exactly when the clock starts. Usually that is when the attack began.
Then agree on when detection counts, such as when an analyst confirms the alert.
Agree on exactly when response ends: containment, full cleanup, or case closure.
For each incident, record those three timestamps and subtract them to get durations.
Average the durations, but also look at the median and the worst cases.
Finally, review the slowest incidents to find the specific step that failed.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital tracking how long patients wait. The average wait looks fine, but one patient waited nine hours and that single case hides the truth. So the hospital also reports the longest waits and the middle value. Security metrics behave the same way. One very slow incident can make an average look terrible, and one very fast incident can make it look falsely good.
takeaways: An average alone hides the story; check the median and worst cases.
Write down your definitions, or the numbers cannot be compared over time.
Watch for teams that improve the number by closing cases early.

topics.title: Netflow and IPFIX
topics.summary: NetFlow and its open equivalent IPFIX are flow-export technologies that summarise network conversations rather than capturing every packet. A router or switch observes packets, groups them into flows keyed by source and destination address, ports, protocol and other fields, and periodically exports records that describe each flow with counters, timestamps and interface information. Because exports are aggregated, the storage and bandwidth cost is a small fraction of full packet capture, which makes it practical to retain flow data for weeks or months across an entire estate. That retention is the core defensive value. Flow records answer who talked to whom, when, how much and over which port, and they stay useful for retrospective investigation long after the packets are gone. Common analytical uses include detecting exfiltration by volume and direction, identifying beaconing through regular inter-arrival patterns, mapping external exposure during incident scoping, and proving that a segmentation policy is genuinely enforced. Flow data is deliberately lossy: it carries no payload, so it cannot confirm what was transferred or match content signatures, and sampling, aggregation timeouts and top-talker reporting on the exporting device all reduce fidelity. Adversaries and ordinary applications can tunnel over permitted protocols, so flow analysis often produces the hypothesis that packet capture or endpoint telemetry must confirm. Practical deployments must handle clock synchronisation, because flow timestamps are useless for correlation when devices disagree, asymmetric routing so both directions are collected, collector capacity and duplicate exports, and consistent interface naming so that a flow can be tied to a physical or logical path. Enrichment with asset inventory, geolocation and threat intelligence turns raw records into something an analyst can prioritise, and keeping flow data beside DNS, proxy and authentication logs resolves most incidents that no single source could explain.
objectives: You will be able to describe how flows are defined, aggregated and exported and what fidelity that costs.
You will be able to triage flow records for beaconing, exfiltration volume and unexpected lateral movement.
You will be able to design a collector pipeline that handles time sync, asymmetry and duplicates.
You will be able to enrich flow data with asset, geolocation and reputation context for prioritisation.
You will be able to test a segmentation policy against observed flow evidence rather than documentation.
You will be able to state when flow metadata is insufficient and packet or endpoint evidence is required.

beginner.definition: NetFlow and IPFIX are ways for network devices to summarise traffic instead of recording every packet. The device groups packets into flows, which are conversations between two addresses, and sends a short record for each one. A record says who talked to whom, when, for how long and how much data moved.
beginner.whyItMatters: Full packet capture is expensive to store, so most teams keep only a few days of it. Flow records are tiny, so you can keep months of them and still answer questions later. When something goes wrong, flows show you which machines spoke to a strange address and how much data left. They will not tell you what was inside the traffic, but they point you to where to look next.
howItWorks: A router or switch watches the packets that pass through it every second.
It groups packets with the same addresses, ports and protocol into one flow.
It counts bytes and packets for that flow and notes the start and end time.
Every minute or so it exports those records to a collector, which stores them.
Analysts then search the records for odd patterns, such as regular small transfers at night.
Enriching records with asset names and known bad addresses makes them easier to rank.
beginner.example: Think of your monthly phone bill. It lists every call: the number dialled, the date, the duration and sometimes the data used. It does not record what you said. That is exactly what a flow record is. If someone made many short calls to the same strange number at three in the morning, the bill would show the pattern clearly. Flow data works the same way and is far cheaper to keep than recordings.
takeaways: Flow records summarise conversations; they never contain the content.
Because they are small, you can keep them for months and look back.
Regular small transfers to one address often mean hidden beaconing.

topics.title: Network Access Control
topics.summary: Network access control is the set of technologies that decides whether a device may join a network and what it may reach once connected. A typical deployment authenticates the device or its user before granting access, commonly through 802.1X with a RADIUS server, MAC authentication bypass for devices that cannot run a supplicant, or a captive portal for guests and unmanaged endpoints. After authentication the platform evaluates posture, covering operating system version, patch level, endpoint protection state, disk encryption and configuration compliance, and then places the device into a role-based segment or access control list. Devices that fail posture checks are quarantined to a remediation network where they can update but cannot reach production systems, and devices that cannot authenticate at all are denied or routed into a registration workflow. The result is that network admission becomes a policy decision with an audit trail rather than a physical fact. Projects fail more often for organisational than technical reasons. Discovery is the first hurdle, because most estates contain printers, cameras, badge readers, medical devices and building systems that predate any authentication requirement and may not support 802.1X, and each needs a documented exception with a compensating control. Rollout must be staged in monitor mode first, where the platform classifies devices and reports what would have happened, before enforcement is enabled, otherwise a misconfiguration locks out staff or takes critical systems offline. Link design also matters, because authentication on switch-to-switch and switch-to-controller uplinks requires careful configuration to avoid authenticating infrastructure. Once operating, network access control supplies valuable telemetry: it knows which device is on which port at which time, which helps incident response locate and isolate a compromised host quickly. Its limitation is that it secures the moment of connection, not the behaviour afterwards, so it complements segmentation and monitoring rather than replacing them.
objectives: You will be able to explain 802.1X authentication flows and where MAC authentication bypass or portals are needed.
You will be able to design posture checks and a quarantine path that does not break remediation.
You will be able to plan a monitor-mode rollout that discovers devices before enforcement begins.
You will be able to identify infrastructure links and headless devices that require documented exceptions.
You will be able to use admission telemetry for rapid host location and isolation during an incident.
You will be able to state the limits of admission control and the complementary controls it requires.

beginner.definition: Network access control, or NAC, decides whether a device may join your network and what it may reach once connected. It checks who or what is connecting, then checks the device's health, such as patches and antivirus. Healthy devices get normal access, unhealthy ones go to a repair network, and unknown ones are blocked or registered.
beginner.whyItMatters: Anyone who plugs a laptop into a wall socket or joins the wireless network is on your network, unless something checks first. One unpatched or infected machine can then spread trouble to everything else. NAC makes joining a decision with a record, instead of a physical fact. It also tells you which device is on which port, which helps you find and isolate a compromised machine quickly.
howItWorks: A device connects to a switch port or a wireless network and asks to join.
It proves its identity with a certificate, a password, or, for simple devices, its hardware address.
The system then checks the device's health, such as updates, antivirus and disk encryption.
A device that passes goes into a network zone that matches its role.
A device that fails goes into a quarantine area where it can be fixed but not cause harm.
Devices that cannot authenticate, like printers, get a documented exception and limited access.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital front desk. Every visitor must state who they are and who they are visiting. Staff receive a badge that opens only the doors they need. A visitor who looks unwell is sent to a separate room before entering the wards. A delivery driver without an appointment waits at reception. The building still has corridors, but each door checks a different list.
takeaways: NAC checks identity and device health before letting a device on the network.
Failed checks should quarantine, not simply lock people out of work.
Roll it out in monitor mode first so you discover odd devices safely.

topics.title: Network Segmentation
topics.summary: A network segment is a bounded group of systems that share a communication policy, and segmentation is the practice of inserting enforced boundaries between those groups so that a single compromised host cannot reach every other asset. Boundaries may be physical, built from separate switches and cabling, logical, built from VLANs with router or firewall access control lists, or identity-based, built from microsegmentation agents and policy engines that decide per workload rather than per subnet. The design goal is to limit blast radius and to create chokepoints where traffic can be inspected and logged. Flat networks fail catastrophically because one phished workstation inherits reachability to file shares, management interfaces, backup infrastructure and directory services. Good segmentation starts from data and service flows rather than from the organisational chart: classify assets by sensitivity, map which systems must talk to which on which ports, then enforce default deny and log the denials until the policy is proven. Segmentation is a programme rather than a purchase. Legacy applications with hard-coded addresses, unmanaged devices, and operational technology that cannot tolerate added latency all generate exceptions that erode the model over time, so each exception needs an owner and an expiry date. Attackers respond by tunnelling permitted protocols, chaining through dual-homed hosts and abusing management planes, which is why monitoring must exist on the boundaries themselves. Administrative tiering, jump hosts and dedicated management networks address the management-plane risk, while cloud security groups, network policies and service meshes reproduce the same ideas with their own drift problems. The practical test of any segmentation scheme is adversarial: assume a host inside a segment is already compromised and ask what it can still reach.
objectives: You will be able to classify assets by sensitivity and derive required communication flows from evidence rather than assumption.
You will be able to design enforced zone boundaries with default deny and documented, expiring exceptions.
You will be able to use flow and firewall logs to detect residual flat-network reachability.
You will be able to describe how administrative tiering and jump hosts reduce management-plane risk.
You will be able to distinguish network, host-based and identity-based microsegmentation and choose appropriately.
You will be able to assess a segmentation design from an assumed-breach perspective and rank the residual paths.

sources.label: RFC 1918: Address Allocation for Private Internets

beginner.definition: Network segmentation means splitting your network into separate groups and putting a control between them. Each group, or segment, holds systems that need to work together. Traffic between segments must be allowed by a rule. The aim is simple: if one machine is taken over, it should not be able to reach everything else.
beginner.whyItMatters: On a flat network, every machine can talk to every other machine. That is convenient until one laptop is infected, because the attacker then has a clear path to file shares, backups and management systems. Segmentation breaks those paths and creates places where traffic can be checked. It also slows an attacker down, which gives your team time to notice and respond. The work is ongoing, not a one-time purchase.
howItWorks: List your systems and sort them by how sensitive and how important they are.
Find out which systems really need to talk to each other, and on which ports.
Group those systems into segments and write rules that allow only the needed traffic.
Block everything else by default and log what gets blocked, so you can spot mistakes.
Review the blocked logs until the rules are correct, then keep the logs for monitoring.
Give every exception an owner and an end date, or the old flat network slowly returns.
beginner.example: Think of an office building where every door opened with the same key. Losing one key meant losing the whole building. Now imagine each floor, the server room and the finance office have their own locks. Your badge opens the doors your job needs and nothing more. A thief who takes your badge can still roam, but only through the rooms you already had. That limit is the whole point of segmentation.
takeaways: Segmentation limits how far one compromised machine can reach.
Start from real traffic needs, not from the organisation chart.
Every exception needs an owner and an expiry date, or the flat network returns.

topics.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
topics.summary: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is a voluntary, outcome-based framework that organises cybersecurity activity into a common vocabulary so that technical teams, executives, auditors and regulators can discuss risk using the same terms. Its core is a set of Functions, historically Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, each broken into Categories and Subcategories that describe desired outcomes rather than prescribing specific products. Around that core sits the Framework Implementation Tiers, which characterise how rigorous and repeatable an organisation's risk management practice is, and the Framework Profiles, which express current and target states so a gap analysis produces a funded roadmap instead of a vague maturity claim. Practitioners use the framework in three concrete ways. First, as a mapping hub: an organisation maps its existing controls from ISO 27001, NIST SP 800-53, CIS Controls and regulatory obligations onto Subcategories once, then reuses that mapping for every new questionnaire. Second, as a reporting device: Function-level scores give executives a defensible view of capability without exposing implementation detail. Third, as a design input for metrics, where each Subcategory outcome gets an operational measurement such as mean time to detect or percentage of assets with current agent coverage. The framework is deliberately technology-neutral and does not itself create legal obligations, which is why it is frequently used as the connective tissue between mandatory regimes rather than as a replacement for them.
objectives: You will be able to describe the Functions, Categories and Subcategories and how they relate to Tiers and Profiles.
You will be able to build a current-state Profile from existing control evidence and a target Profile from business priorities.
You will be able to map ISO 27001, SP 800-53 and CIS Controls onto CSF Subcategories without duplicating effort.
You will be able to define operational metrics that demonstrate progress against Subcategory outcomes.
You will be able to explain to executives why a Tier rating is not the same thing as a maturity score or a certification.
You will be able to use the framework as the common language in a regulator or board conversation about residual risk.

beginner.definition: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is a voluntary guide that organises security work into shared words. NIST means the National Institute of Standards and Technology. The framework groups activity into functions such as govern, identify, protect, detect, respond and recover. Each function holds outcomes, not products, so different teams can compare notes. It creates no legal duty by itself.
beginner.whyItMatters: Security teams and business leaders often talk past each other. One side describes tools and the other side wants to know about risk. The framework gives both a simple shared map, so a report to the board can be short and clear. It also lets you reuse one set of answers for many customer questionnaires.
howItWorks: Describe what your security team does today against each framework outcome.
Mark clearly which outcomes you meet well and which you do not.
Set a target state that matches your business priorities and budget.
Turn the distance between current and target into a funded plan.
Choose a simple measurement for each outcome you want to improve.
Report your progress in plain language to leaders and to customers.
beginner.example: Think of a fitness tracker. It does not tell you which shoes to buy. It shows your current activity, compares it with a goal you set, and turns the difference into a plan. A doctor can read the same numbers without knowing your gym routine. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework works like that for security, giving everyone the same simple measures.
takeaways: The framework is voluntary and gives shared words, not legal duties.
Compare where you are now with a target state you choose.
Simple measures turn a gap list into a funded plan.

topics.title: NIST SP 800-53
topics.summary: NIST Special Publication 800-53 is the United States federal control catalogue for information systems and organisations, and it has become the de facto reference control set for regulated industries well beyond government. Its structure is what makes it useful to engineers: controls are grouped into families such as Access Control, Audit and Accountability, Configuration Management, Incident Response, Risk Assessment and Supply Chain Risk Management, and each control carries a statement, supplemental guidance, assessment procedures drawn from SP 800-53A, and optional control enhancements that allow an organisation to dial specificity up or down. Controls are selected and tailored through the SP 800-37 risk management framework process, where a system is categorised for confidentiality, integrity and availability impact, a control baseline is chosen, and the resulting set is documented in a system security plan with a plan of action and milestones for anything not yet satisfied. The critical practitioner insight is that 800-53 is a catalogue, not a compliance regime by itself: it becomes mandatory through law, contract or agency policy, and the burden of evidence sits with the organisation. Control identifiers are stable and widely reused, which is why so many commercial and cloud compliance mappings, including the FedRAMP baselines, are expressed as 800-53 selections. Teams that implement it well automate evidence collection against assessment procedures rather than treating the catalogue as a documentation exercise.
objectives: You will be able to explain how categorisation, baseline selection and tailoring produce a system-specific control set.
You will be able to read a control family and its enhancements and translate them into implementable configuration.
You will be able to build evidence that satisfies SP 800-53A assessment procedures for audit and accountability controls.
You will be able to author a system security plan with an honest plan of action and milestones.
You will be able to map 800-53 controls to ISO 27001 Annex A and NIST CSF Subcategories to reuse existing work.
You will be able to spot where an inherited control from a cloud provider does not transfer accountability.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-53 security and privacy controls

beginner.definition: NIST SP 800-53 is a large catalogue of security controls published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in the United States. A control is a safeguard, such as an access rule or a log review. The controls are grouped into families like access control, incident response and supply chain risk. It is a menu, not a law.
beginner.whyItMatters: Teams waste months rewriting the same safeguards in different words for each customer. A shared control catalogue lets you describe your work once and reuse it. It also helps you find what you forgot, because the families cover areas people often miss. The catalogue becomes binding through a contract, a law or an agency rule.
howItWorks: Decide how much harm a loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability would cause.
Pick a starting set of controls that matches that level of harm.
Adjust the set for your situation, removing or adding controls as needed.
Write a plan that says who owns each control and how it is implemented.
List anything not yet finished, with a date and a named owner.
Collect evidence that shows each control works, then review it often.
beginner.example: Think of a building code. It lists rules for wiring, stairs and fire doors, but the city decides which rules apply to your building. A small warehouse follows fewer rules than a hospital. An inspector then checks your building against the list. NIST SP 800-53 works like that list for computer systems, and your own rules decide how much of it you must follow.
takeaways: NIST SP 800-53 is a catalogue of controls, not a law on its own.
You tailor the control set to your system and its risk level.
Unfinished controls still need an owner, a date and a plan.

topics.title: Nonce Reuse
topics.summary: Nonce reuse is the failure to supply a unique per-operation value to a cryptographic algorithm that requires one, and it quietly converts otherwise sound constructions into broken ones. The consequences depend on the mode. In counter-mode authenticated encryption such as AES-GCM, reusing a nonce with the same key leaks the XOR of the two plaintexts and exposes the authentication subkey, which allows an attacker to forge messages and, in many deployment patterns, to recover plaintext outright. In stream ciphers, the same keystream is produced twice, so ciphertext XOR reveals plaintext XOR. In signature schemes that take a per-signature secret, reusing it across two different messages lets anyone recover the private key with straightforward algebra, which has caused real-world key compromises in wallets and embedded devices. Nonces are not required to be secret, only unique within the scope of a key, but they must be unpredictable wherever an attacker can influence or predict them. Production failures usually come from weak randomness on constrained hardware, virtual machine clones that resume with identical state, counters that reset after a restart or a snapshot rollback, or application code that derives a nonce from a field like a user identifier, timestamp with poor resolution, or an incrementing database value that resets. Defensive practice means deterministic nonce derivation where the standard permits it, per-message key derivation, hardware random sources, monotonic counters persisted with the key, and monitoring for the duplicate-value signatures of these faults in protocol logs and telemetry.
objectives: Explain the uniqueness requirement for nonces, IVs and per-signature secrets, and why secrecy is not the goal.
Describe the concrete consequences of nonce reuse in GCM, stream ciphers and ECDSA signing.
Identify environment-level causes of repeated nonces such as cloned virtual machines, snapshots and reset counters.
Design a nonce strategy using deterministic derivation or per-message keys that survives restart and scale-out.
Detect nonce reuse indicators in protocol telemetry, signing services and transaction records.
Respond to suspected nonce reuse as a key compromise event rather than a configuration defect.
