beginner.definition: A nonce is a number used once. Nonce reuse means giving the same number twice to a cryptographic operation that expects a fresh one. Nonces do not need to be secret, only unique. Reusing one can break the encryption or, worse, reveal a private signing key.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many crypto systems are safe only if every operation uses a different number. If the same number appears twice, an attacker can compare the two outputs and learn things that should stay hidden. In some designs they can reconstruct the actual key. This happens by accident, for example when a virtual machine is cloned or a counter restarts. The code looks correct, but the numbers repeat.
howItWorks: The system needs a fresh number for each message it encrypts or signs.
The number does not have to be secret, but it must never repeat with the same key.
The number is mixed with the key to produce a unique stream or signature value.
If the number repeats, the same internal value appears twice in two outputs.
Comparing the two outputs cancels out the hidden part and exposes the underlying data.
In signing systems, the same repeat can let an attacker calculate the private key.
beginner.example: Imagine two students using the same one-time pad to write secret notes. Each pad page should be used once. If both students use page seven, then laying their two notes side by side cancels the scrambling and the words become readable. The pad itself was strong. The mistake was using the same page twice.
takeaways: A nonce must be unique, not secret. Use each one only once per key.
Cloned machines, restored snapshots and reset counters are common causes of repeats.
Treat confirmed nonce reuse as a key compromise: rotate the key immediately.

topics.title: OAuth 2.0
topics.summary: OAuth 2.0 is an authorisation framework that lets a client application obtain limited access to a resource on behalf of a user or another service without handling that user's credentials. It defines roles (resource owner, client, authorisation server, resource server), grant types (authorisation code, client credentials, device code, and the deprecated implicit and resource owner password grants), and token types, most importantly the access token and the optional refresh token. The framework deliberately separates authorisation from authentication, which is why building a login flow on OAuth alone produces the confused-deputy problems that OpenID Connect was created to solve. Security depends heavily on implementation choices rather than on the framework's defaults: public clients must use proof key for code exchange to bind the authorisation request to the token request, redirect URIs must be matched exactly, state parameters must be unpredictable and verified, and bearer tokens must be protected in transit and at rest because anyone holding the token can use it. Common real-world failures include open redirectors leaking authorisation codes, permissive redirect URI matching with wildcards or path traversal, tokens stored in browser local storage where cross-site scripting can reach them, excessive scope grants that let a low-privilege client call high-value APIs, and consent phishing in which a user grants a malicious application durable access. Defenders focus on token lifetime, scope minimisation, sender constraint, and the authorisation server's audit log of grants, consents and token issuance.
objectives: You will be able to describe the authorisation code, client credentials and device code flows and select the correct one for a given client type.
You will be able to explain why OAuth 2.0 is not an authentication protocol and how that leads to confused-deputy vulnerabilities.
You will be able to identify insecure redirect URI handling, missing state validation and absent proof key for code exchange in a client registration.
You will be able to evaluate access token lifetime, scope breadth and refresh token rotation against least-privilege expectations.
You will be able to investigate suspicious OAuth consent grants and illicit consent attacks using authorisation server audit logs.
You will be able to explain token sender-constraining options and when bearer token protections are insufficient.

sources.label: RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security

beginner.definition: OAuth 2.0 is a set of rules that lets an application use part of your data without seeing your password. You approve a limited permission, and the app receives a token instead. A token is a temporary key that can be cancelled.
beginner.whyItMatters: People want to connect apps to their accounts without handing over a password. A password would give the app full control forever. OAuth limits what each app may do and lets you withdraw access later. If it is built badly, a small app can quietly read far more than you agreed to.
howItWorks: An app asks your permission to read one specific thing, such as your calendar.
You are sent to the sign-in service, where you approve or refuse that request.
The service gives the app a short code, which the app swaps for a token.
The app uses the token when it calls the service on your behalf.
Tokens expire, and you or the service can cancel them at any time.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel valet ticket. You hand over the ticket, and the valet can fetch your car. The ticket does not open your front door or your bank account. It also expires at the end of the day. If you lose it, the hotel cancels it quickly. That is exactly what a token is meant to do.
takeaways: OAuth 2.0 grants limited access with tokens instead of your password.
Ask for the smallest permission that still does the job.
Anyone who holds a token can use it, so protect and shorten its life.

topics.title: OpenID Connect
topics.summary: OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 that gives clients a standardised way to verify a user's identity and obtain basic profile information. It adds an identity token, a JSON Web Token whose claims describe the authentication event and the subject, and it standardises discovery through a well-known configuration document, key distribution through a JSON Web Key Set, and user information retrieval through a dedicated endpoint. Because the identity token is signed and carries claims such as issuer, audience, subject, issue time and expiry, a relying party can validate it locally without a per-request round trip to the provider, provided it verifies the signature against the published keys, checks that the issuer and audience match its own registration, enforces nonce and expiry, and refuses to accept a token signed with an algorithm it did not expect. Failures cluster in exactly those checks: accepting a token with an unexpected signing algorithm, skipping audience validation so a token minted for a different application is accepted, trusting unverified claims taken from an access token rather than the identity token, and mixing up access tokens and identity tokens in ways that lead to privilege confusion. Hybrid flows, front-channel logout, and the handling of long-lived refresh tokens each introduce their own edge cases. Operational attention belongs on key rollover in the JSON Web Key Set, because a relying party that caches keys indefinitely will fail closed or, worse, fail open depending on its error handling.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish identity tokens from access tokens and explain which claims may be relied on for each purpose.
You will be able to describe the mandatory validation steps a relying party must perform on an identity token.
You will be able to explain how discovery documents and JSON Web Key Sets are consumed and why key caching matters.
You will be able to identify weak configurations such as missing nonce checks, unverified issuers and over-permissive redirect URIs.
You will be able to troubleshoot sign-in failures using identity provider logs and token claims side by side.
You will be able to evaluate front-channel and back-channel logout options for session termination requirements.

beginner.definition: OpenID Connect is a layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 that tells an application who you are. It adds a signed identity token, which is a digital statement about your sign-in. The app can check the signature and trust the details inside.
beginner.whyItMatters: OAuth 2.0 was built for permission, not for proving identity. Teams that use it for login often accept the wrong token or skip important checks. OpenID Connect fixes that by defining exactly what an identity token must contain. Correct validation stops an attacker from replaying a token meant for another application.
howItWorks: The application sends you to the identity provider, which is the trusted sign-in service.
You sign in there, and the provider creates a signed identity token for you.
Your browser carries that token back to the application you wanted to use.
The app checks the signature, the issuer, the audience, and the expiry time.
Only if every check passes does the app treat you as signed in.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital wristband. The admissions desk prints it after checking your details. Every nurse and doctor then trusts the wristband without calling the desk again. But they still check that the band is genuine and belongs to this patient. A copied band from another hospital would fail those checks.
takeaways: OpenID Connect adds identity on top of OAuth 2.0 permission.
An application must verify the token signature, issuer, audience, and expiry.
Never treat an access token as proof of who someone is.

topics.title: Operational Security (OpSec)
topics.summary: Operational security, usually shortened to OpSec, is the practice of controlling the observable traces an activity produces so that they do not reveal capability, intent, identity or infrastructure to an observer. The classic process has five steps: identify the information that must not be disclosed, analyse who is collecting against it, analyse the weaknesses in how the activity is conducted, assess the risk each weakness creates, and apply countermeasures in proportion. In security work the concept applies in two directions. On the adversarial side it explains why intrusions are often quiet, consistent and patient: infrastructure is separated by purpose, personas are maintained consistently across channels, timing follows the target's working rhythm, and released artefacts are sanitised of metadata before use. Understanding that discipline is directly useful to defenders, because every trace an intruder must suppress is a trace worth monitoring, and every inconsistency in a persona or infrastructure set becomes a pivot for attribution at a stated confidence level. On the defensive side, OpSec governs incident response itself: communications move off potentially compromised channels, actions that would alert an intruder are delayed until containment is ready, and information about the investigation is shared strictly on a need-to-know basis. Poor OpSec in either direction produces preventable loss, whether that is a burned capability or an intruder who destroys evidence after noticing that they have been detected.
objectives: You will be able to apply the five-step OpSec process to a security activity and its observable traces.
You will be able to identify which traces an intruder must suppress and convert them into monitoring requirements.
You will be able to explain how inconsistencies in infrastructure and persona support attribution at a stated confidence level.
You will be able to plan incident response communications that do not alert an active intruder.
You will be able to judge when operational silence harms an investigation more than it helps.

beginner.definition: Operational security, often shortened to OpSec, means controlling the traces your activity leaves behind. Those traces are called observables. Good OpSec keeps them from revealing what you can do, what you plan, who you are, or what systems you use. The classic method has five steps: identify, analyse threats, analyse weaknesses, assess risk, and apply countermeasures.
beginner.whyItMatters: Every action leaves a mark somewhere. If you do not manage those marks, someone can read your plans from them. In security work, operational security matters in two directions. Attackers use it to stay hidden, so defenders should study which traces they must hide. Defenders also need it during an incident, because a careless response can warn an intruder that you have noticed them.
howItWorks: List the information you do not want others to learn from your activity.
Work out who could be watching and what they are able to collect.
Find the weak points in how you normally carry out the activity.
Judge how much harm each weak point would cause if it were seen.
Add simple countermeasures where the risk is highest, and no more.
beginner.example: Think about planning a surprise party. You cannot discuss it in the group chat the guest of honour reads. You book the venue under a different name. You keep your story consistent when someone asks about Saturday. Each small choice hides one clue. If you slip once, the surprise is gone. Operational security works the same way: many small habits, chosen on purpose, that together keep your activity from being noticed.
takeaways: Every action leaves a trace, so decide which traces you can afford.
A trace an intruder must hide is a trace you can monitor.
During an incident, quiet and careful communication protects the investigation.

topics.title: Passwordless Authentication
topics.summary: Passwordless authentication is a set of authentication methods in which the user proves possession of a registered authenticator bound to their identity and never supplies a shared secret that can be phished, reused or cracked offline. The two dominant families are asymmetric key credentials based on the Web Authentication standard, where the private key stays in a hardware security key or platform authenticator and the public key is registered with the relying party, and certificate-based authentication, where a device or smart card certificate issued by enterprise certificate authority replaces the password. Both defeat password-centric attacks structurally rather than by policy: there is no secret to spray, no hash to crack, no code to relay to a waitress-style adversary-in-the-middle proxy, and the signature is bound to the origin so that a lookalike domain cannot harvest a usable response. Passkeys extend the same primitive to consumer use by synchronising or device-linking credentials, which improves usability and recovery but changes the threat model, since the credential now follows the user's platform account rather than a single physical token. Deployment work is mostly in the unglamorous details: recovery and enrolment, because account recovery becomes the weakest authentication path once passwords are gone; attestation and device inventory, to decide which authenticators are acceptable; account identifier design, to avoid silently re-enrolling a credential to the wrong person; and legacy systems that cannot speak the protocol and therefore need a brokered or certificate-based compromise. Hybrid environments usually run passwordless for interactive users and retain vaulted secrets for machine identities, where the equivalent control is short-lived certificates and automatic rotation.
objectives: You will be able to explain how asymmetric key credentials resist phishing and credential replay structurally rather than by policy.
You will be able to compare hardware security keys, platform authenticators and synchronised passkeys by assurance and usability.
You will be able to design enrolment and recovery procedures that do not reintroduce a weak authentication path.
You will be able to identify systems that cannot support passwordless authentication and select a brokered or certificate-based alternative.
You will be able to detect suspicious authenticator registration, deletion and re-registration events in identity provider logs.
You will be able to plan a phased migration that keeps break-glass access available without standing passwords for administrators.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-63B: Digital Identity Guidelines, Authentication and Lifecycle Management
Microsoft Learn: Passwordless authentication options for Microsoft Entra ID

beginner.definition: Passwordless authentication lets you sign in without typing a shared secret. Instead, you use something tied to you, such as a security key, your fingerprint, or your phone. The secret never leaves your device. Attackers cannot steal what you never send.
beginner.whyItMatters: Passwords are guessable, reusable, and easy to trick out of people. Even a second code can be relayed by a fake login page. Passwordless sign-in removes the shared secret completely, so a fake page has nothing useful to copy. The remaining risk moves to account recovery, which needs just as much care.
howItWorks: You register a device or a security key with your account, once.
The device creates a key pair, which is a matched set of two keys.
The public key goes to the service, and the private key stays on your device.
To sign in, the service sends a random challenge, which is a fresh question.
Your device signs that challenge, and the service checks the signature.
beginner.example: Think of a wax seal on a letter. Anyone can look at the seal, but only you own the stamp. A forger cannot copy the stamp from the wax mark alone. Each letter gets a different seal, so an old one is useless. That is why a copied sign-in page cannot replay your answer.
takeaways: Passwordless sign-in uses a key on your device, not a shared secret.
No shared secret means nothing useful for a fake login page to copy.
Protect account recovery, because it becomes the easiest way in.

topics.title: Payload Staging
topics.summary: Payload staging is the practice of splitting the code or configuration that achieves an objective into a small delivery component and one or more larger components retrieved after execution begins. It exists because delivery channels impose constraints: an email attachment has a size ceiling, a landing page should look unremarkable, and a single large transfer to an unusual destination is easier to detect than several small ones that blend with normal traffic. A typical staged operation therefore uses a lightweight first stage, often a script or a signed system utility, to establish execution and then pull the remainder from a location the operator controls, frequently over ordinary web or cloud storage protocols. Staging also supports flexibility, because capabilities can be swapped or updated during an engagement without re-delivering the initial component. From a defensive standpoint, staging is a gift as much as a problem: it produces a distinctive chain of events that begins with a user action or an exploited service, continues through an interpreter or signed binary starting unexpectedly, and ends with an outbound fetch from an endpoint that has no business reason to contact that destination. High-value detections combine process ancestry with network context, especially where a document reader, archive tool or script host initiates an outbound connection, and where the destination is new to the estate. Mitigations limit both halves of the chain: blocking macros and script execution from user-writable locations, restricting which binaries may make outbound connections, tightening egress, and maintaining a software inventory so unexpected fetches stand out.
objectives: You will be able to explain why operators split delivery into stages and what each stage reveals to a defender.
You will be able to trace a staged delivery chain through process, file and network telemetry.
You will be able to write detections that pair suspicious parent processes with unexpected outbound connections.
You will be able to list the application control and egress controls that break staged delivery.
You will be able to distinguish in-memory execution from on-disk staging in endpoint evidence.

beginner.definition: Payload staging means splitting an attack tool into two parts. A small first part reaches the target, often inside a document or link. That part then fetches the bigger second part from a server the intruder controls. This keeps the first delivery small and less suspicious. It also lets the intruder swap the second part later.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers split their tools because delivery channels have limits. An email attachment cannot be too large, and a landing page should look normal. One big download to a strange destination is also easy to spot. Splitting the tool produces a chain of events instead: a user opens something, a program starts, and then the machine contacts a new address. Each link in that chain is a chance for you to notice.
howItWorks: The intruder builds a small first part that is easy to deliver and hide.
They host the larger second part on a server or cloud storage they control.
The first part arrives by email, a link, or a weak public service.
When it runs, it quietly connects out and downloads the second part.
The second part now runs in memory or on disk and does the real work.
beginner.example: Imagine ordering a large wardrobe online. The shop does not post the whole thing. It sends you a small card with a pickup code. You take that card to a depot and collect the heavy boxes yourself. The postman only ever saw a thin envelope. Staged attacks use the same idea: a tiny first piece, then a separate collection step that brings the bulky part.
takeaways: A small first stage that fetches more code is a classic pattern.
Watch for ordinary programs, like document readers, making unexpected outbound connections.
Block scripts from running in folders users can write to.

topics.title: PCI DSS
topics.summary: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard is a contractual requirement imposed by the card brands and administered by the PCI Security Standards Council on any entity that stores, processes or transmits account data, or that can impact the security of the cardholder data environment. Unlike principle-based regimes, PCI DSS is prescriptive: it defines requirements for network security controls, secure configuration, protection of stored account data, encryption of transmission over open networks, malware protection, secure development, access restriction by business need to know, identification and authentication, physical security, logging and monitoring, security testing and an information security policy supported by risk assessment. Scope is the central engineering problem, and the standard explicitly encourages segmentation and other scope-reduction techniques so that systems neither connected to nor able to impact the cardholder data environment drop out of assessment. Practitioners should expect annual assessment by a Qualified Security Assessor or completion of a self-assessment questionnaire depending on transaction volume, plus quarterly network scans by an Approved Scanning Vendor and continuous evidence of logging, file integrity monitoring, change control and access review. Version 4.x introduced a customised approach allowing an entity to meet a requirement's intent using a documented compensating control methodology, and shifted many controls into a continually operating model rather than an annual evidence scramble.
objectives: You will be able to define the cardholder data environment and reduce scope through segmentation and data flow analysis.
You will be able to translate the twelve requirement areas into specific configuration and process controls.
You will be able to prepare the evidence an assessor expects for logging, file integrity monitoring and access review.
You will be able to apply the customised approach and document compensating controls that meet a requirement's intent.
You will be able to distinguish self-assessment obligations from a Qualified Security Assessor engagement and quarterly scans.
You will be able to detect where stored sensitive authentication data has leaked outside the approved data flows.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-53 security and privacy controls
OWASP Top 10 Web Application Security Risks

beginner.definition: PCI DSS is a set of security rules for anyone who handles payment card data. PCI DSS stands for Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard. The rules come from the card brands and apply through your contract with them. They cover storing, processing and sending card numbers, and the systems that could affect them.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you take card payments, you cannot simply decide to ignore these rules. Your contract with the card brands requires them, and losing the ability to accept cards can stop your business. The rules also reduce real fraud, because stolen card numbers are easy to sell. Knowing your scope early saves months of extra assessment work.
howItWorks: Draw a map of where card numbers enter, live and leave your systems.
Shrink that area by separating it, so fewer systems are in scope.
Protect stored numbers with encryption and remove data you no longer need.
Restrict access by job need, and give each person a unique login.
Log activity, watch for unexpected changes and test your systems for weaknesses.
Prove all of this to an assessor each year, with evidence not promises.
beginner.example: Think of a shop that keeps cash in one locked room instead of in every drawer. Staff who never touch cash need no key. That is scope reduction. In the same way, if card numbers pass through one separated payment system, the rest of your network is easier to assess. Small, well-guarded areas cost less to protect and prove than a whole building.
takeaways: Your contract with the card brands makes these rules mandatory.
Reduce scope by separating card systems from everything else.
Keep evidence of access reviews, logs and tests all year round.

topics.title: Persistence
topics.summary: Persistence is the collection of mechanisms an intruder uses to retain access across reboots, password changes, session expiry and partial remediation, so that initial access does not have to be won again. Host-based persistence attaches to legitimate startup behaviour: autostart entries, scheduled tasks, system services, logon scripts, shell profiles, and browser or office extensions. Identity-based persistence is often more valuable and harder to see, because it lives in the directory or cloud tenant rather than on an endpoint; examples include newly created accounts, added credentials or keys, modified federation settings, and application registrations with delegated permissions that outlive any single session. Network-based persistence covers configurations that survive host rebuilds, such as remote access profiles, tunnels and backup channels. Every mechanism trades stealth against resilience, and defenders can exploit that trade-off: the more durable the mechanism, the more likely it is to touch a monitored location, generate an audit record, or require a privileged change. Practical detection therefore starts from an accurate baseline of what is allowed to autostart, which scheduled tasks and services normally exist, and which principals hold privileged roles. Deviations from that baseline, combined with audit events for account creation, permission grants and application registration, give far better coverage than hunting for specific tools. Mitigation combines application control, privileged access management with approval workflows, credential hygiene, and centralised logging that an intruder cannot quietly edit.
objectives: You will be able to categorise persistence mechanisms as host-based, identity-based or network-based.
You will be able to explain the trade-off between resilience and stealth for common autostart mechanisms.
You will be able to build a baseline of legitimate autostart locations, services and scheduled tasks.
You will be able to spot tenant-level persistence through account creation, credential addition and application registration.
You will be able to recommend controls that make durable access expensive for an intruder.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)

beginner.definition: Persistence means the methods an intruder uses to keep access after a reboot, a password change, or a partial cleanup. Without it, a single restart could end the intrusion. Persistence can live on a machine, inside an identity system, or in the network itself. It exists so the intruder does not have to break in a second time.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you remove the intruder but leave their persistence behind, they simply come back. This is why cleanups sometimes fail and the same incident reappears weeks later. Persistence often hides in normal startup behaviour, such as scheduled tasks or service accounts, so it looks ordinary. You cannot spot what is unusual unless you first know what is normal. A written baseline of allowed startup items, tasks and admin accounts is your best defence.
howItWorks: After getting in, the intruder looks for places that start programs automatically.
They add their access to an autostart entry, a scheduled task, or a service.
They may also create a new account or add a key in the identity system.
Now the access returns whenever the machine restarts or the user logs in.
Even if you close the first opening, their quiet back door stays open.
beginner.example: Suppose you change the locks on your front door after a break-in. You feel safe again. But the intruder copied a key and hid it under a garden stone. They return a month later without forcing anything. Replacing the lock alone did not help, because the copy was never found. Persistence works exactly like that hidden key. Cleaning up the visible entry point is not enough; you must also find the copies.
takeaways: Removing the intruder is not enough; you must remove their persistence.
Know which programs and tasks are allowed to start automatically.
New accounts and newly added access keys are persistence as well.

topics.title: PICERL
topics.summary: PICERL is a six-phase incident response lifecycle - Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery and Lessons Learned - that gives a security team a shared vocabulary and a gated decision path from the moment an alert fires to the moment an incident is formally closed. Preparation covers work done before anything happens: asset inventories, logging coverage, jump bags, out-of-band communication, standing authority to isolate systems, and rehearsed escalation paths. Identification is the analysis phase, where telemetry from endpoints, identity providers, network sensors and SaaS audit logs is correlated into a defensible statement of what is actually happening, which hosts and accounts are involved, and how confident the team is in that conclusion. Containment splits into short-term measures that stop immediate spread, such as network isolation or credential revocation, and longer-term measures that keep the business running while the adversary is still presumed present. Eradication removes the adversary's foothold - malware, persistence, created accounts, modified configuration - and is where teams most often declare victory too early. Recovery restores service under heightened monitoring, validates that the root cause is genuinely closed, and defines what normal looks like again. Lessons Learned converts the incident into durable change: detection gaps closed, playbooks updated, owners named, and remediation tracked to completion. The phases are not strictly linear. A persistence mechanism discovered during Recovery sends the team back to Containment, and that iteration is expected rather than a sign of failure. What matters is that each transition is justified by evidence, documented with timestamps, and communicated to the people who own the resulting risk decisions.
objectives: Explain each PICERL phase and the evidence-based entry and exit criteria that justify moving to the next one.
Build a Preparation checklist covering logging coverage, standing authority to isolate, out-of-band communications and evidence handling.
Write an Identification statement that separates confirmed fact from inference and states an explicit confidence level.
Choose between short-term and long-term containment actions and defend the tradeoff between spread reduction and business impact.
Distinguish eradication from recovery and explain why restored service is not proof that the adversary is gone.
Design a Lessons Learned process that converts findings into owned, dated remediation items.
Reconstruct a PICERL timeline from multi-source logs and identify the points where the team iterated backwards between phases.

sources.label: SANS Institute - Incident Handler's Handbook and incident response white papers

beginner.definition: PICERL is a six-step map for handling a security incident. The letters stand for Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, and Lessons Learned. It gives a team one shared language, from the first alert to the final review. The steps guide decisions, but you can move back and forth between them.
beginner.whyItMatters: During a real incident, pressure makes people skip steps. They wipe a machine before saving evidence, or they restore service before the attacker is gone. A shared lifecycle keeps the team calm and ordered. Everyone knows what happens next, who decides, and what must be documented before moving on.
howItWorks: Preparation: get ready before anything happens, with logs, contacts, tools, and clear authority.
Identification: work out what actually happened, which systems are involved, and how sure you are.
Containment: stop the spread quickly by isolating machines and cutting off accounts.
Eradication: remove the attacker's software, hidden access, and created accounts for good.
Recovery: bring services back carefully while watching closely for signs of return.
Lessons Learned: review what worked, fix gaps, and give each fix an owner and a date.
beginner.example: Think of how a hospital handles a patient. First the staff prepare the room. Then they identify the problem with tests. They stabilize the patient before treating the cause, then remove it, then help the patient recover, and finally review the case. An incident follows the same rhythm. Skipping the review means the same problem catches you again.
takeaways: PICERL gives six phases: Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, Lessons Learned.
Save evidence before cleanup, and do not confuse restored service with safety.
The phases repeat; going back a step is normal, not a failure.

topics.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography
topics.summary: Post-quantum cryptography is the family of public-key algorithms designed to remain secure against an adversary equipped with a large-scale quantum computer, alongside the migration work required to deploy them. The threat is asymmetric in time: Shor's algorithm would break RSA and elliptic curve cryptography outright, while Grover's algorithm only modestly reduces the effective strength of symmetric primitives, so AES-256 and SHA-384 remain comfortable. The most urgent operational risk is harvest-now-decrypt-later, where traffic captured today is stored for decryption once the capability arrives, which makes long-lived confidentiality requirements the first migration priority. NIST standardised a set of algorithms for key encapsulation and digital signatures built on lattice, hash-based and code-based mathematics, with a hybrid deployment pattern that combines a classical and a post-quantum exchange so that security holds unless both are broken. Migration is harder than swapping a library. Organisations must inventory where public-key cryptography is used, including embedded devices that will never receive an update, hardware modules with fixed algorithm support, certificate and protocol size assumptions that break under larger keys and signatures, performance budgets on constrained links, and the certificate authority and code signing infrastructure that has to issue and validate new algorithm types. Governance questions follow, such as which algorithms are approved, how hybrids are represented in policy, and how long a cryptoperiod must be before quantum resistance becomes mandatory.
objectives: Explain how Shor's and Grover's algorithms affect public-key and symmetric cryptography differently.
Describe harvest-now-decrypt-later and identify which data classes justify early migration.
Compare post-quantum key encapsulation and signature families on trust assumptions, key size and maturity.
Perform a cryptographic inventory that finds public-key usage in code, devices, protocols and third-party services.
Plan a hybrid classical-plus-post-quantum deployment and explain what property the hybrid preserves.
Assess protocol and infrastructure changes needed for larger keys, including certificate handling and constrained links.
Build a migration roadmap with cryptoperiods, priorities and a defensible policy position on algorithm approval.

sources.label: NIST FIPS 203: Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1: Recommendation for Key Management

beginner.definition: Post-quantum cryptography means methods for encryption and signing that stay safe even against a powerful future quantum computer. Today's public key methods, such as RSA and elliptic curves, could be broken by such a machine. RSA and elliptic curves are kinds of maths used to build small, strong keys. The new methods rely on different hard problems instead.
beginner.whyItMatters: An attacker can record your encrypted traffic today and store it until a quantum computer exists. This is called harvest now, decrypt later. Anything that must stay secret for many years, such as health records or government files, is at risk already. Migration is slow, because old devices, certificates and protocols need to change. Starting early is cheaper than rushing later.
howItWorks: First, make a list of everywhere your organisation uses public key cryptography.
Decide which data must stay secret for a long time, since that is the priority.
Choose the approved quantum-resistant algorithms for key exchange and for digital signatures.
Run the new algorithm alongside the old one, so safety holds if either is broken.
Test the larger keys and signatures through your protocols, devices and certificates.
Replace old algorithms step by step and keep the ability to swap again later.
beginner.example: Picture a village that learns a new kind of lock-picking tool may appear in ten years. The tool will not open the new locks. Villagers cannot change every door at once, so they start with the strongroom that holds documents meant to last fifty years. Meanwhile, a thief is already photographing keys through windows. Those photographs become useful the day the tool arrives.
takeaways: Quantum computers would break today's public key methods, but shared-secret encryption stays strong.
Data captured now can be decrypted later, so long-lived secrets need early action.
Build a crypto inventory and plan hybrid algorithms instead of a sudden swap.

topics.title: Privilege Escalation
topics.summary: Privilege escalation is the set of actions that convert ordinary user or service access into authority the account was never intended to hold, whether that means higher rights on the same host or rights that reach across a domain or cloud tenant. Vertical escalation raises the level of permission an identity holds, while horizontal escalation moves to a different identity with comparable rights and is often a stepping stone rather than an end in itself. The underlying causes are consistent across platforms: excessive standing privilege, misconfigured permissions on files, services or container runtimes, unpatched local software, credential material left in memory, configuration files or environment variables, and trust relationships that let a low-trust principal assume a high-trust role. Cloud and container estates add their own variants, including over-broad role assumption policies, instance metadata reachable from a workload, and container configurations that expose the host. Because escalation usually abuses legitimate functionality, signature-based detection alone is inadequate. Useful signals include process trees in which a user-facing application spawns a shell or administrative utility, changes to local or directory group membership, newly granted roles or permissions, and access to privileged interfaces outside a change window. Effective mitigation is architectural rather than detective: least privilege, removal of standing administrative rights in favour of just-in-time elevation, unique local administrator credentials, timely patching, and application control that limits what an unprivileged user can execute. Detection then concentrates on the residual cases where those controls fail or are bypassed.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish vertical from horizontal privilege escalation and give a realistic example of each.
You will be able to identify the misconfiguration classes that most often enable escalation on hosts, directories and cloud tenants.
You will be able to read process ancestry and permission-change telemetry to recognise escalation behaviour.
You will be able to prioritise privilege reduction using standing rights, administrative tiering and just-in-time access.
You will be able to explain how container configuration and instance metadata exposure change the escalation picture.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (T1548)

beginner.definition: Privilege escalation is when someone turns ordinary access into stronger access they were never meant to have. It can happen on one machine, or across a whole company directory or cloud account. Vertical escalation raises the level of permission. Horizontal escalation moves to a different account with similar rights. Horizontal moves are often just a step towards a bigger goal.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most intruders start with a normal user account. That account alone cannot usually read the important data or change system settings. Escalation is the step that changes this. It often abuses ordinary features rather than a software bug: loose file permissions, saved passwords, or roles that are too broad. Reducing standing admin rights and patching quickly removes many of these easy paths before anyone uses them.
howItWorks: The intruder arrives with a low-level account, perhaps a normal user or service.
They check what that account can read, run and change on the system.
They look for weak spots, such as loose file rights or saved passwords.
They use one weak spot to gain more rights, often through a normal feature.
With higher rights they can create accounts, change settings, or reach data.
beginner.example: Picture a visitor in a hospital. Their badge opens the front lobby and the cafe. Then they notice a supply cupboard left unlocked. Inside is a staff badge on a hook. Now they can open the medicine store and the records room. Nobody hacked anything. They simply used a door that should have been shut. Privilege escalation in computer systems is the same: small lapses in permission add up to full authority.
takeaways: Escalation often uses normal features, not clever software bugs.
Give people only the rights their job needs, and no more.
Patch quickly, because old flaws are still a common path upward.

topics.title: Privileged Access Management
topics.summary: Privileged access management (PAM) is the discipline and tooling set that controls, brokers, records and audits the use of accounts with elevated rights, including domain administrators, root, database superusers, cloud root and organisation owner roles, and the service accounts that hold equivalent power. The core problem PAM addresses is that privileged credentials are shared, rarely rotated, widely copied into scripts and configuration files, and almost never attributable to an individual, so a single disclosure can be replayed indefinitely with the full authority of the account. A mature programme removes standing privilege wherever possible by vaulting credentials and checking them out for a bounded window, injecting them into sessions so the human never sees the secret, brokering interactive sessions through a jump host that records keystrokes and commands, and replacing human-held credentials with short-lived certificates or tokens. Just-in-time elevation, approval workflows and break-glass procedures with mandatory post-use review are the mechanisms that make this workable when a human genuinely needs emergency access. Beyond vaulting, PAM covers the secrets that machines use: application credentials, API keys and certificates stored in a managed vault with automatic rotation rather than committed to repositories or baked into images. The detection value is substantial, because privileged session recordings, checkout logs and vault audit trails give defenders a well-defined baseline against which unusual hours, unusual source hosts, direct use of an unvaulted credential, or elevation outside the approved workflow stand out sharply.
objectives: You will be able to inventory privileged identities across on-premises, cloud and database estates and classify them by blast radius.
You will be able to design credential checkout, session brokering and rotation workflows that eliminate standing privilege.
You will be able to explain how session recording, keystroke logging and command-level auditing support investigation and attribution.
You will be able to define break-glass access procedures with approval, time bounds and mandatory post-incident review.
You will be able to detect use of unvaulted credentials, out-of-window elevation and anomalous privileged session sources.
You will be able to extend PAM controls to service accounts, API keys and certificates with automated rotation.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-53: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems
CISA: Cyber Resilience and privileged access guidance

beginner.definition: Privileged access management, or PAM, is the set of tools and habits that control powerful accounts. These accounts can change systems, read any data, and create new administrators. PAM stores their passwords safely, hands them out briefly, and records what happens.
beginner.whyItMatters: Powerful passwords are often shared, copied into scripts, and never changed. Nobody can say who used them. One leak then gives an attacker lasting control of everything. PAM fixes this by keeping secrets in a vault and giving each person a named, time-limited session. The audit trail also tells you what really happened.
howItWorks: You list every powerful account, including service accounts that machines use.
Passwords move into a vault, which is a protected store with strict access.
You check out a password for a short window, or the tool types it for you.
Your session runs through a jump host, which records the commands you use.
The password is rotated when you return it, so the old value stops working.
beginner.example: Think of the keys to a building. In a careless office, ten people copy the master key and nobody knows who has one. In a careful office, the key hangs in a locked cabinet. You sign it out, use it, and return it the same day. A camera records the corridor. If something goes wrong, the sign-out book answers the question.
takeaways: Powerful credentials should live in a vault, not in scripts or notes.
Give named, short sessions so every action has an owner.
Record privileged sessions, because recordings settle arguments during investigations.

topics.title: Process Injection
topics.summary: Process injection is a family of techniques in which code is placed into the address space of another running process so that it executes under that process's identity, privileges and trust context. Attackers use it for three overlapping reasons: to hide malicious execution inside a legitimate process that security tooling already trusts, to inherit access tokens and privileges the injected process already holds, and to survive elementary cleanup because the host process is not the malicious file. The general mechanism is consistent across implementations even when the specific interfaces differ: obtain a handle to a target process, allocate or repurpose memory inside it, write the payload, change that memory to an executable state, and redirect execution there. Variants differ in how visible each of those steps is — remote thread creation requires cross-process handles and leaves distinct artefacts, while approaches that use shared sections, asynchronous procedure calls, or the process's own already-loaded libraries produce different telemetry. Detection depends heavily on visibility into memory and into cross-process operations, so defenders combine endpoint sensor callbacks, memory scanning for executable regions that are not backed by a file on disk, thread creation anomalies, and behavioural signals such as an unexpected process making network connections or reading credential material. Injection alone is not an objective; it is an enabler that usually appears adjacent to credential access, defence evasion and command-and-control. Understanding the mechanism precisely is what allows an analyst to decide whether a flagged event reflects a genuine intrusion or one of the many legitimate products that also inject code.
objectives: Describe the generic injection sequence from handle acquisition and memory allocation to execution redirection.
Compare common variants by the artefacts each produces and the visibility each gives a defender.
Distinguish malicious injection from legitimate application, accessibility and security product behaviour.
Detect unbacked executable memory regions and anomalous cross-process thread creation on a live host.
Correlate injection events with credential access and command-and-control activity to build an incident narrative.
Map injection techniques to their ATT&CK sub-techniques and explain the defensive value of that mapping.

sources.label: Microsoft Learn: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint documentation

beginner.definition: Process injection is a way of putting harmful code inside another program that is already running. The code then runs under that program's identity and permissions. To the operating system, the activity appears to come from a trusted program rather than from anything suspicious. It is a technique, not a complete piece of malware.
beginner.whyItMatters: It helps an attacker hide in plain sight, borrow permissions the running program already has, and survive simple cleanups. It also breaks the assumption that a program's name tells you what the program is doing. Injection alone does not steal data or spread. It is a step that makes later steps easier. Knowing how it works helps you tell real intrusions apart from the many legitimate products that also use it.
howItWorks: The harmful code picks a running program on the machine to hide inside.
It asks the operating system for permission to work with that program.
It reserves space inside the program's memory and copies its code there.
It marks that memory as something the processor is allowed to run.
It makes the program start executing the new code instead of its own.
The code now acts with the trust and permissions of the host program.
beginner.example: Imagine a courier who is allowed into every floor of an office building. A stranger slips a sealed envelope into the courier's bag and writes a new delivery note. The courier, still trusted and still wearing the right badge, walks the envelope to a restricted floor. Security sees a familiar courier doing a normal job. Process injection is that envelope. The host program keeps its good name while carrying out someone else's instructions.
takeaways: Injection hides harmful code inside a program that is already trusted.
Watch for executable memory that is not backed by a file on disk.
Some legitimate software injects too, so confirm the context before reacting.

topics.title: Proxy
topics.summary: A proxy is an intermediary that receives a client request, applies policy, and forwards that request to the destination on the client's behalf, so the client never communicates directly with the remote server. Forward proxies serve outbound traffic and are the classic control point for URL filtering, malware blocking, authentication, logging and caching, while reverse proxies sit in front of servers to terminate TLS, balance load and shield applications from direct exposure. Because a forward proxy sees the full request, including hostname, path, headers and, where transport encryption is terminated, the body, it can enforce category and content rules that a packet filter cannot express. Proxies are also a natural place for authentication, so access decisions can be tied to a user identity rather than an address, and for inspecting protocols that negotiate their own transfers, such as web traffic carrying file downloads or application programming interface calls. The operational challenges are bypass and scale. Applications that ignore system proxy settings, mobile devices that roam off the corporate network, and encrypted protocols on non-standard ports can all sidestep a proxy unless it is combined with egress control that blocks direct outbound connections, so enforcement of proxy use matters more than the feature list. Explicit proxies require client configuration, while transparent interception redirects traffic without client knowledge, which simplifies rollout but breaks certificate-pinned applications and creates privacy obligations. High availability is essential because an inline proxy failure becomes an outage, and capacity must account for decryption overhead. Logging is where the proxy earns its keep: full URLs, identities, response codes, byte counts and file metadata are among the richest sources for detecting beaconing, staged downloads and exfiltration over web services, though the volume makes retention and indexing a real design constraint.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish forward and reverse proxy roles and the controls each enables.
You will be able to triage proxy logs for beaconing, staged payload downloads and exfiltration over web services.
You will be able to compare explicit configuration with transparent interception and their operational trade-offs.
You will be able to design egress control that prevents applications from bypassing the proxy.
You will be able to plan for high availability, capacity and cost limits in a proxy deployment.
You will be able to map proxy telemetry to adversary techniques and state what the logs cannot show.

beginner.definition: A proxy is a middleman for network traffic. Your device sends its request to the proxy, the proxy decides whether to allow it, and then makes the request on your behalf. The remote server never speaks to you directly. Forward proxies handle outbound traffic from users, while reverse proxies stand in front of servers to protect them.
beginner.whyItMatters: A firewall sees addresses and ports, but a proxy can see the full web request, including the site name, the page and the file being downloaded. That extra detail lets you block whole categories of sites and spot a machine quietly sending data out. Proxies also tie access to a person's account rather than an address, so the rules follow the user everywhere. The catch is that anything which ignores the proxy bypasses it completely.
howItWorks: You configure devices, or the network, so web requests go to the proxy first.
The proxy checks who the user is and what category the site belongs to.
If policy allows it, the proxy fetches the page and returns it to the user.
It logs the address, the user, the site, the file details and how much data moved.
For encrypted sites, the proxy may need to decrypt before it can read anything.
You then block direct outbound connections, so nothing can skip the proxy.
beginner.example: Think of a company mail room. Every letter leaves through it, and the staff there check the address, note it in a log and refuse anything on the banned list. Senders never hand letters directly to the post office. If someone climbs out of a window and posts a letter themselves, the mail room never sees it. That is why forcing all traffic through the proxy matters as much as the proxy itself.
takeaways: A proxy sits in the middle and can read the whole web request.
It ties rules to user accounts, not just to network addresses.
If traffic can skip the proxy, the proxy gives you false comfort.

topics.title: Public Key Infrastructure
topics.summary: Public key infrastructure is the combination of certificate authorities, registration authorities, certificate repositories, revocation services and the policies that bind public keys to identities so that parties who have never met can authenticate each other. A certificate is a signed data structure containing a subject public key, an issuer, a validity period, extensions that constrain usage, and the issuer's signature over all of it; a relying party validates that structure by building a chain to a trusted root, checking signatures, validity times, key usage and extended key usage, name constraints, and revocation status through CRL or OCSP. In practice most PKI incidents are not cryptanalytic. They are trust-store problems: an over-broad enterprise root installed on endpoints, a subordinate CA with no name constraints, an internal CA whose private key sits on a network-reachable server, a certificate issued to an unverified requester, a revocation path that clients never actually check, or a machine identity that outlives the employee who owned it. Lifecycle management is equally important, because expiring certificates cause outages while forgotten long-lived ones become stable footholds. Modern practice pushes towards short-lived certificates, automated issuance through ACME-style protocols, hardware-backed CA keys, certificate transparency monitoring for rogue issuance, and continuous inventory of everything presenting a certificate on the network.
objectives: Describe the roles of certificate authority, registration authority, repository and revocation service in an operational PKI.
Validate a certificate chain manually, including signature, validity, key usage, name constraints and revocation status.
Explain why clients frequently fail to enforce revocation and what design choices reduce that exposure.
Identify trust-store risks such as unnecessary enterprise roots, unconstrained subordinate CAs and stale root certificates.
Design a certificate lifecycle process using automation, short validity periods and hardware-protected CA keys.
Use certificate transparency and issuance monitoring to detect rogue or misissued certificates.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1: Recommendation for Key Management
NIST SP 800-32: Introduction to Public Key Technology and the Federal PKI Infrastructure

beginner.definition: Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is the system of rules, people and services that issue and check digital certificates. A certificate is a signed file that binds a public key to a name, like a website address. Certificate authorities sign these files. Your device trusts a small set of root authorities, and everything else must chain back to them.
beginner.whyItMatters: Two strangers on the internet need a way to trust each other. PKI solves that by introducing trusted signers. Without it, you could not tell your bank's website from a copy made by an attacker. Most real PKI failures are not clever maths. They are messy operations: a certificate nobody renewed, a trusted root that should not be there, or a revocation list clients never check.
howItWorks: A certificate authority creates a root key pair and publishes its root certificate.
Anyone who wants a certificate sends a request with their name and public key.
The authority checks the request, then signs a certificate with its private key.
Your device already trusts the root, so it can verify that signature.
The device also checks the dates, the allowed uses and the chain of issuers.
It may also ask whether the certificate was cancelled before its expiry date.
beginner.example: Think of a passport office. The office checks your identity and issues a passport signed with an official stamp. Border guards do not know you, but they recognise the stamp and can verify it against a list of trusted offices. If a passport is reported stolen, the office adds it to a cancellation list. If a guard never checks that list, a stolen passport still works.
takeaways: A certificate is a signed link between a public key and a name.
Trust flows from a small set of root authorities down through a chain.
Expired certificates and unmanaged roots cause most real outages and trust gaps.

topics.title: Ransomware
topics.summary: Ransomware is malicious software or an intrusion campaign whose objective is to deny an organisation access to its own data or systems and then sell that access back, typically by encrypting files, locking virtualisation or backup infrastructure, or threatening to publish stolen data. Modern incidents are rarely a single executable. They are operations that begin with access brokering, phishing, exposed remote services or valid credentials, proceed through discovery, privilege escalation and lateral movement, often harvest data for double extortion before encryption starts, and only then deploy the payload across many hosts at once. The encryption phase is quick and loud, but the preceding dwell time is where defenders have the best chance to intervene, which is why detection strategy emphasises the precursors: mass file rename behaviour, deletion or disabling of shadow copies and recovery catalogs, unexpected use of backup administration interfaces, credential dumping, and the disabling of endpoint protection. Recovery depends far more on preparation than on any live response. Organisations need offline or immutable backups whose restore path has genuinely been rehearsed, a documented decision process for isolation versus shutdown, and pre-negotiated legal, regulatory and communications roles. Paying a demand is discouraged because it funds further crime, does not guarantee restoration, and in some jurisdictions carries sanctions or reporting implications. Because exfiltration frequently precedes encryption, incident scoping must assume data theft even when no leak site is mentioned, and breach notification timelines should be assessed from the moment of first unauthorised access rather than the moment files were encrypted.
objectives: Describe the typical ransomware intrusion lifecycle from initial access and discovery through exfiltration and encryption.
Detect pre-encryption precursors such as recovery-inhibition behaviour, credential access and mass file modification.
Define a backup architecture that resists destruction, including immutability, offline copies and restore rehearsal.
Lead a ransomware incident decision tree covering isolation, shutdown, escalation, legal and regulatory notification.
Explain double extortion and why breach assessment must assume data exfiltration even without proof of theft.
Justify a no-payment position and outline the sanctions, insurance and recovery consequences of paying a demand.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK: Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486)

beginner.definition: Ransomware is malicious software, or a whole intrusion, that blocks an organization from using its own data and then demands payment to give it back. The usual method is encrypting files so they cannot be opened. Many groups also steal data first and threaten to publish it, which is called double extortion.
beginner.whyItMatters: A ransomware event can stop a business completely, and the encryption phase happens fast. The best chance to intervene comes earlier, while the attacker is still exploring the network. Good backups that are offline or cannot be altered are the single most useful preparation. Organizations should also decide in advance who calls which shots, because the middle of an incident is a bad time for those arguments.
howItWorks: The attacker gets in, often through a stolen password, phishing email, or exposed service.
They explore the network, quietly raise their permissions, and reach more machines.
Valuable data is quietly copied out of the network before anything is encrypted.
Backup tools and recovery features are attacked so that restores become hard.
The encryption program then runs across many machines at once, very quickly.
A note appears demanding payment, sometimes with a threat to publish the stolen data.
beginner.example: Imagine a shop where the owner keeps the spare key under the mat and the safe combination in a drawer. A thief who gets inside first locks every door and changes every lock, then offers to sell the keys back. If the owner had kept a copy of the keys in a bank vault across town, the demand would mean nothing. That vault is an offline backup. Ransomware only works as a business when recovery is impossible.
takeaways: Ransomware is usually a long intrusion that ends in a fast encryption event.
Keep backups offline or unchangeable, and practice restoring from them.
Assume data was stolen even if no leak site is mentioned.

topics.title: Reconnaissance
topics.summary: Reconnaissance is the disciplined collection and organisation of information about a target before and during an engagement, producing the map of systems, identities and technologies that every later phase depends on. Practitioners divide it into passive work, which draws on third-party and public sources and leaves no trace on the target, and active work, which sends traffic to target-owned infrastructure and is therefore visible to defenders. Passive sources include domain registration records, certificate transparency logs, DNS history, public code repositories, cloud storage naming conventions, marketing material, job advertisements that name internal platforms, and breach corpora that reveal credential exposure. Active work includes port and service enumeration, protocol fingerprinting, virtual host and content discovery, and banner or TLS inspection; each of these produces network, firewall and web server evidence that a mature security operations centre can alert on. The output is normally a structured inventory annotated with ownership, exposure and business value rather than a raw list of addresses. For defenders, reconnaissance matters because it is the phase with the longest lead time before exploitation: high volumes of denied flows, sequential destination sweeps, unusual user agents, and monitoring of certificate transparency entries for the organisation's own domains all provide early warning. Reconnaissance quality also determines engagement safety, because scope, rate limits and prohibited techniques are agreed before any packet is sent. Understanding what an adversary can learn from open sources is the most honest route to reducing an attack surface rather than cosmetically hiding it.
objectives: You will be able to separate passive from active reconnaissance and state what evidence each leaves in network and application logs.
You will be able to inventory the open sources that reveal an organisation's naming conventions, technology stack and staff identities.
You will be able to describe how enumeration traffic appears in firewall, netflow, DNS and web server telemetry.
You will be able to rank attack surface findings by business impact rather than by count.
You will be able to explain how certificate transparency and historical DNS monitoring feed an early warning capability.
You will be able to draft reconnaissance limits for a rules-of-engagement document, including rate limits and excluded assets.

beginner.definition: Reconnaissance is the careful gathering of information about a target before an attack. It builds a map of systems, people and technologies. Passive reconnaissance uses public sources and leaves no trace on the target. Active reconnaissance sends traffic to the target's own systems, so defenders can see it. Good reconnaissance decides what happens next.
beginner.whyItMatters: Reconnaissance is the longest phase of an attack, so it gives defenders the earliest warning. Before anyone breaks in, you may see address scanning or unusual login attempts. Your own public information matters too: job adverts, code repositories and old domain records can reveal your technology and your naming habits. If you know what an attacker can learn about you, you can reduce that exposure honestly instead of just hiding it.
howItWorks: The attacker decides what they need to learn about the target first.
They collect free public information, such as domain records and job adverts.
They look for weak signals, such as exposed cloud storage or leaked passwords.
Then they send probes to the target and record which services answer.
All of this becomes an inventory of systems ranked by value and exposure.
beginner.example: Think of a burglar planning a robbery. First they walk the street and note which houses look empty. They check social media to see when the family is on holiday. They might ring the doorbell during the day to see if anyone answers. Only then do they choose a house and a time. All of that watching happens before any lock is touched. Reconnaissance in cyber security is exactly this planning stage.
takeaways: Reconnaissance happens before the break-in, so it is your early warning.
Check what your own public information tells the world about you.
Watch for scanning and probing, and treat it as a signal.

topics.title: Risk Register
topics.summary: A risk register is the controlled record of identified risks that an organisation has decided to track, each entry capturing the risk statement, the affected assets and business processes, the threat and vulnerability that make it credible, the existing controls, the assessed likelihood and impact, the resulting inherent and residual rating, the risk owner, the treatment decision and the target date. It is the operational heart of a risk management programme because it converts assessment into accountable action: an entry without a named owner and a due date is an observation, not a managed risk. Practitioners should treat the register as a living engineering artefact rather than an annual spreadsheet. Good registers express risk in a consistent grammar such as cause, event and consequence, so that two analysts score similar situations similarly; they attach evidence such as detection coverage gaps, vulnerability findings, control test results and near-miss incident data; and they record risk acceptance explicitly, with the accepting authority, the rationale and the expiry. Risk scoring should be calibrated against real incident and loss data where it exists, because uncalibrated five-by-five matrices drift toward subjective optimism. Registers also need lifecycle discipline: risks are reviewed on a defined cadence, escalated when treatment slips, closed with evidence, and linked to the frameworks in use, whether ISO 27001 clause six, NIST SP 800-30 or a sector regulator's expectations. Effective registers are visible to engineering, not locked in a GRC tool only compliance staff can open.
objectives: You will be able to write risk statements in a consistent cause, event and consequence structure that different analysts score the same way.
You will be able to attach control evidence, detection coverage and vulnerability data to support likelihood and impact ratings.
You will be able to assign risk owners with authority to accept or treat, and set meaningful target dates.
You will be able to document formal risk acceptance with rationale, accepting authority and review expiry.
You will be able to run a review cycle that escalates overdue treatment and closes risks only with evidence.
You will be able to calibrate a risk matrix against incident and loss data rather than unfounded opinion.

beginner.definition: A risk register is a living list of the risks your organisation has decided to track. Each entry describes the risk, what it could harm, how likely it is and how bad it would be. It also names an owner and a treatment decision. Without those last parts, it is only a list of worries.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most organisations know their problems but nobody remembers who agreed to fix them. Work slips, priorities change and the same discussion returns every year. A register keeps the decision, the owner and the date in one place. It also shows auditors and leaders that you manage risk on purpose rather than by accident.
howItWorks: Write each risk in the same simple shape: cause, event and consequence.
Note which business processes and which computer systems the risk could damage.
Record the controls you already have and how well each one works.
Score the likelihood and impact, then give every entry a named owner.
Choose to treat, transfer, avoid or accept the risk, with a date.
Review the list on a schedule, escalate late work and close with evidence.
beginner.example: Think of a household repair list on the fridge. Writing down that the roof leaks is not enough. You add who will call the roofer, what it may cost and when it must be done. If you decide to live with the leak, you write that down too, so nobody reopens the argument. A risk register is that fridge list for the risks facing your systems.
takeaways: A risk without a named owner and a date is not managed.
Write risks the same way every time so scores stay comparable.
Record accepted risks openly, with the reason and a review date.

topics.title: Role-Based Access Control
topics.summary: Role-based access control (RBAC) is an access control model in which permissions are assigned to roles rather than directly to users, and users receive permissions only through the roles granted to them. The model is usually decomposed into users, roles, permissions, operations and objects, with role hierarchies allowing a senior role to inherit the permissions of a junior one and constraints preventing conflicting combinations from being held simultaneously. In practice RBAC is the default model for Active Directory groups, Linux groups, Kubernetes role bindings, cloud IAM policies and nearly every commercial application, and it succeeds or fails on the quality of role design rather than on the model itself. Roles that accumulate permissions over years, roles that are granted for convenience rather than function, and role explosion where hundreds of near-duplicate roles exist because exceptions were encoded as new roles rather than handled as exceptions, all produce effective privilege that far exceeds intent. Role mining and periodic recertification are the corrective processes: derive candidate roles from observed entitlement usage, consolidate what overlaps, and require an accountable owner to affirm every assignment on a schedule. The persistent gap is that RBAC answers whether a subject holds a permission but not whether the request is appropriate for the moment, which is why organisations layer attribute-based or context-based conditions over role assignment for sensitive operations. Segregation of duties and least privilege are both expressed through RBAC, so careful attention to role-to-permission mapping and to the aggregation of inherited roles is where real assurance comes from.
objectives: You will be able to model users, roles, permissions and role hierarchies for a representative application.
You will be able to explain how role inheritance and the aggregation of multiple roles produce unintended effective privilege.
You will be able to run role mining and recertification to consolidate role explosion and remove unused entitlements.
You will be able to design segregation-of-duties constraints that keep conflicting duties out of one identity.
You will be able to review cloud IAM policies and Kubernetes role bindings for overly permissive or wildcard grants.
You will be able to explain the limits of RBAC for context-sensitive decisions and when to add attribute-based conditions.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-53: Access Control control family

beginner.definition: Role-based access control, or RBAC, gives permissions to roles instead of to people. A role is a job-shaped bundle of rights, such as help desk agent or finance approver. You get rights only through the roles assigned to you.
beginner.whyItMatters: Assigning rights one person at a time does not scale, and it hides mistakes. Roles make access easier to review and to remove when someone changes jobs. But roles also rot. They collect extra permissions over years, and people keep roles they no longer need. Regular review is what keeps the model honest.
howItWorks: You list the permissions your applications support, such as read, write, and delete.
You group related permissions into roles that match real job duties.
You then assign people to whole roles instead of to single permissions.
A senior role may inherit the permissions of a junior role, which saves effort.
You review the assignments on a schedule and remove what is no longer needed.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital. Nobody gives a new doctor a list of individual permissions on their first day. Instead, the doctor joins the physician group, which already carries the usual rights. A cleaner joins a different group with a different set. Changing jobs means changing groups. The group list is short enough to check.
takeaways: You should give permissions to roles, and then give roles to people.
Roles grow over time, so review every assignment on a schedule.
Many roles together can grant more than any single role suggests.
