topics.title: Rootkit
topics.summary: A rootkit is a set of techniques and components designed to keep malicious presence on a system hidden while retaining privileged control, typically by subverting the very mechanisms an administrator would use to observe the machine. That subversion takes several forms. User-mode rootkits hook or patch library functions so that directory listings, process enumerations and registry queries omit the intruder's artefacts. Kernel-mode rootkits load a driver that filters system calls, hides handles, or unlinks entries from kernel data structures, which can make the compromise invisible to ordinary tooling running above them. Bootkits extend persistence into the boot chain, surviving reinstallation of the operating system on the same disk, and firmware implants sit below that in platform code. Virtualisation-based rootkits move the operating system into a guest and let a thin hypervisor mediate what the guest can observe, which is powerful but fragile in practice. The defensive consequence is that on a suspected rootkit host, a negative result from host-resident tooling proves very little. Trustworthy examination requires either an out-of-band method such as booting the system from known-good external media, offline disk analysis, or cross-referencing independent telemetry: network flow records, remote authentication logs, hypervisor-level events and endpoint agent data that does not rely on the compromised operating system's own APIs. Removal is generally a rebuild decision rather than a cleaning exercise, because a partially removed kernel implant leaves an unverifiable system. Prevention focuses on driver signing enforcement, secure boot, measured boot attestation, and blocking the privileged access that rootkit installation requires in the first place.
objectives: Differentiate user-mode, kernel-mode, bootkit, firmware and virtualisation-based rootkit approaches by their position in the stack.
Explain why host-resident discovery tools can return misleading clean results on an infected system.
Plan an out-of-band investigation using external boot media, offline imaging and independent telemetry sources.
Assess driver signing, secure boot and measured boot controls as barriers to kernel and boot-level persistence.
Justify system rebuild over in-place cleaning when kernel or boot integrity cannot be verified.
Describe the evidence handling steps required when firmware or boot-chain compromise is suspected.

beginner.definition: A rootkit is a set of tools that keeps harmful software hidden on a machine while leaving the attacker in control. It hides by interfering with the very tools an administrator uses to look around, such as file and process lists. Some sit deep inside the operating system, and some go deeper still, into the boot process.
beginner.whyItMatters: On a machine with a rootkit, a clean report from a tool running on that machine proves very little, because the tool itself may be fooled. You have to check from outside, using another source of evidence such as network records or remote sign-in logs. Removing a deep rootkit is usually not realistic, so most teams rebuild the machine instead of trying to clean it.
howItWorks: The attacker gains high-level permission on the machine, often as an administrator.
They install components that change how the system reports its own state.
File lists, process lists, and settings queries start to leave out certain entries.
Deeper versions load early in the boot process and hide above the operating system.
A tool running on the machine therefore reports that everything looks fine.
Investigators must compare the machine against external evidence to spot the difference.
beginner.example: Think of a shop where the manager is the thief. Every evening the manager writes the stock report, so the missing items never appear on paper. The accounts balance perfectly, and any auditor reading the manager's own records would find nothing wrong. To catch it, you must count the shelves yourself, at a time when the manager is not present. Checking an infected machine with its own tools is exactly like trusting that report.
takeaways: A rootkit hides by corrupting the tools you would use to find it.
Trust outside evidence such as network and sign-in records, not the host alone.
For deep rootkits, rebuilding the machine is safer than trying to clean it.

topics.title: RSA
topics.summary: RSA is a public-key cryptosystem whose security rests on the presumed hardness of factoring the product of two large primes, combined with modular exponentiation over that product. A key pair consists of a modulus derived from two secret primes, a public exponent usually 65537, and a private exponent derived through the extended Euclidean algorithm. RSA supports both encryption and digital signatures, and it is normally used inside a padding or encoding scheme rather than on raw data, because textbook RSA is deterministic and malleable. Encryption uses OAEP padding; signatures use PSS or the older PKCS#1 v1.5 scheme, and the padding choice is where most real-world breaks have occurred. Practical risks include small key sizes that are within reach of well-resourced factoring efforts, shared or non-random primes generated by faulty entropy sources, Bleichenbacher-style padding oracle attacks against v1.5 encryption, and signature verification code that ignores algorithm identifiers or accepts the wrong hash. Signing is also much slower than verifying, which shapes how RSA is deployed in certificate chains and protocol handshakes. Throughout their lifecycle, RSA keys must be protected against exfiltration, rotated before weakness accumulates, and retired with their certificates, which is why hardware modules and inventory of key material are operational controls rather than cryptographic footnotes.
objectives: Explain the mathematical structure of an RSA key pair and why factoring the modulus compromises both confidentiality and authenticity.
Distinguish OAEP encryption padding from PSS and PKCS#1 v1.5 signature schemes, and state when each is acceptable.
Describe how a padding oracle attack against RSA encryption is exploited and how constant-time error handling mitigates it.
Identify weak key generation in an asset inventory, including undersized moduli and duplicated or non-random primes.
Interpret certificate chain and signature algorithm fields during a review of TLS or code-signing infrastructure.
Assess the migration path away from RSA towards elliptic curve and post-quantum signature schemes in a live environment.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1: Recommendation for Key Management

beginner.definition: RSA is a public key method for encryption and digital signatures. The name comes from its three inventors. It uses two linked keys: a public key anyone may see and a private key you keep secret. Its safety rests on one idea. Multiplying two large prime numbers is easy, but splitting the answer back into those primes is hard.
beginner.whyItMatters: RSA has protected the internet for decades, and you still meet it in certificates, secure connections and signed software. It also shows the cost of getting cryptography wrong. Most real RSA breaks did not come from difficult maths. They came from weak random numbers, keys that were too short, or error messages that leaked small clues. Protecting the private key is the other half of the job.
howItWorks: The computer picks two very large prime numbers and multiplies them together.
That product becomes the public part of the key, and it is shared freely.
The two primes stay secret and form the private key, which must never be shared.
To encrypt, the sender scrambles data with the public key and some padding rules.
Only the matching private key can unscramble it back into readable data.
To sign, the owner scrambles a short fingerprint of the message with the private key.
beginner.example: Imagine a padlock that anyone can snap shut, but only you hold the key that opens it. A friend puts a secret note in a box, locks it with your open padlock and sends it. Anyone can copy the open padlock and send you locked boxes, but nobody can open them. If someone ever copies your key, or your key is made from a guessable number, every box is exposed.
takeaways: RSA uses a public key to lock and a private key to unlock or sign.
Its strength depends on key length and on truly random prime numbers.
Use modern padding and never reveal detailed errors, because clues help attackers.

topics.title: RTO and RPO
topics.summary: Recovery time objective and recovery point objective are the two commitments that translate continuity intent into engineering requirements. The recovery time objective is the targeted duration of time within which a business process, system or service must be restored after a disruption; it is a deadline, not a duration target, and it must sit inside the maximum tolerable period of disruption derived from the business impact analysis. The recovery point objective is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time, expressed as how far back the last usable copy may be; it constrains backup frequency, replication mode and journaling design. The relationship between them is where most programmes break down. An aggressive recovery point objective of minutes implies continuous or near-continuous replication and therefore a second site, transactional log shipping or storage-level mirroring, all of which carry cost, operational complexity and their own failure modes. An aggressive recovery time objective implies pre-provisioned capacity, automated failover, tested runbooks, current infrastructure as code and staff who have actually executed the procedure. Practitioners should treat both figures as properties of a service tier, published with the dependent services and any exclusions, and validate them with regular restoration and failover tests, because an untested objective is a claim rather than a capability. Finally, recovery objectives must account for integrity as well as availability: restoring clean data after destructive or ransomware activity requires immutable or offline copies whose own recovery point is understood.
objectives: You will be able to explain the difference between a recovery time objective and a recovery point objective using concrete service examples.
You will be able to validate stated objectives against an impact-over-time curve from a business impact analysis.
You will be able to derive the backup, replication and failover architecture each objective actually requires.
You will be able to design restoration and failover tests that produce evidence rather than a checkbox.
You will be able to account for data integrity and immutable copies when destructive activity is in scope.
You will be able to identify where a stated objective is unachievable because a dependency has a weaker objective.

beginner.definition: Recovery time objective and recovery point objective are two promises about outages. The recovery time objective is how long a service may stay broken before it must work again. The recovery point objective is how much recent data you may lose. Both are measured in time and both must be tested.
beginner.whyItMatters: Without these numbers, recovery becomes a guess made during a crisis. Teams argue about what to restore first while customers wait. Clear objectives tell engineers what to build: how often to copy data and how fast a switchover must run. They also expose weak links, because a service cannot recover faster than the slowest part it depends on.
howItWorks: Ask the business how long each service may be unavailable before harm starts.
Ask how much recent data the business can truly afford to lose.
Decide how often to copy data so the second answer is possible.
Build the spare capacity and steps needed to meet the first answer.
Write a recovery plan that lists the order and the people involved.
Test the plan often and record the real time and data loss achieved.
beginner.example: Imagine writing a book on a laptop. The recovery point objective is how many pages you are willing to retype, so you save every ten minutes. The recovery time objective is how long you can wait for a repair before your deadline is missed, so you keep a spare machine ready. Both answers cost money, so you choose them together with the person who owns the deadline.
takeaways: Recovery time is about downtime, recovery point is about data loss.
The business sets the numbers; engineers build to meet them.
An untested objective is only a hope, so measure real recoveries.

topics.title: S3 Bucket Policy
topics.summary: An S3 bucket policy is a JSON resource-based policy attached directly to an object storage bucket that controls which principals may perform which actions against that bucket and the objects inside it, optionally under conditions. Because it is resource-based it can grant access to principals outside the owning account, which is what makes it the standard mechanism for cross-account sharing, public content delivery, and service integrations such as logging or content delivery networks. The policy is evaluated together with identity-based policies, access control lists, block-public-access settings, and any service control policies, and an explicit deny in any of those layers prevents the action. The most consequential failure modes are well known: a wildcard principal combined with a wildcard action, a listing permission that reveals object names, a condition intended to restrict access that does not actually match the request shape, and an object that was public before public access blocks were enabled. Security teams monitor bucket policy changes as high severity events because a single edit can expose an entire dataset, and they combine policy review with classification of what the bucket holds, encryption requirements, versioning, logging and lifecycle rules. Effective practice is to prefer identity-based access and role assumption over cross-account wildcards, to enforce encryption and TLS in the policy itself, and to keep public access blocks on unless a documented exception exists.
objectives: You will be able to read a bucket policy and determine whether it permits public or cross-account access.
You will be able to explain how bucket policies interact with identity policies, ACLs and public access blocks during authorisation.
You will be able to write conditions that restrict access by encryption, transport, network origin or principal tags.
You will be able to identify policy patterns that expose object listings or allow unintended read and write access.
You will be able to triage alerts raised by bucket policy changes and public access block modifications.

sources.label: AWS Blocking Public Access to Storage

beginner.definition: A bucket policy is a written rule attached to a cloud storage bucket. A bucket is a container that holds files, and S3 is one popular object storage service. The policy states who may read, write or list the files inside, and under what conditions. The provider checks it on every request.
beginner.whyItMatters: One wrong line in a bucket policy can expose a whole dataset to the world. This happens often in real incidents, and the files can be copied before anyone notices. Unlike a password, the exposure needs no guesswork. That is why bucket policy changes are treated as high-severity events and reviewed carefully.
howItWorks: A request arrives asking to read, write or list objects in the bucket.
The service collects the bucket policy and any identity policy for the caller.
It also applies public access blocks and any organisation-wide guard rules from your company.
If any of those layers contains an explicit deny, the request fails immediately.
Otherwise, if a rule allows the action under the stated conditions, it succeeds.
Bucket logs record the request, so you can see who read what and when.
beginner.example: Imagine a filing cabinet in a shared office. A label on the front says who may open each drawer: the finance team only, or everyone in the building. If you write everyone on the label, any visitor can help themselves. Nothing is broken, no lock is picked, yet the files are gone. A bucket policy is that label.
takeaways: A bucket policy decides who can reach the files, so review every change.
Keep public access blocks on unless there is a documented reason.
An explicit deny in any policy layer always stops the request.

topics.title: Salt
topics.summary: A salt is a unique, non-secret random value that is combined with an input before hashing so that identical inputs produce different digests, and it is a mandatory component of any password storage scheme. Salting defeats precomputed lookup structures such as rainbow tables and prevents an attacker who obtains a password database from learning which accounts share a password, because the same password hashed under different salts yields unrelated digests. Salts must be generated with a cryptographically secure random source, must be long enough to make collisions across a large user base statistically irrelevant, and must be stored alongside the resulting hash so verification remains possible. Salting does not slow down guessing, so it must be paired with an adaptive, memory-hard password hashing function; a salted fast hash is still a fast hash. Other contexts use the term differently. In key derivation a salt binds derived material to a context or generation, and in signature schemes a random per-signature value is sometimes loosely called a salt even though its uniqueness requirements are far stricter and its exposure is catastrophic rather than merely weakening. Common implementation defects include a single global salt shared by every account, salts derived from the username or a timestamp with insufficient entropy, truncated salts, salts generated with a non-cryptographic random function, and migration routines that re-hash existing passwords with a fixed salt during a framework upgrade.
objectives: Explain what salting prevents and what it explicitly does not protect against.
Specify correct salt generation, length and storage requirements for a password authentication system.
Choose an adaptive password hashing construction and tune its cost parameters for a production workload.
Identify defective salt handling during code review, including shared, derived or truncated salts.
Distinguish a password salt from a key derivation salt and a per-signature nonce, and apply the right rules to each.
Plan a credential store migration that rehashes existing passwords without weakening them.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-63B: Digital Identity Guidelines - Authentication and Lifecycle Management

beginner.definition: A salt is a random value added to a password before it is hashed. A hash turns text into a fixed code that cannot be reversed. The same password with different salts gives completely different codes. Salts are stored next to the hash, because the system needs them to check a login later. Salts are not secret.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you store plain hashes of passwords, two users with the same password get the same code. An attacker who steals the list can spot those matches. Worse, they can precompute codes for millions of common passwords and look them up instantly. A salt per user destroys both tricks. Remember, though, a salt does not slow down guessing. You still need a slow password hashing method.
howItWorks: When a user sets a password, the system generates a random salt for that account.
The salt is combined with the password and passed through a slow hashing function.
The system stores the salt and the resulting hash together in the database.
Each account gets its own salt, so identical passwords produce different hashes.
At login, the system reads the stored salt and repeats the same calculation.
If the new hash matches the stored one, the password is correct.
beginner.example: Imagine a school that files student forms by exact wording. Two students who write the same sentence end up in the same folder, which is a privacy problem. So the school adds a random cover page to each form before filing. Now the same sentence lands in a different place every time. The cover page is not secret, but it stops anyone grouping students by what they wrote.
takeaways: Use a unique random salt for every stored password, never one shared salt.
A salt stops precomputed lookups, but only a slow hash slows down guessing.
Store the salt beside the hash, since it is not secret and you need it later.

topics.title: SAML
topics.summary: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an XML-based standard for exchanging authentication and authorisation assertions between an identity provider and a service provider, and it remains the dominant federation protocol in enterprise and government environments. In the common web browser profile, an unauthenticated user is redirected to the identity provider, authenticates there, and is returned to the service provider carrying a signed assertion posted to an assertion consumer service endpoint. The service provider must validate the XML signature over the assertion, confirm the audience restriction matches its own entity identifier, verify the NotBefore and NotOnOrAfter conditions and the subject confirmation method, and reject any assertion that is replayed. Those checks are exactly where real breaches have occurred: libraries that parse untrusted XML without disabling external entity resolution, service providers that trust an unsigned assertion because it arrived over TLS, and implementations that accept a signature covering only part of the document while the attacker modifies another part. Signature wrapping, XML external entity injection, comment-field confusion and assertion replay are the recurring failure modes, and they are implementation defects rather than flaws in the protocol. Metadata, certificate rotation and clock skew are the operational problems that cause outages, while attribute mapping and name identifier format issues cause the subtle authorisation errors that let a user reach an application they should not. For defenders, SAML troubleshooting means reading identity provider sign-in logs alongside the service provider's own assertion handling, and treating any change in signing certificate or assertion consumer endpoint as a change worth alerting on.
objectives: You will be able to trace a SAML web browser SSO flow and name the security checks the service provider must perform on every assertion.
You will be able to explain signature wrapping, assertion replay and XML external entity risks without relying on a specific tool.
You will be able to inspect SAML metadata, signing certificates and attribute mappings for a federation partnership.
You will be able to diagnose common SAML failures such as clock skew, audience mismatch and unresolved name identifiers.
You will be able to design monitoring for assertion consumer endpoint changes and signing certificate rotation.
You will be able to explain why transmitting an assertion over TLS does not remove the need for signature validation.

beginner.definition: Security Assertion Markup Language, or SAML, is a way for one sign-in service to tell another application that you are who you say. The service sends a signed statement, written in a markup format that labels each field. The application checks the signature before trusting the statement.
beginner.whyItMatters: SAML still runs sign-in for many large organisations. The protocol itself is sound, but the checking code is often weak. Some applications trust a statement just because it arrived over a secure connection. Others check only part of the document. Those small gaps have caused real account takeovers, so careful validation matters.
howItWorks: You open an application, and it sees that you are not signed in yet.
The application sends your browser to the identity provider, the trusted sign-in service.
You sign in there, often with a second factor such as a code or key.
The provider builds a signed statement about you and sends it back.
The application verifies the signature, the audience, and the time limits.
beginner.example: Think of a letter of introduction sealed with wax. A trusted office writes that you are a member of staff and stamps it. You carry the letter to another building. The guard there checks the wax stamp and the name on the envelope. If the stamp is missing, or the letter names a different building, the guard refuses you.
takeaways: A signed SAML statement should be verified, never accepted on transport alone.
Check the audience, the time window, and the full signature.
Alert on changes to signing certificates and receiving endpoints.

topics.title: Scope and Rules of Engagement
topics.summary: Scope and rules of engagement are the written boundary that defines what may be tested, when, how, by whom, and what happens when something goes wrong; without documented authorisation from someone entitled to give it, the same activity is simply unauthorised access. A workable document names in-scope assets precisely enough to be unambiguous, lists excluded systems and data categories, and states testing windows with time zones. It defines permitted and prohibited techniques, for example whether denial-of-service testing, social engineering, physical entry or third-party hosted services are allowed, and it records the source addresses that defenders may allow-list. It sets escalation rules: emergency contacts on both sides, stop conditions such as discovery of an unrelated active intrusion or unexpected service degradation, and the obligation to report critical findings immediately rather than at the final readout. It also covers handling of sensitive data encountered during testing, evidence retention and destruction, deconfliction with the security operations centre, and the treatment of cloud or outsourced services where the provider may require separate notification under a shared responsibility model. Practically, the document protects the tester, the client and the defenders: it reduces false positives because the security operations centre knows when legitimate testing is scheduled, gives a tested route for stopping work, and provides the audit trail that regulators and insurers request. Scope should be reviewed whenever the environment changes materially.
objectives: You will be able to draft a scope section that names in-scope and excluded assets unambiguously.
You will be able to list the technique categories that must be explicitly permitted or prohibited in an engagement.
You will be able to define escalation paths, stop conditions and emergency contacts for a test.
You will be able to explain how deconfliction with a security operations centre reduces false positives.
You will be able to describe the authorisation needed for cloud and third-party hosted services.
You will be able to specify evidence handling, retention and data destruction requirements.

beginner.definition: Scope and rules of engagement are the written rules for a security test. They say what may be tested, when, how, and by whom. They also say what to do when something goes wrong. Without written permission from someone allowed to give it, the same testing becomes unauthorised access. This document protects the tester, the client and the defenders.
beginner.whyItMatters: Testing without permission is not testing, it is intrusion. Clear scope keeps everyone safe and legal. It also prevents wasted work on systems nobody cares about. When defenders know a test is booked, they do not treat it as a real attack, which saves hours of false alarms. A good document also names emergency contacts and the conditions that mean stop now.
howItWorks: List every system that is inside the test, using exact names and addresses.
List what is out of bounds, including systems owned by other companies.
State the allowed hours, the time zone, and any speed limits.
Say which techniques are banned, such as service disruption or social tricks.
Agree on emergency contacts, stop conditions, and exactly how findings will be reported.
beginner.example: Imagine hiring builders to fix your kitchen. You would not let them knock down walls in the flat next door. You agree the working hours so the neighbours can sleep. You say clearly that the gas pipe stays untouched. You also swap phone numbers for emergencies. A rules of engagement document is that agreement for a security test. It sets the boundaries before work starts, so nobody is surprised later.
takeaways: No written permission means the testing is simply not allowed.
Name what is out of scope as clearly as what is in scope.
Defenders should know about a planned test before it starts.

topics.title: Secret Scanning
topics.summary: Secret scanning is the practice of detecting credentials, API keys, tokens, private keys and other sensitive material that has been committed to source control, embedded in build artifacts, written into logs, or left in configuration files and container layers. It operates in three places: pre-commit or pre-receive hooks that block a secret before it enters history, continuous scanning of repositories and pipelines that catches what got through, and artifact and runtime scanning that finds secrets baked into images or exposed through debug endpoints. Detection usually combines high-confidence provider-specific patterns with entropy heuristics and verification calls that confirm whether a discovered credential is still live. For a practising engineer the critical insight is that a secret written to version control should be treated as disclosed, because rewriting history does not undo the copies already fetched by every clone, fork and CI cache. The response is therefore rotation first, cleanup second, and only then rewriting history if it is worth the disruption. Effective programmes pair scanning with a secrets manager, short-lived credentials issued by workload identity, and pre-commit enforcement so the cheap prevention happens before the leak. The usual failure modes are scanning only the default branch, ignoring pipeline logs and issue attachments, alerting into a channel nobody owns, and treating the problem as solved once a scanner is installed while long-lived static keys remain the primary authentication method.
objectives: You will be able to explain why a credential committed to version control must be treated as disclosed and rotated rather than merely deleted.
You will be able to design a layered detection approach covering pre-commit hooks, repository history, pipeline logs and container images.
You will be able to distinguish high-confidence provider patterns from entropy-based heuristics and assess the false positive cost of each.
You will be able to write an incident runbook for a live credential exposure covering revocation, rotation, scope review and log analysis.
You will be able to evaluate whether an organisation's credential strategy reduces secret sprawl or merely detects it after the fact.
You will be able to identify the blind spots of a scanner that only inspects the default branch of a repository.

beginner.definition: Secret scanning looks for passwords, keys, and access tokens that were left in the wrong place. These secrets often end up in source code, build logs, or setup files by mistake. The scanner compares what it finds against patterns for known key formats. It warns you so the secret can be replaced before anyone else uses it.
beginner.whyItMatters: A key in your code is like a house key taped to the front door. Anyone who reads the repository can copy it. Deleting the line is not enough, because every clone and backup still holds the old copy. You must treat the key as leaked and replace it. Rotating fast limits the damage an attacker can do.
howItWorks: A pre-commit hook checks your changes before they are saved to history.
A hook is a small script that runs automatically at a set moment.
It looks for key patterns and for random-looking text with high entropy.
Entropy means the text looks random and unpredictable, which real keys usually do.
Continuous scans then check the whole repository, its history, and its logs.
If a live key is found, you revoke it first and clean up afterwards.
beginner.example: Imagine you write your bank card number on a sticky note and stick it to your monitor. You notice a week later and throw the note away. Is your card safe? No, because anyone who walked past could have photographed it. A secret committed to code works the same way. The right response is not just deleting the line. You call the bank and get a new card.
takeaways: A secret in version control is leaked; replace it, do not just delete it.
Scan before committing, then keep scanning history and build logs.
Move secrets into a secrets manager and use short-lived credentials.

topics.title: Secrets Manager
topics.summary: A secrets manager is a managed service for storing, controlling access to, and automatically rotating credentials such as database passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates and private keys, so that applications retrieve them at runtime instead of embedding them in code, images or configuration files. The service encrypts stored values with a key management service key, authorises retrieval with the platform identity system, versions every change, and can run scheduled rotation by invoking a function that creates a new credential and updates both the secret store and the target system. The security value comes from removing long-lived static secrets from build artefacts and repositories, from giving each workload a distinct credential that can be revoked individually, and from producing an audit trail of which identity read which secret and when. Practitioners must still address several hard problems. Workloads need a trustworthy identity to authenticate to the store, which in cloud environments usually means instance or workload identity rather than a bootstrap credential, otherwise the initial secret simply moves rather than disappearing. Caching matters because a rotated credential must not break running services, and rotation must be atomic enough that the old value stops working only after the new one is distributed. Also important are scoping read access so that one compromised workload cannot read every secret, detecting secrets that leak into repositories and images, and monitoring for unusual retrieval patterns.
objectives: You will be able to explain how runtime retrieval, versioning and automatic rotation remove static credentials from build artefacts.
You will be able to scope secret read access so a single compromised workload cannot reach unrelated credentials.
You will be able to design a rotation flow that avoids outages from caching and in-flight connections.
You will be able to use workload identity to authenticate to the store without a bootstrap secret.
You will be able to triage alerts on abnormal retrieval volume, cross-account reads and secret policy changes.
You will be able to respond to a leaked secret by rotating, revoking and confirming the old value no longer authenticates.

beginner.definition: A secrets manager is a service that stores sensitive values such as passwords, API keys and certificates. API keys are strings that let one program call another. Instead of hiding these values in code or config files, your program asks the service for them at run time, and the service checks permission first.
beginner.whyItMatters: Passwords and keys written into code or config files spread everywhere: laptops, build logs, backups and code repositories. Once leaked, they often stay valid for years. A secrets manager keeps them in one guarded place, gives each workload its own credential, and can change them on a schedule. It also records who read which secret and when.
howItWorks: You store a secret in the service and write a policy saying who may read it.
The service encrypts the value using a key that it manages for you.
When your program starts, it proves its identity, often using its cloud workload identity.
It asks for the secret by name and receives the value over an encrypted connection.
A rotation schedule can create a new password and update both the store and the target system.
Every read is written to a log, so unusual access can be spotted.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel safe at reception. Guests do not carry the master key in their pocket, and staff do not write the combination on the wall. When you need something from your box, you show your ID and a clerk opens it for you. The safe also keeps a record of each visit. That record is how you notice a stranger asking for your box.
takeaways: Never store passwords or keys in code, images or config files.
Give each workload its own secret so you can revoke it alone.
Rotate secrets on a schedule and watch the access logs for odd reads.

topics.title: Secure Software Development Lifecycle
topics.summary: The Secure Software Development Lifecycle is a structured way of weaving security activities into every phase of how software is planned, built, tested, released and maintained, rather than bolting security on at the end. In a mature SSDLC, requirements work establishes abuse cases and security acceptance criteria alongside functional ones, design work produces threat models and data-flow diagrams, implementation follows approved patterns and hardened libraries, verification combines static analysis, dependency review and dynamic testing, and release gates confirm that findings are triaged and that artifacts are signed. Operations closes the loop through monitoring, vulnerability intake and a defined patch cadence. For a practising security engineer the importance of the SSDLC is organisational rather than technical: it converts a series of ad hoc code reviews into a repeatable set of gates with named owners, entry and exit criteria, and evidence. That evidence is what makes the process auditable and what lets a security team argue for design-time intervention instead of endless reactive reviews. Typical failure modes are well known. Security work is defined as a gate rather than a service, so developers route around it. Threat models are produced once and never revisited when architecture changes. Tooling generates thousands of findings with no triage SLA, producing alert fatigue and eventual ignoring of the whole pipeline. Exceptions are granted verbally and never expire. The strongest programmes measure how early defects are caught and how quickly accepted risks are revisited, and they treat a blocked release as a process defect to be fixed, not a hero moment.
objectives: You will be able to describe the phases of a secure development lifecycle and name the security activities that belong in each.
You will be able to write security acceptance criteria and abuse cases that are testable by engineering teams.
You will be able to design proportionate release gates that block on high-severity findings without paralysing delivery.
You will be able to explain how threat modelling, static analysis, dependency review and dynamic testing complement each other and where each is blind.
You will be able to define a vulnerability triage workflow with severity mapping, owners, SLAs and expiry-bound exceptions.
You will be able to evaluate whether an SSDLC programme is genuinely embedded or merely documented, using observable evidence.

beginner.definition: The secure software development lifecycle is a way of building security into every stage of a project. Security tasks sit beside normal work from planning to release to maintenance. Each stage has clear checks, named owners, and written evidence. It turns security from a last-minute surprise into a normal part of the schedule.
beginner.whyItMatters: Fixing a security flaw after release can cost many times more than fixing it at design time. It also risks customer data and trust. A lifecycle approach spreads the work across the project instead of dumping it on one team at the end. It gives you evidence to show auditors and customers. Without it, security becomes a bottleneck everyone avoids.
howItWorks: In planning, you write security requirements and misuse cases next to normal features.
In design, you draw the data flows and run a threat modelling session.
While coding, you follow approved patterns and never write secrets into the code.
In testing, you run static checks, dependency reviews, and dynamic scans of the app.
Before release, gates confirm that findings were triaged and files were signed.
After release, you monitor, collect vulnerability reports, and patch on a set schedule.
beginner.example: Think of building a house with a building inspector involved from day one. She reviews the plans, checks the foundation, inspects the wiring, and signs off before you move in. Each visit is short and catches small problems early. Now imagine skipping all that and calling her only after the roof leaks. Same inspector, far bigger bill, and much more stress. That is the difference a lifecycle makes.
takeaways: Build security into every stage instead of adding it at the end.
Give each gate an owner, clear rules, and written evidence.
Make exceptions expire, and review them on a fixed date.

topics.title: SHA-256
topics.summary: SHA-256 is a cryptographic hash function from the SHA-2 family that maps an arbitrary-length input to a fixed 256-bit digest, and it is specified in FIPS 180-4. It belongs to the Merkle-Damgard construction with a Davies-Meyer compression function, processing 512-bit message blocks through 64 rounds over eight 32-bit state words. The function is designed to be preimage resistant, second-preimage resistant and collision resistant, so it is suitable for integrity verification, digital signature pre-hashing, message authentication when combined with a key, and content addressing. It is not a password storage function: its speed makes offline guessing cheap, and password hashing should use a memory-hard, salted construction instead. Integrity use cases bring their own failures, because comparing digests with a non-constant-time equality check leaks information and because hashing a downloaded artifact without binding it to a trusted signature only proves the artifact matches whatever digest was served alongside it. File integrity monitoring, software supply chain attestation, SBOM identification and forensic evidence records all rely on SHA-256 as a common language, so defenders need to know when a digest comparison is meaningful and when it is merely decorative. Extension-attack resistance is also relevant: because plain SHA-256 is a Merkle-Damgard construction, naive secret-prefix MACs built from it are forgeable, which is precisely why HMAC exists.
objectives: Explain the Merkle-Damgard structure of SHA-256 and what preimage, second-preimage and collision resistance each protect.
Distinguish integrity verification from authenticity and state what additional control is required for a trustworthy digest comparison.
Identify why SHA-256 must not be used directly for password storage and which construction to use instead.
Explain how length extension defeats secret-prefix construction and why HMAC is the correct keyed alternative.
Apply SHA-256 correctly in forensic evidence handling, file integrity monitoring and software supply chain records.
Assess the risk from deprecated hash functions still present in a certificate or signature policy.

beginner.definition: SHA-256, short for Secure Hash Algorithm 256, is a hash function. It takes any amount of data and produces a fixed 256-bit fingerprint, usually written as 64 characters. The same input always gives the same fingerprint, and any change, even one letter, gives a completely different one. You cannot turn a fingerprint back into the original data.
beginner.whyItMatters: SHA-256 is how computers check that a file arrived intact. Downloads, software updates and evidence bags all carry a fingerprint. If a single byte changed, the fingerprint no longer matches. But a fingerprint alone proves only that the data matches the fingerprint you were given. It does not prove who created it. You need a signature from a trusted source as well. SHA-256 is also fast, so it is unsafe for storing passwords.
howItWorks: The input data is split into fixed-size blocks, and padding is added at the end.
The function starts with eight fixed numbers that form its working state.
Each block is mixed into that state through many rounds of simple operations.
The operations include adding, rotating bits and combining values with logic rules.
After the last block, the state is written out as the final 256-bit fingerprint.
Changing one input bit scrambles the whole state, so the output looks unrelated.
beginner.example: Think of a wax seal pressed onto a document. The seal pattern depends on the whole document and on a fixed stamp. Change one word and the pattern no longer matches. Anyone with the stamp can make a new seal, so the seal shows the document is intact, not that a stranger wrote it. For that, you also need the writer's own signature.
takeaways: A hash is a one-way fingerprint: you can check it but not reverse it.
SHA-256 detects accidental change; only a signature proves who sent the data.
Never store passwords with a fast hash. Use a slow, salted method instead.

topics.title: Shared Responsibility Model
topics.summary: The shared responsibility model is the contractual and architectural division of security duties between a cloud service provider and its customer, in which the provider secures the cloud itself while the customer secures what they put in the cloud. The split is not uniform: for infrastructure as a service the provider owns the physical facilities, hosts, hypervisor and network fabric, while the customer owns the guest operating system, patching, identity, data and application; for platform as a service the provider absorbs the runtime and middleware, leaving the customer identity, configuration and data; for software as a service the provider operates nearly the whole stack and the customer retains responsibility for accounts, access grants, data classification and how the service is used. Security professionals rely on the model because most cloud incidents occur in the customer's portion of the stack, particularly identity misconfiguration, overly permissive policies, exposed storage and unpatched workloads. Applying it demands more than reading a marketing diagram: teams must map each control in their own framework to a named owner, record the evidence source, and confirm the split for every managed service they adopt, since the boundary shifts service by service and even feature by feature. Auditors expect this mapping to be documented and traceable, and incident responders need it to know who to contact and what telemetry the provider will and will not expose.
objectives: You will be able to explain how responsibility shifts across IaaS, PaaS and SaaS and why the boundary differs per managed service.
You will be able to map a control framework to provider and customer ownership and identify which side supplies the evidence.
You will be able to recognise the misconfiguration classes that repeatedly fall on the customer side of the line.
You will be able to use provider documentation to settle disputed ownership during an incident or audit.
You will be able to brief engineering and procurement teams on the security work they still own after adoption.

beginner.definition: The shared responsibility model describes how security duties are split between a cloud provider and you, the customer. The provider secures the cloud itself, such as buildings, hardware and the network. You secure what you put in the cloud, such as your data, your accounts, your settings and your code.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many people assume the provider handles all security, and that belief causes breaches. The cloud provider does protect the underlying platform, but it cannot know whether your storage should be public or your staff should have admin rights. Most cloud incidents happen in the customer's part of the stack. Knowing where the line falls tells you which work is still yours.
howItWorks: Start by listing the services you use, because the split differs for each one.
For each service, find the provider's own description of who does what.
Sort the duties into groups: physical, platform, operating system, identity, data and configuration.
Write next to each duty the name of the team that owns it and the evidence they keep.
Check the split again whenever you add a new service or a new feature.
During an incident, use the list to know who to call and what logs to expect.
beginner.example: Renting a flat is a good comparison. The landlord keeps the building safe: the roof, the wiring, the front door lock and the fire alarms. You keep your own flat safe: you lock your door, you decide who gets a key, and you insure your belongings. If you leave your door open, that is not the landlord's fault.
takeaways: The provider secures the cloud; you secure what you put inside it.
The split changes with each service, so check it every time.
Write down who owns each duty before you need it in an incident.

topics.title: SIEM
topics.summary: A Security Information and Event Management platform is a centralised system that ingests logs and telemetry from across an estate, normalises them into a common schema, correlates events over time, and evaluates detection rules to raise alerts that a security operations centre can triage. In practice a SIEM is three coupled capabilities: collection and parsing, a searchable hot and warm store with a query language, and a rules and correlation engine with alerting, case management and reporting on top. Its value depends far less on the vendor than on data quality and coverage. A rule is only as good as the fields it can rely on, so normalisation decisions, timestamp handling, and reliable identity resolution across endpoints, identity providers, cloud control planes and network sensors determine whether detections are precise or noisy. Detection engineers therefore treat the SIEM as a product with a content pipeline: they map log sources to what MITRE ATT&CK techniques they can observe, write and version rules, measure precision and recall against known-good and known-bad telemetry, and retire content that only produces fatigue. Common failure modes are predictable. Ingesting everything without enrichment produces volume without context; ignoring time zone and clock skew breaks correlation windows; broad rules with single-event triggers flood analysts; and quiet log sources create blind spots that adversaries exploit precisely because nobody alerted. Effective operators tune the platform deliberately, using allow-lists with expiry dates, entity risk scoring rather than raw severity, and periodic purple-team validation to prove that a technique which should be detected actually is.
objectives: You will be able to explain how a SIEM pipeline collects, parses, normalises and stores telemetry, and identify where parsing errors silently break downstream detections.
You will be able to assess log source coverage against MITRE ATT&CK techniques and state honestly which techniques your estate cannot currently observe.
You will be able to write and tune correlation rules that use entity context, thresholds and time windows rather than single-event triggers.
You will be able to diagnose false-positive floods by tracing an alert back through normalisation, enrichment and rule logic to its root cause.
You will be able to design retention and hot/warm/cold tiering that balances investigation needs, cost and compliance obligations.
You will be able to validate detection content with controlled test telemetry and record the evidence that a rule fires when it should.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-92, Guide to Computer Security Log Management
NIST SP 800-61, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

beginner.definition: A SIEM is a Security Information and Event Management platform. It is one central system that collects logs from across your whole estate. It cleans them into a common shape, stores them, and checks them against detection rules. When a rule matches, the SIEM raises an alert for analysts to review.
beginner.whyItMatters: Logs live in hundreds of places: laptops, servers, cloud accounts and network devices. Without one central system, nobody can see the whole picture. A SIEM is what lets you connect a strange login on one system to a strange file change on another. It is also where your detection rules actually run.
howItWorks: Agents and connectors on your systems forward their logs to the SIEM.
A parser reads each log format and breaks it into named fields, such as user and host.
Normalisation then renames those fields so every source uses the same field names.
The events land in a searchable store, and older data moves to cheaper storage.
Detection rules run against the incoming events and raise an alert on a match.
Alerts go to a queue with case notes, so an analyst can investigate and record a decision.
beginner.example: Imagine a large building where every room keeps its own notebook of who came and went. If something is stolen, you would have to walk to every room and read every notebook. A SIEM is the front desk that collects all those notebooks each night and keeps them in one place. Rules act like a careful clerk who reads them all and shouts when something looks wrong.
takeaways: A SIEM is only as good as the logs you feed it.
Bad log parsing silently breaks the rules that depend on those fields.
Know which log sources you are missing; those are your blind spots.

topics.title: Sigma Rules
topics.summary: Sigma is a vendor-neutral, YAML-based signature format for describing log-based detections, intended to be written once and translated into the query language of whichever SIEM or log platform an organisation runs. A rule separates two concerns that many native rule formats entangle: the detection logic, expressed as named search identifiers with field modifiers such as contains, startswith, endswith, base64offset, re and cidr, and a condition that combines those identifiers with boolean and aggregation operators. Around the logic sits metadata that makes the rule maintainable and machine-readable: a title and description, a stable id, a status, a logsource block naming the product, service or category the rule requires, references, an author, a date, a level and tags that commonly include ATT&CK technique identifiers. The logsource abstraction is what enables portability, because the translator maps product and category onto concrete field names for the target platform, for example expanding a Windows process creation rule into the vendor's specific process, command-line and parent-process fields. The pipelining feature turns Sigma into a small language for composed detections: a base rule can be chained with filters that add exclusions, or several rules combined to require correlated events. Practical advantages are reviewable diffs, reuse of a rule estate across multiple platforms, and coverage tracking. Practical limitations deserve equal weight: translation quality varies, so a converted rule must be validated on real telemetry before it is trusted; generic field mappings can lose fidelity for platforms whose schema differs substantially; and Sigma describes log detections only, so it says nothing about network, memory or endpoint-behaviour detection that never reaches a log pipeline. Treat Sigma as a shared, reviewable source of truth rather than as a guarantee of deployable accuracy.
objectives: You will be able to read and write a Sigma rule with a logsource block, named search identifiers, field modifiers and a boolean or aggregation condition.
You will be able to explain how the logsource abstraction enables translation to different SIEM query languages and where that mapping loses fidelity.
You will be able to use rule metadata to track ownership, required telemetry, status and ATT&CK technique coverage across a rule estate.
You will be able to compose detections with pipelining, including base rules with filters and correlated multi-rule conditions.
You will be able to validate a translated rule against real telemetry and identify the translation errors that break it silently.
You will be able to state which detection domains Sigma cannot cover and what complementary content is needed for them.

sources.label: Sigma: generic signature format for SIEM systems

beginner.definition: Sigma is a shared, vendor-neutral way to write detection rules as text. Vendor-neutral means the rule is not tied to one security product. You describe what to look for, and a translator turns it into the query language your platform understands. It is often called the common language for log detections.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most companies use more than one security platform, and each has its own query language. Writing the same rule five times wastes effort and creates five chances to make a mistake. With Sigma you write it once, review it once, and convert it as needed. It also gives your rules a shared shape, so they are easy to compare and track.
howItWorks: You write the rule in a plain text format with a title, a description and an author.
You state which log source the rule needs, such as Windows process creation events.
You list the patterns to look for, such as a command name or a file path.
You write a condition that combines those patterns, using simple words like and, or, not.
A translator converts the rule into the query language of your chosen platform.
You test the converted rule on real logs, because translation does not always fit perfectly.
beginner.example: Think of a recipe written in a neutral way: flour, water, salt, bake until golden. Any kitchen can follow it, whether the oven is gas or electric. A cook adjusts the timing for their own oven. Sigma rules work like that recipe. You write the detection once in neutral terms, then each platform follows it in its own local dialect.
takeaways: Write a detection once in a neutral format, then translate it.
Always test a translated rule on real logs before you trust it.
Sigma covers log detections only, so files and memory need other tools.

topics.title: SOAR
topics.summary: Security Orchestration, Automation and Response is the discipline and tooling category concerned with turning detection output into repeatable action. Where a SIEM answers what happened, a SOAR platform asks what should happen next and then does as much of it as is safe without a human. Three capabilities are usually bundled: orchestration, meaning integration with other systems through APIs and playbooks; automation, meaning execution of those playbooks with minimal analyst input; and response, meaning the enrichment, containment and case-management actions that result. Typical first automations are unglamorous and high value: enriching an alert with asset ownership, user directory data, threat-intelligence reputation and recent sign-in history; de-duplicating and grouping related alerts into one case; notifying the right on-call queue with a consistent summary; and posting a structured timeline into the ticketing system. The hard part is not the integration, it is the decision boundary. Automations that take destructive action such as disabling an account, isolating a host or blocking an indicator can cause outages and can be abused by an adversary who learns what triggers them, so mature teams stage actions by confidence and reversibility, require approval for anything irreversible, and log every automated decision with its inputs for later review. SOAR also institutionalises response quality: a playbook is a documented, versioned procedure, so junior analysts execute the same steps as seniors, and post-incident review can show exactly which step failed. Common pitfalls include automating a process nobody had defined, brittle integrations with no error handling, and relying on threat-intelligence indicators that expire before the playbook runs.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish orchestration, automation and response capabilities and map each to concrete SOC workflows.
You will be able to design a playbook that enriches an alert before any containment action is considered.
You will be able to classify response actions by reversibility and confidence, and place approval gates where an automated mistake would cause outage or data loss.
You will be able to write idempotent automation steps so that a retried playbook does not duplicate tickets, notifications or containment actions.
You will be able to instrument playbooks with logging that records inputs, decisions and outcomes for after-action review.
You will be able to evaluate a SOAR integration for failure handling, rate limits, credential storage and blast radius before enabling it.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-61, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
CISA Cyber Security Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks

beginner.definition: SOAR stands for Security Orchestration, Automation and Response. It is a platform that connects your security tools together and runs repeatable response steps for you. Orchestration means the tools talk to each other. Automation means the steps run without a person. Response means real actions, such as blocking or collecting evidence.
beginner.whyItMatters: Analysts waste hours copying data between tools: looking up who owns a machine, checking a user's history, opening a ticket. SOAR does that boring work automatically. This gives analysts time to think. But automation can also cause harm, so risky actions still need a human approval step.
howItWorks: An alert arrives from your detection system and lands in the SOAR queue.
The platform automatically gathers facts: who owns the machine, and how important it is.
It checks threat intelligence to see whether the address or file is already known as bad.
It groups alerts about the same event into one case, so the queue stays clean.
For low-risk steps it acts alone, such as sending a summary to the right team.
For risky steps it pauses and asks a human to approve before anything changes.
beginner.example: Think of a busy airport check-in desk. The clerk does not phone the airline to confirm every booking. The computer already knows the passenger, the seat and the baggage rules. It only calls a supervisor when something unusual appears, like an expired passport. SOAR is that check-in system. It handles the routine questions automatically and pulls in a person only when the decision is risky.
takeaways: Automate the boring, repeatable steps first, and keep risky actions behind approval.
Every automated action should be logged with the inputs that caused it.
Do not automate a process that nobody has written down yet.

topics.title: SOC 2
topics.summary: SOC 2 is an attestation report issued under the AICPA Trust Services Criteria that describes how a service organisation designs and, in a Type 2 report, operates controls relevant to the security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy of customer data. It is not a certification and there is no pass or fail: an independent CPA firm expresses an opinion on whether management's description of its system is accurate and whether the selected controls operated effectively over a defined review period. Two report types exist. A Type 1 report speaks to control design at a single point in time and is frequently used to unblock early enterprise deals; a Type 2 report covers design and operating effectiveness across a window, commonly three to twelve months, and is what mature buyers demand. The Common Criteria, organised around control environment, communication and information, risk assessment, monitoring activities and control activities, map closely to how engineering teams already work, which is why SOC 2 readiness often reduces to formalising change management, access review, vulnerability management, incident response and vendor risk processes that already exist informally. For practitioners the practical work is defining the system boundary, producing a control matrix with named owners, gathering evidence on a schedule rather than in a panic, and being precise in the description of the system. Bridge letters and complementary user entity controls matter because responsibilities split between the provider and the customer.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish a SOC 2 Type 1 design opinion from a Type 2 operating effectiveness opinion and explain the review period.
You will be able to define a service organisation's system boundary and the infrastructure, software, people and procedures inside it.
You will be able to map the Trust Services Criteria to existing engineering controls and assign named control owners.
You will be able to design an evidence cadence that keeps access reviews, change tickets and monitoring artefacts audit-ready year round.
You will be able to interpret a bridge letter and complementary user entity controls in a vendor due diligence review.
You will be able to spot the difference between a control that is documented and a control that actually operated.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-53 security and privacy controls

beginner.definition: SOC 2 is an independent report about how a service company protects customer data. SOC stands for System and Organization Controls. An outside accounting firm checks the company's controls and writes an opinion. It is not a certificate, and there is no pass or fail result. Customers read the report to decide whether to trust you.
beginner.whyItMatters: Business customers often refuse to buy from a company that cannot show how it protects data. Filling in a long questionnaire for every deal wastes time and gives inconsistent answers. A SOC 2 report answers most of those questions once, in a form their auditors accept. Preparing for it also forces you to tidy processes you already run informally.
howItWorks: Define the clear boundary of the service that the report will cover.
Choose which trust categories apply to you, such as security and availability.
List your existing controls and give each one a clear named owner.
Collect evidence on a schedule, such as access reviews and change tickets.
Let the outside accounting firm test the controls over the chosen period.
Share the finished report with your customers and fix whatever it flags.
beginner.example: Think of a restaurant hygiene rating shown in the window. The rating comes from an inspector who visited, not from the owner's own claims. A high rating helps customers decide quickly. SOC 2 works the same way for data. The report describes what the inspector saw during a set period, and it also lists the things you, the customer, must still do yourself.
takeaways: SOC 2 is an opinion from an auditor, not a certificate.
Type 1 looks at design; Type 2 covers real operation over time.
Collect evidence all year instead of scrambling before the audit.

topics.title: Software Bill of Materials
topics.summary: A software bill of materials is a machine-readable inventory of the components that make up a piece of software, typically listing each package with its name, version, supplier, unique identifier and the relationships that describe how components nest. The two dominant interchange formats are SPDX and CycloneDX, both of which support integrity hashes and licence metadata, and both of which can be produced per build or per released artifact. The operational purpose is rapid answerability: when a critical vulnerability or a compromised package is disclosed, an organisation that holds accurate SBOMs can determine exposure in minutes by querying inventories rather than by rebuilding and reviewing manifests by hand. That is also why SBOM accuracy, completeness and freshness matter far more than format choice. An SBOM generated once at a release and never regenerated drifts from reality as soon as a hotfix rebuilds a base image. For a practising engineer the practical problems are transitive completeness, identifier normalisation across ecosystems, correlating components to vulnerability data with trustworthy package identifiers, and handling the volume of inventory data without turning it into an unreadable dump. Useful programmes generate SBOMs automatically in the build pipeline, store them alongside the artifact they describe, sign them so their provenance can be checked, and test the whole path with a tabletop exercise that asks how fast the organisation could answer a specific exposure question. Formats without ingestion tooling or a query surface produce compliance artefacts that nobody can use during an incident.
objectives: You will be able to explain what an SBOM must contain to be useful during a vulnerability response, beyond a flat list of package names.
You will be able to compare SPDX and CycloneDX at a level sufficient to choose one for a given toolchain.
You will be able to describe how SBOMs are generated in a build pipeline and why they must be regenerated for every artifact build.
You will be able to design a query workflow that answers exposure questions against stored inventories quickly.
You will be able to explain why signing and provenance attestation of SBOMs matter for supply-chain assurance.
You will be able to evaluate an SBOM programme by running an exposure question and measuring time to a trustworthy answer.

beginner.definition: A software bill of materials is a list of every part inside a piece of software. It names each package, its version, and who supplied it. Think of the ingredient list on a food packet. When a bad ingredient is announced, you check the list instead of guessing.
beginner.whyItMatters: Modern software is mostly other people's code. One popular library can sit inside hundreds of your applications. When that library is found to be unsafe, you need to know quickly where it is used. Without a list, teams spend days rebuilding and searching by hand. With one, you answer in minutes and patch the right systems first.
howItWorks: During every build, a tool reads your dependency files and lists each package.
It records the name, version, supplier, and a unique identifier for each part.
It also notes which packages contain other packages, so the tree is complete.
The finished list is saved next to the exact software build it describes.
When a problem is announced, you search all stored lists for that package.
The list should be rebuilt every time the software is rebuilt, or it drifts.
beginner.example: Imagine a school cafeteria that keeps a full ingredient list for every meal it serves. One morning a supplier recalls a batch of peanut butter. The kitchen checks its lists and finds the three meals that used it. Only those trays are removed. Without those lists, staff would have to open every freezer and read every label by hand. A software bill of materials is that ingredient list for your code.
takeaways: A software bill of materials lists the parts inside your software, like a food label.
Regenerate it for every build, or it will describe the wrong thing.
Store it so you can search it during an emergency, not in a drawer.

topics.title: Software Composition Analysis
topics.summary: Software composition analysis is the automated identification of third-party and open-source components in a codebase or built artifact, together with an assessment of the known vulnerabilities, licence obligations and maintenance risks attached to those components. A typical SCA engine resolves the dependency graph from manifests and lock files, matches resolved versions against vulnerability advisories, and reports the direct and transitive path that introduces each affected package, which matters because most findings arrive through dependencies the team never chose explicitly. Modern supply-chain expectations extend SCA to artifact-level analysis of containers and binaries, where the tool inspects package databases inside an image rather than trusting the build manifest alone. For a practising engineer the hard parts are reachability, version-range ambiguity and remediation logistics. A flagged transitive dependency may never be loaded at runtime, an advisory may apply only to a configuration the project does not use, and the fixed version may be blocked by an incompatible major upgrade somewhere else in the graph. A workable programme therefore gates on new critical findings with an available fix, tracks unfixable findings as accepted risk with an expiry, and uses override or exclusion mechanisms deliberately rather than pinning stale versions forever. The recurring failure modes are reporting the same vulnerable library dozens of times because it appears in several images, ignoring transitive dependencies entirely, and treating an empty scan result on a project that vendors its dependencies as evidence of safety.
objectives: You will be able to explain how a dependency graph is resolved from manifests and lock files and why lock files determine what is actually built.
You will be able to interpret a transitive dependency finding and trace the path that introduces the affected package.
You will be able to assess whether a vulnerable component is reachable and whether the advisory applies to the way the project uses it.
You will be able to define a gating policy that blocks new critical findings with available fixes without freezing the dependency graph.
You will be able to explain how container and binary artifact scanning differs from manifest-based analysis and when each is required.
You will be able to record accepted dependency risk with an owner, a compensating control and a review date.

beginner.definition: Software composition analysis finds the third-party and open-source parts inside your project. It reads your dependency files, matches versions against known vulnerability lists, and reports which packages are affected. It also shows the path that pulled each risky package in, so you know who to ask for a fix.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most of your application is code you did not write. That code can carry known security holes for years. Attackers watch these public lists and target anyone who is slow to update. Composition analysis turns a huge dependency tree into a short list of things to fix. Without it, you are trusting hundreds of strangers blindly.
howItWorks: The tool reads your manifest and lock files to learn every dependency.
A lock file records the exact versions that were really installed.
It builds a tree showing which package brought in each other package.
It compares those exact versions against public databases that list known vulnerabilities.
You get a report naming the package, the flaw, and the upgrade that fixes it.
You then decide to patch, replace, or formally accept the risk.
beginner.example: Think of a car made from parts produced by fifty different factories. One factory announces a brake part that can fail. A good mechanic can look up your car's parts list and tell you within minutes if your model is affected. Composition analysis is that lookup for software. It saves you from recalling every car ever made just to find the few with the bad part.
takeaways: Composition analysis finds risky third-party libraries and shows where they came from.
Indirect dependencies matter most, because you never chose them.
Block new critical findings that have a fix available today.

topics.title: SSO
topics.summary: Single sign-on (SSO) is an authentication architecture in which one identity provider authenticates a principal once and then issues assertions or tokens that multiple relying-party applications accept in place of their own credential stores. Instead of every application holding a password database, each application trusts a federated identity provider such as Entra ID, Okta, Ping or a Keycloak deployment, and receives a signed statement about who the user is and, increasingly, what context the authentication occurred in. The security benefit is concentrated and easy to understate: credentials live in one hardened location with one MFA policy, one lockout policy, one session lifetime and one revocation path, so deprovisioning a leaver becomes a single disable action rather than a hunt through dozens of local account stores. The corresponding risk is that the identity provider becomes a tier-zero system whose compromise grants access to every federated application, and that the session cookie or refresh token becomes the real credential that adversaries pursue. Most real-world SSO incidents therefore involve token theft, consent phishing against the authorisation endpoint, misconfigured assertion validation on the relying-party side, or stale accounts that survive offboarding because a shadow application was never federated. Practitioners must be able to reason about session lifetime, token binding, sign-out propagation, identifier normalisation and the difference between an application that validates a signature correctly and one that merely decodes it. Logging quality matters here: the identity provider's sign-in and audit logs, not the application logs, are usually the authoritative record of who authenticated and from where.
objectives: You will be able to explain the roles of identity provider, service provider and relying party in a federated sign-in flow.
You will be able to describe why the SSO session token, not the password, is the primary credential an adversary targets.
You will be able to evaluate session lifetime, token binding and global sign-out settings against a stated risk appetite.
You will be able to identify common SSO misconfigurations such as unvalidated assertions, wildcard redirect URIs and orphaned application accounts.
You will be able to use identity provider sign-in logs to reconstruct an authentication timeline for incident response.
You will be able to plan deprovisioning so that disabling one identity revokes access to all federated applications.

sources.label: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series: Authentication and Session Management
Microsoft Learn: Microsoft Entra authentication and single sign-on

beginner.definition: Single sign-on, or SSO, lets you sign in once and then use many applications without typing your password again. One trusted service checks who you are. It then issues a signed pass that the other applications accept.
beginner.whyItMatters: Without single sign-on, every application keeps its own password list. Removing a leaver means hunting through dozens of systems. With one sign-in service, you disable one account and access ends everywhere. The trade-off is that this service becomes very valuable to attackers, so it needs the strongest protection you have.
howItWorks: You open an application that you have never used in this browser session.
The application sends you to the identity provider, the shared sign-in service.
The provider checks that you are already signed in, or asks you to sign in.
It creates a signed pass and sends your browser back to the application.
The application checks the pass and starts your session, without its own password.
beginner.example: Think of a theme park. You pay and get one wristband at the gate. Inside, every ride simply scans the band. You do not queue at a ticket booth before each ride. If you lose the band, park staff cancel it at once. The gate becomes the most important place to guard.
takeaways: Single sign-on centralises passwords, policies, and lockouts in one place.
The session token becomes the real credential, so protect it well.
Disabling one identity should revoke access to every connected application.
