topics.title: Statement of Applicability
topics.summary: A Statement of Applicability is the document that records, for every control in the applicable catalogue, whether the organisation includes it, why that decision was made, and where the implementation lives. In an ISO/IEC 27001 management system it is a mandatory artefact that ties the risk assessment and risk treatment process to the controls actually operated, and it acts as the table of contents an auditor follows through the rest of the evidence. A defensible entry contains the control reference and title, an inclusion or exclusion decision, the justification for that decision, the implementation status, a reference to the specific implementation such as a policy section, system configuration or process document, and the control owner. Exclusions are where most documents fail. An organisation cannot legitimately exclude a control simply because it is inconvenient; the justification must show that the control is not applicable to the scope, that the risk it addresses does not exist in the scope, or that an alternative treatment reduces the risk to an acceptable level. Practitioners should keep the statement traceable in both directions: every selected control should map back to at least one assessed risk, and every treated risk should map forward to at least one control or a documented acceptance. Version control matters because the document is audited against a period, and reviewers should be able to reconstruct what the statement said when a given audit took place. It is also useful beyond certification as a concise inventory of the control estate.
objectives: You will be able to build a complete statement that traces every selected control back to an assessed risk.
You will be able to write exclusions that are genuinely justifiable rather than convenience-driven.
You will be able to record implementation references that point to verifiable configuration, policy or process evidence.
You will be able to assign control owners and implementation status that survives an auditor walkthrough.
You will be able to maintain version control so a past audit period can be reconstructed.
You will be able to use the statement as a control inventory for coverage and gap analysis outside certification.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-53 security and privacy controls

beginner.definition: A statement of applicability is a document that lists every security control in a chosen set. For each control it records whether you include it, why you decided that, and where it is implemented. It links your risk assessment to the controls you truly run. Auditors use it as a map of your evidence.
beginner.whyItMatters: When an auditor asks why you skipped a control, a vague answer damages trust. This document gives a written reason for every choice, so nothing looks accidental. It also stops duplicated effort, because you can see which risks already have a control and which have none. Over time it becomes a short inventory of your whole control estate.
howItWorks: List every control in the catalogue that you are working from.
For each one, record include or exclude and give a short reason.
Point to real evidence, such as a policy section or a system setting.
Name the person who owns each control and note its current status.
Check that every treated risk links back to at least one control.
Keep versions, so you can show what the document said during a past audit.
beginner.example: Think of a school trip consent form. A parent ticks each activity their child may join and writes a reason if they say no. The teacher can then plan safely and explain every choice later. A statement of applicability is that form for security controls. Skipping a control is allowed, but you must write down why, and someone must be able to check that reason.
takeaways: Every control entry needs a decision, a reason and a real reference.
Exclusions must be justified by scope or risk, not by convenience.
Every treated risk should point to at least one control.

topics.title: Static Application Security Testing
topics.summary: Static application security testing is the automated analysis of source code, bytecode or binaries without executing the program, looking for patterns that indicate a security defect such as injection sinks reached by untrusted input, unsafe deserialisation, hard-coded cryptographic material or broken access control. Modern SAST engines combine pattern matching with dataflow and taint tracking, so a rule can follow a value from a source such as an HTTP parameter through assignments and function calls to a sink such as a database query. Because it works on the code itself, SAST can find defects on code paths that no test exercises, and it can be run on every commit, which makes it attractive as a pull-request gate. Its central limitation is the false positive rate: without whole-program context and runtime configuration, the engine cannot know whether a path is reachable or whether a sanitiser it cannot model already applies. For a practising engineer the discipline is therefore triage, not detection. A workable programme baselines existing findings, gates only on new high-confidence rules, tunes rules per repository, suppresses with expiring annotations, and assigns rule ownership so that noisy rules are fixed rather than ignored. The common failure modes are treating the raw finding count as a metric, enabling every rule at once and drowning the team, running SAST only on a nightly build so feedback arrives too late to change the design, and allowing unbounded suppressions that silently disable entire rule classes. Pairing SAST with dependency analysis, dynamic testing and code review covers the gaps each tool leaves.
objectives: You will be able to explain how taint tracking differs from pattern matching and what each approach can and cannot detect.
You will be able to configure a SAST scan as a pull-request gate that blocks on new high-confidence findings without failing on legacy debt.
You will be able to triage a SAST finding by tracing reachability and confirming whether a modelled sanitiser applies.
You will be able to write a suppression with a justification, an owner and an expiry date instead of a permanent ignore.
You will be able to explain why raw finding counts are a poor programme metric and what to measure instead.
You will be able to state which defect classes escape static analysis and which complementary testing technique covers each.

beginner.definition: Static application security testing reads your source code without running it. It searches for dangerous patterns, such as secret keys written into the code. Modern tools also follow data from user input to a risky command. It runs on every commit, so problems appear while they are still cheap to fix.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most security bugs start as small coding mistakes. Finding them in review by hand is slow and easy to miss. Static testing checks every line each time you save, so nothing slips through unnoticed. It also finds problems on code paths that your tests never touch. Ignoring it means paying for fixes after release, when they cost far more.
howItWorks: You connect the tool to your code repository, usually in the build pipeline.
The tool parses the code and builds a map of how data moves.
It then checks that map against hundreds of rules for dangerous patterns.
When user input reaches a risky command, it raises a finding.
You review each finding and confirm whether an attacker could truly reach it.
You fix real problems and mark false alarms with a reason and a date.
beginner.example: Think of a proofreader who checks a recipe before anyone cooks it. She reads every line and circles a dangerous instruction, like adding cleaning fluid to a cake. Nothing has been baked, so the fix is just rewording a sentence. Static testing is that proofreader. It reads your code before it ever runs and circles the lines that could hurt you later.
takeaways: Static testing reads code, so it finds bugs before anything runs.
Expect false alarms; triage each finding instead of trusting the count.
Gate only on new high-confidence findings, not on old backlog noise.

topics.title: STIX and TAXII
topics.summary: STIX is a structured language for expressing cyber threat intelligence and TAXII is the transport protocol that moves it between organisations, and together they are the standards that make machine-to-machine sharing practical. STIX is a graph-based data model, serialised as JSON, whose objects fall into domain objects, cyber observable objects and relationship objects. Domain objects describe high-level intelligence such as threat actors, campaigns, intrusion sets, malware, attack patterns, indicators, reports, courses of action and identities. Cyber observable objects describe the technical artefacts an analyst records, including files, processes, network traffic, domain names and registry keys. Relationship objects connect them, so an indicator can reference an attack pattern and a report can bundle the whole product. Patterning gives indicators a precise, testable expression language, which is what allows a detection platform to consume them without hand translation. TAXII is the transport layer: a client polls or subscribes to a server, and the server exposes API roots containing collections of STIX objects. TAXII collections are browsable sets of objects, while channels support publish and subscribe exchange. Versioning and identifier discipline matter operationally. Every object carries a stable identifier and a modified timestamp, and consumers deduplicate and resolve updates on that basis, so sloppy identifier generation causes silent divergence between sharing partners. Real deployments also need trust decisions, because receiving a bundle is receiving attacker-influenced content. Analysts must honour handling markings that express sharing caveats, and they must decide what tooling does when an object is malformed or uses extensions the consumer does not implement. A working pipeline therefore combines schema validation, deduplication, enrichment, confidence handling and a documented policy for what is automatically blocked, what is only hunted, and what is discarded.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish STIX domain objects, cyber observable objects and relationship objects and explain what each is for.
You will be able to validate, deduplicate and update STIX objects using identifiers and modified timestamps.
You will be able to explain how TAXII collections differ from channels and which fits a given sharing requirement.
You will be able to apply handling markings and confidence information when a bundle arrives from a partner.
You will be able to describe the failure modes of an unvalidated feed and the controls that prevent them.
You will be able to write a consumption policy that separates objects to block, to hunt and to discard.

sources.label: OASIS Open repository for STIX tooling
NIST Computer Security Resource Center publications

beginner.definition: STIX is a standard language for describing threats in a way computers can read. The name stands for Structured Threat Information Expression. TAXII, the Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information, is the delivery service that carries it. Together they let security tools share warnings without a human retyping anything.
beginner.whyItMatters: Before shared standards, every team sent warnings by email in its own format. Someone had to read each one and re-enter the details by hand. That is slow and full of mistakes. STIX and TAXII remove the retyping. A detection tool can pull new warnings and act on them within minutes. The trade-off is trust. You are accepting content that other people created, so you must validate it first.
howItWorks: An analyst describes the threat using STIX objects, such as an attacker, a tool or a clue.
Relationships link those objects, so a clue points to a technique and a report groups them.
Each object gets a unique identifier and a modified time, so updates can be tracked.
The objects are packed into a bundle, which is a single file of structured text.
TAXII carries the bundle. A client polls a server collection, or subscribes to receive updates.
The receiving tool validates the content, removes duplicates and decides what to block or hunt.
beginner.example: Think of shipping containers. Every country used to load goods in its own odd shapes, so docks wasted hours repacking. Then everyone agreed on one container size. A crane can now lift any container without opening it. TAXII is the shipping route, and STIX is the standard container. One more thing matters. You still inspect what arrives, because a sealed container can hold anything.
takeaways: STIX describes threat information in a structured way that tools can read.
TAXII moves those descriptions between organisations, removing slow manual retyping.
Always validate incoming bundles, because shared content can be wrong or poisoned.

topics.title: STRIDE
topics.summary: STRIDE is a threat enumeration mnemonic that groups threats into six categories: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. It was developed so that designers without a deep attack background could still systematically ask the right questions about each element of a data-flow diagram. The categories map neatly onto security properties, which is what makes the framework teachable: spoofing attacks authenticity, tampering attacks integrity, repudiation attacks non-repudiation of actions, information disclosure attacks confidentiality, denial of service attacks availability and elevation of privilege attacks authorisation. In practice the mnemonic is applied per element and per flow, with a common convention that processes, data stores, data flows, external entities and trust boundaries each attract a characteristic subset of the six. For a practising engineer STRIDE is most useful as a completeness check rather than a rating scheme, because it deliberately says nothing about likelihood or impact and produces no prioritisation on its own. Teams normally pair it with a scoring method and with attack-library mapping to connect abstract categories to observed adversary behaviour. The known weaknesses are worth stating plainly. STRIDE was framed for classical component-and-network designs and fits cloud identity, serverless and machine-learning pipelines awkwardly. It has no privacy or supply-chain category. Its output is highly dependent on the facilitator's skill, and groups tend to over-report the categories they understand and under-report repudiation and availability. Reviewing a STRIDE session for concrete preconditions and observable failure modes is the cheapest way to raise its quality.
objectives: You will be able to name the six STRIDE categories and state which security property each one attacks.
You will be able to apply the mnemonic element by element to a data-flow diagram without missing entire categories.
You will be able to explain the conventional mapping between diagram element types and the STRIDE categories most likely to apply.
You will be able to convert a bare STRIDE label into a concrete threat statement with preconditions and impact.
You will be able to identify design situations where STRIDE fits poorly, such as cloud identity graphs and machine-learning pipelines.
You will be able to critique a completed STRIDE worksheet for over-reporting and under-reporting bias.

beginner.definition: STRIDE is a checklist of six threat types used when designing a system. The letters stand for spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, and elevation of privilege. Together they cover faking an identity, changing data, denying an action, leaking secrets, blocking access, and gaining extra rights. Walking the list helps a team spot gaps it might miss.
beginner.whyItMatters: Teams often forget whole kinds of attack because nobody names them out loud. STRIDE gives six simple prompts so no category is quietly skipped. It needs no deep attacker knowledge, which means designers and developers can take part. The result is a list of concrete questions early, when changes are still cheap. Skipping it means discovering the same gaps in production.
howItWorks: Draw your system as boxes for components and arrows for data flows.
Mark the trust boundaries, the lines where data moves between different owners.
For every box and arrow, ask the six STRIDE questions in turn.
Write each threat as a real sentence with an actor, an asset, and an impact.
Rate each threat by how likely it is and how much damage it would cause.
Choose a response for each: fix it, transfer it, accept it, or remove the feature.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel with a checklist for each room: is the lock working, is the window shut, is the safe closed, is the smoke alarm fitted, is the phone working? The cleaner walks the same list in every room. She may find nothing in most, but the one room with a broken lock gets fixed. STRIDE is that room checklist for software design. It makes you look at the same six things everywhere.
takeaways: STRIDE gives six prompts: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, disclosure, denial, and privilege.
Use it as a completeness check, not as a risk score.
Write each threat as a concrete sentence, or no fix will follow.

topics.title: Supply Chain Attack
topics.summary: A supply chain attack is an intrusion that reaches a target indirectly by compromising something the target trusts: a software dependency, a build system, a package registry, an update mechanism, a managed service provider, or a hardware or firmware supplier. The attraction for an adversary is leverage. One compromised package or build job can yield access to thousands of downstream organisations, and the resulting code or update often arrives already signed, already approved and already allow-listed. Documented patterns include malicious package versions published to public registries, typosquatted and dependency-confusion package names that resolve to attacker-controlled artifacts, compromised maintainer accounts, injected code in build pipelines that never touches the repository, and tampered vendor updates delivered through legitimate channels. For a practising engineer the defences are layered and mostly about provenance rather than detection: pin and verify dependencies with lock files and integrity hashes, generate and review build provenance, require signed artifacts with verification at install and deploy time, restrict who can publish and with what credentials, and monitor registries and build systems as production infrastructure. Attribution is genuinely hard because the activity happens inside trusted workflows; logs from build systems, registry publish events and artifact signing services often provide the only visibility. The most common organisational failure is assuming that internal dependence on well-known vendors removes the risk, when in practice the exposure is determined by how much unverified code and configuration is consumed, and how quickly a compromised component could be identified and removed from production.
objectives: You will be able to describe the main supply chain attack patterns, including malicious packages, dependency confusion, compromised maintainers and build pipeline injection.
You will be able to explain why signed and approved artifacts still require verification and provenance checks rather than blind trust.
You will be able to design controls for dependency pinning, integrity verification and registry allow-listing.
You will be able to specify telemetry from build systems, package registries and signing services that would reveal a compromised build.
You will be able to assess an organisation's time to identify and remove a compromised dependency from production.
You will be able to distinguish third-party and vendor risk that is genuinely mitigated from assurance that rests on reputation alone.

beginner.definition: A supply chain attack reaches you through something you already trust. Instead of breaking into your systems directly, the attacker compromises a supplier, a software library, a build tool, or an update service. Because the poisoned item arrives approved and signed, nobody questions it. That makes these attacks hard to spot and very wide in reach.
beginner.whyItMatters: One poisoned library can reach thousands of companies at once. That leverage is exactly why attackers like this route. Your normal defenses may not help, because the code looks legitimate and arrives through a trusted channel. If you cannot tell which version you run and where it came from, you cannot respond. You need to find and remove the bad part quickly.
howItWorks: An attacker picks a widely used package or a popular build tool.
They gain control of a maintainer account or publish a look-alike package name.
Your build pulls the package automatically and trusts it, because the name matched.
The harmful code runs inside your pipeline or ships to your customers.
To defend yourself, you pin exact versions and verify integrity hashes for every download.
You also keep a list of your parts so you can react fast.
beginner.example: Imagine you buy milk from a shop you trust every week. One day the delivery truck is hijacked and the bottles are refilled with something harmful. The shop still looks normal and the label is unchanged. You would never suspect it. Supply chain attacks work like that. The attacker never enters your house. They tamper with the delivery before it reaches your door.
takeaways: Trust arrives through suppliers, and attackers target exactly that trust.
Pin versions, check hashes, and require signed artifacts before use.
Know your parts list so you can remove a bad one fast.

topics.title: Tabletop Exercise
topics.summary: A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based rehearsal in which a team walks through a realistic scenario and makes the decisions it would face during a real incident, without touching production systems. Participants are given an inject, such as a triggering event involving a suspicious file server notification, an unexpected identity consent grant, or a reported business email compromise, and the facilitator advances the scenario in stages while asking who would be notified, what evidence would be collected, who has authority to isolate a system, how customers or regulators would be informed, and where the organisation's own procedures break down. Its value lies less in testing tooling than in exposing the seams between teams: security operations, IT operations, legal, communications, HR, executive leadership and third-party providers all have to agree on roles before a real crisis forces the question. Well-run tabletops are grounded in a written scenario and explicit objectives, use a documented playbook as the reference standard, and produce findings with named owners and dates. They differ from functional and simulation exercises, which do exercise live systems and response tooling, and most mature programmes alternate between the two. Frequency and scope should follow risk profile and regulatory expectation, and results feed back into the incident response plan. Because these exercises surface uncomfortable truths, including unclear decision rights, untested contact trees and unowned log sources, their findings are only valuable if remediation is tracked like any other risk treatment.
objectives: Define the purpose of a tabletop exercise and distinguish it from functional, simulation and full-scale testing.
Design a scenario, objective set and inject sequence grounded in risks the organisation actually faces.
Facilitate an exercise that surfaces unclear decision rights, communication gaps and untested assumptions.
Use the incident response playbook as the reference standard and capture where practice diverges from it.
Manage exercise documentation, confidentiality and participant safety so discussion stays candid and useful.
Convert observations into findings with named owners, due dates and a tracked remediation path.
Plan an exercise calendar that matches scenario scope and frequency to risk profile and regulatory expectation.

beginner.definition: A tabletop exercise is a group discussion where your team talks through a made-up security incident. Nobody touches real systems. A facilitator describes events step by step and asks what you would do. It tests your plans, your roles, and your communication before a real crisis arrives.
beginner.whyItMatters: Written plans often hide gaps that only appear when people talk them through. Nobody may know who can switch off a production server. A key phone number may be years out of date. Legal or communications staff may never have met the security team. A tabletop finds these problems cheaply, in a meeting room, instead of during a real breach.
howItWorks: Choose a realistic scenario that matches the risks your organization actually faces.
Write clear objectives, so you know which plans and decisions you want to test.
Gather the right people: security, IT, legal, communications, and business owners.
Give the group the first events and ask who they would call and what they would do.
Reveal later events one at a time and watch where the plan breaks down.
Write findings with a named owner and a due date, then track them like any other task.
beginner.example: Think of a fire drill in an office. Nobody expects a real fire that morning, and no flames appear. People still walk to the meeting point, and someone checks whether the back stairs were locked. The drill shows the locked door, not the smoke. A tabletop exercise is the fire drill for a security incident.
takeaways: A tabletop is a discussion, so nobody risks real systems.
It reveals unclear roles and stale contacts before a real incident.
Every finding needs a named owner and a due date to matter.

topics.title: Terraform Drift
topics.summary: Terraform drift is the divergence between the infrastructure state recorded in a Terraform state file and the actual configuration of the resources deployed in a cloud account, arising when something changes a resource outside the pipeline that created it. The change might be a console fix during an incident, a script in a legacy automation path, a provider-side default that shifted, an imported resource never brought under management, or an attacker deliberately relaxing a control such as a firewall rule or bucket policy. Drift matters because the infrastructure-as-code repository stops being a trustworthy description of reality: a plan run after drift will silently revert the out-of-band change, reviews of pull requests no longer describe the live environment, and a security control that appears present in code may have been removed in production. Detection normally relies on scheduled plans or a refresh-only plan that reports differences without applying them, remote state with locking to prevent concurrent writes, and consistent provider versions so that cosmetic differences do not obscure real ones. Handling drift requires judgement rather than blind application, because some drift is legitimate emergency remediation that should be codified back into the repository, while unreviewed drift in security-relevant attributes is an incident indicator. Mature teams track drift as a metric, alert on changes to sensitive attributes, and reconcile by importing or amending code rather than by overwriting production.
objectives: You will be able to explain how state, configuration files and live resources can diverge and why that breaks review assumptions.
You will be able to interpret a refresh-only plan and separate meaningful drift from cosmetic provider differences.
You will be able to triage unreviewed changes to security-relevant attributes as potential malicious activity.
You will be able to reconcile drift by importing or amending code instead of overwriting production state.
You will be able to describe how remote state, locking and pinned provider versions reduce false drift signals.
You will be able to design a drift detection cadence and reporting path for a platform team.

beginner.definition: Terraform is a tool that builds cloud infrastructure from written files. Drift is the gap between what those files say and what is really running. It appears when somebody changes a resource by hand, through a web console or a script, instead of through the usual pipeline that created it.
beginner.whyItMatters: When drift exists, your written files no longer describe reality. A reviewer approves a safe change, but production may already differ. A firewall rule that looks closed in code may be open in the live account. Worse, an attacker who quietly weakens a control creates drift on purpose. Finding drift turns a silent change into something you can see and question.
howItWorks: Terraform keeps a state file that records what it believes it created.
On a schedule, you run a check that reads the real cloud resources again.
The check compares the real settings with the recorded state and your written files.
Differences are listed as a plain report, and nothing is changed yet.
Your team decides what each difference means: a quick fix, an old script, or an attack.
Safe changes are written into the files, and unwanted ones are reversed.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared kitchen with a written recipe pinned to the wall. One evening someone swaps the salt for sugar to save time and forgets to update the recipe. The next cook follows the pinned recipe and is confused by the result. Drift is that stale recipe: the kitchen and the instructions no longer match.
takeaways: Drift means your written files no longer match the live environment.
Check for drift on a schedule and treat security settings as high priority.
Reconcile by updating the files or importing resources, not by guessing.

topics.title: Threat Hunting Hypothesis
topics.summary: A threat hunting hypothesis is a falsifiable statement about adversary behaviour that is expected to be present in an environment if a specific technique is being used, written so that telemetry can confirm or refute it. It is the element that separates hunting from browsing dashboards. A usable hypothesis names the behaviour rather than a tool, states the observable artifacts that behaviour would create, identifies the data sources required to see those artifacts, and defines in advance what evidence would count as a hit and what would count as absence. A well-formed example is that an adversary using valid accounts for lateral movement will produce authentication events from atypical source hosts or at atypical times for that identity, which can be tested against identity logs joined to asset inventory. The discipline around the hypothesis is as important as its content. Before hunting, the analyst verifies the required log source is actually collected, parsed and retained for the period of interest, because a great many hunts end with the discovery that the question cannot be answered with current telemetry. During the hunt, findings are documented as they are made, including negative results, since knowing that a technique was sought and not found is itself informative for coverage decisions. After the hunt, hits are converted into durable value: a new or tuned detection rule, a logged coverage gap with an owner, or a data source onboarding request. Hunting without that loop produces interesting sessions and no lasting improvement, which is why mature programmes track hunts by hypothesis, data source, technique coverage and number of detections produced rather than by hours spent.
objectives: You will be able to write a falsifiable hunting hypothesis that names behaviour, observable artifacts, required data sources and refutation criteria.
You will be able to derive hypotheses from ATT&CK techniques, threat intelligence reporting and known gaps in existing detection coverage.
You will be able to verify before hunting that the required telemetry is collected, parsed and retained for the relevant time window.
You will be able to execute a structured hunt and document hits and negative results as you go.
You will be able to convert hunt findings into durable outputs such as new detection rules, tuning changes or data source requests.
You will be able to prioritise a hunt backlog by technique risk, current coverage and the cost of answering the question.
You will be able to report hunt outcomes in terms that inform coverage decisions rather than only describing the investigation.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-61, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

beginner.definition: A threat hunting hypothesis is a clear guess about attacker behaviour that you can test with data. It says what you expect to see if a certain technique is being used in your network. Then you search your logs to prove it right or wrong. It is a question with a testable answer, not a vague worry.
beginner.whyItMatters: Detection rules only catch what somebody already thought of. Attackers know the common rules and work around them. Hunting lets you go looking for what your rules missed. Without a clear hypothesis, hunting becomes scrolling through dashboards and hoping. With one, you learn something either way, even when you find nothing.
howItWorks: You start from a known attacker technique, or from a gap in your current coverage.
You write one clear sentence describing the behaviour you expect to find.
You list the evidence that behaviour would leave behind in your logs.
You check first that those logs are actually collected and kept long enough.
You run searches over the relevant time window and record what you find.
You turn any finding into a new detection rule, or log a data gap with an owner.
beginner.example: Imagine a security guard who normally stands at the front door. One slow night, the guard decides to walk the corridors instead, because the cameras cannot see around corners. Before setting off, the guard says: if someone forced a back window, I will find broken glass or a bent frame. That is a hypothesis. The guard either finds the evidence or rules it out.
takeaways: A good hypothesis can be proven wrong, not just confirmed.
Check that you collect the needed logs before you start hunting.
Turn every hunt finding into a rule or a documented gap.

topics.title: Threat Modelling
topics.summary: Threat modelling is a structured design-time technique for reasoning about what can go wrong in a system, who would want to make it go wrong, and which controls would reduce that risk, producing a documented set of threats that engineering teams can act on. The usual workflow has four parts: scope the system and draw its data flows across trust boundaries, enumerate plausible threats against each element and flow, rate them by likelihood and impact, and record a decision for each one as mitigate, transfer, accept or eliminate. Frameworks such as STRIDE help teams avoid blind spots by prompting per category, while attack-library mapping grounds the exercise in techniques that real adversaries use. For a practising engineer the value is not the diagram but the argument it forces: where does authentication actually terminate, which component can impersonate another, what happens when a message is replayed, who can read this store, and what does the audit trail miss. Good threat models are living artifacts tied to architecture decisions, reviewed when data flows or trust boundaries change, and written in language the delivery team already uses. Failures are predictable. The exercise becomes a compliance ritual with no owner and no follow-through. Models are built by a single architect and never validated against the running system. Threats are described abstractly, with no asset, actor or preconditions, so no control follows. Ratings are inflated until everything is critical and prioritisation collapses. Structured abuse-case derivation, adversarial review by a second team, and tracking threat entries to backlog items with acceptance criteria are what separate a useful model from a wall diagram.
objectives: You will be able to scope a system into components, data stores, flows and trust boundaries before enumerating any threat.
You will be able to derive threats from a data-flow diagram across authentication, authorisation, confidentiality, integrity, availability and repudiation concerns.
You will be able to write a threat statement with actor, asset, precondition and impact rather than a vague category label.
You will be able to rate threats using a documented scheme and defend the rating against scope creep.
You will be able to convert accepted threats into tracked backlog items with verification criteria.
You will be able to explain where threat modelling fails and why models decay when architecture changes are not fed back into them.

beginner.definition: Threat modelling is a design-time exercise where you ask what could go wrong with a system and who might cause it. You map how data moves, find the weak points, and decide what to do. The result is a written list of threats and a decision for each. It happens before code is written, when changes are still cheap.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most security problems come from design choices, not from typing mistakes. Once a system is built, changing its structure is slow and expensive. A threat model finds those weak choices while they are still on a whiteboard. It also gives your team shared language about risk. Without it, you react to incidents instead of preventing them.
howItWorks: You draw the system as boxes, arrows, and data stores on one page.
You mark trust boundaries, where data crosses between areas with different owners.
For each element and flow, you ask what an attacker could do.
You write each threat as a sentence with an actor, an asset, and an impact.
You rate the threats and choose to fix, transfer, accept, or remove each one.
You store the model with the design and update it whenever the architecture changes.
beginner.example: Think of planning a trip before you leave home. You look at the route and ask what could go wrong. What if it rains, what if the car breaks down, what if a border is closed? For each risk you decide to carry an umbrella, buy cover, or change the route. Threat modelling is that planning conversation for software. You are still at the kitchen table, so changes cost nothing.
takeaways: Model threats at design time, when changes are cheap and fast.
Write each threat with an actor, an asset, and a real impact.
Keep the model alive and revisit it when the architecture changes.

topics.title: Timeline Analysis
topics.summary: Timeline analysis is the forensic practice of ordering events drawn from multiple evidence sources onto a single, comparable chronological axis so that an investigator can establish sequence, duration, causality and gaps in an intrusion. It is the discipline that turns a pile of artefacts into a story: which account logged in first, when the payload was written, what process created it, whether an outbound connection preceded or followed credential theft, and how long the adversary held access before anyone noticed. Source material includes file system metadata such as creation, modification and access times, file system journals and change records, registry hives and their key last-write values, operating system event and process telemetry, authentication logs from identity providers, browser and application histories, shell histories, container and cloud control-plane audit logs, and network flow or proxy records. The hard parts are rarely tooling and usually interpretation: clocks drift, time zones differ, some sources record local time while others use UTC, several timestamps are updated by ordinary activity, and artefacts can be deliberately manipulated by an adversary who understands the same metadata. A sound timeline states its normalisation decisions, records uncertainty rather than smoothing it away, and distinguishes corroborated events from single-source ones. Analysts typically build a full super-timeline for scoping and a filtered, focused timeline to answer one specific question such as dwell time, lateral movement path or data access. The output feeds incident scoping, legal and regulatory reporting, and detection engineering.
objectives: Define timeline analysis and explain how normalised event ordering establishes sequence, duration and causality.
Identify the artefact sources that contribute to a forensic timeline and state what each one can and cannot prove.
Normalise timestamps across time zones, clock drift and differing source granularity, and document those decisions.
Construct a super-timeline for scoping and a focused timeline for answering a specific investigative question.
Recognise artefact types that an adversary can manipulate and treat single-source events with appropriate caution.
Correlate host, identity, cloud and network telemetry to reconstruct lateral movement and data access.
Translate timeline findings into dwell time, affected scope and detection gaps for reporting.

sources.label: SANS Institute - digital forensics and incident response resources

beginner.definition: Timeline analysis means putting events from many sources into one time order. You line up logins, file changes, program starts, and network connections on a single clock. Then you can see what happened first and what followed. This turns a pile of evidence into a clear story of the intrusion.
beginner.whyItMatters: A single log rarely tells you the whole story. One system records a login, another records a file download, and a third records an outbound connection. On their own, each event looks harmless. In the right order they show an attack. Timeline analysis also tells you how long the attacker had access, which shapes your reports.
howItWorks: Collect events from every source you can, such as hosts, accounts, and network logs.
Convert all times to one time zone, usually UTC (Coordinated Universal Time).
Place every event on a single list, sorted from the earliest to the latest.
Check for clock differences between systems, because small drift can mislead you.
Look for gaps and for events that appear only in one source.
Build a short list of key events to answer one clear question about the incident.
beginner.example: Imagine a busy airport terminal with cameras in different rooms. One camera shows a person at check-in, another shows a bag on a belt, and a third shows a door opening. Alone, each clip is boring. Played on one clock, they show a clear journey. That is what a timeline does with log entries.
takeaways: One event rarely proves anything; the order of events builds the story.
Convert every source to the same time zone and note the difference.
Treat gaps and single-source events as questions, not as facts.

topics.title: TLS Inspection
topics.summary: TLS inspection is the practice of terminating or intercepting encrypted sessions inside a controlled boundary so that security controls can examine the plaintext that would otherwise be opaque. Because most malicious traffic now uses the same transport encryption as legitimate traffic, signature-based network detection, data loss prevention and URL filtering are blind without decryption. Two broad techniques exist. An active proxy terminates the client connection, presents a certificate the client must trust, and opens a separate connection to the server, while passive decryption uses key material or session keys supplied out of band to decrypt copies of traffic without altering the flow. Both depend on trust: active interception requires a private certificate authority whose root is installed on every endpoint, which makes that authority a high-value target and a frequent source of operational breakage when applications use certificate pinning, mutual TLS or embedded trust stores. Inspection is not free. Decryption consumes substantial processor and memory capacity, so throughput, latency and sizing change materially, and uninspected encrypted traffic becomes a growing blind spot as the inspection ratio falls. Privacy and legal constraints are equally important, because intercepting employee banking, health or personal traffic carries regulatory exposure in many jurisdictions, and an internal certificate authority must be protected, logged and audited like any other signing authority. Bypass categories are necessary for pinned applications, software update channels and regulated third parties, and each bypass should have a documented owner. Monitoring must cover the inspection platform itself, since an expired root certificate, a failed cipher negotiation or a silent fail-open policy can disable decryption without anyone noticing.
objectives: You will be able to compare active interception with passive decryption and state the trust requirements of each.
You will be able to explain why certificate pinning and mutual TLS break inspection and how to handle the exceptions.
You will be able to size and monitor a decryption platform for capacity, latency and fail-mode behaviour.
You will be able to define and document bypass categories with owners and review dates.
You will be able to detect a silent drop in inspection coverage and treat it as a control failure.
You will be able to describe the privacy, legal and key-protection obligations created by internal interception.

sources.label: RFC 8446: The Transport Layer Security Protocol Version 1.3

beginner.definition: TLS inspection means opening encrypted traffic inside your own network so security tools can read it. TLS is the encryption that protects web and other traffic. When traffic is encrypted, a firewall can see the address but not the content. Inspection decrypts the session, checks it, and then encrypts it again on the way out.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most traffic is encrypted today, including traffic from attackers. Without inspection, your filters and detection rules are blind to anything hidden inside. That blind spot grows quietly, because nothing breaks and no alert fires. Inspection brings back visibility, but it costs processing power and can break applications that check certificates strictly. It also creates privacy duties, since you are reading traffic that may be personal.
howItWorks: You set up an internal certificate authority, which is a trusted stamp your own network issues.
You install the authority's root certificate on every device your team manages.
The inspection device takes the encrypted session from the client and ends it there.
It reads the plaintext, applies your rules, then starts a fresh encrypted session to the real site.
Applications that pin certificates, meaning they trust only one exact certificate, must be excluded.
You monitor the inspection rate, because a failed certificate can silently switch decryption off.
beginner.example: Think of a post room that opens sealed letters so it can check for banned items. That works only if the sender trusts the post room to open and reseal properly. Some senders use tamper-proof seals and refuse to let anyone open their letters. Those letters must go around the post room. The post room also needs its own official stamp, and if that stamp is stolen, everything it approved becomes suspect.
takeaways: Encryption blinds your defences; inspection restores visibility at a cost.
Inspection needs a trusted internal certificate on every managed device.
Watch the inspection rate, because silent failures are easy to miss.

topics.title: True and False Positives
topics.summary: A true positive is an alert that correctly identifies the behaviour the detection was written to find; a false positive is an alert raised on activity that does not match that behaviour. The pairs that matter operationally are richer than that binary. A true positive may still be benign in context, which is why analysts distinguish a detection that fired correctly on authorised administrative work from one that fired on genuine adversary activity. A false negative is the more dangerous case: malicious behaviour occurred and nothing alerted, either because the log source was absent, the rule logic did not cover the variant, or the telemetry was normalised into a shape the rule never matched. Detection engineers therefore evaluate content on two axes, precision, meaning what fraction of alerts are genuine, and recall, meaning what fraction of real occurrences are caught. Improving one usually costs the other, which is why tuning is an explicit trade-off documented with its rationale rather than an accumulating set of exclusions. Practical classification requires ground truth, and ground truth requires work: confirming with asset owners whether a process is sanctioned, checking change records for scheduled jobs, validating whether an account was legitimately used, or replaying controlled test activity to prove a rule fires. The vocabulary also covers near misses and true negatives, and it is worth stating plainly that a closed alert labelled false positive is a claim of fact, not a dismissal. Teams that keep a labelled corpus of past alerts, including the reasoning, build the empirical basis for tuning, for measuring detection coverage, and for demonstrating improvement over time.
objectives: You will be able to classify alerts into true positive, false positive and false negative with an evidence-based rationale rather than intuition.
You will be able to distinguish a detection that fired incorrectly from one that fired correctly on activity that is benign in context.
You will be able to explain the precision and recall trade-off and describe the operational cost of moving either measure.
You will be able to obtain ground truth for a disputed alert through asset ownership records, change tickets and controlled test activity.
You will be able to identify likely false negatives by reviewing which ATT&CK techniques your log sources and rules can actually observe.
You will be able to maintain a labelled alert corpus that supports tuning decisions and demonstrates detection improvement over time.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-61, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

beginner.definition: A true positive is an alert that correctly found the behaviour the rule was written to catch. A false positive is an alert about activity that does not match that behaviour at all. A false negative is the dangerous one: something bad happened and no alert fired. These three labels describe every alert you will ever see.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you cannot label alerts correctly, you cannot improve your rules. People often close an alert and call it a false positive when they only mean it was harmless. That is a different thing, and it hides useful information. Honest labelling is how a team learns which rules work and which rules waste time.
howItWorks: Read the rule and write down in one sentence what behaviour it is meant to catch.
Open the raw events and check whether that behaviour actually happened at all.
If it happened, the alert is a true positive, even if the activity was allowed.
If it did not happen, the alert is a false positive and the rule needs tuning.
Ask whether the same activity could happen again without any alert at all.
If yes, you have found a false negative, which is the most important gap to fix.
beginner.example: Imagine a shop door alarm that beeps whenever anyone walks out. It beeps for paying customers, which is annoying but harmless. It stays silent when a thief leaves through the loading bay. The beeping is not a false alarm in the strict sense; the door really did open. The silent loading bay is the real problem, and nobody is watching it.
takeaways: Correctly fired but harmless is not the same as a false positive.
A false negative means bad activity happened and nothing told you.
Keep a record of past alerts and how you labelled them.

topics.title: TTP
topics.summary: A TTP is the behavioural layer of threat intelligence: the tactics, techniques and procedures an adversary uses to achieve an objective, expressed independently of the specific tools, hashes or domains observed in any single intrusion. Tactics describe the goal, such as gaining initial access or exfiltrating data. Techniques describe how the goal is achieved, such as abusing a valid account, injecting into a trusted process, or tunnelling command and control inside a protocol the network already permits. Procedures describe the specific implementation an actor prefers, including the exact command line shape, the order of operations and the operational security habits around them. Because TTPs are constrained by how software and operating systems actually work, they change far more slowly than infrastructure. An actor can re-register a domain overnight but cannot easily abandon the need to persist after reboot or to move laterally with stolen credentials. That asymmetry is why behavioural intelligence retains value for months or years while atomic indicators decay in hours, and why the widely used pyramid of pain ranks TTPs near the top for the difficulty they cause an adversary when defenders detect them. In practice, TTP intelligence is codified as technique mappings, detection-as-code rules, hunting hypotheses and control requirements rather than as blocklists. The defensive translation step matters: a report stating that an actor abuses signed system binaries is not actionable until an engineer identifies which telemetry would capture it, which legitimate activity resembles it, and what the detection will cost in analyst time. TTP-driven detection also supports coverage reasoning, because defenders can measure which techniques are instrumented and which are blind spots. The main risks are over-generalisation, where a technique is treated as unique to one group, and abstraction drift, where a mapping is recorded without the procedure detail that would make it detectable.
objectives: You will be able to separate tactics, techniques and procedures and explain why each layer has a different detection lifetime.
You will be able to translate a prose intrusion report into technique mappings and concrete telemetry requirements.
You will be able to explain why TTP-based detection resists adversary infrastructure rotation better than indicator matching.
You will be able to judge when a technique mapping is too generic to be actionable and what procedure detail would fix it.
You will be able to derive hunting hypotheses from a technique and define what evidence would confirm or refute them.
You will be able to measure detection coverage by technique and identify blind spots that no current rule addresses.

sources.label: NIST Computer Security Resource Center publications

beginner.definition: TTP stands for tactics, techniques and procedures. It describes how an attacker behaves, not the specific tools they used. A tactic is the goal and a technique is the method. A procedure is the exact way one group carries it out. Behaviour changes slowly, so it stays useful for a long time.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers swap tools constantly. A web address can change in minutes and a file can be rebuilt in seconds. Blocking those things gives you short lived protection. Behaviour is different. An attacker still needs to log in, move between machines and take data out. If you learn to spot those patterns, your detection lasts far longer. It also hurts the attacker more, because changing habits is hard.
howItWorks: Read the report and find the goal. Was the attacker trying to break in or to steal data?
Name the technique, which is the method used to reach that goal.
Record the procedure, meaning the exact commands, order and habits of that group.
Find the telemetry, which is the log record that would capture this activity.
Write a detection rule, then check how much normal work looks the same.
Track coverage, so you can see which techniques you can spot and which are blind spots.
beginner.example: Think of how a pickpocket works. The tools may be a coat, a bag or simply a pair of hands, and those change. The method does not. They choose a crowd, distract the target and slip away quickly. Guards who learn the method catch thieves using any tools. Guards who only memorise one coat miss everyone else. Defence based on behaviour studies the method, not the coat.
takeaways: TTP describes attacker behaviour, which outlives tools and network addresses.
Turn behaviour into detection rules, and check how much normal activity looks similar.
Measure which techniques you can detect, then hunt the blind spots you find.

topics.title: Volatile Data
topics.summary: Volatile data is state that exists only while a system is powered, running or connected: processor registers and cache contents, random access memory, running processes and their loaded modules, open network sockets and routing tables, logged-on sessions, mounted encrypted volumes, clipboard contents, and in-memory credentials or keys. Because it disappears on shutdown, reboot, logoff, container termination or network disconnection, it is both the most perishable and often the most probative evidence in an investigation. Memory is where fileless malware, injected code, decryption keys, command-and-control configuration and unencrypted artefacts frequently live, and where a rootkit's tampering may be visible even when the file system looks clean. Established practice follows an order of volatility, collecting the fastest-decaying sources first: processor and memory state, then network and process state, then temporary file systems, then disk, then archival media. Acquisition must be planned before the responder types a single command, because ordinary administrative actions such as listing directories, opening a file or running a built-in utility overwrite memory and alter timestamps. Captured data is hashed, documented and stored under chain of custody, and analysis must account for the fact that memory contents are a snapshot of a live and constantly changing system. In virtualised and cloud environments the practical techniques differ, relying on hypervisor snapshots, managed capture APIs and provider tooling, but the ordering logic and the documentation obligations do not change.
objectives: Classify data sources by volatility and apply the correct collection order at an incident scene.
Explain why memory, session and network state often carry evidence that the file system does not.
Plan a volatile data collection sequence that avoids overwriting evidence through routine administrative commands.
Capture memory, process, network and session state using validated tooling and hash the resulting output.
Adapt volatile collection techniques to virtual machines, containers and cloud instances.
Document volatile acquisitions so that they satisfy chain of custody and remain usable in later analysis.
Assess the investigative cost of a reboot, shutdown or logoff and communicate that cost to decision makers.

sources.label: RFC Editor - guidelines for evidence collection and archiving
NIST Computer Security Resource Center - forensic acquisition guidance

beginner.definition: Volatile data is information that only exists while a system is switched on and running. Examples include memory contents, running programs, open network connections, and logged-in sessions. As soon as the machine shuts down, reboots, or disconnects, this data is gone. That makes it the most fragile evidence in an investigation.
beginner.whyItMatters: Some of the best evidence never reaches the disk. Fileless attacks, encryption keys, and active connections live only in memory and system state. If your first action is a restart, that evidence disappears before you can look at it. The order in which you collect data decides what you can still prove later.
howItWorks: Start with the fastest to disappear: memory contents and the running state of the system.
Next capture the active network connections and the list of running programs.
Then record who is logged in and which encrypted drives are currently unlocked.
Only after that move to slower material, such as temporary files and then the disk.
Avoid ordinary commands that change the system, because they can overwrite evidence.
Save each capture with a hash, a time, and a note about who collected it.
beginner.example: Think of snow on a warm morning. If you want to study the shape of the flakes, you must look before the sun climbs higher. Once the snow melts, the pattern is gone and no tool brings it back. Volatile data is that snow. Collect it first, and write down what you saw.
takeaways: Volatile data vanishes on a shutdown, a reboot, a logoff, or a disconnect.
Collect in order of fragility: memory first, then connections, then disk.
Everyday commands change the system, so plan your collection before you type.

topics.title: VPN
topics.summary: A virtual private network establishes an encrypted tunnel between endpoints or gateways so that traffic crossing an untrusted network cannot be read or modified in transit, and so that the endpoints can be treated as members of a logical private network. Site-to-site tunnels join branch offices or cloud networks using IPsec or comparable protocols, while remote-access VPNs connect individual users through a concentrator that authenticates them and places them on an internal subnet. The security properties come from the cryptographic handshake, mutual authentication of peers, and integrity protection of each packet, but the trust model is the weak point. A remote-access VPN that grants full internal reachability reproduces the flat network for every connected device, so a compromised laptop inherits the same access as a workstation on site. Split tunnelling compounds the problem by allowing the endpoint to talk directly to the internet while holding an internal tunnel, which turns the endpoint into a bridge between the two. Operationally, VPN concentrators concentrate risk. They are internet-facing, they authenticate users, and they are frequently targeted by credential stuffing, password spraying and exploitation of unpatched appliances, so they must be patched aggressively, protected with phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, and monitored for unusual session behaviour such as logins from unexpected geographies or impossible travel. Capacity planning matters because a saturated concentrator becomes an availability incident. Many organisations are reducing reliance on broad network-level access in favour of application-level access brokers that authorise a specific service rather than placing a device on the internal network. Where VPNs remain, good practice includes per-user authorisation profiles, session timeouts, device posture checks before access is granted, and complete logging of tunnel establishment and termination.
objectives: You will be able to explain what a VPN does and does not protect once a device is connected.
You will be able to compare site-to-site and remote-access designs and their trust assumptions.
You will be able to assess split tunnelling and full tunnelling against endpoint risk.
You will be able to triage VPN authentication logs for spraying, stuffing and anomalous session behaviour.
You will be able to harden a concentrator with multi-factor authentication, patching discipline and per-user profiles.
You will be able to justify moving sensitive access from network-level tunnels to application-level brokers.

sources.label: RFC 4301: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol

beginner.definition: A virtual private network, or VPN, builds an encrypted tunnel between your device and another network. Traffic inside the tunnel cannot be read or changed by anyone in between. Remote-access VPNs let one person connect to the office, while site-to-site VPNs join two networks, such as a branch and head office, as if they were neighbours.
beginner.whyItMatters: People work from cafes, homes and airports on networks you do not control. A VPN protects their traffic from anyone watching that network. It also lets them reach internal systems without exposing those systems to the internet. But a VPN is not a magic shield. Once connected, the device is usually on your internal network with wide access, so a compromised laptop can spread trouble. Treat the VPN as a door, not a guarantee.
howItWorks: The user's device and the VPN gateway agree on keys, which are secret values used for encryption.
Both sides prove who they are, so you cannot tunnel into a fake gateway.
Traffic is wrapped in encryption and sent across the internet to the gateway.
The gateway unwraps it, checks the user's permissions and forwards it internally.
Replies travel back through the same tunnel, so the session stays protected.
If split tunnelling is on, other traffic goes straight to the internet, outside the tunnel.
beginner.example: Think of an armoured van carrying parcels through a busy city. Nobody on the street can open the doors or swap the contents. When the van arrives, the depot checks the driver's badge before accepting the delivery. The protection covers the journey, not the depot. If the driver then has keys to every room in the building, the van has protected the parcels and handed over the whole site anyway.
takeaways: A VPN protects traffic in transit, not the device at either end.
Require multi-factor authentication, because gateways face constant password attacks.
Give each user only the internal access their role needs.

topics.title: WDAC and AppLocker
topics.summary: Windows Defender Application Control and AppLocker are the two application control mechanisms Microsoft provides for Windows, and understanding their difference matters more than knowing either in isolation. AppLocker is policy-based, configured through Group Policy or a similar management channel, and enforces rules that permit or deny executables, installers, scripts, packaged applications and dynamically loaded libraries on the basis of publisher signature, file path or file hash. It is straightforward to operate, easy to audit in a reporting-only mode before enforcement, and widely used because it can be piloted on a subset of users without touching the underlying platform configuration. WDAC operates at a lower level and expresses policy as a signed binary policy that the kernel enforces, which makes it substantially harder for a local administrator or a malicious process with administrative rights to disable, and it can be used to protect the integrity of the code that is allowed to run at boot and in the kernel. In practice the two are complementary and both are frequently deployed together, because WDAC's strength is its resistance to tampering while AppLocker's strength is granular, easily reasoned-about rules for user-facing applications. The hardest part of either deployment is not the technology but the operational discipline: maintaining accurate inventory of what legitimately runs, designing publisher-based rules rather than brittle path rules, adopting managed installer concepts so that approved deployment tooling can introduce new software without policy churn, running in audit mode long enough to catch the long tail, and planning a change process for the inevitable application that must be allowed next week. A policy that is too permissive provides no protection; one that is too brittle is bypassed by an exception list nobody reviews.
objectives: Compare WDAC and AppLocker across enforcement location, tamper resistance, rule granularity and management model.
Choose between publisher, path and hash rule types and explain the maintainability consequences of each.
Design an audit-then-enforce rollout that gathers the legitimate software inventory before blocking anything.
Explain how managed installer and signed policy concepts reduce operational churn after enforcement.
Detect attempted policy tampering or the abuse of allowed binaries to execute unapproved code.
Plan an exception and change process that keeps the policy tight without blocking business operations.

sources.label: Microsoft Learn: Application control for Windows

beginner.definition: WDAC stands for Windows Defender Application Control, and AppLocker is a related Windows feature. Both decide which programs are allowed to run, an approach called application control or allow-listing. Instead of blocking known bad software, they permit only approved software and refuse everything else. WDAC enforces its rules deeper in the system than AppLocker does.
beginner.whyItMatters: Blocking known bad files only works until something new appears. Allowing only approved software flips the problem, because unknown programs simply cannot start. That stops a lot of malware, including scripts and borrowed system tools. The hard part is not the technology but the upkeep. You need an accurate list of what people really use, or the policy will break their work and get switched off.
howItWorks: You first take an inventory of the software that people and servers genuinely need.
You write rules that allow those programs, using publisher, path, or file fingerprint.
You run the policy in audit mode, which records what would have been blocked.
You review those records, add missing rules, and repeat until the list is stable.
You switch to enforcement mode, so unapproved programs can no longer start.
You keep a change process, because new software will always need approval later.
beginner.example: Imagine a members-only club with a guest list at the door. The bouncer does not try to recognise every troublemaker in the city. He only checks whether your name is on the list, and if it is not, you stay outside. That is much easier than memorising faces. But the list must stay current, or loyal members get refused and the door staff start waving everyone through.
takeaways: Application control allows only approved software and refuses everything else.
Run in audit mode first, and gather a real software inventory before enforcing.
Prefer publisher rules over file paths, which are easy to abuse and hard to maintain.

topics.title: XDR
topics.summary: Extended Detection and Response (XDR) is the practice of fusing telemetry from multiple security domains — endpoint, identity, email, cloud workload, network and SaaS audit logs — into a single detection and response platform so that correlated evidence from several sources produces higher-fidelity incidents than any one source could alone. Where EDR answers host-level questions, XDR is defined by the correlation itself: an email gateway recording a delivered message with an external link, an identity provider logging a successful sign-in from an unusual geography with a satisfied multi-factor challenge, and a cloud audit log showing a new OAuth grant to an unfamiliar application become one incident rather than three unrelated alerts. That consolidation is attractive because it directly attacks alert fatigue and the mean time to detect, but it also concentrates risk. A single platform that holds identity, email and endpoint data becomes a high-value target, its normalisation pipeline can silently drop fields that a responder later needs, and its correlation logic is often opaque enough that analysts cannot explain why two events were joined. Many vendors ship a native XDR that works best with their own sensors, and open or hybrid approaches exist that stitch together existing tools through a data lake and a detection-as-code layer. Practitioners should evaluate XDR on ingestion coverage and latency, schema fidelity, the ability to write and version custom detections, the depth of the response actions available per integration, and how gracefully the platform degrades when one source goes dark. XDR does not replace investigation discipline; it changes where the analyst starts.
objectives: Define XDR precisely and distinguish it from EDR, SIEM and SOAR by the correlation and response scope each provides.
Map the telemetry sources that must be onboarded before cross-domain correlation can produce actionable incidents.
Explain how identity, email and endpoint signals combine to raise confidence above that of any single-domain alert.
Assess schema normalisation risk, including field loss and timestamp skew that degrade correlated detections.
Write and version a custom cross-domain detection rule and describe how it should be tested before production rollout.
Evaluate a vendor XDR deployment against data concentration, response-action depth and graceful degradation requirements.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-137: Information Security Continuous Monitoring

beginner.definition: XDR stands for Extended Detection and Response. It collects security data from several places at once, such as laptops, sign-in systems, email, and cloud services. Then it links related events together so that one clear incident appears instead of many separate alerts.
beginner.whyItMatters: Separate tools each see only a slice of the story. An email alert, an unusual sign-in, and a new cloud permission might look harmless alone, but together they describe a break-in. Linking them raises confidence and cuts the number of alerts an analyst must read. The trade-off is concentration. One platform now holds a lot of sensitive data, so it becomes a valuable target itself.
howItWorks: Sensors in different places send their logs into one shared platform.
The platform rewrites each log into a common shape so events can be compared.
Rules and analytics look for related events across those different sources.
When the pattern matches, the platform raises a single incident with all the evidence.
The analyst investigates from that one place and can respond through the same tool.
Coverage and data quality must be checked, because a missing source hides the story.
beginner.example: Imagine an airport where the check-in desk, the security scanner, and the passport gate each keep their own notes. Alone, none of them sees a problem. Together, they notice the same passenger changed names on three documents in one hour, and they raise one alarm instead of three unrelated ones. That shared picture is what extended detection and response provides. It does not replace the officers at each post, but it lets them compare notes instantly instead of never.
takeaways: XDR joins data from many sources so related events become one incident.
It cuts alert noise, but only if every source actually delivers good data.
One platform holding that much data becomes a target in its own right.

topics.title: YARA
topics.summary: YARA is a pattern-matching language and tool for identifying files and memory regions by their content, widely used by malware analysts, incident responders and detection engineers to classify samples by family, capability or campaign. A rule consists of a metadata block, a set of string definitions, and a boolean condition that decides whether the rule matches. Strings may be text, hexadecimal byte patterns with wildcards and jumps, or regular expressions, and each can carry modifiers that change matching semantics, such as nocase for case-insensitivity, wide for UTF-16 encodings, ascii, fullword to prevent substring hits, and xor to handle simple single-byte obfuscation. Conditions can reference string counts, offsets, file size, the values of the PE header, module imports, and matches from other rules through the of and for...of constructs, which allows composition from weak indicators into stronger composite logic. That compositional ability is the feature that separates useful rules from fragile ones: a single suspicious string is weak evidence, whereas a condition requiring several independent strings, a specific file size range and a particular section characteristic resists trivial modification. YARA is also a source of operational mistakes. Rules written against one sample overfit and miss variants; broad string sets produce false positives across legitimate software; large rule sets slow scanning to the point of being unusable and are often loaded with performance warnings that operators ignore; and short strings without fullword matching collide with unrelated binaries. Authoring quality therefore means testing rules against known-good corpora before deployment, documenting their provenance, retaining a rationale for each indicator, and treating a match as an investigative lead that must be corroborated rather than as automatic proof of malice.
objectives: You will be able to explain the structure of a YARA rule and the roles of the metadata, strings and condition blocks.
You will be able to select appropriate string modifiers and explain how each changes matching behaviour and false-positive risk.
You will be able to write compositional conditions that require independent evidence instead of relying on a single weak indicator.
You will be able to test a rule set against known-good files and quantify the false positives before deployment.
You will be able to identify overfitting to a single sample and rewrite the rule so that it generalises to likely variants.
You will be able to treat a YARA match as an investigative lead and state the corroboration needed before calling a file malicious.
You will be able to assess the performance cost of a rule set and reduce scanning overhead without losing meaningful coverage.

beginner.definition: YARA is a tool and a simple language for finding files or memory by what is inside them. You write a rule that describes text or byte patterns, and YARA reports any file that matches. Analysts use it to sort malware samples into families. A match is a strong hint, not final proof.
beginner.whyItMatters: Hundreds of thousands of new suspicious files appear every day, and file names mean nothing because attackers rename them constantly. YARA lets you describe the inside of a file instead. One good rule can find every copy of a known threat across your whole estate, including files that have been renamed or slightly changed.
howItWorks: You write a rule in a text file with three parts: details, patterns, and a condition.
The details section records who wrote the rule and what it is looking for.
The patterns section lists the text, bytes, or regular expressions to search for.
You can add modifiers, such as ignoring letter case, or matching two byte encodings.
The condition decides which combination of pattern matches counts as a hit.
You test the rule against known good files first to count false matches.
beginner.example: Imagine a lost-property office that identifies umbrellas not by the label, since labels fall off, but by their pattern of panels and the scratch on the handle. Two umbrellas can share a brand and still be different objects. YARA reads the inside of a file the same way. It looks for a distinctive combination of features instead of trusting the name on the outside.
takeaways: Match on what is inside a file, because names can be changed.
Require several patterns together; one weak string causes false matches.
Treat a YARA match as a lead and confirm it before calling it malicious.
