topics.title: Zero Trust
topics.summary: Zero trust is a security model that removes implicit trust from network location and instead evaluates every request against identity, device posture, context and policy before granting the least access needed. The traditional perimeter assumed that anything inside the corporate network was trustworthy and anything outside was not, and remote work, cloud services and mobile devices destroyed that assumption. Zero trust replaces it with explicit verification, so a request from a corporate subnet receives no more privilege than the same request from a home network. Core components include a strong identity provider with phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, a policy decision point that consumes signals from device management and threat detection, segmentation that constrains lateral movement, and pervasive logging so that every decision can be audited after the fact. Reference architectures describe the model in terms of a policy engine, a policy administrator and policy enforcement points, which gives architects shared vocabulary when planning a migration. Migration is incremental, because few organisations can rebuild identity, endpoint management and network policy at the same time. A realistic sequence strengthens identity first, then device assurance, then application-level access brokers that replace broad network reachability, and finally workload-level policy for the highest-value systems. The hard parts are cultural and operational rather than technical: legacy applications that cannot express fine-grained authorisation, service accounts holding standing privilege, and business processes that depend on unrestricted file-share access. Zero trust also fails when telemetry is poor, because a policy engine fed stale or incomplete device data will either block legitimate work or wave through compromised endpoints. Mature implementations measure the share of access decisions made by policy, count standing privileged accounts, and test how quickly access can be revoked.
objectives: You will be able to explain why network location is not an authentication signal and what replaces it.
You will be able to describe the roles of the policy engine, policy administrator and policy enforcement point.
You will be able to identify standing privilege and implicit trust relationships in a real environment.
You will be able to design an incremental migration order across identity, device assurance and application access.
You will be able to evaluate whether telemetry quality is sufficient for policy decisions and where it misleads.
You will be able to measure zero trust progress with defensible metrics rather than vendor claims.

beginner.definition: Zero trust is a security approach that stops treating your own network as safe. It checks every request based on who is asking, what device they use and what they want, then grants the smallest access needed. Being inside the office network gives you no special trust. The name means there is no automatic trust based on location.
beginner.whyItMatters: The old idea was a castle with a wall: safe inside, dangerous outside. Remote work, cloud services and personal phones broke that idea. Attackers who get one password now find themselves already inside the walls. Zero trust removes that free pass, so a stolen account gets only what it is allowed. It also forces you to log decisions, which helps you understand incidents afterwards.
howItWorks: Every request must prove identity, usually with multi-factor authentication, meaning two different proofs.
The system also checks the device: is it managed, patched and free of known problems?
A policy engine compares the request with your rules and decides allow, deny or limited access.
Access is granted to a specific application or data set, not to a whole network.
Every decision and session is logged, so you can review what happened later.
You start with identity and your most valuable systems, then expand step by step.
beginner.example: Think of a modern hotel. The front desk does not hand you a key to every room. Your card opens your room, the gym during opening hours and nothing else. If you lose the card, it can be cancelled within seconds. Staff have different cards, and each open is recorded. That is zero trust: identity plus context, checked every time, with the smallest access that still lets you do your job.
takeaways: Location is not proof of trust; verify every request on its own merits.
Give the smallest access that works, and grant it for a limited time.
Good telemetry matters, because bad device data leads to bad decisions.

topics.title: Account Use Policies
topics.summary: Account use policies constrain how, when, from where, and through which session type an identity may authenticate, rather than what that identity is permitted to read or change. Typical controls include conditional access that demands a compliant device, a trusted network location, an acceptable risk score, or a phishing-resistant authenticator; logon-hour and source-address restrictions; session lifetime and idle timeouts; limits on concurrent sessions; denial of interactive logon for service and shared accounts; and automatic disconnection of dormant or orphaned identities. In practice the difficult part is not writing the rule but keeping it true. Hybrid estates evaluate policy in several places at once, so a rule that is strict in the cloud can be undermined by an on-premises path that still accepts the same credential, and legacy protocols plus emergency break-glass accounts routinely sit outside enforcement. Vendor and batch service accounts resist restriction because their scheduled work cannot satisfy interactive conditions, so teams either carve out permanent exceptions or move the workload onto a managed identity. Understanding what an account is actually used for normally has to precede meaningful restriction, which is why sign-in and privileged-role reporting carry so much weight. The control attacks the value of stolen credentials directly: a valid account is far less useful when the credential cannot be used from an unmanaged host, at an unusual hour, or into a remote desktop service from the internet. It reduces the yield of brute-force and spraying campaigns by removing the paths they target and it damages lateral movement by denying interactive logon where it is not required. Its failure modes are common and honest: exclusions that outlive their justification, session tokens stolen after a correct policy decision, legacy authentication paths, and misconfigured rules that either lock out operations or quietly apply to nobody.
objectives: Explain how account use policy differs from permission policy and why both are required for a defensible posture.
Design conditional access conditions that make a stolen credential unusable from an unmanaged or untrusted host.
Identify legacy authentication paths, service accounts, and break-glass identities that bypass enforcement.
Apply logon restrictions to shared and service accounts without breaking scheduled workloads.
Triage sign-in and privileged-role reports to find dormant, orphaned, and over-privileged identities.
Assess how stolen session tokens can defeat policy that was evaluated correctly at authentication time.

beginner.definition: Account use policies control how and when an account may sign in, not what it can reach. They can demand a managed device, a trusted network, or a second factor. They can restrict where logins come from and end idle sessions. A valid password is far less useful when it only works under the right conditions.
beginner.whyItMatters: When an attacker buys a password from a breach, the password alone should not be enough. Use policies make that true. They block sign-ins from strange countries or unmanaged laptops, and they stop accounts being used for jobs they were never meant for. Together with permission rules, they shrink what a stolen credential can do. They also expose logins that happen at odd hours or from odd places.
howItWorks: Decide the conditions that make a sign-in acceptable, such as a known device or location.
Write the rule so it checks those conditions when the person signs in.
Add session limits, so an idle login closes instead of staying open all night.
Restrict service and shared accounts to the systems they actually need to use.
Test the rules against real work, and fix anything that blocks a legitimate task.
Review the exceptions often, because a temporary rule tends to become permanent.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital wristband. It proves who you are, but it does not let you into every ward. Your badge opens the rooms for your job, during your shift, at your hospital. If someone finds a lost badge, it will not open the pharmacy door at midnight in another building. Account use policies work like that. The credential is only the start; the conditions decide whether the door opens.
takeaways: Combine use policies with permission rules; neither is enough alone.
Make a stolen password useless when it comes from an unknown device.
Review the exceptions often, since every permanent one is a hole.

topics.title: Antivirus/Antimalware
topics.summary: Antivirus and antimalware controls are the endpoint and gateway technologies that identify, block, quarantine, and remediate malicious files, scripts, and behaviour before or during execution. A modern deployment is rarely signature-only: it combines static signatures and hashes, emulation and unpacking of obfuscated content, heuristic and machine-learning scoring, script-scanning interfaces that inspect interpreter content at runtime, behavioural monitoring of process trees and file operations, and cloud reputation lookups for samples the local engine has not seen. Protection is placed at several chokepoints, including the endpoint agent with on-access and on-write scanning, mail gateways that strip or detonate attachments, web proxies that block known-malicious downloads, and server or container layers where scanning is often omitted for performance reasons. Operationally the control is dominated by tuning and by exclusions. Build directories, database data paths, backup volumes, and vendor application folders produce constant false positives, and every documented exclusion becomes a place where an intruder can operate unobserved, which is why exclusion lists deserve the same review discipline as firewall rules. The control reliably defeats commodity and mass-market malware, script-based loaders, well-known ransomware families, and infostealers, and it frequently supplies the first detection signal for an intrusion that other controls missed. Its limitations are structural: novel or lightly modified samples evade signatures, living-off-the-land execution and in-memory payloads leave little on disk to scan, attackers target the agent itself for tampering, encrypted archives and some delivery paths escape inspection entirely, and agents left disabled or excluded on server tiers create large unprotected areas.
objectives: Explain how signature, heuristic, behavioural, and reputation layers complement each other and where each one fails.
Tune detection and exclusions for production workloads without creating blind spots an intruder can exploit.
Interpret malware alerts alongside process, script, and network telemetry during initial triage.
Evaluate agent tamper protection and coverage gaps across servers, containers, and remote endpoints.
Assess why script-based, in-memory, and living-off-the-land execution evade file-based detection.
Prioritise quarantine and remediation actions when a detection lands on a critical production system.

beginner.definition: Antivirus and antimalware software finds, blocks, and removes malicious files, scripts, and programmes. Modern tools do more than match known virus signatures, which are unique patterns of known bad files. They unpack hidden code, watch for suspicious behaviour, and check reputations online. Protection sits on endpoints, mail gateways, and web gateways. The weakest parts are usually the exclusion lists.
beginner.whyItMatters: Common malware still spreads widely, and it usually arrives by a file, a link, or an email attachment. Antimalware catches a lot of that before it runs, and it often gives the first warning of a wider problem. It is not a complete defence. New or slightly changed samples slip past pattern matching, and code that runs only in memory leaves little to inspect. So it belongs in a stack, not alone.
howItWorks: Files are scanned when they are written and again when they are opened.
The engine compares them with signatures of known malicious code and checks online reputation.
Behaviour rules watch process chains, such as a document starting a script interpreter.
Matches are blocked, quarantined, or removed, and an alert goes to your team.
Administrators tune exclusions carefully, because every exclusion creates a blind spot for attackers.
Coverage is checked across servers and containers, where agents are often missing.
beginner.example: Think of a building with a metal detector at the main entrance. It stops a lot of everyday trouble, especially the obvious cases, and the guard recognises common weapons. But someone who hides a tool inside a laptop, or who already works in the building, walks past it. The detector is worth having, yet nobody would rely on it as the only protection for a bank vault.
takeaways: Keep exclusions short, documented, and reviewed, because they are blind spots.
Expect new and in-memory code to slip past file scanning.
Check that agents actually run on servers, containers, and remote devices.

topics.title: Application Developer Guidance
topics.summary: Application developer guidance is the set of practices, standards, and tooling that cause security requirements to be expressed in code rather than bolted on after release. It begins with threat modelling during design, where the team enumerates trust boundaries, data flows, and the abuse cases a feature enables, and continues through secure coding standards that name the safe primitive for each risky operation: parameterised queries instead of string-built statements, contextual output encoding, framework-provided session and anti-forgery handling, safe deserialisation, and explicit allow-lists for file paths and redirects. In delivery pipelines the guidance is enforced by automated checks, including static analysis, dependency and container scanning, secret detection, composition analysis against a maintained inventory, and infrastructure-as-code policy evaluation, with a severity threshold that actually fails a build instead of producing a report nobody reads. Durable programmes also govern build artifacts, signing releases and verifying dependencies so the build path itself is not a supply-chain vector, and they invest in developer enablement through security champions and lightweight review rather than pure gatekeeping. The control removes whole classes of exploitable weakness from public-facing applications, shrinking the reachable initial-access surface and the injection, authorisation, and deserialisation flaws that follow. It also constrains privilege-abuse paths that depend on flawed authorisation logic and reduces the chance that a product ships insecure defaults. Its honest limits are that scanners miss logic and business-flow flaws, false positives breed desensitisation, transitive dependencies are difficult to govern, remediation debt accumulates faster than it is cleared, and guidance changes nothing unless it changes the code that ships.
objectives: Run a design-stage threat model that produces security requirements a team can implement and test.
Map common vulnerability classes to the safe coding primitives and framework features that prevent them.
Wire static analysis, dependency scanning, and secret detection into a pipeline with a gate that fails builds.
Govern third-party and transitive dependencies using composition analysis and maintained inventory data.
Interpret scanner findings well enough to separate genuine defects from noise without ignoring either.
Evaluate insecure product defaults, especially features that ease user execution, before a release ships.

beginner.definition: Application developer guidance is the set of rules, habits, and tools that help teams build security into software while they write it. It covers design reviews, safe coding standards, and automatic checks in the build pipeline. The aim is simple: stop common weaknesses from reaching users in the first place.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most break-ins start with a flaw someone wrote into an application. A missing permission check or a badly built database query can hand an attacker the whole system. Fixing code after release is slow and costly. Building it well from the start removes entire families of weakness, so your team has fewer urgent problems and your users face less risk.
howItWorks: During design, the team draws how data flows and marks the trust boundaries where untrusted input enters.
For each risky operation, the guidance names one safe habit, such as a query that keeps data separate from the command.
The build pipeline then runs automatic checks for known code patterns, old libraries, and secrets left in files.
A severity threshold fails the build, so a serious finding must be fixed before the code ships.
Releases are signed, and dependencies are tracked so the build path itself is not a weak link.
Developers get short reviews and a security helper on the team, so guidance reaches daily work.
beginner.example: Think of a restaurant kitchen. Instead of inspecting every plate at the door, the kitchen follows rules while cooking: keep raw meat away from salad, wash hands, use separate boards. Inspectors still visit, but the rules do most of the work. Developer guidance is like that. The team follows safe habits as they write code, and the pipeline acts as a quick inspector. Fewer bad plates reach the customer, and nobody is chasing problems all night.
takeaways: Agree the security rules during design, not after the first incident.
Automate the checks, and let a serious finding stop the release.
Scanners miss logic flaws, so careful human review still matters every time.

topics.title: Audit
topics.summary: Audit is the control that makes an environment observable: the deliberate collection, retention, and review of security-relevant events so that unauthorised activity can be detected, reconstructed, and attributed. Implementation in a real estate spans several layers that must be joined together. Operating system audit policy is tuned to capture process creation with command-line arguments, authentication outcomes, account and group changes, service installation, scheduled task creation, and privilege use. Directory and identity services capture sign-in events, token issuance, and administrative role assignment. Network infrastructure contributes flow records, proxy and DNS logs, and firewall decisions. Cloud control planes contribute API activity trails for every subscription, account, and project. Endpoint agents contribute process lineage, driver and module loads, and file integrity information. All of it converges into centralised storage with normalised time, retained long enough to support an investigation that begins months after initial access, and protected from the very accounts it is meant to observe. Audit is the foundational control behind every other detection capability: without it, threat hunting, incident response, and forensics are guesswork. It directly supports detection of remote service use, account creation and discovery, autostart persistence, defence impairment, and data staging or exfiltration behaviour, because those actions leave configuration and authentication traces. The honest limitations are volume and quality. Default audit policy is either too sparse to be useful or so verbose that signal drowns in noise and licensing cost, and collecting events without a review process produces archives nobody reads. Failure modes include logging only on servers and not on workstations or build agents, leaving audit records in a writable location for any local administrator, failing to synchronise clocks so timelines cannot be correlated, expiring retention before an intrusion is discovered, and disabling a noisy audit subcategory after a false alarm instead of tuning the detection.
objectives: Explain how to design a tiered audit policy covering endpoint, identity, network, and cloud control-plane telemetry.
Describe how to normalise timestamps, field names, and identifiers across heterogeneous log sources for correlation.
Explain how log retention, immutability, and segregation of duties protect audit records from the accounts they observe.
Identify the audit gaps that most often make an incident timeline unreconstructable and prioritise closing them.
Describe the audit subcategories or event sources that support detection of persistence, account manipulation, and defence impairment.
Explain how to tune noisy audit sources without discarding the events that matter for investigation.
Evaluate an existing logging estate against detection and forensic requirements and produce a prioritised remediation plan.

beginner.definition: Audit is the practice of recording security-relevant events so you can see what happened and prove it later. It covers sign-ins, account changes, program starts, service installs, and cloud activity. Records are collected in one place, kept long enough to be useful, and protected from tampering. Without these records, investigations become guesswork.
beginner.whyItMatters: When something goes wrong, the first question is what happened and when. Good records answer that in minutes instead of weeks. They also let you hunt for quiet activity that no alert covered. An attacker who knows the logs are thin can work slowly and stay unseen. Records must be protected too, because erasing them is often part of an attack.
howItWorks: Choose the events worth recording, such as logins, new accounts, and service installs.
Turn on the same settings across servers, workstations, cloud accounts, and network devices.
Send everything to one central store, with clocks synced so times line up.
Keep the records long enough to cover an investigation that starts months later.
Protect the store so local administrators cannot edit or delete their own traces.
Review the records with searches and alerts, or the archive becomes a shelf nobody reads.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital keeping notes for every patient visit. If a patient returns with a fever, the notes show which ward they were in and who treated them. Without notes, the staff can only guess. The notes are also kept securely, because a record that anyone can rewrite is worth very little. Audit logs are the hospital notes for your computers and accounts.
takeaways: Decide what to record, then check that it is actually arriving.
Sync clocks and centralise logs, or you cannot build a timeline.
Protect audit records from the administrators they are meant to observe.

topics.title: Disable or Remove Feature or Program
topics.shortTitle: Disable or Remove Feature or Program
topics.summary: Disable or remove feature or program is the reduction of attack surface by eliminating software, protocols, services, and interpreter features that the business does not need. It is the least glamorous control and consistently one of the most effective, because every removed component is a class of vulnerability, a persistence location, and an execution path the adversary can no longer use. In real environments it is implemented as a hardening baseline applied through configuration management: removing or blocking legacy scripting hosts and command-line download utilities where they are not required, disabling macro execution from internet-sourced documents, turning off deprecated authentication protocols and unauthenticated file sharing versions, uninstalling unused agents and management tools that carry their own privileged services, removing sample applications and default accounts from internet-facing systems, disabling unnecessary remote access features and file-transfer endpoints, and pruning optional operating system capabilities and kernel modules on servers. The control is powerful because it works before detection matters: the technique fails outright rather than generating an alert that someone must triage. It addresses user execution through document and script features, abuse of command and scripting interpreters, exploitation of public-facing applications that would not exist in a minimal build, and remote services that only function because an unnecessary protocol is enabled. It also removes the defence-impairment surface, since tooling that is not installed cannot be tampered with. The honest limitations are organisational. Nobody wants to be the team that broke a business process, so removal requests are contested, and the knowledge of who depends on a legacy component is usually incomplete. Applications are frequently reinstalled silently by a vendor update, a configuration baseline that is applied once drifts back within a quarter, and the hardened image is rarely the one used for the emergency build during an incident. Failure modes include disabling a feature only on workstations while servers keep it enabled, relying on a registry setting that a per-application local override can bypass, forgetting the disaster recovery and test environments, and removing a component with no inventory record so that no one can tell whether it came back.
objectives: Explain how to build a hardening baseline from an accurate software, protocol, and service inventory.
Identify the interpreter features, legacy protocols, and default components that most reliably reward removal.
Describe how configuration management and compliance scanning keep a hardened baseline from drifting back to default.
Explain how disabling an unnecessary feature changes detection requirements by removing an execution path entirely.
Describe how per-application overrides and vendor updates can silently re-enable a component that was disabled.
Explain why test, disaster recovery, and emergency build environments must receive the same baseline as production.
Evaluate a proposed removal against business dependency, rollback options, and residual risk, and document the decision.

beginner.definition: This mitigation means removing software, services, and features that the business does not actually need. Every extra component is another possible weakness, another place to hide, and another way to run code. A smaller build is easier to defend and easier to understand. It is one of the least exciting controls and one of the most effective.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers love features nobody uses. Old scripts, unused agents, and legacy file sharing are common ways in and common ways to stay hidden. If the component is gone, the attack simply fails, and your team never has to investigate it. The difficulty is social, not technical. Someone usually depends on the old thing, so you need good records before you remove it.
howItWorks: Build an accurate inventory of installed software, running services, and enabled network protocols.
Ask each business owner which items they truly rely on, and record the answers.
Remove or block the rest, starting with the riskiest and least used.
Apply the same baseline to test, backup, and emergency systems, not only production.
Scan regularly for drift, because updates and installers quietly bring features back.
Keep a rollback plan for each removal, so a mistake can be undone quickly.
beginner.example: Think of clearing out a garage. Every old tool, can of paint, and broken chair is something that could trip you or catch fire. You keep what you use, and you get rid of the rest. The hard part is not the lifting, it is the argument about the box nobody remembers opening. A clear garage is quicker to search and safer to work in.
takeaways: Remove what you do not need; unused features are free help for attackers.
Check that updates and installers do not quietly switch features back on.
Ask owners before you remove, and keep a rollback path ready.

topics.title: Encrypt Sensitive Information
topics.summary: Encrypting sensitive information means ensuring that data is unreadable to anyone who does not hold the corresponding key, both while it is stored and while it travels between systems. In production the requirement resolves into a small set of concrete patterns: full-disk encryption bound to a hardware root of trust so a stolen laptop yields nothing without the platform, database and column-level encryption for regulated fields, object storage configured for server-side encryption under a customer-managed key, secret managers that remove plaintext credentials from configuration files and build pipelines, and modern TLS with validated certificates for every service-to-service and client connection. Key management is where such programmes succeed or fail. Envelope encryption through a key management service or hardware security module keeps data keys short-lived and auditable, rotation schedules and a cryptographic agility plan limit the blast radius of a compromised key, and separation of duties prevents the team that operates the data from also controlling the keys that protect it. The control blunts exfiltration over command-and-control channels and public web services by reducing what stolen bulk data is worth without its keys, protects credentials and tokens at rest so that an exposed file share or backup does not immediately become account takeover, and makes salted, deliberately slow storage of password material expensive to attack offline. Its limitations are real: data must be decrypted somewhere, and that endpoint, its memory, and its logs are the practical attack surface; keys stored beside the data reduce encryption to presentation; a legitimate session used by an intruder is unaffected; and aggressive inspection or key escrow can quietly undo the protection. Encryption changes the economics of a breach rather than preventing one.
objectives: Explain the difference between encryption at rest, in transit, and at the application layer, and where each genuinely helps.
Design an envelope-encryption scheme with a key management service or hardware security module that keeps data keys short-lived.
Identify where keys, tokens, and plaintext secrets leak through configuration files, backups, and pipeline variables.
Assess certificate lifecycle and cipher configuration as continuing operational risks rather than one-time build tasks.
Evaluate how key custody, escrow, and separation of duties determine the real strength of an encryption deployment.
Plan key rotation and cryptographic agility without breaking dependent services or losing historical data access.

beginner.definition: Encrypting sensitive information means scrambling data so only someone with the right key can read it. You do this for data on disk and for data moving across a network. Keys matter most: if the key sits beside the data, the protection is only a disguise. Good practice keeps keys separate, rotates them, and limits who can use them.
beginner.whyItMatters: A stolen laptop, a leaked backup, or a misconfigured storage bucket can expose everything inside. Encryption means the thief has a locked box instead of readable files. It also protects data in transit, so someone watching the network cannot read it. Be honest about the limit: someone using a valid login sees decrypted data normally. Encryption changes what a breach costs, rather than stopping one.
howItWorks: Decide which data needs protection, and classify it by how sensitive it is.
Turn on full-disk encryption, so a lost laptop cannot be read without its key.
Encrypt traffic between services with modern secure connections and valid certificates, which prove a service identity.
Move passwords and keys out of configuration files and into a managed secret store.
Keep data keys in a key service, and rotate them on a schedule you can follow.
Separate the people who run the data from the people who control the keys.
beginner.example: Think of posting a bank statement in a locked briefcase rather than a postcard. Anyone who finds the briefcase on the street still cannot read the contents. That is encryption at rest. The key is the combination, so you never keep the combination taped to the handle, and you change it if someone might have seen it. Also remember that the bank staff can still open the briefcase during business hours.
takeaways: Encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit, then guard the keys.
Never store the key next to the data it protects.
Encryption reduces the cost of a breach; it does not stop one.

topics.title: Execution Prevention
topics.summary: Execution prevention is the set of endpoint and policy controls that stop unauthorised code from ever running, rather than detecting it after it starts. In practice it is implemented as a layered stack: application allow-listing through Windows Defender Application Control or AppLocker, PowerShell constrained language mode and script block logging paired with a hardened execution policy, Microsoft Office macro restrictions enforced by group policy, and on Linux systems mount-level noexec flags plus integrity tooling. The control works because it denies the final common step of nearly every intrusion: the moment a payload is handed to a scripting host, a signed binary proxy, or an office application. It breaks behaviours such as user execution of a malicious attachment, abuse of command and scripting interpreters, and the broad family of living-off-the-land binary abuse where legitimate signed tools are repurposed to launch attacker code. Operational reality is unforgiving. Effective allow-listing requires months of audit-only telemetry, a disciplined change process for every legitimate software update, and a publisher-certificate strategy that survives vendor re-signing. Blocking PowerShell outright is rarely feasible; constrained language mode and AMSI integration are the practical compromise, and both are trivially weakened by an unmanaged host or an excluded directory. Common failure modes include allow-listing only the user-writable portions of the filesystem while leaving temporary and download directories executable, forgetting that signed interpreters such as mshta and rundll32 can load remote content, and deploying policy to workstations while leaving jump servers and build agents in audit mode indefinitely. Attackers adapt by moving to in-memory execution, signed binary proxy chains, and interpreter features that fall outside the constrained set, so execution prevention must be paired with memory-level detection and strict egress control to remain meaningful.
objectives: Explain how application allow-listing policies such as WDAC and AppLocker are designed, piloted in audit mode, and enforced without breaking business software.
Describe the practical difference between blocking a scripting interpreter outright and constraining its language mode, and when each is defensible.
Identify the signed binary proxy execution paths and interpreter features that most often bypass execution prevention controls.
Explain how Office macro, ActiveX, and add-in policy settings reduce user-execution risk and where they are commonly misconfigured.
Describe how noexec mounts, integrity verification, and package trust work on Linux and Unix endpoints as execution prevention.
Evaluate the operational cost of allow-listing in a changing environment and design a change-management path that keeps policy current.
Explain why execution prevention must be complemented by memory-level detection and egress control rather than treated as a complete control.

beginner.definition: Execution prevention stops unauthorised programs from running at all. Instead of watching for bad behaviour later, it uses a list of software allowed to start. Anything not on the list is blocked. It also restricts risky features, such as office documents that carry macros (small scripts inside a document) and script interpreters that run text as code.
beginner.whyItMatters: Almost every intrusion ends with code running on a machine. If that code cannot start, the attack fails, even if the attacker got in. This control works before any alert is needed, which saves your team time. It does have a real cost. Building the allow list takes patience, and a blocked program can interrupt work, so the change process must be smooth and well tested.
howItWorks: Start in audit mode, where the tool only records what would have been blocked.
Study the records for weeks, and add the software your teams really need.
Turn on enforcement, so unknown programs can no longer start on the machine.
Restrict document macros and script features that attackers use to launch code.
Keep a clear path to add new software, or staff will find ways around the rules.
Remember that signed system tools can still be abused, so watch what they do.
beginner.example: Think of a nightclub with a guest list. The bouncer lets in people whose names are on the list and turns away everyone else, no matter how confident they look. A famous face does not get in without a name on the list, because attackers often wear familiar clothing. The club also closes the side door where staff used to slip people in. Execution prevention is that guest list for code.
takeaways: Pilot allow lists in audit mode before you block anything.
Block unauthorised code early, then still watch memory and network.
Make adding approved software easy, or people will bypass the control.

topics.title: Exploit Protection
topics.summary: Exploit protection is the family of host and process hardening features that make memory-corruption and similar software flaws harder to turn into reliable code execution. It is implemented through operating system mitigations that are compiled into binaries and enforced at load time, including address space layout randomisation, data execution prevention, control-flow integrity and control-flow guard, stack and heap integrity checks, structured exception handling overwrite protection, and arbitrary code guard, alongside runtime exploit protection settings that can be applied per process through platform tooling. In practice a security team defines a baseline of mitigations, audits which production binaries and third-party agents opt out, and remediates the opt-outs through vendor updates or configuration. The control raises the cost of vulnerability exploitation and, critically, causes attacks that depend on predictable memory layouts or writable executable regions to fail outright or to crash the target process, which generates high-value telemetry. It addresses exploitation of public-facing applications, client-side exploitation, and privilege escalation that relies on memory corruption in privileged services, and it complicates process injection techniques that require executable memory in a remote process. Honest limitations matter here. Mitigations are not a patch: a logic flaw, a design weakness, or a misuse of legitimate functionality is entirely unaffected. Whole classes of modern attacks, including those abusing legitimate scripting hosts and credential access through operating system interfaces, do not touch memory corruption at all. Mitigations are frequently disabled during troubleshooting and never re-enabled, and older in-house or line-of-business binaries often cannot be rebuilt with control-flow integrity. Failure modes include system-wide opt-outs applied to make a single legacy application run, per-process exclusions that quietly accumulate, and treating a mitigation audit as a one-time project rather than a continuous control that must be re-verified after every application update.
objectives: Explain each major exploit mitigation and the specific exploitation primitive it is designed to disrupt.
Describe how to audit per-process mitigation opt-outs across a production estate and prioritise remediation.
Explain how control-flow integrity and arbitrary code guard change the feasibility of process injection and memory corruption exploitation.
Describe how exploit mitigation enforcement differs between system-wide policy and per-application configuration.
Identify the vulnerability classes that exploit protection does not address at all, and the compensating controls required.
Explain how mitigation-related crashes appear in endpoint telemetry and how to triage them as potential exploitation attempts.
Evaluate the operational tradeoffs of enforcing strict mitigation policy against legacy line-of-business software.

beginner.definition: Exploit protection is a set of built-in defences that make software flaws harder to turn into working attacks. It includes randomising where code sits in memory, marking areas as non-executable, and checking that programmes follow their intended path. When an attack breaks these rules, the programme often crashes instead of being taken over. That crash is also a useful warning.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many serious attacks depend on a bug that lets an attacker write into memory and then run their own code. These defences do not remove the bug, but they make the attacker job much harder and less reliable. Failures often show up as crashes, which gives your team something to investigate. The limits matter: these settings do nothing against weak passwords, bad permissions, or abuse of legitimate tools.
howItWorks: Operating systems apply these protections to a programme automatically when it starts.
Memory positions are randomised, so an attacker cannot rely on a fixed address.
Sections of memory are marked non-executable, so injected code cannot run there.
Checks confirm that a programme jumps only to valid, expected places in its code.
Security teams audit which programs are exempt, because opt-outs quietly weaken everything.
A crash caused by a broken rule is reviewed as a possible attack attempt.
beginner.example: Think of a warehouse where every pallet has a random location each day. A thief who studied last week layout finds nothing where it should be. Some shelves also refuse to hold anything that could be set on fire, and a guard checks that workers only walk the marked routes. A thief who trips these rules sets off an alarm instead of escaping with goods.
takeaways: Turn these defences on, then find and fix the programmes that opt out.
Treat unusual crashes on sensitive services as possible attack attempts.
Remember they do not help against stolen passwords or weak permissions.

topics.title: Filter Network Traffic
topics.summary: Filtering network traffic is the practice of permitting only the protocols, destinations, ports, and services an organisation has explicitly justified and denying everything else at control points the defender owns. In production it is never one device but a stack of them: perimeter and internal firewalls enforcing zone-to-zone policy, web proxies and secure web gateways applying category and reputation decisions, recursive resolvers with policy zones that block or sinkhole unwanted domains, cloud security groups and network ACLs, Kubernetes network policies and service mesh authorisation, and host firewalls that drop traffic before it reaches the wire. The engineering reality is that filtering is a change-management problem at least as much as a technical one. Rules accumulate, business owners resist removals, emergency openings become permanent, and a single any-any rule quietly rebuilds the flat network that segmentation was meant to replace. Mature teams therefore keep rule ownership metadata, review rulesets on a schedule, use hit counters to retire rules that never match, and ship denied traffic into detection pipelines instead of leaving it in a device buffer. The control interrupts command-and-control over common application-layer protocols by forcing beacons toward destinations the organisation does not permit, and it makes DNS-based tunnelling visible and blockable by channelling all resolution through controlled resolvers. It raises the cost of exfiltration over C2 channels and public web services, constrains remote service abuse such as unrestricted RDP or SMB across zones, and removes reachable services that opportunistic exploitation depends on. Its limitations are honest: inspection degrades against encrypted traffic, attackers ride allowed SaaS and cloud endpoints, domain fronting and fast-changing infrastructure defeat static allow-lists, and a filter that generates constant false positives will eventually be bypassed by the operators it inconveniences.
objectives: Explain how traffic filtering policy is enforced at perimeter, internal, cloud, cluster, and host layers, and where each layer's blind spots sit.
Design an egress allow-list that constrains command-and-control over web protocols and DNS without breaking legitimate business traffic.
Triage firewall, proxy, and resolver deny logs for beaconing, tunnelling, and exfiltration patterns rather than dismissing them as noise.
Identify rule sprawl, shadowed rules, and unowned any-any entries during a review of an existing ruleset.
Assess how TLS inspection, domain fronting, and permitted SaaS traffic limit what network filtering can actually observe.
Justify where inline blocking is worth the availability risk and where a monitor-only position is the defensible choice.

beginner.definition: Filtering network traffic means allowing only the connections you have decided to permit and refusing all the rest. You apply the rules at several points, such as a firewall (a guard that checks network traffic), a web proxy, and a name resolver. The rules use addresses, ports, and destinations. The aim is to shrink the paths traffic can take.
beginner.whyItMatters: Malware often needs to talk to a server on the internet to receive orders or send stolen data. Filtering breaks that conversation. It also blocks scanning and remote access tools from crossing between zones. The risk is that filters grow messy over time. A rule added for one emergency can quietly reopen the whole network. So filtering needs care, review, and good records of why each rule exists.
howItWorks: Write down what each system must reach, based on real traffic records rather than guesses.
Allow those connections, and deny everything else unless a person approves it.
Control outbound traffic as well, because most attacks need a way out.
Send refused traffic to your monitoring tools instead of leaving it unread.
Tag each rule with an owner and a reason, so old rules can be retired safely.
Review the rule set regularly and delete entries that never match anything.
beginner.example: Think of a secure office with a reception desk. Visitors may enter only the meeting room they are expected in. The receptionist keeps a list of approved visits, and anyone else is politely turned away. The list is checked often, so an old approval is not still valid next year. A desk that waved everyone through would make the locked doors inside pointless. Traffic filtering is that reception desk for network connections.
takeaways: Default to deny, then allow only what you can justify.
Filter what leaves the network, and not only what tries to enter.
Give every rule an owner and a reason, then review it.

topics.title: Multi-factor Authentication
topics.summary: Multi-factor authentication is the requirement that a login present at least two independent evidence types, so that possession of a password alone is insufficient to establish a session. In real environments it appears in several forms with very different security properties: hardware-backed phishing-resistant factors using FIDO2 or platform credentials, push notifications through an authenticator application, time-based one-time codes, and legacy telephony methods such as SMS or voice callbacks. It is deployed for interactive user sign-in, for privileged and administrative access through a bastion or privileged access workstation, for remote access gateways including VPN and virtual desktop entry points, and increasingly for machine identities where certificate or workload identity stands in for a second factor. The control directly breaks password spraying, credential stuffing, and the reuse of harvested credentials, and it removes the immediate value of most credential phishing because the stolen password cannot complete a session. It also meaningfully constrains lateral movement that depends on reusing captured password hashes or plaintext credentials, since the second factor is not present in memory. The honest limitations are where most breaches still occur. Push-based and code-based factors are vulnerable to real-time relay, where an attacker proxies the authentication prompt to the victim and the victim approves it. Legacy protocols that cannot present a second factor become a bypass path unless they are disabled or brokered. Service accounts, scheduled tasks, and API clients typically cannot perform interactive multi-factor authentication and are excluded, creating a large credential-only attack surface. Failure modes include enrolling users but never enforcing, allowing remembered sessions for months, leaving a break-glass account with a static password, and treating the presence of any second factor as equivalent to a phishing-resistant one.
objectives: Explain the difference between phishing-resistant hardware-backed factors and relayable factors, and the risk each carries.
Describe how to roll out multi-factor authentication for interactive sign-in, remote access, and privileged administration in phases.
Identify the legacy authentication paths and non-interactive accounts that bypass multi-factor enforcement and describe how to close them.
Explain how real-time prompt relay and adversary-in-the-middle proxying defeat push and code factors in practice.
Describe how conditional access, device state, and session lifetime policy combine with multi-factor authentication.
Evaluate an authentication estate and rank the residual risks that multi-factor authentication does not remove.

beginner.definition: Multi-factor authentication asks for two different kinds of proof before letting someone in. Usually that means something you know, such as a password, plus something you have, such as a phone app or a hardware key. A stolen password alone then fails. Some factors are much stronger than others, so the choice matters.
beginner.whyItMatters: Passwords leak constantly, and people reuse them. Multi-factor authentication makes a leaked password far less useful. It stops automated guessing campaigns and most phishing, which means fake messages that try to steal your login. If your account has it, an attacker needs more than a password. The honest limit is that weak factors, such as a code you type in, can still be relayed by a clever attacker in real time.
howItWorks: You enter your password, and the service asks for a second proof.
You approve a prompt, type a short-lived code, or touch a hardware key.
The service checks the second proof and only then creates the session.
Admins enforce this for remote access, cloud consoles, and powerful accounts first.
Old login methods that cannot ask for a second proof are switched off or brokered.
Hardware keys resist fake pages best, because the key checks the real site address.
beginner.example: Think of a bank vault that needs a key and a code. A thief who copies the key still cannot open the door alone. Some vaults instead ring a guard who unlocks remotely, and a clever thief can trick the guard into opening it. That is the difference between a hardware key and a phone prompt. The best vaults also refuse to open for staff who forget the code, and never leave a spare door unlocked.
takeaways: Turn on multi-factor authentication for remote access and admin accounts first.
Prefer hardware keys over codes and prompts where you can.
Close old login paths that skip the second check entirely.

topics.title: Network Intrusion Prevention
topics.summary: Network intrusion prevention is the inline inspection and blocking of traffic that matches known attack patterns, malicious infrastructure, or anomalous protocol behaviour, usually delivered through a next-generation firewall, a dedicated prevention appliance, or a cloud-native inspection service. Unlike intrusion detection, which only alerts on a copy of the traffic, prevention sits in the path and can drop a session, reset a connection, or quarantine a source, which raises both its value and its risk. Detection content combines signature and protocol-anomaly rules for exploitation attempts and malware callbacks, reputation and threat-intelligence feeds for addresses and domains, transport fingerprinting that can distinguish suspicious clients even inside encryption, and behavioural thresholds for scanning, brute force, and tunnelling. Teams enable signature sets selectively, tune and suppress noise until a blocking policy is trustworthy, and frequently run in detect-only mode first to measure what a block would have broken. The control provides virtual patching for vulnerable public-facing services that cannot be fixed immediately, interrupts command-and-control over web protocols and DNS, cuts off large-scale exfiltration toward known or suspicious external services, and contains fast-moving ransomware by dropping the file-sharing and remote-service traffic it uses to spread laterally. Its limitations are equally concrete: encryption and evasion techniques such as fragmentation, encoding, and polymorphic payloads reduce inspection fidelity, traffic that stays inside an allowed cloud service is hard to distinguish from legitimate use, east-west blind spots and sensor placement gaps leave internal movement uninspected, capacity limits force bypass under load, and every false positive is an outage that erodes the organisation's willingness to keep the control in blocking mode.
objectives: Explain the operational difference between detection-only and inline prevention and when each posture is appropriate.
Tune signatures, suppressions, and thresholds until a blocking policy is safe to enforce in production.
Triage prevention alerts for exploitation attempts, beaconing, and tunnelling rather than closing them as noise.
Apply virtual patching to an exposed service while the underlying vulnerability remains unremediated.
Assess the fidelity limits created by encrypted traffic, evasion techniques, and permitted cloud services.
Plan fail-open and bypass behaviour so that an inspection outage does not become a business outage.

beginner.definition: Network intrusion prevention is the inspection of network traffic as it passes, with the power to block what looks like an attack. It sits directly in the path of the traffic, unlike a monitoring tool that only watches a copy. It uses known attack patterns, reputation lists, and unusual behaviour to decide. Blocked traffic never reaches the target.
beginner.whyItMatters: Some attacks happen in seconds, faster than any person can react. An inline blocker can stop those attempts automatically. It also buys time when a known flaw has no fix yet, by blocking the attempts that target it. The catch is risk: a wrong block can cut off real business traffic. That is why teams start in alert-only mode, tune the rules, and only then switch on blocking.
howItWorks: Traffic passes through the device, which reads the packets and rebuilds the session.
Rules compare the traffic against known attack patterns and lists of bad addresses.
Behaviour rules watch for scanning, repeated guessing, or quiet and regular callbacks.
A match can raise an alert, drop the session, or block the source for a while.
Teams run in alert-only mode first, then suppress false alarms before enabling blocks.
Encrypted traffic limits inspection, so the device may rely on patterns and reputation instead of content.
beginner.example: Think of an airport security queue. Every bag passes a scanner before boarding, and a suspicious bag is stopped there and then. The scanner follows a list of known threats, but it also reacts to anything unusual. If the scanner were only recording bags for later review, a dangerous item would already be on the plane. The tradeoff is real too: a scanner set too strictly delays honest travellers.
takeaways: Blocking is more powerful than alerting, and riskier, so tune first.
Use prevention to cover a flaw you cannot patch yet.
Encryption and allowed cloud services limit what inspection can see.

topics.title: Network Segmentation
topics.summary: Network segmentation is the practice of dividing an enterprise network into zones with defined trust levels and restricting traffic between them to what each zone genuinely needs. In modern environments it is implemented less by firewall interfaces and more by a combination of internal micro-segmentation policy enforced on the host or in the virtual network fabric, virtual local area network and routing separation, private endpoints that remove public reachability from data services, and identity-aware proxies in front of administrative interfaces. The purpose is to convert a single compromised host from a launching point for the whole estate into a contained incident. Segmentation breaks the behaviours that carry most intrusions from foothold to impact: internal reconnaissance that depends on broad reachability, lateral movement over remote service protocols such as remote desktop, server message block, and secure shell, and command-and-control that relies on unrestricted outbound access from user subnets. It also constrains exfiltration, because staging servers must reach a route that policy permits rather than any internet destination. The operational reality is that segmentation is a data problem before it is a firewall problem. Nobody can write correct policy without an accurate, current map of which systems talk to which on which ports, and that map is almost never in the documentation. Failure modes are predictable: allow rules written once for a migration and never removed, a broad any-to-any rule between two production zones created during an incident and left in place, flat management networks where hypervisors, backup infrastructure, and jump hosts share a broadcast domain with user devices, and cloud security groups that permit the entire corporate range because enumerating real sources was inconvenient. Segmentation also creates a false sense of safety when the identity plane remains flat, since a single set of reusable administrative credentials can still cross every zone boundary. Segmentation must therefore be paired with privileged access management, multi-factor authentication, and outbound egress filtering rather than treated as a standalone control.
objectives: Explain how to build a traffic dependency map and use it to design zone policy rather than guessing at requirements.
Describe the difference between network-level segmentation, host-based micro-segmentation, and identity-aware proxying of administrative access.
Identify the specific lateral movement protocols and internal reconnaissance behaviours that segmentation is intended to disrupt.
Explain how egress restriction from server and user zones constrains command and control and data exfiltration paths.
Describe how private endpoints and removal of public reachability reduce exposure of data services.
Identify the common failure modes that erode segmentation policy over time and the review process that prevents them.
Evaluate whether segmentation alone is sufficient given a flat identity plane and recommend complementary controls.

beginner.definition: Network segmentation means splitting a network into zones and allowing only the traffic each zone really needs. A flat network lets any computer reach any other computer. A segmented network puts walls between groups, such as users, servers, and payment systems. The goal is to keep one broken machine from becoming a path to everything else.
beginner.whyItMatters: Once an attacker gets one computer, the next step is usually to look around inside. On a flat network they can scan, find servers, and copy data from anywhere. Segmentation limits that movement and also restricts what can leave the network. It turns a company-wide incident into a small one. It also slows the fast spread of ransomware (malware that locks files and demands payment).
howItWorks: First, map which systems talk to which, on which ports, and how often.
Group systems into zones by trust level and by the data they handle.
Write rules that allow the traffic the map proves is needed and deny the rest.
Add host-level rules on servers, so a machine can be protected even inside a trusted zone.
Control outbound traffic too, so a compromised host cannot reach any internet address.
Review the rules on a schedule and remove temporary openings that were never closed.
beginner.example: Think of an office building with locked doors between departments. A visitor in reception cannot wander into the finance office or the server room. Staff who need to reach another floor use a door that opens only for them and only at certain times. If someone slips in through reception, they are stuck in one corridor. A building with every door propped open would let them walk anywhere.
takeaways: Assume one machine will be breached, and plan limits around that.
Segment the network to reduce movement, then review the rules regularly.
Segmentation still fails if administrators share one powerful login everywhere.

topics.title: Password Policies
topics.summary: Password policies are the enforced rules that govern how credentials are created, stored, transmitted, throttled, and retired across an identity estate. Current practice has moved away from mandatory rotation and character-mix requirements toward minimum length, screening against corpora of known-breached passwords, per-account throttling and lockout, and secure storage using salted, deliberately slow hashing. Forced periodic changes with symbol substitution reliably produce predictable mutations that add little entropy, while punishing users and generating helpdesk load. Implementation spans several planes that rarely share one policy: on-premises directory domains with both domain-wide and fine-grained settings, cloud identity providers with their own complexity, lockout, and banned-password controls, hybrid synchronisation that can silently preserve legacy behaviour, service and machine accounts that frequently sit under a separate or exempt policy, and application-local credential stores that no central policy reaches at all. Lockout thresholds deserve deliberate tuning because a low threshold hands an adversary a denial-of-service lever against any username they can guess, so risk-based throttling is usually the better trade than a hard lockout. The control raises the cost of online brute force and password spraying, and breached-password screening at set and change time makes credential stuffing materially less productive. It also reduces the chance that a weak or reused credential becomes the valid account an intruder needs. Its limits are decisive: once stored hashes leave the estate, policy protects nothing, spraying under the lockout threshold remains viable, legacy authentication protocols can bypass modern settings, helpdesk resets are a social-engineering target, and credential reuse on external sites is outside the organisation's control entirely.
objectives: Explain why length, breached-password screening, and throttling outperform forced rotation and character-complexity rules.
Tune lockout and throttling thresholds against the denial-of-service risk they create for known accounts.
Identify the identity planes that escape a central password policy, including service accounts and application-local stores.
Interpret credential storage requirements well enough to judge what a stolen password database is worth to an attacker.
Evaluate how password spraying evades common lockout settings and which telemetry exposes it.
Articulate where password policy stops being useful and multifactor authentication must take over.

beginner.definition: A password policy is the set of rules that control how passwords are created, stored, checked, and retired. Modern advice favours long passwords, screening against lists of passwords already leaked, and limits on repeated guessing attempts. It no longer favours forcing people to change good passwords every month. The policy applies to every system, not only the main directory.
beginner.whyItMatters: Weak or reused passwords remain one of the easiest ways in. Attackers take a list of leaked passwords and try them across many accounts, hoping one fits. A good policy raises the cost of that guessing and blocks passwords already known to be breached. It also matters that bad storage does not undo the work: if a stolen password file is easy to crack, the policy on the front door means little.
howItWorks: Set a minimum length, such as twelve or more characters, because length helps more than odd symbols.
Check new passwords against lists of passwords exposed in past breaches, and refuse matches.
Store passwords with a salted slow hash, which is a one-way scramble that takes real effort to reverse.
Throttle repeated failed logins from one source, and alert on guessing spread across many accounts.
Tune lockout carefully, because a strict lockout lets an attacker freeze any account they can name.
Apply the rules to service accounts, applications, and cloud logins, not just the main directory.
beginner.example: Think of a door lock on a shared office. A short, obvious code is easy for a burglar to try, and the same code reused on every door is worse. The building manager now insists on longer codes, refuses codes already published in an old breach list, and fits a delay after several wrong tries. Staff also stop changing a good code every month, because that only pushed them to write it on a sticky note.
takeaways: Prefer long passwords and breached-password checks over forced monthly changes.
Slow repeated guessing, and watch for many accounts tried at once.
Password policy cannot fix a password you reuse on outside websites.

topics.title: Privileged Account Management
topics.summary: Privileged account management is the discipline of limiting, controlling, and monitoring the accounts and roles that can change security-relevant configuration, access sensitive data, or administer other systems. Real implementations combine several mechanisms: a tiered administrative model that separates directory, server, and workstation administration so that no single credential can cross tiers, dedicated administrative accounts that are never used for mail or browsing, credential vaulting with automatic rotation for shared and service accounts, just-in-time elevation that grants a role for a bounded window with approval and full session recording, and the removal of standing local administrator rights from standard user workstations. The control removes the two conditions attackers rely on most: reusable credentials with broad reach, and quiet elevation paths that leave no approval trail. It breaks behaviours including account discovery and enumeration of privileged groups, credential access through cached secrets and process memory on administrative workstations, exploitation of elevation control mechanisms such as user account control misconfiguration and setuid binaries, and the use of remote services to move laterally with administrative shares. It also directly constrains impact, because destructive actions such as recovery inhibition and mass encryption require privileged reach that a tightly brokered model does not grant by default. Honest limitations are mostly organisational. Tiered models collapse when administrators reuse a single identity across tiers because it is convenient, and vaulting is defeated if the vault becomes a single unmonitored credential store reachable from the same flat network as everything else. Just-in-time access fails when approval becomes a rubber stamp or when emergency break-glass accounts retain permanent standing privilege. Service accounts remain the hardest case, because they cannot always be rotated without an outage and are frequently excluded from management scope. Failure modes include allowing interactive logon for service identities, leaving former administrators in privileged groups, permitting administrative sessions from ordinary workstations, and never reviewing who actually used the privilege that was granted.
objectives: Explain how a tiered administrative model is designed and how credential reuse across tiers defeats it.
Describe how credential vaulting, rotation, and just-in-time elevation are implemented and where they typically break down.
Identify the privileged account and elevation control weaknesses that most often enable privilege escalation in practice.
Explain how removing standing local administrator rights changes attacker options on workstations.
Describe how service and machine accounts should be scoped, monitored, and rotated without causing outages.
Explain how session recording and approval trails turn privileged access management into a detection source.
Evaluate a privileged access estate, including break-glass accounts, and recommend a remediation sequence.

beginner.definition: Privileged account management controls the logins that can change important settings, reach sensitive data, or manage other systems. It limits who holds these powerful accounts, lends the rights only when needed, and records what is done. Default administrator rights are removed from everyday workstations. The aim is to make quiet, wide-reaching access rare instead of normal.
beginner.whyItMatters: An attacker who finds one administrator password can often take the whole company. Powerful logins are reused, shared, and left over from old projects. When that happens, the intruder looks like a normal administrator doing normal work. Managing these accounts properly means powerful access is short, approved, and visible. It also blocks the mass damage from ransomware (malware that locks files and demands payment) because wiping backups needs administrator rights.
howItWorks: Administrators work in separate tiers, so a workstation admin login cannot also manage the directory.
Powerful accounts are stored in a protected vault and their passwords rotate automatically.
When a job needs admin rights, the person requests them for a limited window and a reason.
Every privileged session is recorded, so their actions can be reviewed and traced later.
Standard workstations no longer give staff permanent administrator rights, which blocks many attacks.
Service accounts are scoped to the one task they perform and monitored for odd use.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel master key. It opens every room, so it is never handed out for a whole shift. A cleaner who needs one room signs the key out, uses it, and returns it. The desk keeps a record of who took it and when. If a key goes missing, the locks can be changed quickly. Privileged accounts are master keys, and this discipline keeps them from living in someone's pocket.
takeaways: Give administrator rights for a short time and a clear reason.
Do not reuse one powerful login across several different systems.
Record privileged sessions so unusual actions can be seen and reviewed.

topics.title: Software Configuration
topics.summary: Software configuration as a mitigation is the deliberate hardening of applications, operating systems, and cloud services away from their permissive defaults, followed by the work of keeping that hardened state true over time. It covers disabling features that exist mainly as attack surface, such as legacy file-sharing dialects, name-resolution fallbacks that answer broadcast queries, obsolete scripting engines, and macro execution from internet-sourced documents; constraining command interpreters with logging and restricted language modes; requiring elevation through a separate administrative account for management tooling; and configuring services so that authentication, transport security, cipher suites, and audit settings match a defined baseline. In cloud estates the same idea appears as account-level and resource-level settings, public-access blocks, instance metadata hardening, and organisation policies that stop a workload owner from reverting a control by accident. The operational reality is drift. Baselines are applied at build time and then eroded by an application that needs an exception, an upgrade that resets a value, a container image that still ships the old configuration, or an operator under pressure who weakens a control to restore service. Teams that succeed treat baselines as code, scan continuously against them, alert on drift, and route exceptions through a named owner with an expiry date instead of leaving them undocumented. The control weakens defence-impairment attempts directly, because central logging configuration and tamper-protected agents remove the easiest routes to silencing telemetry, and it closes the autostart, macro execution, and script-interpreter behaviours that commodity intrusions depend on. Its limits are practical: an exception-heavy baseline is theatre, hardening that breaks operations gets rolled back, and no organisation controls the configuration of every third-party service it relies on.
objectives: Explain how a hardening baseline is derived, applied, and verified rather than assumed to be in place.
Identify default features and services that should be disabled or constrained, and the business justification each removal requires.
Detect configuration drift across endpoints, servers, container images, and cloud accounts using continuous scanning.
Assess how defence-impairment techniques exploit permissive logging and agent configuration.
Design an exception process with ownership, compensating controls, and expiry so that hardening stays credible.
Interpret the tradeoff between tightening configuration and preserving availability for legacy applications.

beginner.definition: Software configuration as a defence means changing settings away from the easy defaults and keeping them that way. It covers turning off unused features, closing legacy protocols, requiring logging, and hardening cloud services. Default settings are chosen for convenience, not safety, so they often help an attacker. The real challenge is drift, because settings quietly slip back over time.
beginner.whyItMatters: A single permissive setting can undo several other controls. If logging can be switched off by a local administrator, your audit trail is only a suggestion. If an old file sharing protocol stays enabled, an attacker gains a path that should not exist. Hardening removes these easy routes. It also stops small mistakes from growing, because a defined baseline tells you when something has changed.
howItWorks: Start from a recognised hardening baseline for each type of system you run.
Turn off services, protocols, and features that no one has asked for.
Set logging and protection settings so they cannot be quietly switched off.
Apply the same baseline to every server, workstation, container image, and cloud account.
Scan continuously and alert when a setting drifts away from the baseline.
Give each exception a named owner, a written reason, and an expiry date.
beginner.example: Think of a new flat with factory settings on the heating, the alarm, and the door entry. It works, but the default door code is written in the manual and the alarm is off. Moving in properly means changing the code, arming the alarm, and closing the windows that were open for viewing. Months later you check again, because the alarm can be switched off by anyone who gets annoyed by it.
takeaways: Change the defaults, then check regularly that they stayed changed.
Treat every exception as temporary, with an owner and an end date.
Preventive settings are useless if they can be switched off quietly.

topics.title: Update Software
topics.summary: Updating software is the systematic replacement of vulnerable code with vendor-fixed versions across every asset class an organisation operates, from operating systems and hypervisors through network appliances, container base images, firmware, and third-party libraries. The operational reality is dominated by inventory and scheduling rather than by the patch action itself, because you cannot update what you do not know exists. The control therefore rests on authoritative asset discovery, software composition analysis, a bill of materials for everything the organisation builds, and a change process capable of reaching production servers, field devices, remote laptops, and appliances that are only manageable through a vendor console. Effective programmes rank risk instead of chasing one score: vendor severity, evidence of exploitation in the wild, and whether the asset is internet-facing jointly decide what enters an emergency channel with a short deadline, while lower-risk internal findings wait for a scheduled ring. Where patching is genuinely impossible, teams apply compensating controls and record time-boxed risk acceptance with a named owner. The control breaks the most common initial-access path, exploitation of unpatched public-facing applications and remote-access gateways, and it removes the client-side and local privilege-escalation flaws that follow user execution. Its limitations are well understood: firmware and industrial systems rarely tolerate a reboot, shadow IT and embedded appliances escape inventory, vendors ship delayed or partial fixes, zero-days exist before patches do, and the update channel is itself a supply-chain target. Updating also fails quietly when installation reports success but the service is never restarted, or when an old container image is rescheduled from a registry that still holds it.
objectives: Explain how asset inventory, composition analysis, and risk ranking combine to produce a defensible patch cadence.
Distinguish emergency remediation of internet-facing systems from routine monthly rings and define the trigger for each.
Identify the asset classes that routinely escape inventory and describe how to bring them under management.
Apply compensating controls and time-boxed risk acceptance where patching genuinely cannot occur.
Assess the supply-chain risk introduced by the software update channel itself.
Verify that a patch has taken effect at runtime rather than trusting successful installation output.
Prioritise remediation using vendor severity, exploitation evidence, and exposure together.
