beginner.definition: Account discovery is the search for the list of people, services and machines that have accounts in an environment. The intruder wants to know which identities exist before choosing one to steal or reuse. It is a paper exercise as much as a technical one. Knowing the names of the accounts is the first step towards using them.
beginner.whyItMatters: An account name is half of every login. If an intruder learns which accounts exist, guessing or targeting becomes far easier. Service accounts are especially valuable because they often have broad rights and passwords that are rarely changed. Most companies have dozens of tools that list accounts for legitimate reasons, so the challenge is telling a routine inventory apart from quiet reconnaissance.
howItWorks: The intruder already has a foothold and looks around for anything that lists identities.
On a single machine they read the local account list, often with a simple built-in command.
In a company directory they send search requests that return user, group and computer records.
In cloud platforms they call identity interfaces that list users, roles and service principals.
A service principal is a non-human identity that software uses to log in.
They now hold names, and those names feed the next stage of the attack.
beginner.example: Imagine a burglar who slips into an office at lunchtime. They do not open any drawers. Instead they photograph the staff noticeboard, which lists every employee, their department and their extension. Later they know exactly who to call and who to pretend to be. Nothing was taken, but the photograph was the most valuable thing in the building.
takeaways: Account names are valuable on their own, even before any password is known.
Know which of your tools legitimately list accounts, and from which machines.
A wide directory search from an ordinary workstation is a strong warning sign.

topics.title: Application Layer Protocol
topics.summary: Application layer protocol abuse is the embedding of command and control inside protocols that networks and users expect to see, so the traffic resembles ordinary application use. The mechanism is protocol mimicry. An implant formats its tasking and responses to fit a legitimate carrier such as a web request, a name resolution query, a mail protocol or a file transfer service, then follows that carrier's conventions closely enough to survive inspection: valid request structure, plausible headers, expected ports, and timing that resembles a human or an agent rather than a metronome. Encrypted carriers hide payload contents but not the metadata around them, so detection shifts to connection characteristics such as destination reputation and age, certificate properties, client fingerprints that disagree with the claimed application, user agent strings that never appear elsewhere in the estate, uniform request sizes, and beacon intervals with low jitter sustained over long periods. Unencrypted or partially visible carriers expose more. Name resolution tunnelling encodes data in query names, producing long high entropy labels, elevated query rates and concentration on a single authoritative server, while web based tasking often shows repeated URI patterns, unusual content types and cookie values that carry state. The technique appears on every platform, from Windows workstations and Linux servers to containers, network appliances and cloud workloads, and it is frequently paired with exfiltration over the same channel. The investigative difficulty is that the same protocols carry enormous legitimate traffic. Software updates, telemetry agents, cloud synchronisation, package repositories and partner integrations all generate steady outbound requests. Analysts distinguish malicious use by prevalence and ownership: whether the destination is seen anywhere else in the organisation, which process makes the connection, whether the domain was registered recently or resolves to hosting with no business relationship, and whether the beacon survives reboots or follows a specific user between systems. Enrichment and deviation from baseline, not the choice of protocol, drive the verdict.
objectives: Explain how implants shape command and control traffic to conform to web, name resolution and other application protocols.
Use connection metadata such as certificate properties, client fingerprints and destination age when payload contents are encrypted.
Detect name resolution carried tasking through label entropy, query rate and authoritative server concentration.
Establish prevalence baselines for destinations, user agents and client fingerprints across the estate.
Attribute outbound connections to the responsible process and separate implant traffic from update and telemetry agents.
Map command and control findings to exfiltration and follow-on activity within a single incident timeline.

beginner.definition: Application layer protocol abuse means hiding the link to a compromised machine inside everyday internet traffic. The intruder shapes their commands to look like normal web requests, name lookups or email, so the traffic blends in. It is the digital version of using a familiar envelope so nobody opens it. The contents are hidden in plain sight.
beginner.whyItMatters: Almost all business traffic leaves through the same doors, so blocking a protocol would stop real work. When commands travel inside ordinary traffic, they are very hard to pick out by content, especially if the traffic is encrypted. You also need to spot the hidden channel before stolen data can ride out through it. That task is easier if you know what normal looks like.
howItWorks: The hidden software on the victim machine waits, then contacts a controller on a timer.
It wraps its message in a protocol the network already allows, such as web or name lookup.
The message follows the rules of that protocol, with proper structure and normal ports.
The controller replies in the same style, so the exchange looks like ordinary application use.
When contents are encrypted, defenders must judge by timing, size and destination instead.
Very regular timing, or an address used nowhere else, is often the giveaway.
beginner.example: Imagine writing to a friend every day at nine in the morning. Your letters look like ordinary birthday cards, and the post office never questions them. Inside, the first letter of each line spells out a secret message. To anyone opening the envelope it reads like small talk. Only the clockwork timing, and the fact that nobody else writes to that address, makes it interesting.
takeaways: Modern intrusions hide their control traffic inside protocols your business needs.
When you cannot read the contents, judge the connection: timing, size and reputation.
A destination that appears only on one machine in the company is worth investigating.

topics.title: Application Layer Protocol: DNS
topics.summary:
DNS command and control describes adversary use of the Domain Name System to carry instructions and data between an implant and its controller, usually by encoding information into the queried name itself and receiving instructions in resource records returned by the authoritative server. The technique works because outbound name resolution is permitted almost everywhere, is rarely inspected beyond reputation filtering, and is often logged with more consistency than other egress protocols. Variants include high-volume subdomain encoding for data transfer, low-and-slow single-label lookups for tasking, and the use of DNS over HTTPS to hide the query content inside ordinary web traffic.

The strongest artefacts are in resolver and naming data. Atypical query characteristics include very long or high-entropy labels, unusually deep label hierarchies under a single parent domain, a very high count of unique subdomains for one registered domain from a small set of hosts, and query types that a normal client population never emits in volume, such as text or null record requests. Timing analysis is equally important: automatic retry behaviour in the client stack, which yields near-constant intervals across a few resolver replicas, is a recognisable pattern. Where responses can be observed, unusually large answer sections or records carrying encoded payload deviate from normal caching behaviour. Endpoint evidence is often the decisive layer, since the process making the queries can be identified and tied to a file origin and command line.

Legitimate high-volume DNS exists in the form of content delivery networks, security vendors performing lookups, and misconfigured applications that fail repeatedly against the same name. Investigations separate these by host population, domain registration age, absence of the domain from any approved service inventory, and whether the queried labels decode to structured data rather than readable service names.
objectives: Explain how encoded labels and resource record responses allow bidirectional communication over name resolution.
Identify query entropy, label length, unique subdomain counts, and record type anomalies as detection signals.
Interpret DNS retry timing patterns caused by client resolver behaviour and why they appear so regular in logs.
Correlate resolver telemetry with endpoint process data to attribute queries to a specific binary or script.
Evaluate the visibility loss introduced by encrypted DNS transports and describe compensating controls.
Map DNS command and control to ATT&CK and rank resolver policy, egress restriction, and host telemetry by effectiveness.

beginner.definition: DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's phone book. It turns a name you type, such as example.com, into a number a computer can reach. Attackers can also hide instructions and stolen data inside those name lookups. Because almost every network allows DNS out, this channel is hard to block.
beginner.whyItMatters: Every computer must be able to look up names, or almost nothing works, so DNS traffic is allowed everywhere. It is also rarely inspected in detail and often logged well, which suits an attacker. A program can quietly send small pieces of data out in the names it asks for and receive short replies in return. If you never look at name lookups, this whole channel stays invisible to you.
howItWorks: The attacker registers a domain name and runs a server that answers for it.
Malware on the victim machine builds a long name, such as a string of random characters.
It asks the local resolver to look that name up, and the request travels out through the firewall.
The attacker's server reads the hidden data in the name and replies with a short coded answer.
The malware repeats this often, so the rhythm and the odd names become visible in resolver logs.
beginner.example: Imagine sending secret notes out of a building by writing them on the outside of parcels. The courier reads only the address, so the parcel passes every checkpoint without question. Your friend at the other end reads the address and learns everything. The contents of the parcel never matter. DNS tunnelling, the name for hiding data in lookups, works exactly like that, using a delivery system every building already trusts.
takeaways: DNS is allowed almost everywhere, so it is a favourite hiding place for attackers.
Very long or random-looking names, asked over and over, deserve a closer look.
Send all lookups through your own resolver, so you can see and log them.

topics.title: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
topics.summary:
Web protocols command and control describes adversary use of HTTP and HTTPS to carry instructions and exfiltrated data between an implant and its controller. The traffic is designed to resemble ordinary web browsing: it uses standard ports, valid transport encryption, conventional request methods and headers, and often a legitimate-looking hostname or a domain fronted by a content delivery network. Because the channel is encrypted and rides on the same infrastructure the business depends on, network inspection cannot rely on payload signatures, and detection shifts toward metadata, timing, and behavioural consistency.

Observable artefacts are concentrated in proxy, DNS, TLS, and endpoint data. Proxy logs capture the requested host, full URL path, method, user agent, response size, and byte counts in each direction, and beaconing appears as a strikingly regular interval between requests to the same endpoint from a single internal host, often continuing outside working hours. TLS metadata may reveal a self-signed or unusual certificate, a mismatch between the certificate subject and the requested hostname, or a client that fails to perform expected revocation checks. DNS logs show resolution of the controller domain, sometimes to hosting ranges rather than content networks. On the endpoint, the responsible process is frequently an unexpected binary or a legitimate one with no reason to make network connections, and its command line and file origin provide additional context.

Benign web traffic is the largest data source in any environment and includes software updates, telemetry, and cloud applications, several of which also beacon on fixed intervals. Investigations therefore combine multiple weak signals: an unusual process making regular requests, to a domain with a short registration history, with a consistent user agent that matches no deployed software, and either a long-lived connection or a request pattern that persists through nights and weekends.
objectives: Explain how adversaries shape HTTP and HTTPS traffic to resemble legitimate browsing and why payload inspection fails.
Identify beaconing through interval regularity, byte-size consistency, and persistence outside business hours in proxy logs.
Analyse TLS metadata such as certificate subject, issuer, and validity to surface infrastructure that does not match its hostname.
Correlate endpoint process telemetry with proxy and DNS records to attribute a network connection to a specific binary.
Build baselined detection logic that suppresses known update and cloud application beaconing without losing coverage.
Map web protocol command and control to ATT&CK and describe the value and limits of each mitigation available.

beginner.definition: Web protocols are the rules your browser uses to fetch pages, mainly HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) and its encrypted version HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure). Attackers can hide their control traffic inside the same rules, so the connection blends into ordinary web browsing. The infected computer looks like it is visiting a website.
beginner.whyItMatters: After breaking in, an attacker needs a way to send orders to the infected machine and receive stolen data back. Web traffic is perfect for that, because almost every network allows it out. The content is encrypted, so nobody can read it, and blocking all web traffic would stop the business. You must therefore look at behaviour, such as a machine calling the same address every few minutes, rather than at the content.
howItWorks: The attacker sets up a server on the internet that will act as the controller.
Malware on the victim machine contacts that server using ordinary web requests.
It asks for new instructions at regular intervals, and this rhythm is called beaconing.
Stolen files are sent back inside normal-looking requests, so they leave the network quietly.
Proxy logs show the regular rhythm, and endpoint logs show which program made the connection.
beginner.example: Think of a spy who hides messages inside ordinary shopping catalogues. The postman delivers them without suspicion, because the catalogue is a normal thing to receive. The spy's handler writes the real orders in code between the furniture photos. Nobody reading the outside of the envelope learns anything. Malicious web traffic works the same way, wrapped in the same requests that load every shopping site you visit.
takeaways: You cannot read encrypted web traffic, so focus on patterns instead of content.
A regular call home every few minutes, day and night, is a classic warning sign.
Match the network connection to the program that made it, because that identifies the malware.

topics.title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
topics.summary: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution covers persistence achieved by configuring code to run automatically when a system starts, when a user logs on, or when a session state changes. Rather than one mechanism, the parent technique collects the many autostart surfaces an operating system offers: registry keys and startup folders on Windows, launch agents, launch daemons and login items on macOS, init scripts, systemd units, cron entries and shell profiles on Linux, plus vendor extension points such as print monitors, authentication packages, security support providers and browser helper components. Adversaries favour these locations because they are legitimate features, they execute early or in a privileged context, and they are frequently ignored by users and asset owners alike. The evidence is largely static and configuration-based: registry values pointing at unusual binaries, new or modified service and unit definitions, changes to shell startup files, scheduled tasks with logon triggers, and file creation in autostart directories. Because thousands of such entries are legitimately present on any mature endpoint, the useful question is not whether autostart entries exist but whether one changed recently, points to an unsigned or user-writable location, runs with higher privilege than the account that created it, or coincides with other incident activity on the same host. Baselines built from known-good images, combined with change tracking on autostart locations and file integrity monitoring, reduce an unmanageable list to a small set of reviewable differences. That same baseline supports recovery, because persistence removal during containment has to be complete without breaking the legitimate startup software an organisation depends on.
objectives: Enumerate the principal autostart locations on Windows, Linux and macOS and the privilege each confers on the executed code.
Use baselining and change tracking to reduce autostart review to a manageable set of differences.
Interpret endpoint telemetry for processes launched at boot, logon or session state change.
Judge suspicious autostart entries by path writability, signature state, parent privilege and recency.
Plan persistence removal during containment without breaking legitimate startup software.
Write detection logic for new autostart entries that reference user-writable or unsigned binaries.

beginner.definition: This is persistence built into the way a computer starts. The attacker sets their program to run automatically at boot, at logon, or when a session changes. These are normal operating system features, so the change often hides among hundreds of other startup entries.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you only clean the infected file, this entry starts it again after the next restart. That is why an incident can seem to return. Startup locations also run early and sometimes with high rights. The fix is not to remove everything, but to know what changed recently and why.
howItWorks: The attacker gains access and wants their code to survive a restart.
They add an entry to a startup list, a registry key (a settings store on Windows), or a scheduled task.
The entry points to a file they control, often in a user-writable folder.
After a reboot or logon, the system runs that file automatically.
The code may start with the rights of the user or of the system itself.
Defenders compare today's startup list against a known good baseline from the same machine.
beginner.example: Think of a building where the front door is checked every morning. The attacker does not fight the guard. They add their own key to the cleaner's keyring, so their helper walks in at 6 a.m. with the cleaning crew. Every morning the guard sees a normal start of day. Only a careful list of who holds keys would show the extra one.
takeaways: Removing malware is not enough; remove the entry that restarts it.
Keep a baseline of startup entries and review every difference.
Be suspicious of startup entries that point at user-writable folders.

topics.title: Brute Force
topics.summary: Brute force is a credential access technique in which an adversary makes repeated authentication attempts, systematically varying one or more credential components, until a logon succeeds. The mechanism is simple: the attacker obtains a valid account identifier, then submits candidate secrets such as passwords from a word list, mutated variations, default vendor credentials, PINs or short numeric codes against whichever authentication interface is reachable, including VPN gateways, webmail portals, SSH, remote desktop services, database listeners and application programming interfaces. Modern variants avoid hammering a single account. Password spraying submits one weak candidate across many accounts to stay below per-account lockout thresholds, while credential stuffing replays username and password pairs harvested from unrelated breaches, betting on password reuse. The technique appears on every platform: Windows domain services such as Kerberos and NTLM, Linux and Unix authentication stacks reachable over SSH, network device management planes, cloud identity providers and consumer facing applications. The telemetry that matters most is authentication logging. On Windows this means records of failed and successful logons, account lockouts and Kerberos pre-authentication failures; on Linux it means authentication daemon, sudo and pluggable authentication module messages; identity providers expose sign-in logs with failure reason, source address, client application and risk score, and VPN concentrators record the source address and assigned session. Investigators distinguish brute force from ordinary user error by looking at volume and shape: many failures against few accounts from few sources, or few failures against many accounts from distributed sources, unusually uniform request timing, impossible travel between successes, and a success that immediately follows a burst of failures. Benign causes include stale saved credentials on a mobile client, a service account whose password was rotated without updating configuration, and an automation script that never received the new secret, so a finding usually needs corroboration before it is treated as malicious.
objectives: Explain how brute force, password spraying and credential stuffing differ in request volume, account targeting and detection signature.
Identify the authentication telemetry sources that record guessing attempts across Windows, Linux, network devices and cloud identity providers.
Write SIEM-style queries that surface distributed low-volume spraying which per-account lockout thresholds never trigger.
Distinguish malicious guessing from stale saved credentials, misconfigured service accounts and password rotation drift.
Prioritise authentication alerts by exposure, separating internet facing services from internal systems behind segmentation.
Recommend mitigations that combine multi-factor authentication, throttling, lockout policy, credential screening and monitoring of successful logons after failure bursts.

beginner.definition: Brute force is guessing at logins until one works. The intruder tries many passwords against a known account name, or one common password against many names. Automated tools make thousands of attempts possible in minutes. Two related variants are spraying, one weak password across many accounts, and stuffing, reusing password pairs stolen from other websites.
beginner.whyItMatters: People reuse passwords, and old breach lists are still traded online. A single weak password can open a remote access gateway and let an intruder walk in. Spraying is quiet by design, because each account sees only a few failures and never locks. Watching failed logins across the whole company, not just one account, is how you catch it.
howItWorks: The intruder first needs a list of account names, which is easy to find or guess.
They send the login attempts automatically, often from many different addresses at once.
Spraying uses one common password, such as a season plus a year, on every account.
Stuffing replays username and password pairs taken from an unrelated website breach.
Each account sees only a few failures, so lockout rules may never trigger at all.
A success straight after a burst of failures is the clearest warning.
beginner.example: Think of a thief with a ring of ten common keys. Instead of forcing one door, they walk a long corridor and try all ten keys once on every door. Each door sees only ten attempts, so nothing locks and nobody complains. Eventually one door opens, and the thief walks in as if they had a key all along.
takeaways: Spraying stays under the lockout limit by spreading few attempts across many accounts.
Count failed logins across all accounts, not per account alone.
Multi-factor authentication stops guessing even when the password is correct.

topics.title: Brute Force: Credential Stuffing
topics.summary:
Credential stuffing is an automated credential access technique in which the adversary replays username and password pairs obtained from a breach of one service against authentication endpoints of other services, exploiting the fact that people reuse passwords across systems. Because each attempt uses a valid credential for some unrelated site, failure rates are low enough that modest volumes of traffic produce a meaningful number of successful logins, and per-account lockout counters are rarely triggered since each account typically sees one attempt. Attacks are usually executed from distributed residential proxy networks or botnets so that source reputation and address-based throttling do not stop the campaign.

Artefacts appear in authentication and web telemetry. Identity provider or application logs show a large number of logins from many distinct addresses that share a narrow fingerprint: identical client or user agent strings, identical header ordering, uniform inter-request timing, and no preceding session or page views. The ratio of successful to failed logins is often unusually high compared with normal user behaviour, and the first action after a successful login frequently differs from that account's historical pattern, such as immediately creating access tokens, changing registered authentication methods, or reading mailbox rules. Account recovery and password reset events may cluster afterwards if the legitimate user is displaced.

Benign lookalikes include shared network address translation egress, corporate proxy pools, and users travelling. What separates stuffing is the breadth of accounts touched, the uniformity of the client fingerprint, the absence of normal session establishment, and the correlation of the username set with a known third-party breach. Detection therefore depends on joining authentication outcomes with network-level fingerprinting rather than on any single log source.
objectives: Explain how password reuse and third-party breach data make stuffing viable, and why per-account lockout does not stop it.
Identify the client fingerprint characteristics that distinguish automated replay from genuine interactive login.
Correlate successful authentications with post-login behaviour to determine whether an account was actually taken over.
Analyse source address distribution and proxy patterns to differentiate stuffing infrastructure from corporate egress.
Prioritise accounts for forced reset and session revocation based on observed post-authentication activity.
Map credential stuffing to ATT&CK and describe the controls that reduce impact when passwords are already compromised.

beginner.definition: Credential stuffing is an attack that replays username and password pairs stolen from one website against a different website. It works because many people reuse the same password everywhere. Each attempt uses a real password, just not for this service. Lockouts rarely fire, because each account is usually tried only once.
beginner.whyItMatters: Breaches at other companies become your problem, because your users hold accounts elsewhere too. An attacker does not need to break your defences, only to find one reused password. A single success can open a mailbox, a file store or an administrative console. This traffic also comes from many different addresses and looks like real logins, so it is genuinely hard to spot without looking at patterns.
howItWorks: An attacker obtains a large list of usernames and passwords from a breach at some other company.
Automated tools try those pairs against your login page, thousands of times per hour.
Most attempts simply fail, but the reuse rate means that some logins succeed.
Bot traffic is spread across many addresses, so blocking one address changes nothing.
The attacker checks what each working account can reach, then acts quickly before anyone resets a password.
beginner.example: Imagine a master key that fits one brand of padlock. Thieves steal a box of those keys from a shop, then walk a street trying each key on every door of that brand. The key was never made for these houses, but it opens them anyway because the owner bought the same lock. Credential stuffing works like this. The password was stolen somewhere else, yet it still opens your door.
takeaways: People reuse passwords, so a breach elsewhere can unlock an account here.
Multi-factor authentication breaks stuffing, because a stolen password is not enough on its own.
Ten logins from ten countries in one minute is not normal user behaviour.

topics.title: Brute Force: Password Spraying
topics.summary:
Password spraying is a credential access technique in which an adversary attempts a small number of commonly chosen passwords against a large number of accounts, inverting the traditional brute force pattern of many attempts against one account. The objective is to stay below per-account lockout thresholds and below anomaly thresholds that trigger on repeated failures for a single identity, while still finding the few accounts in any population that use a weak or seasonal password. Spraying is frequently directed at externally exposed authentication surfaces such as webmail, remote access portals, virtual desktop gateways, and identity provider endpoints, and it is often distributed across many source addresses to avoid source-based rate limits.

The distinguishing telemetry is a burst of failed authentications that is broad but shallow: many distinct usernames, few attempts each, a short time window, and a small set of repeated password-derived failure patterns. Domain controller and identity provider logs record the authentication package, the client address, the user agent or client string, and the exact failure reason, which separates a wrong password from a disabled account or a logon outside permitted hours. Successful authentication following the spray, particularly from a new address or an unusual client, is the pivot point that converts reconnaissance into an account compromise. Where multifactor authentication is enforced, the spray may still succeed against legacy protocols that do not support it, which is why protocol-level breakdown matters.

Legitimate causes of distributed failure bursts include stale credentials in a scheduled job, a misconfigured service account, or a user with an outdated cached password. The reliable discriminators are the ratio of distinct accounts to attempts, the synchronisation of retry timing, the absence of an interactive client fingerprint, and whether the source addresses belong to hosting or proxy ranges rather than corporate networks.
objectives: Explain why low-and-slow spraying evades per-account lockout thresholds and how distributed source addresses defeat source-based rate limiting.
Construct SIEM queries that surface broad shallow failure bursts and distinguish them from single-account noise.
Interpret authentication failure reasons and client fields to separate wrong-password events from policy or account-state events.
Identify which legacy or non-interactive authentication protocols bypass multifactor enforcement in a given environment.
Prioritise a spray investigation when a success occurs, and describe the immediate containment and reset sequence.
Map spraying behaviour to ATT&CK and mitigation coverage, and state where detection depends on external-facing service logging.

beginner.definition: Password spraying is a guessing attack that tries one or two common passwords against a long list of usernames. It is the opposite of trying thousands of passwords on one account. The goal is to stay under the lockout limit, which usually counts failures per account. One lucky match gives the attacker a real working login.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most organisations lock an account after several wrong passwords, which stops an attacker from hammering one account. Spraying sidesteps that defence by spreading a few attempts across many accounts. People also choose predictable passwords, such as a season plus a year, so a small number of guesses can succeed somewhere. If your login page faces the internet, you will be sprayed, and you may never notice without good logs.
howItWorks: The attacker collects a list of valid usernames from public sources or a previous breach.
They pick one or two passwords that many people are likely to use.
They try that password once against every account, spread over a short period.
Because each account sees only one failure, the lockout counter never triggers.
Any success is followed by a normal login, which is the moment the attack becomes serious.
beginner.example: Imagine a thief walking down a hotel corridor with a single key card. They try it on every door, once each. No lock alarms, because a single failed swipe is normal. Most doors stay shut, but a few open. Password spraying is that walk. The thief never attacks one room hard enough to raise the alarm, and they only need one careless guest to leave a door unlocked.
takeaways: Watch for many usernames failing once each, instead of one account failing many times.
Turn on multi-factor authentication, so a guessed password alone is not enough.
Block passwords built from seasons, years or the company name.

topics.title: Command and Scripting Interpreter
topics.summary: Command and Scripting Interpreter describes the abuse of native command interpreters and scripting runtimes to execute code on a target host, chain further actions, and stage additional payloads without necessarily writing a conventional executable to disk. The parent technique covers interpreters such as PowerShell, the Windows command shell, Unix shells, Python, JavaScript engines and platform-specific automation hosts, and it appears on Windows, Linux, macOS, network appliances and inside container and cloud execution contexts wherever a shell or runtime is reachable. At a mechanism level the adversary runs an interpreter interactively, passes commands as arguments, or loads script content from a local file, a remote share, or an encoded blob that is decoded into memory at execution time. The telemetry this produces is rich but noisy: process creation records showing interpreter binaries with unusual parent processes, command lines containing encoded or obfuscated arguments, script block and module logging on Windows, process accounting and execve audit records on Linux, shell history files, and the child processes the interpreter subsequently spawns. Investigators separate malicious from benign use by examining the parent-child relationship, the user and session context, the working directory and destination of any download, whether the interpreter was launched by a service or scheduled task, whether logging captured the full script content, and whether the same interpreter and argument pattern recurs across hosts at a rate that matches an automated campaign rather than an administrator. Change windows, software deployment tooling and signed management agents explain a large share of legitimate interpreter invocations, so the bar for escalation should be unusual lineage, unusual content or unusual timing rather than the mere presence of the interpreter.
objectives: Describe how interpreters such as PowerShell, the Windows command shell and Unix shells are invoked and how their command lines differ from routine administrative use.
Identify the process-creation, script-block, module and shell-history telemetry that records interpreter execution across Windows and Linux estates.
Explain how encoded or obfuscated interpreter arguments are surfaced in logging and where visibility gaps typically appear.
Distinguish adversary interpreter abuse from legitimate automation, configuration management and software deployment activity.
Design detection logic that keys on process lineage, argument content and cross-host recurrence rather than on interpreter presence alone.
Assess how interpreter logging configuration and constrained language modes change both visibility and attacker cost.

beginner.definition: A command and scripting interpreter is a built-in tool that runs typed commands or small programs, such as a command shell or a scripting language. Every operating system has them, and administrators use them daily. Intruders abuse the same tools because they are already installed and trusted. Nothing new has to be downloaded, so fewer alarms sound.
beginner.whyItMatters: Because these tools are legitimate, blocking them outright would break normal work. Intruders can therefore run commands, gather information and fetch more tools without ever placing an obvious virus file on disk. The traces they leave are in the command line and the process that started it. If you do not log those details, you lose the evidence you need.
howItWorks: The intruder needs a way to run something, often through a document, a script or a scheduled job.
They start a built-in interpreter, such as a Windows shell or a Unix shell.
The commands may be typed, read from a file, or hidden inside encoded text.
Encoded text is a scrambled form that the interpreter turns back into commands as it runs.
The interpreter then downloads or creates the extra tools that the intruder wants next.
Logs record the interpreter, its arguments and the child programs it started.
beginner.example: Think of a repair worker who arrives with no tools at all. They do not need to smuggle anything past the door, because a full toolbox already sits in the building and everyone is allowed to use it. They open the toolbox and fix, or break, whatever they like. Afterward the toolbox looks exactly as it did before.
takeaways: Built-in shells and scripting tools are useful to you and to intruders alike.
The command line and the parent program are the details that reveal misuse.
Turn on script logging so you can read what actually ran, not just that it ran.

topics.title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
topics.summary:
PowerShell is a task automation and configuration management framework from Microsoft, consisting of a command-line shell and an associated scripting language built on the .NET runtime. It is a first-class execution mechanism on Windows and is also available on Linux and macOS, which makes it attractive to adversaries because it ships with the operating system, is signed by Microsoft, and gives direct access to the .NET framework, WMI, Active Directory, and the registry without dropping a compiled binary to disk. Execution ranges from a simple encoded command passed to powershell.exe, to in-memory assembly loading through reflection, to full script blocks delivered over a remote session.

The telemetry footprint is unusually rich compared with most interpreters. Process creation records the full command line, which frequently exposes switches such as -enc, -nop, -w hidden, or -exec bypass. Script Block Logging writes the de-obfuscated script text to the event log, and Module Logging captures cmdlet invocations even when the script itself is heavily encoded. PowerShell transcription can record console input and output to files, and the Antimalware Scan Interface reports suspicious script content to the registered antivirus engine. Network-enabled cmdlets produce connections associated with the responsible process, and constrained language mode changes appear in the runtime's own logging.

Benign administrative use is pervasive in most enterprises, so volume alone proves nothing. Investigations distinguish malicious from routine activity by correlating parent process and user context, looking for scripting that originates from Office applications, web browsers, or service accounts that should never run interactive shells, and by comparing the target hosts against software deployment and configuration management baselines. Scripts arriving from temporary directories, download URLs appearing inside command lines, and execution outside change-management windows are stronger signals than the presence of PowerShell itself.
objectives: Explain how the PowerShell host resolves execution policy, what that policy actually constrains, and why it is not a security boundary in production.
Identify the specific process creation fields and log sources that expose encoded, obfuscated, or in-memory script execution.
Interpret Script Block Logging and Module Logging output and reconstruct a script's behaviour from the de-obfuscated text.
Correlate suspicious PowerShell process ancestry, such as Office or browser parents, with subsequent network and file activity.
Distinguish delegated administrative automation from adversary tradecraft using user context, host baseline, and change windows.
Map observed PowerShell behaviour to the relevant ATT&CK technique and describe the residual detection gaps in the environment.

beginner.definition: PowerShell is a command line and scripting tool that is built into Windows. You type commands or run a script, and the tool performs tasks for you. It can manage files, users, services and almost any part of the operating system. It is also included in Windows by default, which is why attackers like it.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers can run PowerShell without downloading any extra program, because it already sits on the machine. It is signed by Microsoft, so security tools often trust it. It can also load code straight into memory, so nothing is written to disk for a virus scanner to find. That combination makes it one of the most popular ways to run malicious commands on Windows.
howItWorks: An attacker sends a command to PowerShell, often hidden inside an email document or a script.
The command line is recorded when the process starts, so the arguments are visible to defenders.
Windows can also log the full script text after it unravels any encoding, which is very useful.
PowerShell then reaches out to the network, changes files, or creates new accounts for the attacker.
You match the parent process with what followed, so you can tell an admin task from an attack.
beginner.example: Imagine a kitchen where every cook already owns a full set of knives. A stranger walks in, picks up a knife from the rack, and starts cooking something nobody ordered. Nothing was smuggled through the door and the knife itself is completely normal. The only clue is that the wrong person is holding it, at the wrong time, making the wrong dish. PowerShell attacks look exactly like that on a computer.
takeaways: PowerShell is a normal tool, so judge it by who ran it and what happened next.
Turn on script logging, because it reveals commands that were hidden behind encoding.
Be suspicious when an office document or browser starts a PowerShell session.

topics.title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell
topics.summary:
A Unix shell is a command interpreter such as sh, bash, zsh, ksh, or dash that provides an interactive interface and a scripting language for Unix-like operating systems, including Linux, macOS, and the BSD family. It exposes pipelines, redirection, job control, variable and command substitution, and access to the full set of system utilities, which together make it a complete execution environment. Adversaries use it to run reconnaissance, download and stage payloads, establish persistence through cron or shell profile files, and pivot to remote hosts using the same credentials. Because the shell is the primary administrative interface on these systems, its presence is normal and only behaviour inside it differentiates intent.

Telemetry comes from several layers. Process execution auditing via the kernel audit subsystem, EDR process telemetry, or container runtime logs captures the argv of each spawned process, and the parent-child tree shows whether a shell was launched by a web server, database service, or container entrypoint. Shell history files record interactive commands but are trivially edited and often disabled. Scripts written to disk leave file creation and permission change events, and interactive shells frequently write to /tmp, /var/tmp, or the home directory, which may appear in file integrity monitoring. Audit records for executed syscalls supplement process data where the agent does not capture full argument vectors.

Legitimate shells are everywhere: package installers, container entrypoints, health checks, and administrator sessions. Investigations therefore anchor on context rather than on the interpreter. Shells spawned by internet-facing daemons, execution under an account whose normal role is non-interactive, odd execution paths, base64 decoding pipelines, and outbound connections immediately following shell creation are the reliable signals. Building a baseline of which service accounts execute shells on which hosts converts a very noisy dataset into a workable detection surface.
objectives: Explain how shell features such as pipelines, substitution, and redirection shape both behaviour and the arguments visible in telemetry.
Interpret process execution audit records and reconstruct a shell command sequence from parent-child lineage.
Assess how shell history, container logs, and file integrity monitoring each contribute to or mislead an investigation.
Distinguish shells spawned by internet-facing services from routine administrative or automation-driven execution.
Design a service account and host baseline that reduces false positives for shell execution detections at scale.
Map observed Unix shell behaviour to ATT&CK and identify which residual gaps require additional instrumentation.

beginner.definition: A Unix shell is the text command tool on Linux, macOS and similar systems. Common examples are bash (Bourne Again Shell), sh (Bourne shell) and zsh (Z shell). It runs single commands and whole scripts, and it can join tools together with pipes. On these systems it is the main way people administer a machine.
beginner.whyItMatters: Because the shell is the normal way to manage a Linux server, its presence proves nothing. An attacker who reaches a web server can use the very same shell to look around, download tools, and add a scheduled job that survives a reboot. The tricky part is that automated software also opens shells all day. You need to know which services may run a shell on which host, or every alert looks plausible.
howItWorks: A program starts a shell on the server, and the parent program is the most useful clue.
The system records the command and its arguments when each new process starts.
The shell can chain tools with pipes, so one short command line may do several different jobs.
The attacker may download a tool, run it, then hide a scheduled task or a startup script.
You compare the account and the host against your baseline to decide whether this should happen.
beginner.example: Picture a large shared workshop where everyone is allowed to use the power tools. A visitor picking up a drill attracts no attention at all. But if that visitor is not on the staff list, drills three cabinets open, and a new lock appears on the back door, the picture changes. A Unix shell is that workshop. Nothing about the tool is wrong, so you judge the person, the hour and the mess left behind.
takeaways: On Linux and macOS the shell is normal, so watch the account and the parent process.
A web server or database service opening a shell is rarely good news.
Shell history files can be edited, so do not rely on them as your only evidence.

topics.title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
topics.summary:
The Windows Command Shell, implemented by cmd.exe, is the legacy interpreter for batch files and interactive command execution on Windows. It provides built-in commands for file manipulation, process and service control, network configuration, and scheduled task creation, and it acts as a launcher for other utilities. Adversaries favour it because it is universally present, is not typically removed by hardening, and blends with a very high volume of legitimate administrative and installer traffic. Typical abuse patterns involve chaining built-in commands together with shell redirection and the command separator to perform discovery, staging, and cleanup within a single short-lived process.

The artefacts left behind are concentrated in process creation telemetry. The parent process is often more informative than cmd.exe itself, because the shell is frequently spawned by a document reader, a script host, a service, or a webshell. Command lines containing long chains of separators, repeated directory traversal toward temporary or public directories, and redirection into executable file types are notable. Script Block Logging does not cover cmd.exe, so visibility depends on command line auditing, the process creation event source used by the endpoint agent, and file and registry events generated by whatever the shell touched. Batch files executed from user-writable paths leave a file creation record that may be deleted immediately afterwards.

Routine use includes login scripts, software deployment wrappers, backup jobs, and diagnostic commands run by administrators. The distinguishing factors are context and sequence: an unusual parent, a service account running console utilities interactively, network share access immediately preceding shell execution, and command content that maps to discovery or staging rather than to a scheduled maintenance task. Comparing the observed command line against the standard image of the host and against known automation accounts resolves most apparent positives.
objectives: Describe how cmd.exe parses command separators, redirection, and quoting, and why that parsing shapes what appears in log records.
Extract and interpret parent-child process relationships that indicate a shell spawned by an unexpected host application.
Build SIEM-style queries that surface anomalous command shell usage while suppressing known installer and login script noise.
Reconstruct a short shell session from command line auditing, file creation, and registry events when no script logging is available.
Explain the visibility limitations of resource kit tooling historically used to log console activity and how it fails on modern systems.
Map observed shell behaviour to ATT&CK and document the specific telemetry gaps that remain in the environment.

beginner.definition: The Windows Command Shell is the older text tool on Windows, started by a program called cmd.exe. You type short commands and it runs them, and batch files are simply lists of those commands saved in a file. It has been part of Windows for decades. Many maintenance tasks still rely on it today.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers use this shell because it is everywhere and nobody removes it. It can chain many small commands into one line, so a single short process can search a system, copy files and clean up. Legitimate installers and login scripts produce a huge amount of the same traffic. If you have no baseline of what normal looks like, you will either miss the attack or drown in false alarms.
howItWorks: Something starts the command shell, and the program that started it is often the biggest clue.
The full command line is recorded when the process starts, so you can read what was asked.
The shell runs built-in commands and calls other small tools that already exist on Windows.
Those tools touch files, services and the network, and each action leaves its own record.
You rebuild the short story from the starting program, the command line and the events that followed.
beginner.example: Think of a cleaner who carries a master trolley with every tool on it. Nobody questions a cleaner pushing a trolley down a corridor, because that happens a hundred times a day. But if the trolley appears in the server room at midnight, and the same trolley turns up in three other locked rooms, you start asking questions. The Windows command shell is that trolley. The tool is ordinary, but the place and the timing give it away.
takeaways: The command shell is normal on Windows, so context matters more than the program name.
A document reader or web server starting a shell is a strong warning sign.
Keep command line logging on, because it is your main record of what the shell did.

topics.title: Create Account
topics.summary: Create Account describes adversary creation of new accounts to maintain access after an initial foothold is lost or remediated. The accounts involved can be local or domain user accounts, accounts holding administrative rights, cloud and SaaS identities, service principals, or machine accounts created through directory APIs, and they can be created on a single host, in the enterprise directory, or in a hosted tenant the organisation only partially monitors. The technique is favoured because a fresh account survives the password resets that remediation applies to compromised existing accounts, blends into the constant background churn of real onboarding, and can be granted additional rights quietly if the adversary already holds privilege. The mechanism usually involves ordinary administrative interfaces rather than exploits: command-line account management utilities, remote management protocols, directory and cloud identity APIs, and application-specific user administration consoles. The artefacts are concentrated in directory and audit telemetry, including account creation events, group membership additions, privilege role assignments, cloud provider audit records, and the authentication activity of the new identity afterwards. Benign account creation is continuous in most environments, driven by hiring, contractor onboarding, automation and service deployment, so an investigation should weigh the identity of the creator, the interval between creation and first use, the privileges requested or assigned, how naming and description conventions compare with organisational standards, and whether the creating identity was itself recently established or recently elevated. Accounts created and then used immediately, added straight into a privileged group, or authenticating from unexpected infrastructure are the cases that warrant escalation, and reviewing them against a documented joiner process is usually what separates a real incident from a noisy one.
objectives: Identify the account types an adversary can create and the visibility each provides to the defender.
Interpret directory, local and cloud audit records to reconstruct who created an account and when.
Detect create-and-use patterns by comparing account creation with subsequent authentication activity.
Evaluate naming, privilege and approval controls that make rogue accounts distinguishable from legitimate ones.
Explain how identity governance and periodic access review limit the lifetime of adversary accounts.
Write detection logic for privileged account creation and for sensitive group membership changes.

beginner.definition: Creating an account is when an attacker adds a brand new user identity to a system, a network directory, or a cloud service. That new login is not stolen, so it keeps working even after the real breaches are found and passwords are reset.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most clean-up work focuses on the accounts an attacker stole. A quiet new account can sit outside that list for months. It looks like normal staff onboarding, so nobody questions it. If the attacker gives it extra rights, they can return whenever they like. Regular access reviews are how you find accounts nobody actually hired.
howItWorks: The attacker already has a foothold, meaning some access to one machine or one cloud tenant.
They use normal admin tools, not a software bug, to add a new user account.
The new account can be local to one machine or shared across the whole company directory.
They may also create cloud identities, service accounts, or accounts for automation.
If they already hold rights, they quietly add the account to a privileged group.
Later they simply log in again, and the original fix no longer keeps them out.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel that changes every lock after a break-in. The thief had copied a key, so the new locks work. But while inside, the thief also added a new key card to the system and wrote a name on it that sounds like staff. The hotel keeps it active because it looks normal. The thief walks back in through the staff entrance weeks later.
takeaways: A stolen account can be fixed; a newly created one must be found.
Compare each new account against a real hiring or change record.
Review privileged group membership often, and remove what you cannot explain.

topics.title: Data Encrypted for Impact
topics.summary: Data encrypted for impact is the technique of rendering data unusable to its owner by encrypting it in place, typically to extort payment or to degrade an organisation's ability to operate. The mechanism relies on the same cryptographic primitives that protect data legitimately: a symmetric cipher such as AES with a randomly generated key for bulk file content, and asymmetric or hybrid wrapping of that key so the victim cannot recover it without the adversary's secret. Implementations vary. Some call operating system cryptographic interfaces, some ship a self-contained binary, and some abuse legitimate administration and backup tooling already trusted in the environment. Targets are chosen for operational value: user documents on workstations, file shares, database files, virtual machine disks and datastores, cloud object storage, and increasingly the backup repositories that would otherwise permit recovery. The technique appears on Windows, Linux, macOS, hypervisor platforms and cloud infrastructure, and it is frequently preceded by credential access, discovery and defence evasion, then accompanied or followed by inhibition of system recovery. Telemetry is distinctive at scale even when individual operations look ordinary. Investigators look for a single process touching thousands of files in a short window, bulk renames or extension changes, mass modification of file timestamps, sudden entropy shifts in stored content, note files written across many directories, deletion or truncation of shadow copies and snapshots, and storage performance anomalies. Endpoint detection platforms surface the responsible process tree, its parent, the account it runs under and the command line that launched it; file server and storage logs show the fan-out; backup and hypervisor audit logs show snapshot removal. Distinguishing this from benign encryption is a matter of scope and context. Full disk encryption tools, archive utilities, backup agents, synchronisation clients and mass deployment scripts all write many files, but they run on a known schedule, under known service accounts, with change records, and without note files or recovery tampering. Correlation of encryption activity with recovery inhibition, unusual account use and concurrent exfiltration is what turns a performance problem into a confirmed impact event.
objectives: Explain how hybrid encryption makes bulk data unrecoverable while keeping the decryption key outside the victim environment.
Recognise the file system, storage and backup telemetry that indicates mass encryption rather than normal archival or synchronisation.
Correlate encryption activity with recovery inhibition, credential access and exfiltration to confirm an impact event.
Separate legitimate full disk encryption, backup and deployment tooling from malicious encryption using scope, account and change records.
Prioritise response steps that preserve evidence and protect remaining recovery capability before containment.
Design detection coverage for hypervisor, cloud object storage and backup platforms rather than endpoint file systems alone.

beginner.definition: This is the act of scrambling a victim's files with strong encryption so nobody can read them. The attacker keeps the only key that can unlock the data. It is the step that turns a network intrusion into a business shutdown, and it is the core of most ransomware attacks.
beginner.whyItMatters: Locked files stop work immediately: invoices, patient records, design files, and the systems that run production. The attacker asks for payment to hand back the key. Paying does not guarantee recovery and may be illegal in some places. What really decides your fate is whether clean, offsite backups exist and were tested before the attack.
howItWorks: The attacker gets in earlier, often through a stolen login or a phishing email.
They look around to find valuable data, file shares, and backup systems.
They often delete recovery points first, so restoring your data becomes much harder.
A key is created, and files are rewritten in scrambled form at high speed.
File names or extensions change, and a ransom note demanding payment appears in many folders.
Defenders notice one process touching thousands of files within a few minutes.
beginner.example: Think of a warehouse where every box is sealed with a new padlock, and only the thief holds the keys. Staff can still walk the aisles, but nothing can be picked or shipped. The thief leaves a note on the door asking for money. If the company kept a second warehouse with untouched stock, it can keep serving customers while the mess is cleaned up.
takeaways: Backups are only useful if they are separate, recent, and tested.
Fast detection of mass file changes limits how much data you lose.
Never assume that paying a ransom will bring your data back.

topics.title: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
topics.summary: Exfiltration over a command and control channel is the transfer of collected data out of a victim environment using the same communication path the adversary already uses to task and control implanted tooling. The mechanism matters because it removes a separate, conspicuous egress channel from the operation: the implant beacons to its controller, receives instructions, and returns results inside the same session, often over HTTPS to blend with ordinary web traffic but also over DNS, mail protocols, or a custom binary protocol on a non-standard port. Data is typically staged first, compressed and sometimes encrypted or encoded, then split into chunks that fit the profile of the carrier protocol, with the encoded bytes placed in request bodies, headers, URI parameters or DNS query names. Because command and control traffic is already expected to be periodic, exfiltration rides inside a pattern defenders must baseline before they can spot the change. The technique appears on endpoints, servers and cloud workloads alike, and the observable artefacts differ by vantage point. Network flow records show asymmetric byte counts, with outbound volume far exceeding inbound, across long lived sessions to the same destination. Web proxies and inspection logs show repeated uploads, unusual content types, large request bodies and consistent request sizes or timing. Name resolution logs show elevated query volume, long or high entropy subdomains and repeated queries to a single authoritative server. Endpoint telemetry captures the preceding collection and staging: archive creation, bulk file reads, access to database exports, clipboard or screen capture. Distinguishing malicious transfer from benign uploads requires context. Cloud synchronisation, update reporting, telemetry agents, backup replication and video conferencing all produce sustained outbound flows. Investigators therefore weigh destination reputation and age, whether the destination appears on any approved list, which process owns the connection, whether timing is machine regular, and whether the transfer coincides with staging activity on the same host.
objectives: Explain how an implant multiplexes command, control and data transfer over a single channel and why that complicates egress monitoring.
Interpret network flow asymmetries, long lived sessions and repeated upload patterns as candidate exfiltration rather than routine traffic.
Correlate endpoint staging artefacts such as archive creation and bulk file reads with outbound network volume on the same host.
Analyse name resolution carried transfer patterns using query volume, label entropy and authoritative server concentration.
Tune proxy, network detection and data loss prevention rules to reduce false positives from synchronisation, patch delivery and telemetry reporting.
Describe containment choices that stop the transfer without destroying evidence of the channel or the staged data.

beginner.definition: Exfiltration over a command and control channel means the intruder sends stolen data out using the same link they already use to control their hidden software. Command and control is the channel an attacker uses to give orders to a machine they compromised. One path carries both orders and stolen files, so there is no second, obvious exit route.
beginner.whyItMatters: Data leaving your network is the part of an attack that cannot be undone. If the intruder reuses a channel you already expect to see, your monitoring may treat it as normal. Outbound traffic that quietly grows, or uploads that repeat on a schedule, can be the last chance to stop a leak. Watching outbound volume matters as much as watching inbound attacks.
howItWorks: The intruder collects files of interest and copies them to one folder on the victim machine.
They pack the files into an archive and often shrink or scramble them.
The hidden software already talks to its controller on a regular schedule.
Instead of sending a small reply, it now sends pieces of the archive back.
The data is split into chunks that fit the shape of normal traffic.
Because the channel already looks familiar, only volume and timing give it away.
beginner.example: Imagine a delivery van that comes to your office every morning with paperwork and leaves with a signed receipt. Nobody questions the van. Now imagine the driver also carries out a few boxes from the storeroom on each trip. The route is unchanged, the schedule is unchanged and the van looks the same. Only the weight of the van and the shrinking storeroom tell you something is wrong.
takeaways: Stolen data usually leaves through a channel the attacker already uses for control.
Sessions where far more data goes out than comes in deserve a closer look.
Alert on unusual upload volume, not just on suspicious files arriving.

topics.title: Exfiltration Over Web Service
topics.summary: Exfiltration over a web service moves data out of an environment through legitimate, publicly available or tenant sanctioned online services rather than through adversary controlled infrastructure. The mechanism sidesteps the assumption that egress to unknown destinations is the thing worth blocking. Instead, the transfer goes to a code repository, object storage bucket, file sharing site, paste service, webmail account, messaging platform or collaboration tool that either already appears on an allow list or is indistinguishable in a proxy log from ordinary collaboration. Two patterns dominate. The first uses the provider's public interface or web front end from an endpoint or server, uploading data with an authenticated or anonymous session over an encrypted channel. The second abuses services already provisioned inside the organisation, where the adversary has obtained an account and moves data into a personal folder, shares it externally, or grants a third party application permission to read it. Telemetry sits at three layers. Network and proxy logs show upload volume, session duration and destination service, but the payload is encrypted, so detection depends on comparing volume and frequency against the user's or host's baseline. Cloud and software as a service audit logs are richer: file creation, download, external sharing, permission changes, mailbox rule creation and third party application consent grants are recorded with actor, time and client application. Endpoint telemetry captures the preceding collection and staging steps, such as archiving directories, exporting mailboxes, reading databases or capturing screen content. The challenge is baseline noise. Synchronisation clients, build pipelines, backup products, log shippers and ordinary document collaboration generate large uploads continuously. Investigators distinguish malicious use by whose account is acting, whether the destination or sharing scope is new for that user, whether volume departs sharply from history, whether activity occurs outside working hours or from an unusual client, whether a new application consent appeared shortly before, and whether staging activity is visible on the source host at the same time. Sanctioned service visibility is only useful if the organisation has inventoried which services it actually uses.
objectives: Explain how legitimate web services and tenant sanctioned applications can serve as exfiltration channels.
Use cloud and software as a service audit logs to identify uploads, external sharing and permission changes by actor and client.
Baseline per user and per host upload volumes to detect transfers that hide inside encrypted traffic.
Detect malicious third party application consent as a precursor to data access and transfer.
Correlate endpoint collection and staging artefacts with service side upload activity.
Prioritise sanctioned service abuse over generic egress alerts using data classification and account context.

beginner.definition: This is sending stolen data out through ordinary online services, such as file sharing sites, code repositories, webmail, or workplace chat tools. Because these services are allowed and encrypted, the transfer looks much like normal work traffic. The attacker avoids using strange servers that defenders might block.
beginner.whyItMatters: Blocking unknown destinations does not help when the data leaves through a service you already trust. The payload is encrypted, so you cannot read it in transit. You can only compare the size, timing, and frequency of uploads against normal behavior. This is often the last stage before public release, so detection here limits real damage.
howItWorks: The attacker has already gathered data and put it into one file or archive.
They sign in to a normal cloud or file sharing account, sometimes a free one.
Data is uploaded over an encrypted connection, exactly like a routine backup.
They may instead move files into a personal folder inside company systems.
Sharing links are then sent out, or an outside app is granted access to the files.
Defenders compare upload volume per user against that user's normal pattern.
beginner.example: Think of a postcard versus a sealed courier parcel. Guards at the gate read postcards, so nothing private travels that way. A courier van with a company logo passes without a second look. The thief loads boxes into that van and drives out. Nothing was hidden or forced; the escape route was simply one everyone already trusted.
takeaways: Watch how much each account uploads, not just where it connects.
Review external sharing and app permissions on cloud services regularly.
Encrypted traffic still leaves clues in volume, timing, and destination.

topics.title: Exploit Public-Facing Application
topics.summary: Exploit Public-Facing Application covers adversary exploitation of weaknesses in internet-reachable software to obtain code execution, data access or a foothold inside a network. The targets are the services an organisation deliberately exposes: web applications and their frameworks, remote access and virtual private network gateways, file transfer and mail servers, content management systems, and the APIs behind them. The mechanism is usually a flaw in input handling, authentication or deserialisation that lets an attacker influence server-side behaviour, but the category also includes misconfiguration such as an exposed administrative interface, a default credential on an appliance, or a debug endpoint left reachable, as well as exploitation of a dependency the application implicitly trusts. Time matters a great deal, because exploitation commonly follows public vulnerability disclosure closely and internet-wide scanning means exposed hosts are probed continuously, so telemetry often shows attempts against many assets rather than one carefully chosen request. The evidence lives in web and reverse proxy access logs, web application firewall and intrusion detection alerts, application error logs, process creation on the host running the service, and network flow records. An investigation must separate attempted exploitation from successful compromise, which requires correlating an anomalous request with a subsequent child process, a new file, an outbound connection or a configuration change on the same asset within a coherent time window. Heavy legitimate traffic, commercial vulnerability scanners and benign crawlers generate enormous volumes of superficially malicious requests, so triage should weight requests that returned a success status, that plausibly reached the vulnerable code path, and that were followed by follow-on activity on the affected host.
objectives: Identify which internet-facing assets and software versions carry exploitation risk and how exposure is verified rather than assumed.
Read web, proxy and application logs to distinguish probing from a request that reached vulnerable code.
Correlate a suspicious request with post-exploitation evidence such as child processes, new files or outbound connections.
Explain how virtual patching, web application firewall rules and rapid patching differ in coverage and operational cost.
Build a prioritisation method that combines exploit availability, exposure and asset criticality.
Write detection logic that keys on exploitation behaviour rather than on attacker-controlled request strings alone.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker takes advantage of a weakness in software your company deliberately puts on the internet. Web sites, remote access gateways, mail servers and file transfer services are common targets. The goal is to get a foothold inside, often without any password at all.
beginner.whyItMatters: Anything you publish on the internet is being probed all day long by automated scanners. A single unpatched server can hand an intruder a way in. Small delays matter: attackers often start using a published flaw within days of the fix being released. If you do not know what you expose, you cannot protect it.
howItWorks: You publish a service to the internet, such as a web shop or a staff portal.
An automated scanner in the outside world finds that service and notes its software version.
A known weakness in that version is tried, sometimes thousands of times a day.
If the request reaches the faulty code, the attacker may run their own commands.
They then download tools, create a login, or connect out to another system.
Defenders spot it by matching a strange request with later activity on the same server.
beginner.example: Picture a shop with a serving hatch open to the street. Anyone walking past can knock, and hundreds do every hour. Most just try the handle. One person knows the hatch latch is broken, reaches in, and unlocks the back door for friends. The shop only notices hours later when stock is missing. Closing the hatch, or fixing the latch the day the fault is known, is what keeps the shop safe.
takeaways: Keep a list of everything you expose to the internet, and check it often.
Patch internet-facing systems quickly, because automated scanners never stop looking.
A strange request is only noise until you see what happened next on that host.

topics.title: External Remote Services
topics.summary: External Remote Services describes adversary use of legitimate remote access services to gain an initial foothold or to re-enter an environment from outside the perimeter. The services involved are ones the organisation exposes deliberately for business reasons: virtual private network concentrators, remote desktop gateways, remote shell and file transfer services, and hosted remote management or desktop-as-a-service platforms. Because the service is expected to be reachable and the protocol itself is legitimate, the technique sits on the boundary between initial access and persistence, and identical session types appear in both contexts. At a mechanism level an adversary authenticates with credentials obtained elsewhere, uses a valid account issued to a contractor or third party, exploits or misconfigures the gateway itself, or registers an account with a cloud-hosted remote access platform that the organisation cannot see at all. The telemetry lives mainly in the gateway and identity layers: authentication records with source address, client and device attributes, session start and duration, concurrent session anomalies, and configuration changes to the service, after which endpoint records show what the session did once established. Investigations separate legitimate remote work from abuse by examining the source network and its reputation, whether the account was expected to use that client and that geography, whether the session coincided with password spraying or credential stuffing activity, and whether the same account performed administrative actions outside its normal pattern. Strong controls tie every exposed service to multifactor authentication and device posture rather than treating network reachability as sufficient proof of identity, and they log enough session context to reconstruct who connected from where and when.
objectives: Inventory externally reachable remote access services and identify which are business-essential.
Read gateway authentication and session logs to establish source, client and duration for a session.
Correlate a remote session with identity anomalies and with post-authentication endpoint activity.
Evaluate multifactor, device posture and session recording controls for each remote access path.
Explain how third-party and hosted remote management platforms complicate visibility and attribution.
Write detection logic for remote sessions from unexpected geographies or concurrent with credential attacks.
